lessons.plain: These are the common shapes an application can take and the ways its parts can talk. A monolith is one big program doing everything. Microservices split that program into small independent services. Event-driven means parts react to announcements that something happened instead of calling each other directly. Fanout sends one announcement to many listeners at once. When several services must finish a job together, they can coordinate in two ways. With choreography, each one reacts to the others, like dancers who know their cues. With orchestration, a conductor tells each one when to play. Choosing a shape decides how easily the system grows, fails, and gets debugged.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop must charge the card, book a courier, and email a receipt after every order. Would you rather have one central program call each step in order, or have each step listen for news and act on its own? What could go wrong with each?
lessons.teach:
A monolith is one application deployed as a single unit, with all features in one codebase and usually one shared database. Microservices split the work into small services. Each owns one business capability and its own data, is deployed independently, and talks to the others over the network. Event-driven architecture means components react to events, which are records that something happened, such as OrderPlaced. A producer publishes an event, and consumers that subscribed to it act on it. Fanout means publishing one event once and having it delivered to many consumers. On AWS, a common way to do this is an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish/subscribe service) delivering copies to several Amazon SQS queues (managed queues), one per consumer, so each consumer works at its own pace.

When services cooperate on one process, they can coordinate in two ways. In choreography, nobody is in charge: each service listens for events and emits its own, and the process emerges from those reactions. In orchestration, a central coordinator calls each step in order, tracks progress, and handles failures. On AWS this is typically AWS Step Functions, a managed workflow state machine.

Why it works: decoupled parts scale, fail and deploy separately. Events let you add a new consumer without changing the producer.

Worked example: Order service saves an order and publishes OrderPlaced to a topic. Fanout delivers copies to three queues. Billing charges the card and publishes PaymentTaken. Shipping waits for PaymentTaken and books a courier. Email sends a receipt. That is choreography. In the orchestrated version, a state machine runs Charge, then Ship, then Email, and runs Refund if shipping fails. The whole flow is visible in one place.

Common mistake: assuming microservices or choreography is always better. A small team is often faster with a monolith, and long choreographed chains are hard to trace. Nobody can easily say where order 42 is stuck.

Consequence in a running system: if a choreographed consumer fails silently, the process stalls and no central component reports an error. Orchestration gives you one place to see and retry failed steps, at the cost of a central dependency.

questions.prompt: A city library system wants to announce new books. When a librarian adds a book, the catalog service publishes one BookAdded event. Three consumers must each get their own copy: a search indexer (fast), a recommendation engine (slow, runs heavy jobs), and a notification service that emails members. The slow recommendation engine must not hold up the other two. Step 1: the catalog service publishes BookAdded once to an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish/subscribe service). Step 2: ??? Step 3: each consumer reads from its own source and processes BookAdded at its own speed, so a backlog in recommendations does not delay search or email. What is Step 2?
choices: Subscribe a single shared Amazon SQS queue to the topic and let all three consumers read from that one queue
Have the catalog service skip the topic and call each of the three services directly, one after another
Subscribe three separate Amazon SQS queues (managed queues) to the topic, one per consumer, so each gets its own copy
Start an AWS Step Functions state machine that runs the indexer, then recommendations, then notifications in order
questions.why: Fanout means one publish to the topic delivers a copy into a separate queue per consumer, which lets each consumer work at its own pace without blocking the others.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing company's trip process works like this: the trip service emits TripEnded, the fare service hears it and emits FareCalculated, and the rating service hears FareCalculated and asks the rider for a rating. No component directs the steps; each service just reacts to events and emits its own. Which coordination style is this?
choices: Monolithic, because all three services handle the same trip
Fanout, because one event is copied to many queues at once
Choreography, because the process emerges from services reacting to events
Orchestration, because the services run in a fixed order
questions.why: Choreography means no service is in charge and the overall process emerges from each service listening for events and publishing its own.

questions.prompt: A three-person startup is building the first version of a booking app for dog groomers. They have one small codebase idea, a single database, and need to ship quickly. A consultant insists they must start with fifteen microservices because microservices are always better. Based on the trade-offs of these patterns, what is the most reasonable response?
choices: Agree, because microservices always scale and deploy faster for any team size
Use fanout for every request so each feature gets its own queue from day one
Disagree, because a small team is often faster with a monolith deployed as one unit
Use choreography between fifteen services so no central dependency exists
questions.why: Assuming microservices are always better is a common mistake; a small team often moves faster with a monolith, one application deployed as a single unit.

questions.prompt: A video platform processes uploads with choreography: the upload service emits VideoUploaded, the transcoder emits VideoTranscoded, and the thumbnail service then emits ThumbnailReady so the video can be published. One day the thumbnail service starts failing silently, without emitting anything or raising an alarm. What is the most likely result, and which pattern would have made it easier to spot?
choices: The transcoder automatically retries the thumbnail step, because choreography tracks progress centrally
The upload service reports the error to users, because producers in event-driven systems wait for every consumer
Videos stall unpublished with no central error report; orchestration (e.g. AWS Step Functions) gives one place to see and retry failed steps
Videos publish anyway without thumbnails, because fanout skips any consumer that fails
questions.why: In choreography no component tracks the whole process, so a silent consumer failure stalls it unnoticed, whereas an orchestrator tracks each step and can show and retry failures.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between choreography and orchestration, and where fanout fits in. Name one tradeoff that would make you choose orchestration for a multi-step order process.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both choreography and orchestration coordinate several services on one business process. In choreography there is no boss. Each service subscribes to events, does its part, and publishes a new event that the next service reacts to. Fanout is the delivery mechanism that makes this cheap: one OrderPlaced event goes to a topic and gets copied to a queue for each interested consumer, so billing, shipping and email all hear about it without the producer knowing they exist. In orchestration, a central coordinator such as a Step Functions state machine calls each step in order and decides what happens on failure, for example issuing a refund if shipping fails. Choreography is loosely coupled and easy to extend, but the flow is scattered and hard to trace. For an order process with strict ordering and compensation steps, I would choose orchestration because I get one place to see the state and retry failures. The cost is a central component that every step depends on.
rubricPoints: Defines choreography as services reacting to each other's events with no central controller.
Defines orchestration as a central coordinator, such as a workflow state machine, driving the steps.
Explains fanout as one published event delivered to many independent consumers.
Names a real tradeoff, such as traceability and failure handling versus coupling to a central component.
Distinguishes monolith from microservices by deployment unit and data ownership, or links patterns to event-driven design.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between monolith, microservices, choreography, orchestration and fanout is a judgment call best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios and their tradeoffs.

lessons.plain: State is anything a program remembers between one request and the next, such as a shopping cart, a login session or a running total. A stateful component keeps that memory inside itself, so a follow-up request must reach that same copy. A stateless component keeps nothing between requests. Every request carries what it needs, or the component looks it up in a shared store. Think of a coffee shop. If only one barista remembers your usual order, you must wait for that barista. If your order is written on a shared board, any barista can serve you. Stateless designs are easy to copy, replace and scale.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function adds each new item to a shopping cart kept in a variable in its own memory. Traffic grows, so the platform starts a second copy of the function. A customer's next request lands on the second copy. What do you think that customer sees in their cart?
lessons.teach:
A stateful component stores data about earlier requests inside itself, in memory or on its local disk. It needs that data to answer the next request correctly. A stateless component treats every request as independent. Anything it needs comes in with the request or is read from an external store. An external store is a shared service outside the component, such as a DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database) or a cache service.

Statelessness matters because modern platforms run many identical copies of your code and create or destroy them at will. AWS Lambda runs each function in an execution environment, which is an isolated container holding one copy of your code. Lambda adds environments when traffic rises, removes them when traffic falls, and never promises that a given request reaches a given environment. Any copy can serve any request only if no copy holds unique data.

Worked example: a function keeps a visit counter in a global variable. Request 1 hits environment A, and the counter becomes 1. Request 2 arrives while A is busy, so Lambda starts environment B, where the counter starts at 0 and becomes 1. Request 3 hits A, and the counter becomes 2. The true count is 3, but no copy knows that. Later A is recycled and its count is gone. The fix is to keep the counter in DynamoDB and have each request apply an atomic increment there. The function becomes stateless and every copy sees the same total.

A common mistake is treating the memory or /tmp folder of a warm environment as storage because it often survives between invocations in testing. Reusing that space is fine for things you can rebuild, like a database connection or a cached config file. It is never fine for data you cannot lose. In a running system, relying on it causes vanished sessions, wrong totals and bugs that only appear under load.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket app runs a Lambda function that keeps each user's held seats in a dictionary stored in a global variable. Trace what happens for one user. Step 1: The user holds seat 14. The request lands on execution environment P, and P's dictionary now shows seats [14] for that user. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: The user clicks checkout. That request lands on environment Q, and Q's dictionary shows only seat [15], so the user pays for one seat and seat 14 silently disappears. Fix: store held seats in a DynamoDB table so every copy reads the same data. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The user holds seat 15. Lambda starts environment Q by copying P's memory, so Q's dictionary shows seats [14, 15].
The user holds seat 15. The request lands on environment P again, and P's dictionary now shows seats [14, 15].
The user holds seat 15. The function writes seat 15 to a DynamoDB table, and Q's dictionary shows seat [15].
The user holds seat 15. P is busy, so Lambda starts environment Q with an empty dictionary, and Q's dictionary now shows seat [15].
questions.why: A new environment starts with its own empty memory, so only the seat added there (15) exists in Q, which explains why checkout on Q sees seat 15 alone.

questions.prompt: A team at a shipping company runs several identical copies of an address-validation service. Which description makes that service stateless?
choices: All copies save validation results to their own local disk so the results survive restarts.
Each copy is pinned to one customer, so that customer's requests always reach the same copy.
Each copy remembers the last address it validated so it can answer repeat requests faster and more accurately.
Each request carries the address to check, and any extra data the service needs is read from a shared external store.
questions.why: A stateless component treats every request as independent, getting what it needs from the request or an external store, so any copy can serve any request.

questions.prompt: A photo-tagging Lambda function writes several things to the /tmp folder of its execution environment. Which item is it acceptable to rely on finding there in a later invocation, as long as the code can rebuild it when it is missing?
choices: A list of user sessions showing who is currently logged in.
A copy of a labeling model file downloaded from storage, which can be downloaded again if missing.
The running count of photos tagged today, used for billing customers.
A photo a user just uploaded that has not been saved anywhere else yet.
questions.why: Warm-environment storage is fine for things you can rebuild, like a re-downloadable file, but never for data you cannot lose.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking site stores logged-in users' sessions in the memory of its Lambda function. It worked perfectly in testing with one tester. After launch, under heavy traffic, users are randomly logged out mid-booking. What is the most likely cause?
choices: New execution environments start without the sessions held in other environments' memory, so requests landing on them see no login.
DynamoDB is deleting the session records when too many users read them at the same time.
Lambda copies sessions between environments too slowly when traffic rises, so some copies lag behind.
The function timeout is too short, so Lambda logs users out after each invocation ends.
questions.why: Under load Lambda adds environments that each have their own empty memory and never guarantees a user reaches the same one, so in-memory sessions vanish; they belong in an external store.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a stateful and a stateless component, why Lambda code should be stateless, and one cost or limit of moving state out to an external store.
lessons.modelAnswer: A stateful component remembers things from earlier requests inside itself, so later requests must reach that same copy. A stateless one keeps nothing between requests and gets what it needs from the request or from a shared store like DynamoDB. Lambda can start new execution environments, run several at once and recycle them whenever it likes, so it never guarantees which copy handles a request. Data kept in one environment's memory is invisible to the others and disappears when that environment ends. Stateless code lets any copy serve any request, so scaling and replacing copies is safe. The tradeoff is that every state read or write is now a network call. That adds delay and cost, and the store itself must handle the load and concurrent updates, for example with atomic increments. Keeping a reusable connection or cache in memory is still fine, because losing it costs only speed, not correctness.
rubricPoints: Defines stateful as keeping data from earlier requests inside the component.
Defines stateless as treating each request independently and using the request or an external store for any needed data.
Explains that Lambda creates, runs in parallel and recycles execution environments with no request affinity.
Gives a consequence of in-memory state, such as lost or inconsistent data under scaling.
Names a tradeoff of external state, such as extra latency, cost or concurrent-update handling.
Notes that in-memory reuse is acceptable only for rebuildable things like connections or caches.

suggested.rationale: No listed mission or engine directly tests where state lives, and the core skill is explaining why state belongs in a shared store and what that move costs.

lessons.plain: Coupling describes how much one part of a system depends on another being present, healthy and unchanged. Tightly coupled parts call each other directly and wait for an answer, so if one stalls or breaks, the other does too. Loosely coupled parts talk through something in between, such as a queue, so each can keep working, scale or change on its own. Think of a phone call versus a mailbox: on a call both people must be free at the same moment, but a letter can sit in a mailbox until the reader is ready.
lessons.guessPrompt: An order service calls a billing service directly and waits for its reply. Billing goes down for five minutes. What happens to customers who try to order during those five minutes, and what could you place between the two services so their orders are still accepted?
lessons.teach:
Coupling is the degree to which one component depends on another. A component is any separately running piece, such as a Lambda function or a web service. Two components are tightly coupled when one calls the other directly, waits for the result, and must know its address and exact interface; a failure or slowdown in either one immediately hurts the other. They are loosely coupled when they communicate through an intermediary, so neither needs the other to be running at the same moment.

The most common intermediary is a managed queue, such as Amazon SQS: a service that stores messages until something reads them. The producer is the component that writes a message; the consumer is the component that reads and processes it. The queue acts as a buffer, absorbing bursts and outages.

Worked example. Tightly coupled version: a customer places an order; the order function calls billing over HTTP; billing is down; the call times out; the order function returns an error; the customer's order is lost. Loosely coupled version: the order function writes an 'order placed' message to the queue and immediately tells the customer it was accepted; billing is down, so messages pile up safely in the queue; billing recovers and reads the backlog; every order is billed, just later. Billing can also be scaled, redeployed or rewritten without touching the order code, as long as the message format stays the same.

Common mistake: assuming that adding a queue automatically makes components loosely coupled. If the producer then waits for a reply message before answering the user, or the consumer breaks whenever the producer adds a field to the message, the two are still tightly coupled in practice.

Loose coupling has costs. Work finishes later rather than instantly, the producer cannot show the final result right away, and tracing a problem across a queue is harder. In a running system, tight coupling lets one slow dependency cause a cascading failure, where each caller fails in turn; loose coupling contains the failure to a growing backlog that can be drained once the broken part is fixed.

questions.prompt: A video-sharing startup lets users upload clips. The upload function (the producer, the component that writes messages) puts a 'clip uploaded' message on an Amazon SQS queue (a managed queue that stores messages until something reads them) and immediately tells the user 'upload received'. A separate transcoding function (the consumer, the component that reads and processes messages) converts each clip. Trace a 3-hour transcoder outage. Step 1: At 14:00 a bad deploy crashes the transcoder. Step 2: Users keep uploading, and the upload function keeps writing messages and replying 'received'. Step 3: ??? Step 4: At 17:00 the team fixes the transcoder and it starts reading again. Step 5: Every clip is transcoded, just later than usual. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: The upload function times out waiting for the transcoder and returns an error to each user.
The messages pile up in the queue as a backlog, stored safely until a consumer reads them.
The upload function keeps calling the transcoder directly over HTTP until it comes back online.
The queue rejects new messages because no consumer is reading, so those uploads are lost.
questions.why: A queue is a buffer that holds messages while the consumer is down, so the outage becomes a growing backlog that is drained after the fix instead of lost work or user errors.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, the payroll service calls the tax-calculation service directly over HTTP, waits for the answer before continuing, and has the tax service's exact address and request format written into its code. How are these two components coupled?
choices: Tightly coupled, because payroll calls tax directly, waits for the result, and must know its address and interface.
Tightly coupled only if both services are written in the same programming language.
Loosely coupled, because they are deployed as two separate services.
Loosely coupled, because HTTP is a standard protocol that any service can use.
questions.why: Tight coupling means one component calls another directly, waits for it, and depends on its address and exact interface, so a failure or slowdown in tax immediately hurts payroll.

questions.prompt: A grocery delivery app adds a queue between its checkout function and its stock-reservation function. However, checkout still waits for a reply message from stock-reservation before answering the shopper, and stock-reservation crashes whenever checkout adds a new field to the message. Are these components loosely coupled?
choices: Yes, because any component that communicates through a queue is loosely coupled.
Yes, because the two functions no longer need to know each other's address.
No, because loose coupling requires both functions to run in the same Lambda function.
No, because checkout still waits on stock-reservation and stock-reservation breaks on message changes, so they are tightly coupled in practice.
questions.why: Adding a queue does not by itself loosen coupling; if the producer still waits for a reply and the consumer breaks on message format changes, a failure in one still directly hurts the other.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing site replaces a direct call from its booking function to its email-confirmation service with an SQS queue between them. Which is a real cost the team accepts by making this change?
choices: The email service must now be running at every moment that a booking is made.
The booking function must now know the email service's exact address and interface.
Bookings will be lost whenever the email service is down, because the queue cannot store messages.
Confirmation emails may be sent later rather than instantly, and tracing a problem across the queue becomes harder.
questions.why: Loose coupling trades instant completion and easy tracing for resilience: work finishes later, the final result is not shown right away, and following a problem across a queue is harder.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between tightly and loosely coupled components using an example from an order system, and name at least one cost or tradeoff of making things loosely coupled.
lessons.modelAnswer: Tight coupling means one component calls another directly and waits for it, so it depends on that other component being up, fast and unchanged. If our order function calls billing directly and billing is down, orders fail too, and a slow billing service can drag everything down in a cascading failure. Loose coupling puts an intermediary, usually a queue like SQS, between them. The order function, the producer, drops a message on the queue and returns; billing, the consumer, reads it whenever it is ready. A billing outage just becomes a backlog that drains later, and each side can scale or be redeployed independently. The tradeoff is that work completes later, the customer cannot get the final billing result immediately, and debugging across the queue is harder. Also, a queue alone is not enough: if the producer waits for a reply or the consumer breaks on any message change, they are still effectively coupled.
rubricPoints: Defines coupling as how much one component depends on another being available and unchanged.
Explains that tightly coupled components call each other directly and fail or slow down together.
Explains that loosely coupled components communicate through an intermediary such as a queue that buffers messages.
Uses a concrete example showing an outage turning into a backlog instead of lost work.
Names a tradeoff such as delayed completion, no immediate result, or harder tracing.
Notes that a queue does not decouple components if they still wait on each other or share a brittle message format.

suggested.rationale: A messaging lab where the learner inserts a queue between a producer and a failing consumer would let them watch an outage become a drainable backlog instead of lost requests.

lessons.plain: A synchronous call is one where the caller asks for something and waits, doing nothing else, until the answer comes back. An asynchronous call is one where the caller hands the request off, gets a quick receipt saying it was accepted, and carries on while the work happens later. Think of a coffee shop: ordering at the counter and standing there until your drink is handed over is synchronous. Dropping your dry cleaning off and getting a ticket is asynchronous. You leave, the work happens without you, and you find out how it went some other way.
lessons.guessPrompt: A customer clicks Buy on a shopping site. Which of these should the customer's browser wait for before showing 'Order placed': checking the card was accepted, or sending the confirmation email? Why?
lessons.teach:
In a synchronous pattern, the caller sends a request and blocks, meaning it waits, until it receives a response or an error. The caller learns the outcome directly, so it can show a result or retry. The cost is that the caller is tied up for the whole duration, and any slowness or failure downstream lands on it. In AWS Lambda, a synchronous invocation (called RequestResponse) returns the function's result to the caller. An HTTP API in front of a function works this way.

In an asynchronous pattern, the caller hands off the work and gets back an acknowledgement that it was accepted, not a result. The work runs later. Often a queue sits in between. A queue is a managed buffer that holds messages until a worker reads them, and Amazon SQS is one. When Lambda is invoked asynchronously (the Event type), Lambda answers right away with HTTP 202 Accepted, holds the event in its own internal queue, and runs the function afterward. If the function throws an error, Lambda retries it on its own, by default up to two more times.

Here is a worked example: checkout. First, the browser calls an API, which invokes a function synchronously. Second, the function validates the cart, charges the card, writes the order, and returns an order ID. The customer needs that answer, so waiting is correct. Third, the function puts a message on a queue saying the order was created, then returns. Fourth, a separate worker reads the message and sends the receipt email. If the email service is slow, the customer never notices.

A common mistake is doing slow or unreliable work inside the synchronous path. An API gateway typically gives up after roughly 29 seconds, so a long report or a flaky third-party call ends in timeout errors for users, even if the work later finishes. The opposite mistake is assuming an asynchronous caller will hear about failures. It will not, so errors must be captured somewhere else, and retried work must be safe to run twice.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's booking app is built in four steps. Step 1: the patient's phone app calls an HTTP API, which invokes a Lambda function synchronously, meaning the app waits for the answer. Step 2: the function checks that the 10:30 slot is free, books it, and prepares the booking reference BK-7741 that the patient must see on screen. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: a separate worker function reads a message from the queue and sends an SMS reminder through a third-party text provider that sometimes takes 40 seconds to respond. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The function puts a 'booking created' message for BK-7741 on a queue, then returns BK-7741 to the app without waiting for any SMS.
The function invokes the worker synchronously with RequestResponse and returns BK-7741 once the worker reports that the SMS was delivered.
The function returns BK-7741 straight away and skips the queue, because the worker in Step 4 will notice the new booking on its own.
The function calls the text provider itself and waits for the SMS to be sent, then returns BK-7741 so the patient knows both the booking and the reminder succeeded.
questions.why: Handing the slow, unreliable SMS work to a queue lets the patient get the booking reference immediately while the 40-second text provider never sits in the waiting path, and the queue message is what gives the Step 4 worker something to read.

questions.prompt: A warehouse system invokes a Lambda function that recalculates stock levels, using the asynchronous invocation type (Event). What does the calling system receive right after it makes the call?
choices: The recalculated stock levels, once the function has finished running.
An error message if the function fails, so the caller can retry it itself.
An HTTP 202 Accepted acknowledgement that Lambda has taken the event, with no function result.
Nothing at all until Lambda has finished its automatic retries.
questions.why: With the Event type, Lambda replies at once with 202 Accepted, holds the event in its own internal queue, and runs the function later, so the caller gets an acknowledgement rather than a result.

questions.prompt: A gym chain sends 'membership renewed' events to a Lambda function using asynchronous invocation. The function adds 500 reward points to the member's account, then crashes with an error before it finishes logging. Members are now sometimes ending up with 1,000 or 1,500 extra points. What explains this, and what is the right fix?
choices: The function is too slow for the caller to wait on, so the fix is to switch to synchronous invocation.
The caller saw the error and resent the event, so the fix is to stop the caller from resending events.
Lambda automatically retried the failed event, running the points step again, so the work must be made safe to run twice.
The queue lost the first message and delivered a duplicate, so the fix is to remove the queue entirely.
questions.why: After an error, Lambda retries an asynchronous event on its own, by default up to two more times, so each retry adds another 500 points unless the work is safe to repeat, and the caller never hears about the failure to begin with.

questions.prompt: A city council's open-data site has a 'Download annual budget report' button that calls an HTTP API, which invokes a Lambda function synchronously. Building the report takes about 2 minutes. Users report error messages, yet the finished reports appear in storage afterwards. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Lambda retries synchronous calls automatically up to two more times, and the retries collide with each other.
The report was saved to storage, so the error must come from the browser rather than from anything in the request path.
The API gives up after roughly 29 seconds, so users get a timeout error even though the function keeps running and finishes the report.
Synchronous invocation always returns HTTP 202 Accepted, which the browser treats as an error.
questions.why: Doing slow work inside the synchronous path means the waiting caller hits the API's roughly 29-second limit and sees a timeout, even though the work itself later completes.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between synchronous and asynchronous calls, and how you would decide which to use for a given step. Name at least one tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: With a synchronous call, the caller waits for the answer. That is simple: you get the result or the error immediately and can react. The downside is that the caller is stuck for the whole call. A slow or failing dependency makes the caller slow or failing too, and front doors like API gateways cut you off after a fixed timeout. With an asynchronous call, you hand the work off, often through a queue or an async Lambda invocation, and get only an 'accepted' back. That keeps the caller fast and absorbs spikes. The tradeoff is that the caller never sees the result directly. Failures surface elsewhere, automatic retries can run the same work more than once, and you need a separate way to report status. My rule: if the user needs the answer to continue, like a payment approval, keep it synchronous. If the work can happen later, like emails or reports, make it asynchronous.
rubricPoints: Synchronous means the caller waits for the result or the error.
Asynchronous means the caller gets an acknowledgement and the work runs later, often through a queue.
Synchronous ties the caller to downstream speed and timeouts.
Asynchronous hides failures from the caller, so errors and retries must be handled elsewhere.
Choose synchronous when the caller needs the answer to proceed, and asynchronous for work that can be deferred.

suggested.rationale: Designing a command and acknowledgement path makes the learner decide which steps must wait for an answer and which can be handed off and confirmed later.

lessons.plain: Fault-tolerant code keeps doing its job, or fails cleanly, when something it depends on misbehaves. Networks drop packets, databases get briefly overloaded, and calls sometimes hang. Resilient code expects this. It waits a limited time for each call, retries only the failures that might succeed on a second try, and spaces those retries out. It also makes sure that repeating an action does no extra harm. Think of a careful courier. If nobody answers the door, they come back later rather than knocking nonstop. They never deliver the same parcel twice. They give up after a few attempts and report back.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your code saves an order to a database, and the database replies 'too busy, try later'. Should the code retry immediately, wait and retry, or give up at once? What would change if the reply were 'this order is missing a customer ID'?
lessons.teach:
Fault-tolerant code survives failures in the things it calls. It uses four habits.

The first habit is to classify errors. A transient error is temporary and may succeed on retry. Examples are a timeout, a throttling response (the service refusing extra requests because you exceeded its rate), or a 5xx server error. A permanent error will fail every time. Examples are bad input, a missing permission, or a 4xx validation error. Retry only transient errors.

The second habit is to set timeouts. A timeout is the longest you will wait for a call. Without one, a hung dependency freezes your code until the whole function is killed.

The third habit is exponential backoff with jitter. Exponential backoff doubles the wait after each failure. Jitter randomizes each wait so that many clients do not retry at the same instant. Always cap the number of attempts.

The fourth habit is idempotency, meaning that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once. You can get this by sending a unique idempotency key with the request, or by writing with a condition such as 'only if this ID does not already exist'. It matters because a call can time out after the work actually happened.

Here is a worked example. A Lambda function (AWS's run-on-demand code service) writes to DynamoDB, a managed key-value database. Attempt 1 is throttled, so the code waits a random 0 to 100 ms. Attempt 2 is throttled again, so it waits a random 0 to 200 ms. Attempt 3 succeeds. If attempt 3 had failed, a cap of three attempts means the code raises the error. The event is then not lost, because it can be retried later or set aside for inspection. The AWS SDKs, which are the libraries for calling AWS from code, already retry many transient errors this way. Tune their settings rather than stacking a second, hidden retry loop on top.

A common mistake is to retry everything immediately and without limit. Permanent errors then loop forever. Thousands of instant retries become a retry storm that keeps an overloaded service down. In a running system, retries without idempotency can also cause duplicate charges or duplicate records.

questions.prompt: A small bookshop's order function calls a shipping company's label service. It uses exponential backoff with jitter, starting at a 0 to 50 ms wait, and a cap of four attempts. Attempt 1 gets a 503 (a 5xx server error), so the code waits a random time between 0 and 50 ms. Attempt 2 also gets a 503. [Missing step.] Attempt 3 then gets a 503, so the code waits a random time between 0 and 200 ms. Attempt 4 succeeds and the label is created. What is the missing step after attempt 2?
choices: Wait a random time between 0 and 100 ms, then make attempt 3
Raise the error, because a second 503 shows it is permanent
Wait exactly 100 ms, then make attempt 3
Make attempt 3 immediately, since the first wait was already used
questions.why: Backoff doubles the upper limit of the wait from 50 to 100 ms, jitter picks a random point inside it, and a 5xx error is transient, so the retry continues within the cap.

questions.prompt: A warehouse inventory function calls a database and sees four different errors over a day. Which one is a transient error that is reasonable to retry?
choices: A validation error because the request had a date in the wrong format
A request rejected because a required field was left empty
A throttling response because the function exceeded the table's request rate
An access-denied error because the function lacks permission to write to the table
questions.why: Throttling is temporary and may succeed after a wait, while missing permissions and bad input will fail every time no matter how often they are retried.

questions.prompt: A gym's billing function asks a payment service to charge a member's card. The call times out, but the charge actually went through. The function retries and the member is charged twice. Which change best prevents the double charge?
choices: Send a unique idempotency key with each charge so a repeated request has no extra effect
Raise the attempt cap so the retry is more likely to succeed
Retry the charge immediately instead of waiting, so it finishes sooner
Remove the timeout so the function always waits for the payment service to answer
questions.why: An idempotency key makes doing the charge twice have the same effect as doing it once, which matters because a call can time out after the work already happened.

questions.prompt: A travel app's function calls an outside weather service, and no timeout is set on that call. One afternoon the weather service hangs and never replies. What happens to the function?
choices: It returns cached weather data until the service recovers
It treats the hang as a permanent error and skips the weather data
It automatically retries with jitter after a few milliseconds
It stays frozen waiting for the reply until the whole function is killed
questions.why: A timeout is the longest you will wait for a call, so without one a hung dependency freezes the code until the whole function is killed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a function that writes payment records resilient to a flaky database, and name one tradeoff or limit of retrying.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd sort the errors. Throttling, timeouts and 5xx responses are transient, so I'd retry those. Validation failures or access denied will never succeed, so I'd fail fast on those. Every call gets a timeout, so a hung database can't freeze the function. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter, and the number of attempts is capped. That stops us from hammering a struggling service in lockstep. I'd lean on the SDK's built-in retry settings rather than adding a second loop. Because a timed-out call may still have succeeded, each payment write carries an idempotency key or a conditional write, so a retry can't create a second charge. The tradeoff is that retries add latency and use up the function's time budget. Too many attempts can also make an outage worse. So past the cap, we surface the error and let the event be retried or parked later.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes transient errors, which are worth retrying, from permanent errors, which should fail fast.
Sets timeouts on calls so a hung dependency cannot stall the code.
Uses exponential backoff with jitter and caps the number of attempts.
Makes retried operations idempotent, for example with an idempotency key or a conditional write, to avoid duplicates.
Names a tradeoff such as added latency, a consumed time budget, or retry storms worsening an outage.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner build retries with backoff and add idempotency keys, which are the core habits of this objective.

lessons.plain: An API is the front door other programs use to ask your application for something. On AWS, a managed API gateway (Amazon API Gateway) sits at that door like a receptionist. Before passing a request inward, it can check the form is filled in correctly (validation), rewrite the form into the layout your back office expects (request transformation), and on the way out reshape the reply and choose the outcome code the caller sees, such as 404 for not found (response transformation and status code override). Your backend code stays simpler, and callers get clear, consistent answers.
lessons.guessPrompt: A caller sends an order whose quantity field says "two" instead of a number. Is it better to reject that at the front door or let your function receive it and fail? Why?
lessons.teach:
In API Gateway's REST APIs, each request passes through four stages. The method request is what the caller sends. The integration request is what reaches the backend, such as a Lambda function. The integration response is what the backend returns. The method response is what the caller finally receives.

Validation checks the method request. A model is a JSON Schema, a description of the allowed body shape. A request validator turns on checks of the body against the model, or checks that required headers and query parameters are present. A failed check returns 400 and the backend never runs, so you pay for no invocation and your code never sees bad data.

Transformation uses mapping templates. These are small templates, written in the Velocity Template Language (VTL), that rewrite a payload between stages. Status code override means choosing the method response code. You can match the backend's error message with a pattern, or set $context.responseOverride.status inside a template.

Worked example, POST /orders. The model requires quantity to be an integer of at least 1. First, a caller sends quantity "two". The validator rejects it with 400, and Lambda is not called. Second, a valid request arrives. The request template renames customerId to customer_id and adds $context.requestId. Third, Lambda throws an error whose message starts "NotFound". The integration response pattern .*NotFound.* maps that to 404, and a response template returns a clean JSON error.

Common mistake: these templates apply only to a non-proxy (custom) integration. With Lambda proxy integration, the request passes through untouched, and your function must return its own statusCode, headers and body. A second trap affects a non-proxy integration with no error pattern. A failed function can come back to the caller as 200 with an error body. Clients then treat failures as success, retries never happen, and monitoring under-reports errors.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic exposes PATCH /appointments through an API Gateway REST API with a non-proxy (custom) Lambda integration. Their model requires durationMinutes to be an integer from 15 to 60, and a request validator checks the body. Step 1: a caller sends durationMinutes 90. The validator rejects it with 400 and the Lambda function never runs. Step 2: a valid request arrives. The request mapping template renames petId to pet_id and passes it to the function. Step 3: the function succeeds and returns a body saying the change is queued for a vet to approve. The team wants the caller to receive status 202 instead of the default 200. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the caller receives 202 with the queued-change body. What is the missing Step 4?
choices: Switch to Lambda proxy integration so the response mapping template can set the 202 for them
Add an integration response pattern .*queued.* so the success body is matched like an error message and mapped to 202
Add 202 to the model so the request validator returns it after the body passes the check
In the response mapping template, set $context.responseOverride.status to 202
questions.why: Setting $context.responseOverride.status inside a mapping template chooses the method response code, and here there is no backend error message for a pattern to match.

questions.prompt: In an API Gateway REST API, a ride-sharing team's Lambda backend returns a payload that API Gateway has not yet reshaped for the caller. Which of the four request stages is this?
choices: Integration response
Method response
Method request
Integration request
questions.why: The integration response is what the backend returns, before it becomes the method response that the caller finally receives.

questions.prompt: A bookshop API uses Lambda proxy integration on GET /titles. A developer adds a response mapping template that should rename fields and set a 404 when a title is missing, but callers see no change at all. What explains this?
choices: Mapping templates apply only to non-proxy integrations; with proxy integration the function must return its own statusCode, headers and body
The template must match the error with a pattern like .*404.* before it can rename any fields
Proxy integration applies response templates only to error responses, so the successful responses pass through unchanged
Mapping templates only take effect after a request validator and a model are attached to the method
questions.why: With Lambda proxy integration the request and response pass through untouched, so templates are ignored and the function itself must build the status code, headers and body.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's API uses a non-proxy (custom) Lambda integration with no error patterns in the integration response. The function starts failing on 5% of calls. What is the most likely effect?
choices: Callers receive 200 with an error body, so clients treat failures as success, do not retry, and monitoring under-reports errors
The request validator returns 400 and stops the failing calls before the function runs
API Gateway automatically returns 500 for every failure because the function threw an error
Callers receive 404, because API Gateway maps any unmatched error message to not found
questions.why: Without an error pattern to choose a different method response code, a failed function can reach the caller as 200 with an error body, which hides the failure from clients and monitoring.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use the API layer to validate input, reshape requests and responses, and return the right status codes, and name one tradeoff of doing this in the gateway instead of in the Lambda code.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd attach a JSON Schema model and a request validator to the method. Malformed bodies or missing required parameters then get a 400 at the gateway, and we never pay for a Lambda invocation on junk. With a non-proxy integration, mapping templates let me rename fields or add context like the request ID before the function sees the request. Integration responses let me match error messages, say anything containing NotFound, to a 404, and shape a consistent error body. Without those error mappings, a failed function can reach the client as a 200, which hides failures. The tradeoff is that logic gets split. Templates are written in VTL, and they are harder to unit test and version than application code. Also, choosing proxy integration gives up templates entirely, so the function must build its own status codes and headers.
rubricPoints: Validation uses a model (JSON Schema) and a request validator, and it rejects with 400 before the backend runs.
Mapping templates rewrite requests and responses between the caller and the backend.
Status codes are overridden by matching backend errors in integration responses or by setting a response override.
Templates and error mappings only apply to non-proxy integrations, while proxy integration passes everything through.
It names a tradeoff, such as logic split across gateway config and code, or VTL being hard to test.
It notes that unmapped errors can surface to callers as 200.

suggested.rationale: No OpsForge mission or planned engine exercises an API gateway's validation and mapping stages, so reasoning through exam-style request scenarios gives the most practice.

lessons.plain: A unit test is a small piece of code that checks one piece of your own code, such as a single function, gives the right answer for a given input. It runs on your laptop in seconds, without touching real cloud services. AWS SAM (the Serverless Application Model) is a free framework for describing and building serverless apps. Its command-line tool can also run your Lambda function on your machine. Think of a flight simulator: pilots practise every switch on the ground before a real plane leaves the gate, so mistakes are cheap and fast to find.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function saves an order to a database table. If your test talks to the real table every time it runs, what problems might you hit when you run that test fifty times a day, or on a teammate's laptop?
lessons.teach:
A unit test checks one unit of code, usually a single function, in isolation. You call the function with a known input and assert, meaning check, that the output or side effect matches what you expect. Isolation is the key idea. Anything outside your code, such as a DynamoDB table, a queue or another API, is replaced by a stub or mock. A stub is a fake object that returns canned answers. A mock is a fake that also records how it was called. Tests stay fast, free and repeatable because nothing depends on the network, on credentials or on data someone else changed.

AWS SAM is an open-source framework. A template file declares your functions and resources, and the sam command-line tool works with that file. The sam build command packages your code and its dependencies. The sam local generate-event command prints a realistic sample event, for example a queue message or an API request. The sam local invoke command runs your function once inside a local container that mimics the Lambda runtime. A container is an isolated package of the runtime and your code, and SAM needs Docker installed to run it. The sam local start-api command serves your API routes on your own machine.

Here is a worked example. Your handler reads orderId from the event and calls put_item on a table. First, you write a unit test that passes a fake event and a stubbed DynamoDB client. You then assert that put_item was called once with orderId 42. Second, if the event has no orderId, you assert that the handler returns a 400 error and never calls put_item. Third, you generate a sample queue event with SAM, save it as event.json and run sam local invoke with that file. This confirms the handler name, runtime and packaging all work.

A common mistake is to think sam local invoke is isolated. Your code runs locally, but any SDK call still reaches real AWS using your credentials. A careless local run can write to or delete production data. Keep unit tests stubbed, and point local invokes at a test table through an environment variable.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental startup has a Lambda handler that reads rentalId from an API request and calls send_message on a queue client. A developer works through it like this. Step 1: write a unit test that passes a fake API event with rentalId 7 and a mock queue client, then assert that send_message was called once with rentalId 7. Step 2: use sam local generate-event to print a sample API request, set rentalId to 7 in it, and save it as rental.json. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: run sam local invoke with rental.json. Docker starts a local container that mimics the Lambda runtime, and the handler runs once. Which action belongs in Step 3 so that Step 4 cannot put a message on the company's real production queue?
choices: Nothing extra is needed, because sam local invoke runs the function in an isolated container that never reaches real AWS.
Set an environment variable for the function so that its queue URL points at a separate test queue instead of the production one.
Switch to sam local start-api, because serving routes on your own machine keeps every SDK call local.
Run sam build again, because packaging the code switches the SDK into an offline mode for local runs.
questions.why: Code run by sam local invoke still sends real SDK calls to AWS using your credentials, so you have to point it at a test resource through an environment variable to protect production.

questions.prompt: A developer at a ticketing company tests a checkout function. In the test, the real payment client is replaced by a fake object. Whatever it receives, the fake always returns the answer "approved", and it keeps no record of how it was called. What is this fake object called?
choices: A stub
A sample event
A mock
A container
questions.why: A stub is a fake that only returns canned answers. A mock would also record how it was called.

questions.prompt: A team at a recipe-sharing site has a SAM template that declares three API routes backed by Lambda functions. A developer wants to open those routes on their own laptop and send requests to them repeatedly from a browser while they work. Which SAM command fits this goal?
choices: sam local generate-event
sam build
sam local invoke
sam local start-api
questions.why: sam local start-api serves your API routes on your own machine. sam local invoke runs a function only once, with a single event.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's unit test for a stock-count function connects to a shared development DynamoDB table. The test passes on Monday. On Tuesday it fails, even though nobody touched the code, because a colleague deleted some rows in that table. What is the best fix?
choices: Run the test with sam local invoke so the shared table is automatically isolated.
Give the test production credentials so it reads from a more stable table.
Ask the team to stop editing the shared development table while tests run.
Replace the table client with a stub or mock that returns known data, so the test no longer depends on outside data.
questions.why: A unit test should be isolated. Stubbing the table makes the test fast and repeatable, and it no longer depends on data that someone else can change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a stubbed unit test and running your function with sam local invoke, and name one thing each approach cannot catch.
lessons.modelAnswer: A unit test calls my handler function directly with a fake event. It swaps out the DynamoDB client for a stub, so it runs in milliseconds with no network and no credentials. I can check my own logic, such as rejecting an event with no orderId or calling put_item with the right fields. It cannot tell me whether my SAM template points at the right handler, whether my dependencies are packaged, or whether the real table accepts my item. sam local invoke builds my function and runs it in a local container that mimics Lambda, using a sample event from sam local generate-event. That catches packaging and configuration mistakes. It is slower and needs Docker, though, and any SDK calls go to real AWS with my credentials. It can also miss real-cloud differences such as IAM permissions or concurrency limits. So I run many unit tests constantly and a few local invokes, always against a test table.
rubricPoints: A unit test exercises one function in isolation with known inputs and asserted outputs.
External services are replaced with stubs or mocks so tests are fast, free and repeatable.
sam local invoke runs the function in a local container that mimics Lambda, which needs Docker and uses sample events.
Local invokes still call real AWS services through the SDK, so they should target test resources.
Each approach misses something: unit tests miss packaging or configuration problems, and local runs miss real-cloud permissions or scale behaviour.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner write real unit tests around error handling, which is the core habit that SAM-based Lambda testing builds on.

lessons.plain: A messaging service is a go-between that holds messages so one program can hand off work without waiting for another program to finish it. Think of a restaurant ticket rail. The waiter clips an order to the rail and walks away. A cook takes the ticket, makes the dish, then throws the ticket away. If the cook drops the ticket half-done, it goes back on the rail for someone else. Amazon SQS, a managed queue, works this way. Amazon SNS, a managed publish-and-subscribe topic, works more like a loudspeaker that copies each announcement to every listener.
lessons.guessPrompt: A worker program takes a message off a queue, then crashes before it finishes the job. What do you think should happen to that message, and how could the queue know the job was never finished?
lessons.teach:
Writing code against a messaging service means using the SDK, the library that calls the service API, to send, receive and acknowledge messages. With Amazon SQS, a producer calls SendMessage, or SendMessageBatch for up to ten messages at once. A consumer calls ReceiveMessage, does the work, then calls DeleteMessage using the receipt handle, a token that identifies that particular delivery. With Amazon SNS, a publisher calls Publish on a topic, and SNS pushes a copy to every subscriber.

The design rests on the visibility timeout. When a consumer receives a message, SQS hides it for that many seconds instead of removing it. If the consumer deletes the message in time, the message is gone. If the consumer crashes or runs too long, the message becomes visible again and another consumer can retry it. This is why a standard queue gives at-least-once delivery: the same message can arrive more than once. A standard queue also does not promise ordering. A FIFO queue keeps order within a message group ID and drops repeats that share a deduplication ID inside a short window.

Here is a worked example with a 30-second visibility timeout. A consumer receives order 42 at t=0, and the message is hidden. The consumer charges the card at t=5. The consumer crashes at t=6 before calling DeleteMessage. At t=30 the message reappears. A second consumer receives it and charges the card a second time.

The common mistake is assuming that receiving a message removes it, or setting the visibility timeout shorter than the real processing time. The fix has three parts. Make processing idempotent, meaning it is safe to repeat, for example by checking the order ID before charging. Set the visibility timeout longer than the worst-case processing time. Delete the message only after the work succeeds.

One more setting matters for polling. Use long polling by setting WaitTimeSeconds up to 20. Short polling returns empty responses immediately, which wastes API calls and money.

In a running system, getting these wrong shows up as duplicate side effects, a queue that never drains, or a high bill from empty receive calls.

questions.prompt: A city library runs a worker that reads overdue-notice jobs from an Amazon SQS standard queue (a managed message queue) and emails each member. The queue's visibility timeout, meaning how long SQS hides a received message, is 45 seconds. Today one job is slow and takes 70 seconds. Trace it. Step 1: At t=0 Worker A calls ReceiveMessage and gets the notice for member 118, and SQS hides the message for 45 seconds. Step 2: Worker A starts building the PDF and sending the email, which will take 70 seconds. Step 3: (missing). Step 4: At t=70 Worker A finishes, calls DeleteMessage with its receipt handle, and member 118 has received two identical emails. Which statement is the missing Step 3?
choices: At t=45 the message becomes visible again, Worker B receives it and sends a second email to member 118.
At t=45 Worker B receives the message, but the standard queue drops it as a repeat before the second email goes out.
At t=45 the visibility timeout expires, so SQS deletes the message and Worker B never sees it.
At t=45 SQS sees Worker A is still busy and extends the hidden period on its own, so no other worker can see the message.
questions.why: When the visibility timeout runs out before DeleteMessage is called, SQS makes the message visible again, and another consumer receives it and repeats the work. That repeat explains the duplicate email.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team's inventory-sync worker calls ReceiveMessage in a tight loop on an SQS queue that is usually empty. The AWS bill shows millions of receive calls that returned nothing. Which code change most directly cuts these wasted calls?
choices: Raise the visibility timeout to 20 seconds so that each message stays hidden for longer.
Send messages with SendMessageBatch so that each call carries up to ten messages.
Set WaitTimeSeconds to 20 on ReceiveMessage so that each call waits for messages to arrive.
Replace the queue with an SNS topic so that the worker no longer has to poll.
questions.why: Long polling, set with WaitTimeSeconds up to 20, makes each receive call wait for messages instead of returning empty at once. Fewer calls come back empty, so fewer calls are wasted and billed.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing app sends seat-booking messages for many events. Bookings for the same event must be processed in the order they were sent, and an accidental resend of the same booking within a short window should be ignored. Which setup fits?
choices: Use an SNS topic so that every subscriber gets each booking in the exact order it was sent.
Use a FIFO queue with the event as the message group ID and a deduplication ID per booking.
Use a standard queue and rely on its ordering guarantee and its built-in duplicate removal.
Use a standard queue with a longer visibility timeout so that bookings arrive in order.
questions.why: A FIFO queue keeps order within a message group ID. It also drops repeats that share a deduplication ID inside a short window. A standard queue promises neither of these.

questions.prompt: A developer at a payroll startup writes a consumer that calls ReceiveMessage, then immediately calls DeleteMessage, then credits an employee bonus. One night the consumer crashes after the delete but before the credit. What happens to that bonus job?
choices: The job is lost: the message was already deleted, so it never reappears and the bonus is never credited.
SQS restores the deleted message because the consumer crashed while still holding the receipt handle.
The bonus is credited twice, because at-least-once delivery always repeats every message.
The message reappears after the visibility timeout, and another consumer credits the bonus.
questions.why: DeleteMessage removes the message for good, so no retry can happen. This is why a consumer should delete a message only after the work has succeeded.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a consumer should receive, process and delete SQS messages, why the same message can be processed twice, and what tradeoff you face when choosing the visibility timeout.
lessons.modelAnswer: The consumer calls ReceiveMessage with long polling, so it waits up to 20 seconds instead of hammering the API with empty calls. Receiving a message does not remove it. SQS only hides it for the visibility timeout. We do the work and then call DeleteMessage with the receipt handle. We delete only after the work succeeds. If we crash or run past the timeout, the message reappears and gets retried. That retry is the point, but it also means a standard queue delivers at least once, so our handler must be idempotent, for example by recording the order ID before charging. The tradeoff is in the timeout length. If it is too short, slow jobs get processed twice at the same time. If it is too long, a message from a crashed consumer sits invisible for a long while before anyone retries it. Set the timeout a bit above the worst-case processing time.
rubricPoints: Receiving a message hides it for the visibility timeout rather than removing it.
The consumer must explicitly delete the message with its receipt handle after the work succeeds.
Standard queues deliver at least once, so handlers must be idempotent.
A visibility timeout that is too short causes duplicate processing, and one that is too long delays retries.
Long polling reduces empty responses and cost.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a queue that grows while nothing drains it makes the learner trace the receive, process and delete cycle that this objective teaches.

lessons.plain: Every AWS service, such as a database or a queue, is controlled through an API: a set of web requests it accepts, like "put this item" or "send this message". You could build those requests by hand, but you would have to format them exactly and prove who you are on every one. An AWS SDK (software development kit) is a library for your programming language that does that paperwork for you. It is like ordering through a trusted courier who already knows the address, carries your ID, and tries again if the shop is briefly too busy.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your code asks a database service for a record and the service replies "too many requests, slow down", what do you think a well-built library should do before giving up, and why?
lessons.teach:
An AWS service API is a set of operations, each reached by an HTTPS request to a service endpoint, the web address for that service in a given Region (a geographic group of AWS data centers). Every request must be signed: the caller uses credentials, an access key ID plus a secret key (and often a temporary session token), to compute Signature Version 4 (SigV4), a cryptographic stamp proving who sent the request and that it was not altered. AWS then checks the caller's IAM (Identity and Access Management) permissions before acting.

An SDK, such as boto3 for Python, wraps all this. You create a client for one service and Region, then call methods named after API operations. The SDK serializes your arguments into the request format, finds credentials through the credential provider chain (an ordered search: environment variables, a local profile, then the role attached to the compute running the code, like a Lambda execution role), signs the request, sends it, and turns the reply into objects or raises an exception. It also retries throttling and temporary server errors with exponential backoff, waiting longer between each attempt, and offers paginators for operations that return results in pages.

Worked example: a Lambda function reads an order. Step one, outside the handler, the code creates a DynamoDB client once. Step two, inside the handler, it calls get_item with the table name and key. Step three, the SDK picks up the function's temporary role credentials from the environment, signs, and sends. Step four, DynamoDB returns a throttling error; the SDK waits briefly and retries, and the second attempt succeeds. Step five, your code receives the item.

A common mistake is pasting long-lived access keys into source code. They leak through repositories and never rotate; relying on the execution role instead gives short-lived credentials automatically. Another is ignoring pagination: a list call returns only the first page, so a running system silently processes part of the data. Creating a new client on every invocation also adds latency to each request.

questions.prompt:
A regional bakery chain runs a nightly Python script on a virtual server (an Amazon EC2 instance) to list about 4,500 receipt files stored in an S3 bucket in the eu-west-1 Region. The instance has a role attached that allows listing that bucket. No environment variables hold credentials, and no local profile exists on the server.

Step 1: The script creates one S3 client for eu-west-1 using boto3.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The SDK signs each request with SigV4 and sends it to the S3 endpoint for eu-west-1.
Step 4: Because the script uses a paginator, the SDK keeps requesting pages until all 4,500 file names are returned.
Step 5: One page request hits a temporary server error. The SDK waits briefly, retries, and the retry succeeds.

What happens in Step 2?
choices: The SDK sends the requests unsigned because it found no keys, and S3 accepts them because the server is in the same Region as the bucket.
The script stops with an error, because the SDK can only read credentials from environment variables.
The credential provider chain finds nothing in environment variables or a local profile, so it moves on and uses temporary credentials from the role attached to the instance.
The SDK skips the IAM permission check, because requests coming from an AWS-hosted server are trusted automatically.
questions.why: The credential provider chain searches in order (environment variables, then a local profile, then the role attached to the compute), so with the first two empty it uses the instance role's short-lived credentials.

questions.prompt: A developer at a parking-app company asks what Signature Version 4 (SigV4) actually does for each request their code sends to an AWS service. Which answer is correct?
choices: It decides whether the caller's IAM permissions allow the requested operation.
It is a cryptographic stamp, computed from the caller's credentials, that proves who sent the request and that the request was not altered.
It picks the correct service endpoint for the Region the client was created for.
It encrypts the reply that comes back from the service so that no one else can read it.
questions.why: SigV4 is computed from the credentials to prove the sender's identity and the integrity of the request; AWS checks IAM permissions separately, after the signature.

questions.prompt: A warehouse company's Lambda function calls a list operation once to fetch shipment records. The table holds about 3,200 records, but the function only ever processes the first 1,000. No error is raised and no retries are logged. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The code makes a single list call and never asks for the following pages, so it only receives the first page of results. Using a paginator would fetch all of them.
The function's temporary role credentials expired partway through the reply.
The client was created for the wrong Region, so only part of the data was visible.
The SDK hit throttling and quietly dropped the remaining 2,200 records instead of retrying.
questions.why: List operations return results in pages, so code that ignores pagination silently processes only the first page without raising any error.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking startup's Lambda function has a long-lived access key ID and secret key pasted directly into its source code, which is stored in a shared repository. Which change best fixes this?
choices: Remove the keys from the code, grant the needed permissions to the function's execution role, and let the SDK's credential provider chain pick up short-lived credentials automatically.
Move the client creation inside the handler so that the keys are re-read on every invocation.
Keep the keys in the code but turn off SDK retries, so that fewer signed requests are sent with them.
Replace the keys once a year by editing the source code and redeploying.
questions.why: Hard-coded long-lived keys can leak through repositories and never rotate, while the execution role supplies short-lived credentials that the SDK finds on its own.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an AWS SDK does for you when your code calls a service like DynamoDB, and name one thing the SDK will not handle for you or one tradeoff of its built-in behavior.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each AWS service exposes an HTTPS API, and every request has to be signed with credentials using SigV4 so AWS knows who is calling and can check IAM permissions. The SDK hides that work: we create a client for a service and Region, call a method like get_item, and it serializes the arguments, finds credentials through the provider chain (in Lambda, the execution role's temporary credentials), signs, sends, and parses the reply or raises an error. It also retries throttling and transient errors with exponential backoff. Limits: it will not fix missing IAM permissions, and it only returns one page of results unless we use a paginator or loop. The retry behavior is a tradeoff too: retries add latency and, for non-idempotent writes, could repeat an action, so we should not hardcode keys, should reuse clients, and should design writes to be safe to repeat.
rubricPoints: Services are called through signed HTTPS API requests to a Regional endpoint.
The SDK serializes requests, signs them with SigV4, and parses responses or errors.
Credentials come from the provider chain, ideally a role, not hardcoded keys.
The SDK retries throttling and transient errors with exponential backoff.
Paginated results must be followed, or data is silently missed.
Names a limit or tradeoff, such as added latency from retries or missing IAM permissions.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises SDK calls directly, so explaining what the SDK does on each request is the best way to check real understanding.

lessons.plain: Streaming data is a never-ending flow of small records, such as vehicle positions, clicks or sensor readings, that you want to handle within seconds rather than in a nightly batch. Think of a conveyor belt in a factory: items keep arriving in order, several workers can watch the same belt, and the belt keeps a recent stretch visible so a worker who fell behind can catch up. On AWS, a managed stream service holds that belt for you. Producers put records on it, and consumer code reads them in order, keeps track of how far it got, and processes them in near real time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A stream splits its traffic across several lanes. If every vehicle's position update must be processed in the order it was sent, what would you use to decide which lane a record goes into?
lessons.teach:
A data stream is an ordered, append-only log of records that many readers can replay. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is AWS's managed version. Records stay for a retention period, 24 hours by default and extendable, and reading a record does not delete it, unlike a queue.

Capacity comes from shards. A shard is one lane of the stream with fixed write and read limits, roughly 1 MB or 1,000 records per second in. Each record carries a partition key, which is a string the producer chooses. The service hashes that key to pick a shard, so records with the same key always land on the same shard. Each record also gets a sequence number, its position in the shard, and order is guaranteed only within one shard. Hashing spreads many keys across shards for throughput, while keeping each key on one shard preserves order for that entity.

Worked example: vehicles send positions with partition key = vehicle ID into a 4-shard stream. Truck 17's key hashes to shard 2. Its 10:00:01 and 10:00:02 positions both go to shard 2 with rising sequence numbers. A Lambda event source mapping, which is a poller that pulls batches from each shard and invokes your function, hands truck 17's records over in order. Meanwhile truck 40 on shard 3 is processed in parallel.

Two related services are worth knowing. Amazon Data Firehose is a managed delivery pipe that buffers records and writes them to storage such as S3 with no consumer code, but you cannot replay from it. DynamoDB Streams emits a change record for every item write to a table, and it is read the same way.

A common mistake is choosing a low-cardinality partition key, meaning one with few distinct values, such as a region field that has only two values. All traffic piles onto one or two hot shards and gets throttled, and adding shards does not help.

In a running system, one bad record that makes the function throw causes the whole batch to retry. The shard stops advancing and lag grows until the record expires. Limit retries, enable bisect-on-error so failing batches are split, report partial batch failures, and send failures to an on-failure destination.

questions.prompt:
A bank streams card transactions into a Kinesis data stream with 5 shards. Each record uses the card number as its partition key. A partition key is the string the producer picks, and the service hashes it to choose a shard. Trace one card.

Step 1: The key for the card ending 4412 hashes to shard 4.
Step 2: The card's 09:15:10 purchase is written to shard 4 and gets a sequence number, which is its position in that shard.
Step 3: (missing) The card's 09:15:30 refund arrives.
Step 4: A Lambda event source mapping is a poller that pulls batches from each shard and invokes your function. It reads shard 4 and processes the refund after the purchase. Meanwhile, card 9031 on shard 1 is processed in parallel.

Which statement correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: The refund goes to whichever shard is least busy, so the write load stays even across all 5 shards.
The refund also lands on shard 4, because the same key always hashes to the same shard, and it gets a higher sequence number.
The refund is given the same sequence number as the purchase, so the two records are grouped together.
The refund can land on any shard, because Kinesis keeps order across the whole stream, not just within one shard.
questions.why: The same partition key always hashes to the same shard, and order is guaranteed only within a shard, so the refund lands on shard 4 with a later sequence number and is read after the purchase.
