questions.prompt: A retailer sends clickstream events through a message queue. Once a consumer reads a message, the message is gone. A second analytics team now wants to reread the last 12 hours of the same events with its own application. Which property of Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, a managed data stream, solves this?
choices: Each shard deletes a record after it is read, but a backup copy goes to a second shard for other readers.
DynamoDB Streams keeps a copy of every event, so the second team can replay from there.
Records stay for a retention period, and reading does not delete them, so several readers can replay the same records.
Amazon Data Firehose, a managed delivery pipe, keeps buffered records so any team can replay them later.
questions.why: A stream is an append-only log: records stay for the retention period (24 hours by default, and it can be extended) whether or not they have been read, so many readers can replay them. You cannot replay from Firehose, and DynamoDB Streams only records writes to a table.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site writes events to a Kinesis stream with 8 shards, using the event type as the partition key. There are only three values: view, add, and buy. Writes are being throttled even though most shards sit nearly idle. What is the best fix?
choices: Increase the shard count to 16 so the stream has more total write capacity.
Make the Lambda function's batch size larger, so it reads the hot shards faster.
Raise the stream's retention period, so records wait longer before they are written.
Switch to a partition key with many distinct values, such as a session ID, so writes spread across all the shards.
questions.why: Three key values can only hash to at most three shards, so traffic piles onto hot shards. Adding shards does not help a low-cardinality key (one with few distinct values); a key with many distinct values spreads writes across all the shards.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function reads a Kinesis stream through an event source mapping. One malformed record makes the function throw an error. Hours later, one shard has not moved forward and its lag keeps growing, while the other shards are fine. What explains this, and what should the developer configure?
choices: Kinesis cannot replay records. Move the data to Amazon Data Firehose, so failed records can be retried automatically.
The whole batch keeps retrying, so the shard is stuck. Limit retries, enable bisect-on-error, report partial batch failures, and add an on-failure destination.
The function is short on memory. Raise its memory setting, so the malformed record can be parsed on the next attempt.
The shard is over its write limit. Add more shards, so the bad record is moved to a less busy shard.
questions.why: A record that makes the function throw causes the whole batch to retry, and this blocks the shard until the record expires. Limiting retries, splitting failing batches with bisect-on-error, reporting partial batch failures, and sending failures to an on-failure destination let the shard advance again.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Kinesis data stream keeps per-vehicle order while still scaling, and name one limit or tradeoff they must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Kinesis stream is a log split into shards, and each shard is a lane with fixed throughput. Every record we write carries a partition key. Kinesis hashes it to choose a shard, so all records with the same key, say one vehicle ID, land on the same shard with increasing sequence numbers. That gives us order per vehicle, while different vehicles spread across shards and get processed in parallel by Lambda reading batches from each shard. The tradeoff is that order only holds within a shard, not across the stream. The key also needs many distinct values; a key like region creates a hot shard that throttles no matter how many shards we add. Finally, a single failing record can block its shard, because Lambda retries the batch. So we cap retries, bisect batches, and send failures to a destination.
rubricPoints: A stream is an ordered, retained log that consumers can replay, unlike a queue that deletes messages.
Shards provide capacity, and each has fixed read and write limits.
The partition key is hashed to a shard, so the same key keeps its order on one shard.
Ordering is guaranteed only within a shard, not across the whole stream.
A low-cardinality key creates hot shards and throttling.
A failing record can block its shard unless retries, bisecting and failure destinations are configured.

suggested.rationale: Choosing between a stream, a delivery pipe and a queue, and reasoning about partition keys and stuck shards, is best practised through exam-style scenarios, because no current mission drives a stream directly.

lessons.plain: Amazon EventBridge is a managed event router. One part of your system announces that something happened, such as an order being placed, and EventBridge decides who else should hear about it. Think of a post office sorting room. Senders drop letters into one slot, and sorting rules read each envelope and send copies only to the people who asked for that kind of letter. The sender never needs to know who the readers are. You can add a new reader later without changing the sender. That independence between the two sides is called loose coupling.
lessons.guessPrompt: An orders service announces "order placed" events. Billing wants every order. A fraud checker wants only orders over 1,000 dollars. How could one central router send each team only what it wants, without the orders service knowing either team exists?
lessons.teach:
An event is a small JSON record saying something happened. It has a source (who sent it), a detail-type (what kind of event it is), and a detail (the data itself). An event bus is the channel that events are published to. AWS gives you a default bus, and you can create custom buses for your own applications. A rule is attached to a bus. It contains an event pattern, which is a JSON filter that an event must match, and up to five targets, which are the destinations that receive matching events. Targets can be Lambda functions, queues, or workflows.

This works because publishers and consumers only share the bus and the shape of the event. Nothing calls anything directly. Delivery to targets is asynchronous.

Here is a worked example. Your code calls PutEvents with source "shop.orders", detail-type "OrderPlaced" and detail {"amount": 1500}. Rule A's pattern lists only that source and detail-type, so the event matches and goes to the billing queue. Rule B adds a numeric condition that amount must be greater than 1000. 1500 passes, so the fraud Lambda is invoked too. An order for 200 dollars would reach billing only.

If a target fails, EventBridge retries it with backoff, for up to 24 hours by default. After that the event is dropped unless you attach a dead-letter queue to that target. A dead-letter queue is a queue that holds events that could not be delivered. Delivery is at least once, so a target can see the same event twice. Handlers must therefore be idempotent, which means processing the same event twice has the same effect as processing it once.

A common mistake is writing patterns that never match. Matching is exact and case-sensitive, so "orderplaced" will not match "OrderPlaced". Another mistake is a target that publishes an event matching its own rule, which creates an infinite loop and a runaway bill. In a running system, a pattern that silently matches nothing means downstream work just never happens, and no error is raised.

questions.prompt:
A city library system uses EventBridge. Trace what happens to one event.
Step 1: The returns app calls PutEvents with source "city.library", detail-type "BookReturned" and detail {"daysLate": 3}.
Step 2: Rule X's event pattern lists only that source and detail-type. The event matches, so it is delivered to the shelving queue.
Step 3: Rule Y's pattern lists the same source and detail-type, plus a numeric condition that daysLate must be greater than 7. Its target is the late-fee Lambda.
Step 4: ???
Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Rule X already matched this event, so EventBridge stops checking rules and Rule Y is never evaluated at all.
3 is not greater than 7, so Rule Y does not match. Only the shelving queue receives this event.
Rule Y's condition fails, so EventBridge treats it as a failed delivery and retries the late-fee Lambda with backoff.
Rule Y matches because its source and detail-type match, so the late-fee Lambda gets the event and checks daysLate itself.
questions.why: Every condition in a pattern must match, and 3 fails the greater-than-7 condition, so only Rule X's target receives the event.

questions.prompt: A team at a gym-booking company writes a rule whose pattern requires detail-type "classbooked". Their code publishes events with detail-type "ClassBooked". The pattern is otherwise correct. What happens in the running system?
choices: The events match anyway, because EventBridge ignores letter case when it compares detail-type values.
No event matches, and the rule's targets never run. No error is raised, so the downstream work silently stops happening.
EventBridge raises a pattern-mismatch error that shows up in the publisher's PutEvents response.
The events go to the target's dead-letter queue, because they did not match the rule's pattern.
questions.why: Matching is exact and case-sensitive, so the rule matches nothing, and a pattern that matches nothing produces no error.

questions.prompt: A parking app's EventBridge rule sends "PaymentReceived" events to a Lambda function that adds loyalty points. The team notices a customer was given points twice for one payment. The function had no errors. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team do?
choices: Delivery is at least once, so duplicates can happen. Make the handler idempotent, so a repeat event has no extra effect.
The rule has two targets. Remove one of them so the event can only be delivered one time.
EventBridge always delivers every event twice. Halve the points added in each invocation.
The pattern is case-sensitive and matched twice. Change the pattern to use lowercase values.
questions.why: EventBridge delivers at least once, so a target can see the same event twice, and only an idempotent handler keeps the result correct.

questions.prompt: A weather-alert service's rule targets a Lambda function that was broken by a bad deployment for two full days. No dead-letter queue is attached to that target. With default settings, what happens to the alert events published during the outage?
choices: EventBridge retries each one with backoff for up to 24 hours. After that, events still undelivered are dropped and lost.
They are sent back to the publisher as errors from its PutEvents call, so the publisher can resend them.
They are moved automatically to a default dead-letter queue that AWS creates for every rule.
They wait on the event bus indefinitely and are delivered when the Lambda function works again.
questions.why: Failed targets are retried for up to 24 hours by default, and after that events are dropped unless a dead-letter queue is attached to the target.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how an EventBridge rule decides where an event goes, and name one limit or tradeoff they must design around.
lessons.modelAnswer:
Our services publish events to an event bus. Each event is JSON with a source, a detail-type and a detail payload. Rules sit on the bus. Each rule has an event pattern, a filter that must match the event's fields, and up to five targets, such as a Lambda function or an SQS queue. Every rule whose pattern matches gets a copy, so one event can fan out to several consumers. The publisher never knows who is listening, which keeps the services loosely coupled.

The tradeoff is that delivery is asynchronous and at least once. Failed targets are retried for up to a day and then dropped unless we attach a dead-letter queue, so we configure one. Duplicates are possible, so our handlers must be idempotent. Patterns are exact and case-sensitive. A typo matches nothing and raises no error, so we need to test our patterns.
rubricPoints: An event carries a source, a detail-type and a detail, and it is published to an event bus.
A rule pairs an event pattern filter with one or more targets.
Every matching rule receives the event, which allows fanout and keeps publishers decoupled from consumers.
Delivery is asynchronous and at least once, so handlers must be idempotent.
Failed deliveries are retried and then dropped unless a dead-letter queue is attached.
Patterns match exactly, so a mismatch fails silently.

suggested.rationale: The planned messaging and events engine would let the learner publish events, write patterns, and watch matches, retries and dead-letter behaviour happen.

lessons.plain: When your code calls someone else's service, such as a payment provider or a weather API, that service will sometimes be slow, briefly broken, or down for hours. Resilient integration means writing your code so those failures do not take your own application down with them. You try again when a failure looks temporary, you wait a little longer between each try, and you stop calling altogether when the other side is clearly broken. It is like phoning a busy shop. You redial after a minute, then after five. If the line stays dead all morning, you stop calling and leave a message instead.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your code calls a payment service that just returned an error. Should you retry immediately, retry after a growing pause, or not retry at all? Does your answer change if the error said 'service temporarily unavailable' versus 'card number invalid'?
lessons.teach:
Resilient integration is a set of patterns for calling a third-party service, meaning a service you do not control, without letting its failures cascade into yours.

Start by sorting errors. A transient error is temporary, such as a timeout, a 503 'unavailable' or a 429 'too many requests'. Trying again later may succeed. A permanent error, such as a 400 'bad request' or a 401 'unauthorized', will fail every time, so retrying only wastes time.

A retry is simply sending the call again. Exponential backoff means the wait doubles after each failure, for example 100 ms, then 200 ms, then 400 ms. Jitter adds a random amount to each wait so that thousands of clients do not all retry at the same instant. Always cap the number of attempts. Always set a timeout too: this is the longest you will wait for a single response, and without it one hung call can freeze your code. Retries are only safe if the call is idempotent, meaning repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. An idempotency key is a unique ID sent with the request so the provider can spot and ignore duplicates.

A circuit breaker is a guard that stops calls to a service that keeps failing. It has three states. Closed means calls flow normally. Open means calls are refused immediately after too many recent failures. Half-open means that after a cooldown, one trial call is allowed through, and its success closes the breaker again. While the breaker is open, you use a fallback: cached data, a default value, or a message placed on a queue to process later.

Worked example: a Lambda function (AWS's run-on-demand code service) calls a shipping API with a 2-second timeout. Attempt 1 times out. It waits about 100 ms plus jitter, and attempt 2 gets a 503. It waits about 200 ms, and attempt 3 succeeds. The total stays well under the function's 10-second limit.

A common mistake is retrying instantly with no limit. That piles extra load onto an already struggling service, and inside Lambda it can burn the whole function timeout, so the function fails anyway and costs more.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking app runs a Lambda function that calls an outside seat-map service. The function wraps the call in a circuit breaker that opens after 4 failures in a row and has a 20-second cooldown. Trace what happens. Step 1: the seat-map service starts returning 503 errors, and after 4 straight failures the breaker opens. Step 2: for the next 20 seconds, every call is refused at once, without contacting the service, and the app shows the last cached seat map as a fallback. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: that call succeeds, so the breaker closes and normal calls resume. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: The cooldown ends and the breaker closes by itself, so all waiting requests go straight to the service.
The cooldown ends, but the breaker stays open until an engineer resets it by hand after checking the service.
The cooldown ends, and every request refused during the open period is resent together to test the service.
The cooldown ends, the breaker moves to half-open, and exactly one trial call is allowed through to the service.
questions.why: After the cooldown, a breaker goes half-open and lets a single trial call through, and only that call's success closes it again, which protects a service that may still be recovering.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company's Lambda function calls a partner's restaurant-menu API. Which response from the partner is worth retrying with exponential backoff?
choices: 401 Unauthorized, because the API key was rejected
429 Too Many Requests, because the partner is throttling callers
400 Bad Request, because the request body was badly formed
400 Bad Request, because a required field was missing
questions.why: A 429 is a transient error that may succeed after a wait, while 400 and 401 errors are permanent and will fail every time, so retrying them only wastes time.

questions.prompt: A clinic's Lambda function asks an outside messaging provider to send an appointment-reminder text. The call times out after 3 seconds, but the provider may have sent the text anyway. The function is set to retry. What best prevents the patient from getting two identical texts?
choices: Send a unique idempotency key with each request so the provider can recognise a repeat and ignore it
Raise the per-call timeout to 30 seconds so the first attempt never times out
Remove the jitter from the backoff so the retry arrives at a predictable moment
Retry immediately with no wait, so the duplicate arrives before the provider finishes
questions.why: Retries are only safe when the call is idempotent, and an idempotency key is the unique ID that lets the provider spot and ignore a duplicate request.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Lambda function has a 12-second limit and calls an outside customs-check service. The developer added capped retries with backoff but set no timeout on each individual call. One day the customs service accepts a connection and then never replies. What is the most likely result?
choices: The first call hangs, uses up the whole 12 seconds, and the function fails before any retry runs
The retries keep the function healthy, because the attempt cap ends the hung call
The backoff doubles the wait automatically, so the function moves on to attempt 2
The circuit breaker opens at once, because a call with no reply counts as a 401 error
questions.why: Without a per-call timeout, nothing ends a single hung call, so it uses up the function's entire time limit and the retry logic never gets a chance to run.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a Lambda function's calls to an unreliable third-party API resilient, covering retries, backoff, and circuit breakers, and name one tradeoff or limit of retrying.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd decide which errors are worth retrying. Timeouts, 503s and 429s are transient, so they get retries. A 400 or a 401 won't fix itself, so I fail fast and log it. Every call gets its own timeout so a hung request can't eat the function's runtime. Retries use exponential backoff with jitter: the waits grow and are randomized, so we don't hammer the provider or retry in lockstep with other clients. I cap attempts so the total stays inside the Lambda timeout. Because a retry might repeat a request that actually succeeded, I send an idempotency key so it can't double-charge. If failures keep coming, a circuit breaker opens and we stop calling for a cooldown, serving cached data or queuing the work instead. The tradeoff is that retries add latency and extra load, and they're only safe on idempotent operations.
rubricPoints: Distinguishes transient errors worth retrying from permanent errors that should fail fast.
Describes exponential backoff with jitter and a cap on attempts.
Mentions per-call timeouts that fit within the overall function timeout.
Explains that retries need idempotency, for example an idempotency key, to avoid duplicate effects.
Describes the circuit breaker states (closed, open, half-open) and a fallback.
Names a tradeoff such as added latency, extra load on the provider, or the risk of duplicates.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner build retries with backoff and idempotency keys, which is the core of resilient third-party integration.

lessons.plain: Amazon Q Developer is an AI coding assistant from AWS. It plugs into your code editor, terminal and the AWS web console. While you type, it can suggest the next lines of code. You can also ask it questions in a chat window, have it explain unfamiliar code, draft unit tests, or scan your work for security weaknesses. Think of it as a well-read pair programmer sitting beside you. It is quick and knows many patterns, but it sometimes guesses wrong. You still own every line you accept, so you read it, test it and decide.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an AI assistant writes a working-looking Lambda function that reads from a database, what are two things you would still check yourself before putting it into production?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Q Developer is a generative AI assistant for software work. Generative AI means a model that produces new text or code from a prompt, which is the instruction you type. Q Developer runs as a plugin in IDEs (integrated development environments, the editors where you write code, such as VS Code or JetBrains tools), in the command line, and in the AWS console.

Its main abilities are these. Inline suggestions complete code as you type, based on your file and comments. Chat answers questions such as how to page through DynamoDB results with the SDK (software development kit, the library your code uses to call AWS). It can explain selected code, generate unit tests, and run security scans that flag risks like hard-coded secrets or injection flaws. Reference tracking warns you when a suggestion closely matches public open-source code and shows its license, so you can decide whether you may use it. It can also help upgrade or transform older code.

Why it helps: it was trained on large amounts of code and AWS material, so common patterns arrive fast.

Worked example. You write a comment: save an order to the Orders table. Step 1: Q suggests a handler that calls put_item. Step 2: you read it and notice the table name is typed directly into the code, so you change it to read an environment variable. Step 3: you ask chat to generate unit tests, and you run them. Step 4: you run a security scan, which finds a logged customer email, so you remove that log line. Step 5: you commit.

Common mistake: accepting suggestions without review. The output can look confident yet use a slow full-table scan, skip error handling, or call an API that does not exist. In a running system, this leads to throttled tables, unexpected costs, or leaked data. Treat Q Developer as a fast first draft, and keep your normal review, tests and pipeline checks in place.

questions.prompt: A developer at a bike-sharing startup asks Amazon Q Developer chat, an AI assistant inside her code editor, to write a Lambda function that returns every ride for one rider from a DynamoDB table named Rides. Step 1: Q suggests code that runs a full-table scan of Rides and filters the results in memory, with no error handling. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: She asks chat to generate unit tests for the function and runs them. Step 4: She runs a security scan, which flags an API key typed directly into the code, so she moves it out of the code. Step 5: She commits. What is the missing Step 2?
choices: Read the suggestion, notice the slow full-table scan and the missing error handling, and rewrite it to look up only that rider's items and handle errors.
Accept the suggestion as written, because the unit tests in Step 3 will catch any problem with it.
Run the security scan early, because it will flag the full-table scan as a risk.
Skip review, because Q was trained on large amounts of AWS material and its suggestions are reliable.
questions.why: Q's output is a fast first draft, so you review it yourself and fix problems such as a full-table scan or missing error handling before testing, scanning and committing.

questions.prompt: A developer at a weather-data company accepts an inline suggestion from Amazon Q Developer. Q shows a notice that the suggestion closely matches public open-source code and displays that code's license. Which feature produced this notice, and why does it matter?
choices: Reference tracking, which shows the license so the developer can decide whether the code may be used.
Unit test generation, which checks whether the matching code behaves correctly.
The security scan, which blocks the code from being committed until it is rewritten.
Code transformation, which rewrites older code to replace copied open-source sections.
questions.why: Reference tracking warns when a suggestion closely matches public open-source code and shows its license, so you can judge whether you are allowed to use it.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a hotel-booking firm is handed a 200-line function written by a colleague who has left. He does not understand what it does and wants a plain-language walkthrough before changing it. Which Amazon Q Developer ability fits this need best?
choices: Turning on reference tracking for the project.
Relying on inline suggestions as he edits the function.
Running a security scan on the file.
Selecting the code and asking Q to explain it.
questions.why: Q Developer can explain selected code, which directly answers what an unfamiliar function does.

questions.prompt: A team at a ticketing company starts using Amazon Q Developer. One member proposes removing code review and pipeline checks for any code Q generates, since Q 'knows AWS well.' What is the most likely result in a running system?
choices: Nothing changes, because Q only suggests APIs that exist and patterns that perform well.
Costs fall, because Q's suggestions always use the cheapest DynamoDB operations.
Only formatting issues slip through, because Q handles error handling automatically.
Confident-looking but flawed code ships, causing problems like throttled tables, surprise costs or leaked data.
questions.why: Q's output can look confident yet use slow scans, skip error handling or call nonexistent APIs, so dropping review and checks lets those flaws reach production.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what Amazon Q Developer can do for your team's Lambda and DynamoDB work, and name one limit or risk you must manage when using it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Amazon Q Developer is an AI assistant that works inside our editor, the terminal and the AWS console. As we type, it suggests code. We can chat with it about things like SDK calls, ask it to explain code we didn't write, have it draft unit tests, and run security scans that catch problems such as hard-coded secrets. Reference tracking tells us when a suggestion resembles open-source code and which license applies. This speeds up first drafts a lot. The limit is that it can be wrong while sounding sure. It might use a full scan where a query is the right call, skip error handling, or invent an API. So we still review every suggestion and run our tests and pipeline checks. Responsibility for the code stays with us, not the tool.
rubricPoints: Defines Q Developer as a generative AI assistant in the IDE, CLI and console.
Names concrete abilities: inline suggestions, chat, code explanation, test generation, security scanning.
Mentions reference tracking and open-source license awareness.
States that output can be wrong or insecure even when it looks correct.
Says the developer must still review, test and own accepted code.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises this tool, and the key skill is articulating what it does and why its output still needs human review.

lessons.plain: Many company databases and internal services live inside a private network in the cloud, walled off from the internet. A Lambda function, which is a small piece of code the cloud runs on demand, normally runs outside that wall, so it cannot reach them. You can tell Lambda to plug into the private network, like giving a visiting contractor a badge for one office building. The badge lets them reach the rooms inside, but they now come and go through that building's doors. If the building has no exit to the street, they cannot pop out to the internet unless you add one.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you move a function inside a private network so it can reach a private database, what do you think happens to its ability to call services out on the public internet, and why?
lessons.teach:
A VPC (virtual private cloud) is your own isolated network in AWS. It is split into subnets, which are address ranges, and a private subnet has no direct route to the internet. A security group is a stateful firewall attached to network interfaces that lists which traffic is allowed in and out. By default a Lambda function runs in an AWS-owned network and can reach the internet and public AWS endpoints, but it cannot reach anything with only a private address in your VPC.

To reach private resources, you configure the function with a VPC, one or more subnets, and a security group. Lambda then creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs), which are virtual network cards placed in your subnets, and routes the function's traffic through them. The function's execution role needs permission to create and manage those interfaces. AWS provides a managed policy for this.

Worked example: a function must read a database in private subnets and then send a message to a managed queue (SQS). Step one, attach the function to two private subnets in different Availability Zones (separate data centres in a region) so it keeps working if one zone fails. Step two, give it a security group, and change the database's security group to allow the database port from that Lambda security group. Step three, the database call now works. Step four, the queue call hangs, because the queue's endpoint is public and the private subnet has no way out. Fix it with either a NAT gateway, a managed device that lets private subnets make outbound internet calls, or a VPC endpoint, a private doorway to an AWS service that keeps traffic off the internet.

A common mistake is putting the function in a public subnet and expecting internet access. Lambda's interfaces never get public IP addresses, so that does not work. In a running system the symptom is function timeouts rather than clear errors, which leads to retries and wasted billed time.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company has an internal inventory API running on servers in private subnets of its VPC. A new Lambda function must call that API and then write a record to DynamoDB, a managed AWS database with a public endpoint. Here is the setup, with one step missing.

Step 1: Attach the function to three private subnets, each in a different Availability Zone, so one zone failing does not stop it. The execution role already has the AWS managed policy for creating network interfaces.
Step 2: ______
Step 3: The call to the inventory API now succeeds on its port.
Step 4: The DynamoDB write hangs until timeout, so the team adds a VPC endpoint for DynamoDB. The write then succeeds without traffic leaving for the internet.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Grant the execution role permission to read the inventory servers, because the role decides which private addresses the function may reach
Add a NAT gateway so the function can reach the inventory servers' private addresses
Give the function a security group, and change the inventory servers' security group to allow the API port from that Lambda security group
Move the inventory servers into a public subnet so the function can reach them from Lambda's default network
questions.why: Once the function's network interfaces are in the subnets, the traffic still has to pass the servers' firewall, so the servers' security group must allow the API port from the function's security group.

questions.prompt: A ticketing startup attaches its Lambda function to a public subnet in its VPC. The function needs to call an outside payment provider on the internet. Every call times out. What is the most likely reason?
choices: Lambda's network interfaces never get public IP addresses, so a public subnet does not give the function internet access
The execution role is missing permission to call internet addresses
The function's security group is stateful, so it drops the payment provider's replies
Public subnets block all outbound traffic unless a VPC endpoint is added for the payment provider
questions.why: Lambda's network interfaces only get private addresses, so even in a public subnet the function needs a path such as a NAT gateway to reach the internet.

questions.prompt: A developer at a weather service adds VPC settings to a Lambda function: two private subnets and a security group. The update fails before the function ever runs. The settings look correct. What should they check first?
choices: Whether the subnets have a route to the internet
Whether the security group allows inbound traffic from the internet
Whether the function's execution role has permission to create and manage network interfaces
Whether a VPC endpoint exists for Lambda in the VPC
questions.why: Lambda places elastic network interfaces in your subnets on the function's behalf, so the execution role must allow creating and managing them, and AWS offers a managed policy for this.

questions.prompt: A bank's Lambda function runs in private subnets and must send messages to SQS, a managed queue service. Security rules say this traffic must never travel over the public internet. Which option meets the rule?
choices: Add a NAT gateway so the private subnets can make outbound calls to the queue
Remove the VPC settings so the function uses Lambda's default network
Add a VPC endpoint for SQS so the function reaches the queue through a private doorway
Move the function to a public subnet so it can reach the queue's public endpoint
questions.why: A VPC endpoint gives private subnets a private path to an AWS service that keeps traffic off the internet, while a NAT gateway works by sending traffic out to the internet.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would let a Lambda function query a database in a private subnet, and name the tradeoff or limit that comes with attaching the function to the VPC.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd attach the function to the VPC by giving it private subnets in at least two Availability Zones and a security group. Lambda places network interfaces in those subnets, so the function needs an execution role that can create them. Then I'd edit the database's security group to allow its port from the Lambda security group, rather than from a broad address range. The tradeoff is that the function now lives by the VPC's routing. It loses its default internet access, so calls to public endpoints like SQS or a third-party API will just time out. To fix that I'd add a VPC endpoint for AWS services, which keeps traffic private, or a NAT gateway for general internet access, which costs money. Putting the function in a public subnet doesn't help, because Lambda interfaces never get public IPs.
rubricPoints: Attaching the function requires choosing subnets and a security group, ideally across multiple Availability Zones.
Lambda reaches the VPC through network interfaces, and the execution role must allow creating them.
The private resource's security group must allow traffic from the function's security group.
Once in the VPC, the function loses default internet access and outbound calls time out without a route.
A NAT gateway or VPC endpoints restore access to the internet or AWS services.
A public subnet does not give Lambda internet access because its interfaces get no public IP.

suggested.rationale: Tracing a packet from a function's subnet through security groups, routes, NAT, or an endpoint is exactly the reasoning a virtual network path tracer would make the learner practise.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is a piece of your code that a cloud service runs only when something asks for it, with no server for you to manage. Configuring it means choosing its settings. These include how much memory it gets, how long it may run, and how many copies may run at once. They also include which language runs it, where execution starts, what shared code it carries, and what wakes it up. Finally, you choose where its results go afterward. Think of hiring temporary workers. You decide the size of each desk, the length of each shift, the maximum headcount, the toolkit everyone shares, and who hands them work.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function handles 50 requests every second, and each request takes 2 seconds to finish. Roughly how many copies of the function must be running at the same moment to keep up?
lessons.teach:
AWS Lambda is a managed function service. Each copy runs in an execution environment, a small isolated sandbox. These are the settings you control.

Memory runs from 128 MB to 10,240 MB. CPU power rises in proportion, so more memory also means faster compute. Timeout is the longest one invocation (a single run) may last. The default is 3 seconds and the maximum is 900 seconds (15 minutes). When the limit is hit, the run is stopped. The runtime is the language environment, such as Python or Node.js. The handler is the named function in your code where execution starts, written as file.function.

Concurrency is how many invocations run at the same moment. A Region account limit, often 1,000 by default, is shared by all your functions. Reserved concurrency sets aside a slice for one function and also caps it there. Provisioned concurrency keeps environments warm so they skip startup delay.

A layer is a separate package of shared libraries that many functions can attach. An extension is a helper process that runs beside your code in the same environment, such as a monitoring agent. A trigger is the event source that invokes the function, such as an HTTP API, a file upload, or a queue. A destination is where Lambda sends a record of success or failure after an asynchronous (fire-and-forget) invocation. Targets include a queue, a notification topic, an event bus, or another function.

Worked example: requests arrive at 50 per second and each takes 2 seconds. Concurrency is roughly rate times duration, so 50 × 2 = 100 environments busy at once. If you set reserved concurrency to 60, the remaining 40 requests per second are throttled (refused with a too-many-requests error). Synchronous callers see failures.

A common mistake is cutting memory to save money. Less memory means less CPU, so each run takes longer. You are billed for memory multiplied by duration, so the bill can rise. Longer runs also raise concurrency and can push past the timeout.

In a running system, a wrong timeout or concurrency cap causes dropped requests, throttling, or half-finished work that gets retried.

questions.prompt:
A print shop runs an image-resizing Lambda function at 512 MB of memory. Each run takes 1.0 second, and about 20 runs arrive per second. To save money, the team cuts memory to 256 MB. Because less memory also means less CPU, each run now takes 2.5 seconds. Lambda bills memory multiplied by duration (counted here in MB-seconds).

Step 1: Cost per run before the change = 512 MB × 1.0 s = 512 MB-seconds.
Step 2: Cost per run after the change = ?
Step 3: Concurrency before = 20 per second × 1.0 s = 20 environments. Concurrency after = 20 per second × 2.5 s = 50 environments.
Conclusion: The change raised both the bill and the number of environments busy at once.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: 256 MB × 2.5 s = 640 MB-seconds, which is more than the 512 before
256 MB ÷ 2.5 s = 102.4 MB-seconds, so the cost per run drops sharply
512 MB × 2.5 s = 1,280 MB-seconds, so the cost per run more than doubles
256 MB × 1.0 s = 256 MB-seconds, so the cost per run is cut in half
questions.why: The bill uses the new memory (256 MB) multiplied by the new, longer duration (2.5 s), which gives 640 MB-seconds, more than the original 512.

questions.prompt: A developer at a bike-rental company writes the starting function for a Lambda function. The function is named process_rental and it sits in a file named rentals.py. What should the handler setting be?
choices: process_rental.rentals
rentals.process_rental
rentals.py
process_rental
questions.why: The handler names where execution starts in the form file.function, so the file rentals followed by the function process_rental gives rentals.process_rental.

questions.prompt: A library's Lambda function builds a monthly report, and each run normally needs about 40 seconds. The team never changed the timeout setting from its default. What happens when the function runs?
choices: Lambda gives it more memory so it can finish within the limit
It finishes normally, because Lambda allows up to 15 minutes by default
It is stopped at 3 seconds, leaving half-finished work that may be retried
Lambda pauses it at 3 seconds and resumes it on the next invocation
questions.why: The default timeout is 3 seconds, and when the limit is hit the run is stopped, so the report is left unfinished and may be retried.

questions.prompt: A travel agency's AWS account has a Region concurrency limit of 1,000. The team sets reserved concurrency of 250 on its booking function. Which statement is true?
choices: Booking keeps 250 environments warm so they skip startup delay
Other functions can still use all 1,000 when booking is idle
Booking can run at most 250 at once; other functions share the other 750
Booking is guaranteed 250 and can also borrow up to the full 1,000
questions.why: Reserved concurrency both sets aside a slice of the shared account limit for one function and caps that function there, so booking stops at 250 and the remaining 750 is shared by everything else.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how memory, timeout, and concurrency interact for a Lambda function, and describe one tradeoff you face when setting reserved concurrency.
lessons.modelAnswer: Memory is also our CPU dial. More memory makes each run faster, and we pay for memory multiplied by duration, so raising it can cost the same or less. Timeout is a hard stop on one run. Too short and real work gets killed halfway; too long and a hung call holds a slot and racks up cost. Concurrency is roughly request rate times duration. At 50 requests a second and 2 seconds each, we need about 100 environments at once. Slow code therefore eats concurrency, and memory and timeout feed straight into it. Reserved concurrency guarantees this function a share of the account limit so others can't starve it. The tradeoff is that it is also a ceiling. Set it too low and a traffic surge gets throttled. Set it too high and it starves other functions in the account.
rubricPoints: Memory also scales CPU, and cost is memory multiplied by duration.
Timeout stops a run at a hard limit, with a default of 3 seconds and a maximum of 15 minutes.
Concurrency is roughly request rate multiplied by duration, drawn from a shared account limit.
Reserved concurrency both guarantees capacity and caps it, so setting it too low causes throttling.
Handler, runtime, layers, extensions, triggers, and destinations are each named with their correct role.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a function that throttles during a traffic surge makes the learner reason directly about concurrency limits, duration, and memory settings.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is a small piece of code that a cloud service runs for you whenever an event arrives. Environment variables are named settings, such as TABLE_NAME=orders-dev, that you attach to the function from outside the code. The code reads them when it starts. Parameters are settings kept in a separate central store and fetched by the code, which suits shared or secret values. Think of a rental car. The car (your code) is the same for every driver, but the seat and mirror positions (the settings) are adjusted per driver. You never rebuild the car to change them.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function writes to a database table called orders-dev in testing and orders-prod in production. Where would you keep that table name so that the exact same code works in both places without editing it?
lessons.teach:
An environment variable in AWS Lambda (a managed service that runs your function on demand) is a key-value pair stored in the function's configuration. The runtime hands it to your code at start-up, for example through process.env in Node.js or os.environ in Python. All the variables on one function together are limited to about 4 KB. Lambda also sets its own reserved variables, such as AWS_REGION, and you cannot override those.

This works because configuration lives apart from code. You deploy one code package and give each stage different values. A published version is a frozen, numbered snapshot of the code plus its configuration. Once you publish it, its environment variables cannot change. An alias, a named pointer such as prod, chooses which version runs.

Variables are encrypted at rest with AWS KMS, the managed key service, using a default key or a customer managed key you control. Anyone who can view the function's configuration can still see the values in plain text. For secrets and shared settings, use a parameter store instead. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store holds String, StringList and SecureString (encrypted) values. AWS Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation, which means it replaces the secret on a schedule. Your function's IAM role, the identity it runs as, needs permission to read them.

Worked example. First, set TABLE_NAME=orders-prod and DB_SECRET_NAME=prod/db on the function. Second, outside the handler, which is the entry function called once per event, the code reads TABLE_NAME and fetches the secret named in DB_SECRET_NAME. Third, it caches both in memory. Fourth, every invocation reuses the cached values until Lambda retires that execution environment, the reused container running your code.

A common mistake is fetching the parameter inside the handler on every call. Under load, this adds latency to each request and can hit the store's request-rate limits. The calls then get throttled, and invocations fail even though your code is correct. A second common mistake is pasting a plain password into an environment variable, where it is visible to anyone who can view the function.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental company runs a Lambda function that writes ride records to a queue and calls a payment partner's API. A developer wires it up like this. Step 1: on the function's configuration, set RIDES_QUEUE_URL to the staging queue's address and PAYMENT_KEY_PARAM=/bikes/staging/payment-key, the name of a SecureString in Parameter Store. Step 2: give the function's IAM role permission to read that one parameter. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: each invocation that lands in the same execution environment reuses the stored queue address and key without calling Parameter Store again. Which choice is the missing Step 3?
choices: Outside the handler, read RIDES_QUEUE_URL, fetch the parameter named in PAYMENT_KEY_PARAM once, and keep both values in memory.
Publish a version, then change PAYMENT_KEY_PARAM on that published version whenever the partner issues a new key.
Inside the handler, read RIDES_QUEUE_URL and fetch the parameter named in PAYMENT_KEY_PARAM at the start of every call, so each request gets the newest key.
Copy the decrypted payment key into a new environment variable named PAYMENT_KEY so the code never needs to call Parameter Store.
questions.why: Code outside the handler runs once when the execution environment starts, so fetching and caching there is exactly what lets Step 4 reuse the values without another call to the store.

questions.prompt: A media team has published version 12 of its thumbnail Lambda function with LOG_LEVEL=warn, and the alias live points at version 12. They now want LOG_LEVEL=debug on the code that live runs. What must they do?
choices: Change LOG_LEVEL in the function's unpublished configuration, publish a new version, and point the live alias at that new version.
Override AWS_REGION to force Lambda to reload version 12 with the new value.
Edit LOG_LEVEL directly on version 12; the alias picks up the change immediately.
Set LOG_LEVEL on the live alias itself, because aliases store their own environment variables.
questions.why: A published version is a frozen snapshot whose environment variables cannot change, so the new value needs a new version, and the alias is the pointer that chooses which version runs.

questions.prompt: During a flash sale, a ticketing company's Lambda function handles about 3,000 requests per second. Its handler fetches a discount-rate parameter from Parameter Store at the start of every call. Requests slow down, then many invocations fail with throttling errors, although the code logic has no bugs. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The environment variables exceed about 4 KB; split them across two functions.
The function's IAM role lacks permission to read the parameter; add read permission.
The parameter is a String instead of a SecureString; change its type to SecureString.
Every call is hitting the store's request-rate limits; fetch the parameter once outside the handler and cache it in memory.
questions.why: Fetching inside the handler on every call adds latency and can exceed the parameter store's request-rate limits, so calls get throttled and invocations fail even though the code is correct.

questions.prompt: A clinic's scheduling function needs a database password that security policy says must be replaced automatically every 30 days. Where should the function get the password?
choices: From a Parameter Store String parameter, since every Parameter Store value is encrypted and rotated automatically.
From a reserved Lambda variable, since Lambda manages and refreshes those values itself.
From an environment variable encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, since that encryption keeps it hidden from anyone who views the function.
From AWS Secrets Manager, which can rotate the secret on a schedule, with the function's IAM role allowed to read it.
questions.why: Secrets Manager adds automatic rotation; environment variables stay readable in plain text to anyone who can view the configuration, String parameters are not encrypted, and reserved variables are set by Lambda and cannot be overridden.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would put a value in a Lambda environment variable and when you would fetch it from Parameter Store or Secrets Manager, and name one tradeoff of each approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Environment variables are key-value settings stored on the function itself, so the same code can run in dev and prod with different values like a table name or a log level. They are free, instant to read, and become frozen when you publish a version. The tradeoff is that anyone who can view the function's configuration sees them, they are capped at about 4 KB in total, and changing one means updating the function. For secrets or values shared across many functions, I would use Parameter Store, which offers SecureString, or Secrets Manager, which adds rotation. I would only keep the parameter's name in an environment variable. The tradeoff there is an extra network call and IAM permissions to grant. So I fetch the value once outside the handler and cache it. Fetching on every invocation adds latency and can get throttled under load.
rubricPoints: Environment variables are key-value settings on the function configuration, read by code at start-up.
They let one code package run in different stages with different values.
Published versions freeze environment variables, and aliases choose which version runs.
Secrets belong in Parameter Store SecureString or Secrets Manager, not plain environment variables.
Fetch parameters outside the handler and cache them to avoid latency and throttling.
The function's IAM role needs permission to read parameters and decrypt them.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner wire a secret into a deployment through configuration without exposing it, which is the core judgement behind choosing environment variables versus a secure parameter.

lessons.plain: When a cloud function is handed a job and nobody waits for the answer, the job can fail with no one noticing. AWS Lambda, a service that runs your code when an event arrives, handles this with two safety nets. A dead-letter queue is a holding area where failed events are parked so a person or program can inspect and replay them later. A destination is a forwarding address that receives a record of what happened, on success or on failure. Think of a parcel service: undeliverable parcels go to a lost-and-found shelf, and delivery receipts can be mailed back to the sender.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function is triggered by file uploads and nobody waits for its reply. It crashes on one particular file every time. Without any extra setup, what do you think eventually happens to that upload event, and how would you find out?
lessons.teach:
Lambda destinations and dead-letter queues apply mainly to asynchronous invocation. That means the caller hands Lambda an event and leaves without waiting for a result. Lambda places the event in its own internal queue and runs your function from there. If the function throws an error, Lambda retries it, by default up to two more times. You can configure retries from zero to two, and you can set a maximum event age of up to six hours. After that, the event is discarded unless you have planned where it goes.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is an Amazon SQS queue (a managed message queue) or an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish-and-notify service). Lambda sends the original event there once the retries are used up. It only catches failures, and it keeps little more than the payload.

A destination is a target you name for the outcome of an asynchronous invocation. You can set an on-success target, an on-failure target, or both. Targets can be SQS, SNS, another Lambda function, or Amazon EventBridge (a managed event bus). A destination receives an invocation record: the original event plus context such as the error message and how many attempts were made. Because of that richer record, destinations are generally preferred over a DLQ.

Worked example: a file upload asynchronously invokes a function, and the function crashes on a malformed file. On attempt 1 it fails. Lambda waits, then attempt 2 fails. Lambda waits longer, then attempt 3 fails. Retries are now exhausted, so Lambda writes an invocation record to the on-failure SQS queue. An engineer reads the error from that queue, fixes the code, and replays the event.

A common mistake is putting a function-level DLQ on a function triggered by an SQS queue and expecting it to catch failures. That kind of trigger is polled by an event source mapping, not invoked asynchronously. For SQS triggers, failures are handled by a redrive policy on the source queue itself. For streams, you set an on-failure destination on the mapping instead. Another frequent miss is forgetting to give the function's execution role permission to send to the target. In a running system, either mistake means failed events vanish silently and no one can replay them.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic runs a reminder function. A scheduler invokes it asynchronously each evening with an event listing tomorrow's appointments. The team set retry attempts to 1, not the default of 2, and named an Amazon SNS topic (a managed publish-and-notify service) as the on-failure destination. Tonight the text-message provider is down. Step 1: attempt 1 times out and fails. Step 2: Lambda waits, runs attempt 2, and it fails again. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the on-call engineer gets a notification showing the error message and the attempt count, waits for the provider to recover, and replays the event. What is Step 3?
choices: Lambda discards the event at once, because on-failure destinations are only used when retries are set to zero.
Lambda waits longer and runs a third attempt, because asynchronous invocations always get two retries no matter what is configured.
Lambda sends only the raw appointment payload to the SNS topic, with no error details, the same way a dead-letter queue would.
With its single retry used up, Lambda sends an invocation record (the original event plus the error message and attempt count) to the SNS topic.
questions.why: The team allowed one retry, so after the second failed attempt the retries are exhausted, and Lambda sends the full invocation record, including error and attempt count, to the on-failure destination.

questions.prompt: A team is choosing between a dead-letter queue (DLQ) and an on-failure destination for an asynchronously invoked Lambda function. Which statement correctly describes a key difference between them?
choices: A DLQ can target another Lambda function or Amazon EventBridge, while a destination can only target Amazon SQS.
A destination lets Lambda keep retrying forever, while a DLQ caps the maximum event age at six hours.
A destination receives an invocation record with the original event plus context such as the error message and attempt count, while a DLQ keeps little more than the payload.
A DLQ can capture both successful and failed invocations, while a destination can only capture failures.
questions.why: Destinations get the richer invocation record and can cover success and failure, while a DLQ only catches failures and holds little beyond the payload, which is why destinations are generally preferred.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's label-printing function is triggered by an Amazon SQS queue (a managed message queue) through an event source mapping, which polls the queue. The team attached a function-level dead-letter queue to the function, but messages that keep failing never show up there. What should they do so repeatedly failing messages are kept for replay?
choices: Set the maximum event age to six hours so the function-level DLQ starts receiving the failed messages.
Configure a redrive policy on the source SQS queue, since the function is polled rather than invoked asynchronously.
Switch the function-level DLQ from an SQS queue to an SNS topic, because SQS-triggered functions can only use SNS.
Raise the function's retry attempts from 2 to 5 so the function-level DLQ has more time to catch the failure.
questions.why: An SQS trigger is polled by an event source mapping, not invoked asynchronously, so the function-level DLQ never applies; failures are handled by a redrive policy on the source queue.

questions.prompt: A payroll team invokes a Lambda function asynchronously and sets an Amazon EventBridge event bus (a managed event bus) as its on-failure destination. During testing, the function fails every attempt, yet no records ever arrive on the event bus. Which cause, named in common mistakes, most likely explains this?
choices: EventBridge cannot be used as an on-failure destination, only as an on-success destination.
On-failure destinations only receive records after the maximum event age of six hours has passed.
The function's execution role lacks permission to send events to the EventBridge target.
Asynchronous invocations never use destinations; only stream-based mappings support them.
questions.why: If the execution role is not allowed to send to the target, Lambda cannot deliver the invocation record, so failed events vanish silently and cannot be replayed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a Lambda dead-letter queue and an on-failure destination, when each one actually applies, and one limit or tradeoff they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: Both catch events that keep failing after Lambda's built-in retries, but only for asynchronous invocations, where the caller does not wait. With synchronous calls, the caller gets the error back and must handle it. A dead-letter queue is an SQS queue or SNS topic. It receives the original event once retries run out, and it handles failures only. A destination can fire on success or on failure. It can point at SQS, SNS, another function, or EventBridge, and it sends a richer record that includes the error and the attempt count. That makes destinations easier to debug and replay. The big limit is that neither function-level option covers SQS-triggered functions, because those are polled through an event source mapping. There, you rely on the source queue's own redrive policy. The function's role also needs permission to write to the target, or the failures are simply lost.
rubricPoints: States that DLQs and destinations apply to asynchronous invocations after Lambda's retries are exhausted.
Distinguishes a DLQ, which catches failures only and holds the payload, from destinations, which cover success or failure and send a richer record.
Names valid targets, such as SQS and SNS for a DLQ, plus Lambda and EventBridge for destinations.
Notes that SQS-triggered functions use the source queue's redrive policy instead of a function DLQ.
Mentions that missing configuration or permissions leads to silently lost events.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner deal with events that keep failing and piling up, which is exactly the problem dead-letter queues and failure destinations exist to contain.

lessons.plain: Testing a Lambda function means feeding it a realistic event and checking that it does the right thing, both on your own machine and once it runs inside AWS. A Lambda function is a piece of code that AWS runs for you whenever an event arrives, such as a message landing on a queue. Because the function only wakes up when an event arrives, you test it by handing it a sample event. Think of rehearsing a play: first you rehearse in your living room with props, then you do a dress rehearsal on the real stage, because some problems only show up there.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function works perfectly when you run it on your laptop with fake versions of the database. After deploying, it fails on every message. Before reading on, guess one thing that could be different about the real environment that your laptop test could never have caught.
lessons.teach:
Testing Lambda code means invoking the handler with a realistic event and checking its output and side effects. The handler is the function Lambda calls; it receives an event (a JSON document describing what happened) and a context object (details about the running invocation, such as time left). Since the event is the input, the quality of your test depends on how realistic that event is.

There are two layers. Local invocation runs the function on your machine. AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model, a tool for defining and running serverless apps) can generate sample events shaped exactly like a real service would send, and run your handler inside a container that mimics the Lambda runtime. This is fast and cheap. Integration testing then deploys the function to a separate test environment and invokes it against real AWS services, such as a real queue and a real DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database). The Lambda console also lets you save named test events and invoke the deployed function directly.

Worked example: a function reads orders from an SQS queue (a managed message queue) and writes each to DynamoDB. Step one, generate a sample SQS event; note each record's body arrives as a string, so the handler must parse it. Step two, invoke locally with that event and confirm it parses and builds the right item. Step three, deploy to a test stack, send a real message to the test queue, then read the table and assert the item exists. Step four, check the function's logs for errors.

Common mistake: hand-writing the event and testing only against mocks (fake stand-ins for services). Mocks never check permissions, so a missing IAM permission (the rule allowing the function to write to the table) passes every local test. In a running system the function then fails with an access-denied error on every message, and the queue retries them repeatedly. Only a test against real services in a test environment catches that class of problem.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup has a Lambda function that runs when a user uploads an image to an S3 bucket (S3 is a managed file-storage service). The function reads the event, works out the image's file name and size, and writes a record to a DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database) called PhotoIndex. Their testing plan so far: Step 1, use AWS SAM (a tool for defining and running serverless apps) to generate a sample S3 upload event, so the event has exactly the shape the real service sends. Step 2, invoke the handler locally inside SAM's Lambda-like container with that event, and confirm it pulls out the file name and builds the right record. Step 3 is missing. Step 4, check the function's logs in the test environment for errors. Which choice is the best Step 3?
choices: Rerun the local test with a mock (a fake stand-in) of DynamoDB that always reports a successful write, to confirm the save logic works.
Deploy the function to production, upload a real image to the live bucket, and watch whether users report missing photos.
Deploy the function to a separate test stack, upload a real image to the test bucket, then read the PhotoIndex test table and assert the new record exists.
Hand-write a smaller event with only the file name in it and invoke the handler locally again to check the record is still built.
questions.why: Only an integration test against real services in a separate test environment, checking the actual table afterward, proves the function can really write the record, including that it has the needed permission.

questions.prompt: When Lambda calls a function's handler, it passes two inputs. Which statement correctly describes them?
choices: The event is a JSON document describing what happened, and the context object gives details about the running invocation, such as time left.
The event and the context object are both JSON copies of the same incoming message, one parsed and one left as a string.
The event is a sample file generated by SAM, and the context object is a list of saved test events from the Lambda console.
The event is the function's IAM permissions, and the context object is the JSON message the function must process.
questions.why: The event is the input describing what happened, while the context object describes the current invocation itself, such as how much time remains.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Lambda function must write bookings to a DynamoDB table. A developer worries the function might be missing the IAM permission (the rule allowing it to write to the table). Which test would actually catch that problem before release?
choices: Invoking the handler locally with a SAM-generated event while DynamoDB is replaced by a mock.
Checking that the handler parses the event correctly and builds the right item in memory.
Deploying to a separate test environment and invoking the function against the real test table, then checking the write succeeded.
Hand-writing a detailed event that includes every booking field and running unit tests on the handler.
questions.why: Mocks never check permissions, so only invoking the deployed function against a real table in a test environment reveals a missing IAM permission.

questions.prompt: A payroll team's Lambda function reads messages from an SQS queue (a managed message queue) and saves each to DynamoDB. Every local test, run against mocks, passed. After deployment, every message fails with an access-denied error and the same messages keep coming back to the function. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The SAM-generated sample event had the wrong shape, so the handler cannot parse any real message body.
The Lambda console's saved test events were deleted, so the deployed function no longer knows how to process messages.
The function lacks the IAM permission to write to the table; mocks never check permissions, so local tests could not catch it.
The function's context object reported too little time left, so DynamoDB refused each write as access-denied.
questions.why: An access-denied error on every message after mock-only testing points to a missing IAM permission, and the queue keeps retrying the failed messages.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would test a Lambda function that reads from a queue and writes to DynamoDB, and name one limit of testing it only locally.
lessons.modelAnswer: I test it in two layers. First, locally: I use SAM to generate a sample SQS event so the shape is realistic, including the fact that the message body is a string I must parse. I invoke the handler with that event and check it builds the right item. That loop is fast and free. Second, I deploy to a separate test stack and run an integration test: put a real message on the test queue, then read the real table and confirm the item landed, and check the logs. The limit of local-only testing is that mocks and local runs don't exercise real permissions, real service limits or real network paths. A missing IAM permission passes locally and then fails on every message in production. The tradeoff is that real-service tests are slower and cost a little, so I keep them few and focused.
rubricPoints: Tests invoke the handler with an event, and the event should be realistic, ideally generated rather than hand-written.
Local invocation with a tool like SAM gives a fast, cheap feedback loop.
Integration tests run the deployed function against real services in a separate test environment and check side effects.
Local tests with mocks cannot catch permission, configuration or real-service problems.
Real-service tests are slower and cost money, so they are kept focused.

suggested.rationale: No current mission has the learner invoke Lambda with generated events, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario about which test layer would catch which failure builds the judgment the objective needs.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is a small piece of your code that a cloud provider runs only when something asks for it, with no server for you to manage. On its own it does nothing useful. It becomes useful when it is wired to other services: something must start it, and it usually needs to read or write somewhere else, such as a database or a queue. Think of a light switch wired into a house. The switch matters only because of what triggers it and what it powers. Integrating Lambda means choosing how it gets started and granting it permission to reach what it touches.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function runs whenever a file lands in a storage bucket, and it saves a record into a database table. How many separate permissions do you think must be set up for this to work, and which way does each one point?
lessons.teach:
Integrating Lambda with other AWS services means two jobs. The first is choosing how the function gets invoked, meaning started. The second is letting the function call other services once it is running.

There are three invocation models. In synchronous invocation, the caller waits for the answer. An example is API Gateway, a managed HTTP front door, which passes the result straight back to a user. In asynchronous invocation, the caller hands over the event and leaves. Lambda queues it internally and retries on failure. Amazon S3 (object storage), SNS (a managed publish-and-subscribe service) and EventBridge (a managed event bus) work this way. With an event source mapping, Lambda itself runs a poller, a background reader that pulls batches of records from SQS (a managed queue), Kinesis (a managed stream) or DynamoDB Streams (the table's change log), then calls your function with each batch.

Permissions point two ways. A resource-based policy is a rule attached to the function. It says who may invoke it, for example "the S3 service, for this bucket". An execution role is an identity the function takes on while it runs. Its policy says what the function may call, for example "PutItem on this DynamoDB table". Event source mappings are different. Because Lambda does the reading, the execution role needs permission to read the queue or stream.

Worked example. A user uploads photo.jpg. S3 checks the function's resource policy, finds it allowed, and invokes the function asynchronously. The function runs under its execution role and calls DynamoDB PutItem. DynamoDB checks the role, allows the write, and the record is saved. If that write throws an error, Lambda retries the asynchronous event.

A common mistake is granting the trigger but forgetting the execution role permission. The function starts fine and then fails with an access-denied error on every call. A related trap applies to SQS. If the queue's visibility timeout is shorter than the function's timeout, a message can reappear while it is still being processed. Another copy of the function then handles it a second time, which causes duplicate work in a running system.

questions.prompt: A logistics company publishes a message to an SNS topic named order-events whenever a customer pays. A Lambda function named route-order is subscribed, and it must add a task to an SQS queue named shipping-tasks. Trace it. Step 1: SNS publishes the payment message to the topic. Step 2: SNS checks route-order's resource-based policy, sees that the SNS service may invoke it for this topic, and invokes the function asynchronously. Step 3: route-order runs under its execution role and calls SendMessage on shipping-tasks. Step 4: ??? Step 5: The task is stored in the queue. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Lambda's poller reads the new message from shipping-tasks and calls route-order again with it as a batch.
SNS checks its own topic permissions to confirm that route-order may write messages into shipping-tasks.
SQS checks route-order's execution role, finds SendMessage allowed on shipping-tasks, and accepts the message.
SQS checks route-order's resource-based policy to confirm that the function is allowed to send to shipping-tasks.
questions.why: Once the function is running, any service it calls checks the execution role, the identity the function takes on, to decide whether the call is allowed.

questions.prompt: A team connects an SQS queue named invoice-jobs to a Lambda function through an event source mapping, so Lambda pulls batches of messages and hands them to the function. Which permission setup lets Lambda read from invoice-jobs?
choices: Give the function's execution role permission to receive and delete messages from invoice-jobs.
Add a resource-based policy to the function that lets the SQS service invoke it for invoice-jobs.
Add a resource-based policy to the function that lets any AWS account read from invoice-jobs.
No permission is needed, because Lambda can always read any queue in the same account.
questions.why: With an event source mapping, Lambda itself does the reading, so the function's execution role must be allowed to read the queue.

questions.prompt: A ticketing service uses an SQS queue with a visibility timeout of 20 seconds. Its Lambda function, triggered from that queue, has a timeout of 60 seconds and sometimes runs for about 45 seconds. What is the most likely problem in the running system?
choices: Lambda stops the function at 20 seconds, so long runs always end with a timeout error.
The message reappears during processing, another copy of the function handles it, and work is duplicated.
SQS deletes the message after 20 seconds, so a slow run loses the ticket entirely.
The function fails with an access-denied error each time it runs longer than 20 seconds.
questions.why: When the visibility timeout is shorter than the function's run time, the message becomes visible again mid-processing and a second invocation processes it too.

questions.prompt: A weather startup wants a Lambda function to process sensor readings arriving in a Kinesis stream. Which description matches how the function gets invoked?
choices: Kinesis invokes the function synchronously and waits for each reading's answer before sending the next.
Kinesis hands each reading to Lambda and leaves, and Lambda queues it internally like an S3 upload.
The function must run continuously and call Kinesis itself in a loop to fetch new readings.
Lambda runs a poller that pulls batches of records from the stream and calls the function with each batch.
questions.why: Kinesis is a source used through an event source mapping, where Lambda's own poller reads batches of records and passes them to the function.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Lambda function gets wired to the services around it: the ways it can be started, and the two kinds of permission involved. Name one limit or tradeoff of choosing an asynchronous or polled trigger instead of a synchronous one.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Lambda function needs two things wired up: what starts it and what it is allowed to touch. It can be started synchronously, as when API Gateway waits for a reply. It can be started asynchronously, as when S3, SNS or EventBridge hand off an event and leave while Lambda retries on failure. Or it can be started by an event source mapping, where Lambda polls SQS, Kinesis or DynamoDB Streams and passes in batches. Inbound permission lives in the function's resource-based policy, which says who may invoke it. Outbound permission lives in the execution role, which says what the function may call, and for polled sources that includes reading the queue. The tradeoff with asynchronous or polled triggers is that the caller never sees the result directly. Retries can deliver the same event twice, so the handler must tolerate duplicates. Failures also show up later rather than immediately.
rubricPoints: Names synchronous, asynchronous, and event source mapping (polling) invocation with an example of each.
Explains the resource-based policy controls who may invoke the function.
Explains the execution role controls what the function may call, including reading a polled source.
Identifies a tradeoff such as no direct result to the caller or duplicate delivery from retries.
Mentions a concrete failure such as access denied or SQS visibility timeout shorter than function timeout.

suggested.rationale: Debugging a queue-triggered function makes the learner work directly with how Lambda polls a queue, retries batches, and interacts with the services wired to it.

lessons.plain: Tuning a Lambda function means adjusting how it is set up so it answers faster without wasting money.
