AWS Lambda is a service that runs your code only when an event arrives, and you pay for the time it runs. The main dial is memory: turning it up also gives the function more processing power. Other levers are doing slow setup work once instead of on every call, and keeping some copies warm and ready. Think of a food truck. A bigger grill costs more per hour but cooks faster, so a busy lunch can cost the same or less overall.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function runs for 2 seconds at its smallest memory setting. If you quadruple the memory and it now finishes in under half a second, do you think the bill per call goes up, goes down, or stays the same? Why?
lessons.teach:
Lambda performance tuning means choosing settings and code structure so each invocation (one run of the function) finishes quickly at a sensible cost. There are three main levers.

The first lever is memory. You set memory from 128 MB up to about 10 GB, and Lambda gives you CPU power in proportion. A CPU-heavy or network-heavy function at low memory is starved of processing power, not short of RAM. Billing is measured in GB-seconds, which is memory in gigabytes multiplied by run time in seconds. So more memory does not always cost more.

Here is a worked example. At 128 MB (0.125 GB) a function takes 2.0 seconds, so 0.125 × 2.0 = 0.25 GB-seconds. At 512 MB (0.5 GB) it takes 0.45 seconds, so 0.5 × 0.45 = 0.225 GB-seconds. It is four times faster and slightly cheaper. Measure several sizes and pick the point where extra memory stops shortening the run. Open-source tools such as Lambda Power Tuning automate this test.

The second lever is the cold start. A cold start is the extra delay when Lambda must create a fresh execution environment, meaning it loads your code, starts the runtime, and runs your setup. Code outside the handler (the entry function Lambda calls per event) runs once per environment, and warm environments reuse its results. Smaller deployment packages and fewer imported libraries shorten cold starts. Provisioned concurrency keeps a chosen number of environments already initialized, for a fee. SnapStart, available for some runtimes, resumes from a saved snapshot instead of initializing from scratch.

The third lever is reuse. A common mistake is creating SDK clients or database connections inside the handler. Every call then pays the connection setup again. Create them once, outside the handler.

In a running system, an untuned function runs long, holds concurrency slots longer, and gets throttled sooner. It can also hit its timeout, which triggers retries and possibly duplicate work.

questions.prompt:
A bakery chain runs a Lambda function that resizes product photos. The team measures it at two memory sizes. Billing is in GB-seconds (memory in gigabytes multiplied by run time in seconds).

Step 1: At 256 MB (0.25 GB) the function takes 3.0 seconds, so 0.25 × 3.0 = 0.75 GB-seconds.
Step 2: At 1024 MB (1 GB) the function takes 0.6 seconds.
Step 3: [missing]
Step 4: The team keeps testing a few larger sizes and stops where extra memory no longer shortens the run.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Memory went up four times, so cost goes up four times: 4 × 0.75 = 3.0 GB-seconds.
1 × 0.6 = 0.6 GB-seconds, which is less than 0.75, so 1024 MB is both five times faster and cheaper.
1 × 0.6 = 0.6 GB-seconds, which is more than 0.75, so the faster size costs extra.
1024 × 0.6 = 614.4 GB-seconds, so the larger size costs far more and should be rejected.
questions.why: GB-seconds use memory in gigabytes (1 GB) times run time (0.6 s), giving 0.6, which is lower than 0.75, so the bigger setting finishes faster and costs less.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company notices that the first request after a quiet period takes about two seconds longer than later requests, even though the code does the same work each time. What is the best explanation?
choices: A cold start: Lambda had to create a fresh execution environment, loading the code, starting the runtime, and running setup before handling the event.
Billing in GB-seconds adds delay to the first invocation of every hour.
The function was throttled because its timeout was set too high.
The handler always runs slower the first time because it has less memory than later invocations.
questions.why: A cold start is the extra delay of building a new execution environment; later requests reuse the warm environment and skip that setup.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm's Lambda function opens a new database connection and creates a new SDK client inside the handler on every event. Run times are higher than expected. Which change addresses this most directly?
choices: Create the client and connection in code outside the handler, so each warm environment sets them up once and reuses them.
Lower the memory so each invocation is cheaper per second.
Turn on provisioned concurrency so the handler stops creating connections.
Raise the timeout so the connection setup has more time to finish.
questions.why: Code outside the handler runs once per environment and warm environments reuse the result, so connection setup is no longer paid on every call.

questions.prompt: A clinic's report-generation Lambda function does heavy number crunching at 128 MB. It sometimes hits its timeout, and the resulting retries create duplicate reports. Which tuning step fits the problem best?
choices: Keep 128 MB, because more memory always costs more money.
Add provisioned concurrency, because it makes each invocation compute faster.
Move the per-report calculations outside the handler so they run only once per environment.
Raise the memory, since CPU power scales with memory, then measure run time at several sizes to find where extra memory stops helping.
questions.why: A CPU-heavy function at low memory is starved of processing power, so more memory gives more CPU and shorter runs, often at similar or lower GB-second cost, which avoids timeouts and the retries they trigger.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make a slow Lambda function faster, and name one tradeoff or limit of the approach you pick.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd measure the function at several memory sizes, because Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory. A slow function at 128 MB is often starved for CPU. Cost is memory times duration, so a bigger size that finishes much faster can cost the same or less. I'd pick the size where adding memory stops cutting run time. Past that point you just pay more for nothing. Next I'd move SDK clients and database connections outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them. I'd also trim the package and its imports to shorten cold starts. If users still feel cold-start delay on a latency-sensitive path, I'd consider provisioned concurrency. Its tradeoff is that you pay for those warm environments even when idle, and it only covers the number you provision. It doesn't fix slow code itself.
rubricPoints: Memory setting also scales CPU, so raising it can speed up compute-bound work.
Cost is memory times duration, so faster at higher memory can be equal or cheaper.
Initialize clients and connections outside the handler so warm invocations reuse them.
Cold starts come from creating new environments and shrink with smaller packages, provisioned concurrency, or SnapStart.
Names a real tradeoff, such as provisioned concurrency costing money while idle or diminishing returns from more memory.

suggested.rationale: Tuning is mostly reasoning through tradeoffs like memory against cost and cold starts against provisioned spend, so working exam-style scenarios teaches it best, and no current mission isolates it.

lessons.plain: Processing data in near real time with Lambda means running a small piece of code within seconds of new data arriving, instead of waiting for a nightly batch job. Lambda is AWS's managed function service: you supply the code, and AWS runs it whenever something triggers it. Records arrive from a stream, a queue, or a delivery service. Lambda picks them up in small groups, your code cleans or reshapes each record, and the result goes on to storage or another service. Think of a sorting clerk at a mail conveyor belt. They grab a handful of envelopes, restamp each one, and pass them along, all day.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a function receives 100 records at once and record number 37 is malformed and makes the code throw an error, what do you think happens to the other 99 records?
lessons.teach:
Near-real-time processing with Lambda means a function transforms records seconds after they are produced. The sources are an ordered stream (such as Kinesis Data Streams or DynamoDB Streams, which keep records in order within a shard, a partition of the stream), a queue (SQS, a managed message queue), or a delivery service (Kinesis Data Firehose, which can call a Lambda function to transform data before writing it to storage).

For streams and queues, Lambda uses an event source mapping. This is a managed poller that reads records on your behalf and hands them to your function as a batch, a list of records delivered in one call. Two settings control it. Batch size is the maximum number of records per call. Batching window is how long the poller may wait to fill a batch. Bigger batches cost fewer invocations but add delay. Small batches with no window give the lowest latency.

Worked example: vehicles send raw GPS readings to a Kinesis stream. The poller collects up to 100 readings and invokes the function. The function loops over the records and decodes each one, because stream data arrives base64-encoded, a text-safe encoding of raw bytes. It converts the units, drops readings that are missing coordinates, and writes the clean items to DynamoDB. It returns success, and the poller advances past those records.

Common mistake: letting one bad record throw an error for the whole batch. By default a failed batch is retried as a unit. On an ordered stream, that shard stops moving while the same poison record (one that fails every time) fails again and again until it expires. Data behind it goes stale, and records that already succeeded get processed more than once.

There are three fixes. Catch errors per record. Turn on partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures), so the function reports only the IDs of the records that failed. Set a retry limit with an on-failure destination, a place where Lambda sends details of records it gives up on. Because retries can still repeat records, the writes must be safe to run twice.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing company sends website click events to a Kinesis stream. An event source mapping (the managed poller) hands the function batches of up to 50 records. Partial batch responses (ReportBatchItemFailures) are turned on. In one batch, record 17 contains malformed data that fails every time it is processed. The function handles the batch like this. Step 1: loop over the 50 records, base64-decoding each one. Step 2: wrap each record's processing in its own try/catch, so record 17's error is caught and does not stop the loop. Step 3: write the 49 good records to DynamoDB, using writes that are safe to run twice. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the poller treats the other 49 records as done, and only record 17 is retried, until a retry limit sends its details to an on-failure destination. Which choice is the missing Step 4?
choices: Throw an error from the function so Lambda knows that something in the batch went wrong
Return a response that lists only the ID of record 17 as failed
Return success with an empty failure list, and log record 17 so someone can inspect it later
Raise the batch size to 100 so the bad record is spread across a larger batch
questions.why: With partial batch responses turned on, the function reports only the IDs of the records that failed, so only record 17 is retried instead of the whole batch.

questions.prompt: A bank's fraud team processes card transactions from an SQS queue with Lambda. They want each alert raised as soon as possible after the message arrives, even if that means paying for more function calls. How should they set the event source mapping?
choices: A large batch size with no batching window, so batches fill instantly
A small batch size with a long batching window, to save on invocations
A small batch size with no batching window
A large batch size with a long batching window, so each call handles more messages
questions.why: Small batches with no batching window give the lowest latency, because the poller does not wait to fill a batch; the cost is more invocations.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm uses Lambda to process a DynamoDB Stream with default settings: no per-record error handling, no partial batch responses and no retry limit. One record in a shard is a poison record that makes the function throw an error every time. What happens?
choices: The poison record is sent straight to an on-failure destination after its first failure
The whole batch is retried as a unit, so the shard stops moving and the good records in it are processed again each time
Lambda skips the bad record automatically and continues with the next records in the shard
Only the poison record is retried, while the rest of the shard keeps moving
questions.why: By default a failed batch is retried as a unit; on an ordered stream the shard is blocked until the poison record expires, data behind it goes stale, and records that already succeeded are repeated.

questions.prompt: A gym chain's Lambda function reads check-in events from a Kinesis stream and writes to DynamoDB. Because retries can deliver the same record more than once, the writes must be safe to run twice. Which write meets that need?
choices: Add 1 to the member's running visit total for every check-in record processed
Write the item using the check-in's unique event ID as its key, so a repeat simply overwrites the same item
Insert each check-in as a new item with a freshly generated random ID
Append each check-in to a list attribute on the member's item every time it is processed
questions.why: Writing by the event's own ID gives the same result whether it runs once or twice, while incrementing, appending or random IDs would double-count a repeated record.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a Lambda function processes records from a stream in near real time. Include how batch size and batching window trade latency against cost, and what goes wrong when one record in a batch keeps failing.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lambda doesn't watch the stream itself. An event source mapping polls the stream and calls our function with a batch of records. Our code loops over them, decodes each one, transforms it, and writes the result somewhere such as DynamoDB. Batch size caps the number of records per call, and the batching window lets the poller wait to fill a batch. Larger batches and longer windows mean fewer invocations and lower cost, but each record waits longer, so latency goes up. The big risk is a poison record. By default, one exception fails the whole batch, and the batch is retried. On an ordered stream that blocks the shard, so data piles up and goes stale, and the good records get reprocessed. So we catch errors per record and report only the failed item IDs with partial batch responses. We also cap retries and send failures to a destination. Our writes are idempotent, meaning safe to repeat, because duplicates still happen.
rubricPoints: An event source mapping polls the source and invokes the function with batches of records.
The function decodes and transforms each record, then writes it onward.
Batch size and batching window trade latency against invocation count and cost.
One failing record fails and retries the whole batch by default, which can block an ordered shard.
Per-record error handling, partial batch responses, and retry limits with a failure destination contain poison records.
Retries can deliver duplicates, so writes must be safe to repeat.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner diagnose events piling up behind a poison record, which is the central failure in batch-based near-real-time processing.

lessons.plain: Amazon DynamoDB is a managed database that stores items, which are records, and finds each item by a key you choose up front. Picture a huge filing room. The partition key tells the clerk which cabinet holds the item. An optional sort key decides the order of the folders inside that cabinet. If you later need to look things up a different way, you build an index. An index is a second, re-sorted copy of the data, like a card catalogue sorted by a different field. Lookups are fast when they match a key you designed. When they do not, the database has to search everything.
lessons.guessPrompt: An orders table is filed by customer ID. A support agent knows only an order number, not the customer. How could the database find that order quickly without searching every order?
lessons.teach:
Every item in an Amazon DynamoDB table (a managed key-value and document database) is located by its primary key, the unique identifier you pick when you create the table. A simple primary key is only a partition key. DynamoDB hashes that value to choose which partition, an internal storage slice, holds the item. A composite primary key adds a sort key. Items that share a partition key are stored together and ordered by the sort key, so you can request a range, such as all of one customer's orders since March. The pair of keys must be unique together. Neither part has to be unique on its own.

This works because a hash jumps straight to one partition, and sorted storage lets a range read start and stop precisely. Cost therefore stays flat as the table grows. The catch is that fast reads exist only for the key shapes you designed.

A secondary index is an extra copy of selected data that is keyed differently. A global secondary index (GSI) can use any attributes as its partition and sort key. You can add one after the table exists, and it has its own capacity. Its reads are eventually consistent, meaning a fresh write may show up a moment later. A local secondary index (LSI) keeps the table's partition key but uses a different sort key. It must be defined when the table is created. Projection is the set of attributes copied into an index: keys only, chosen attributes, or all attributes.

Worked example: an Orders table uses customerId as the partition key and orderDate as the sort key. Step 1: to get customer 42's orders this month, DynamoDB hashes 42, goes to one partition, and reads that date range. Step 2: to find order A-981 by number alone, the table keys cannot help. Step 3: you add a GSI whose partition key is orderId, then look up A-981 in that index directly.

A common mistake is designing keys around entities instead of the access patterns the application needs. When a needed lookup has no matching key or index, the code falls back to reading the entire table. In a running system, that means slow responses and costs that grow with table size. Each index also adds write cost, because every write must update the index copies too.

questions.prompt: A weather company stores sensor data in a DynamoDB table that already exists and is in production. Its partition key is deviceId and its sort key is readingTime. Step 1: to get device D-7's readings from the last hour, DynamoDB hashes D-7, goes to one partition, and reads that time range in order. Step 2: a new feature needs device D-7's readings ordered by temperature instead of time, and the table's sort key cannot do that. Step 3: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: Make temperature part of the table's partition key so that every reading is grouped by its temperature
Add a local secondary index (LSI) now that keeps deviceId as the partition key and uses temperature as its sort key
Add a global secondary index (GSI) with deviceId as its partition key and temperature as its sort key, then query that index
Read the whole table, then filter and sort the results by temperature inside the application code
questions.why: An LSI must be defined when the table is created, but a GSI can use any attributes as its keys and can be added to an existing table, giving a fast keyed read for this new pattern.

questions.prompt: A clinic's Appointments table uses a composite primary key: patientId as the partition key and slotTime as the sort key. Which pair of items can both be stored in the table?
choices: patientId P-5 at slotTime 09:00, and patientId P-5 at slotTime 09:00 with a different doctor attribute
No pair, because each patientId may appear only once in the whole table
patientId P-5 at slotTime 09:00, and patientId P-8 at slotTime 09:00
Two items that both have patientId P-5 and no slotTime value at all
questions.why: With a composite key, only the partition key and sort key together must be unique, so two different patients can share the same slot time.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app writes a new booking to its table, then immediately queries a global secondary index (GSI) keyed on eventId. The booking is missing from the result, but appears when the query runs again a second later. What best explains this?
choices: The booking's attributes were not projected into the index, so it can never appear there
The GSI shares capacity with the table, so the table write had to finish before the index existed
The GSI was added after the table was created, which makes its results incomplete
GSI reads are eventually consistent, so a fresh write can take a moment to show up in the index
questions.why: Reads from a GSI are eventually consistent, meaning a just-written item may appear in the index slightly later.

questions.prompt: A delivery company designed its Parcels table with parcelId as the only key. The app now often needs every parcel for one courier on one day, and no index supports that lookup. As the table grows from thousands to millions of parcels, what happens to that request?
choices: It stays fast and cheap, because DynamoDB hashes the courier name to find the right partition
It returns only the parcels stored in the first partition, so results become incomplete
It fails with an error, because DynamoDB refuses requests that have no matching key
It falls back to reading the entire table, so responses slow down and costs grow with table size
questions.why: Without a key or index matching the access pattern, the code must read the whole table, so time and cost rise as the table grows.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how partition keys, sort keys, and secondary indexes decide which lookups a DynamoDB table can answer quickly. Include one tradeoff of adding a global secondary index.
lessons.modelAnswer: DynamoDB finds items by primary key. The partition key is hashed to pick the storage partition. If we add a sort key, items with the same partition key sit together in sorted order, so we can fetch ranges like a customer's orders between two dates. The two keys together must be unique. Any lookup that does not start from those keys forces a full-table read, which is slow and costly. So we list our access patterns first and design keys to fit them. When we need another lookup, such as by order number, we add a secondary index, which is a re-keyed copy of chosen attributes. A GSI can use any attributes and can be added later. A local index keeps the partition key, swaps the sort key, and must be defined at table creation. The tradeoff with a GSI is that every write also updates the index, which costs more. Its reads are also eventually consistent, so a brand-new item may not appear immediately.
rubricPoints: The partition key is hashed to choose where an item is stored.
The sort key orders items within a partition and enables range lookups.
Partition key plus sort key must be unique together.
Keys should be designed from access patterns, or lookups fall back to reading the whole table.
A GSI can use any attributes and can be added later, while an LSI shares the partition key and must be defined at table creation.
Indexes add write cost, and GSI reads are eventually consistent.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine builds DynamoDB tables, so reasoning through exam-style access-pattern scenarios to choose keys and indexes is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A partition key is the field a database uses to decide where each record is physically stored. DynamoDB, Amazon's managed key-value database, splits a table across many storage slices called partitions and hashes the partition key to choose one. High cardinality means the key has many distinct values, such as a customer ID, rather than a few, such as yes or no. Think of a supermarket with twenty checkouts: if every shopper is sent to a lane by surname initial, the lines stay even, but if everyone is sent by shirt colour, two lanes jam while the rest sit idle.
lessons.guessPrompt: You store a million orders and choose the order's status (pending, shipped, or delivered) as the key that decides where each order is stored. If most orders are pending, what do you think happens to the storage slice holding pending orders when traffic spikes?
lessons.teach:
A partition key is the attribute DynamoDB passes through a hash function, a calculation that turns any value into a seemingly random number, to choose which partition stores an item. A partition is one slice of storage and compute, and each one can serve only a limited rate of traffic, roughly 3,000 reads and 1,000 writes per second. Cardinality is the number of distinct values a key can take. A hot partition is one slice receiving far more traffic than the others.

Why high cardinality helps: the hash scatters different values across partitions almost randomly, so many distinct values spread requests over many slices. Few distinct values can only ever land on a few slices, however large the table grows.

Worked example: a table of orders keyed by status has three values. Step one: 5,000 writes per second arrive, 90 percent of them pending. Step two: all pending writes hash to the same partition, roughly 4,500 per second against a limit near 1,000. Step three: DynamoDB throttles, meaning it rejects the excess requests with a throughput-exceeded error, even though other partitions are nearly idle. Now key by orderId instead. Each write has a unique value, the hash spreads them across all partitions, and each partition carries a small, even share.

Common mistake: assuming high cardinality alone guarantees balance. If one key value, such as a single celebrity user or today's date, receives most of the traffic, that value still sits on one partition and runs hot. Balance needs many values and traffic spread fairly evenly across them. A frequent fix for a hot value is write sharding: appending a small random or calculated suffix to the key so its writes spread over several partitions.

In a running system, a hot partition shows up as throttling errors, SDK retries, rising latency, and failed Lambda invocations while your overall table capacity looks underused. Adding capacity barely helps, because the bottleneck is one slice, not the table.

questions.prompt: A fitness app stores workout logs in a DynamoDB table whose partition key is deviceType. That key has only two values: "watch" and "phone". Assume each partition handles roughly 1,000 writes per second. Step one: 3,000 writes per second arrive, and 80 percent come from watches. Step two: [missing]. Step three: DynamoDB throttles, rejecting the excess writes with a throughput-exceeded error, while the partition holding "phone" items sits mostly idle. Fix: change the partition key to workoutId, which is unique for every log, so the hash spreads writes across all partitions. Which statement correctly fills in step two?
choices: The hash function randomizes each watch write separately, so the 2,400 watch writes spread evenly over all partitions and none exceeds its limit.
The watch writes land on one partition, but 2,400 per second is below that partition's limit of about 3,000, so no throttling is expected.
All watch writes share the value "watch", so they hash to the same partition: about 2,400 writes per second against a limit near 1,000.
The 3,000 total writes exceed the table's overall capacity, so every partition starts rejecting writes in equal measure.
questions.why: Identical key values always produce the same hash, so every watch write goes to one partition, and 2,400 writes per second is far above the roughly 1,000-writes-per-second limit of a single partition.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticketing service is designing a DynamoDB table that will receive heavy write traffic during ticket sales. Which partition key is most likely to spread writes evenly across partitions?
choices: saleChannel, which is either "web" or "app"
seatSection, which has six values (A to F)
ticketId, which is unique for every ticket sold
venueCountry, which has about 20 values
questions.why: ticketId has the highest cardinality, meaning the most distinct values, so the hash scatters writes across many partitions instead of a few.

questions.prompt: A social media app records likes in a DynamoDB table keyed by postId, which has millions of distinct values. One post goes viral and receives about 8,000 likes per second, and the app starts seeing throttling errors on that post only. What is the best explanation and fix?
choices: postId is a poor key; switching to postType (such as photo or video) will group likes together and reduce load.
The table as a whole is out of capacity; raising the table's provisioned write capacity will fully solve the problem.
The key has too few distinct values; switch to a key with even more values, such as a timestamp, and the throttling will stop.
All likes for that one postId hash to a single partition, so it runs hot; write sharding, adding a small suffix to that key, spreads its writes over several partitions.
questions.why: High cardinality does not help when one value gets most of the traffic, because that value still lives on one partition; write sharding spreads that single hot value across several partitions.

questions.prompt: A delivery-tracking team sees throughput-exceeded errors from DynamoDB, repeated SDK retries, rising latency, and failing Lambda invocations. Yet their monitoring shows the table is using only about 15 percent of its total capacity. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The table needs more total capacity, because throttling always means the whole table has run out of throughput.
The table holds too many items, which spreads them across too many partitions and slows every request.
The Lambda function's timeout is too short, which makes DynamoDB return throughput-exceeded errors.
A hot partition: the partition key concentrates traffic on one slice that hits its own limit while the rest of the table sits underused.
questions.why: Throttling while overall capacity looks underused is the signature of a hot partition, where one slice is overloaded even though the table as a whole is not, so adding table capacity barely helps.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we should key our DynamoDB table on something like userId rather than accountType, and name one situation where even a high-cardinality key can still cause trouble.
lessons.modelAnswer: DynamoDB hashes the partition key to decide which partition stores each item, and every partition can handle only so many reads and writes per second. accountType has maybe three values, so all traffic for the most popular type lands on one partition. That partition gets throttled even while the rest of the table sits idle, and paying for more table capacity won't fix it. userId has millions of distinct values, so the hash spreads requests across many partitions and each one carries a small, even share. The limit is that cardinality alone isn't enough: access must also be spread out. If one user, or one key like today's date, gets most of the requests, that single value still lives on one partition and runs hot. For that case we could shard the key by adding a suffix so its writes are split across several partitions, at the cost of more complex reads.
rubricPoints: The partition key is hashed to choose which partition stores an item.
Each partition has a per-second throughput limit, so concentrated traffic gets throttled.
Many distinct key values spread requests evenly across partitions.
Low-cardinality keys create hot partitions even when total table capacity is unused.
High cardinality is not enough if a few values receive most of the traffic.
Write sharding with a key suffix can spread a hot value, at the cost of more complex reads.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a partition key is a design judgement best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios: compare candidate keys and predict where traffic would concentrate and throttle.

lessons.plain: When a database keeps several copies of your data on different machines, a new write reaches them one after another, not all at once. A consistency model is the promise the database makes about which version a read will see. Eventually consistent means a read might briefly return the old value, but every copy catches up soon. Strongly consistent means a read always returns the latest successful write. Think of a shared family calendar synced to several phones: glance at any phone and you might see yesterday's plan for a moment, or you can phone the person who made the change and get the definite answer, which takes a bit more effort.
lessons.guessPrompt: A user changes their delivery address and the app immediately reloads the profile page. If the database keeps three copies of the record and the read may be answered by any one of them, what might the user see, and why?
lessons.teach:
A consistency model defines which version of data a read returns after a write. Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value and document database, stores each item on several replicas (copies) spread across Availability Zones, which are separate data centres in one region. A write is confirmed once enough replicas accept it; the rest catch up, usually within about a second.

An eventually consistent read, DynamoDB's default, may be answered by any replica, so it can return slightly stale (out-of-date) data. A strongly consistent read, requested by setting ConsistentRead to true on GetItem, Query or Scan, is answered by the replica that holds the latest confirmed write, so it reflects every write that succeeded before it.

The tradeoff is cost and reach. Capacity is billed in read capacity units (RCUs). One RCU buys one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second, or two eventually consistent reads of that size, so strong reads cost twice as much. Strong reads are also unavailable on global secondary indexes (alternate key views maintained in the background), and across regions in global tables (multi-region replicated tables), and they can fail if the leading replica is unreachable, where an eventual read could still succeed.

Worked example: a Lambda function writes order 42 with status PAID. One step later, it reads order 42 with default settings. The read lands on a replica that has not received the update, returns PENDING, and the function sends a payment reminder. Change the read to ConsistentRead=true and the same trace returns PAID, so no reminder goes out.

Common mistake: putting ConsistentRead=true on a query against a global secondary index and expecting fresh data; DynamoDB rejects it. If you need read-after-write correctness there, read the base table by key instead.

In a running system, choose strong reads only where a stale answer causes wrong actions, such as balances or read-after-write checks, and keep the cheaper eventual reads for feeds, dashboards and lists.

questions.prompt: A cinema chain's booking service stores seats in a DynamoDB table whose partition key is the seat ID. A Lambda function must hold seat C7 and then confirm the hold before it charges the customer's card. Step 1: the function writes seat C7 with status HELD. Step 2: DynamoDB confirms the write once enough replicas have accepted it, while the other replicas are still catching up. Step 3: the function immediately calls GetItem on seat C7 to check the hold. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the read returns HELD, so the function charges the card and does not re-offer the seat. Which choice correctly fills Step 4?
choices: Set ConsistentRead to true on the GetItem call, so the replica holding the latest confirmed write answers the read.
Make two default reads in a row and trust whichever status appears in both, since a repeated read always reaches a fresh replica.
Run the check as a query on a global secondary index keyed by seat ID, with ConsistentRead set to true.
Keep the default read settings, because DynamoDB always answers a read from the same replica that accepted the write.
questions.why: A strongly consistent read on the base table is answered by the replica holding the latest confirmed write, so it is guaranteed to see HELD right after the write succeeds.

questions.prompt: A weather-station dashboard reads items from a DynamoDB table. Every item is 3 KB. The team decides it needs 600 strongly consistent reads per second. How many read capacity units (RCUs) does this need?
choices: 300 RCUs
600 RCUs
1,200 RCUs
150 RCUs
questions.why: One RCU covers one strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB per second, so 600 such reads need 600 RCUs. Eventually consistent reads would need only 300.

questions.prompt: A fitness app stores users in a DynamoDB table keyed by user ID. It also has a global secondary index keyed by email. Right after sign-up, a Lambda function queries the email index with ConsistentRead set to true to confirm the new account exists. What happens, and what is the right fix?
choices: The query silently falls back to an eventually consistent read, so it is fine to leave as is.
DynamoDB rejects the request. For read-after-write correctness, read the base table by its key, the user ID, instead.
The query succeeds and always returns the new account, because the setting forces the index to update first.
The query succeeds but costs half as much, because index reads are billed at the eventual rate.
questions.why: Strongly consistent reads are not available on global secondary indexes, so DynamoDB rejects the request. A fresh result requires a strong read on the base table by key.

questions.prompt: A digital wallet company uses DynamoDB for several features. For which feature is paying for strongly consistent reads most justified?
choices: Checking a customer's balance immediately before approving a withdrawal
Rendering an internal dashboard of daily sign-up counts
Listing the merchants a customer has saved as favourites
Showing a scrolling feed of recent promotional offers
questions.why: A stale balance could approve a withdrawal that should be refused, which is a wrong action. Feeds, dashboards and lists can tolerate data that is a second old, so the cheaper eventual reads fit them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between strongly consistent and eventually consistent reads in DynamoDB, when you would pay for strong reads, and at least one limit or tradeoff that comes with them.
lessons.modelAnswer: DynamoDB keeps each item on several replicas. A write is confirmed before every replica has it, so a default, eventually consistent read can hit a lagging copy and return old data for a short time, usually under a second. If I set ConsistentRead to true, the read goes to the replica with the latest confirmed write, so I always see writes that succeeded before my read. I'd use strong reads where acting on stale data is harmful, like reading an order right after marking it paid or checking a balance before spending. The tradeoffs: a strong read uses twice the read capacity, it isn't available on global secondary indexes or across regions in global tables, and it can fail when the leading replica is unreachable. For feeds, lists and dashboards, eventual reads are cheaper and good enough.
rubricPoints: Data lives on multiple replicas and writes reach them at slightly different times.
Eventually consistent reads are the default and may return briefly stale data.
Strongly consistent reads return the latest confirmed write, requested with ConsistentRead.
Strong reads cost twice the read capacity of eventual reads.
Strong reads are not supported on global secondary indexes or across regions in global tables.
Choose strong reads only where acting on stale data causes wrong behaviour.

suggested.rationale: Investigating dispatchers who see minute-old positions makes the learner experience stale reads from lagging replicas first-hand and decide where a fresher read is worth its cost.

lessons.plain: A DynamoDB table stores records called items, and each item is filed under a key. A query is like asking a librarian for every book on one specific shelf: you name the shelf, and only that shelf is read. A scan is like walking every aisle and opening every book, then throwing away the ones you did not want. Both can return the same answer, but the scan does far more work, and you pay for all of it. The bigger the table grows, the worse the scan gets, while a well-aimed query stays fast.
lessons.guessPrompt: A table holds one million customer orders, and you need the 20 orders belonging to one customer. If one method reads only that customer's orders and another reads every order and then discards the rest, roughly how many times more data does the second method read?
lessons.teach:
In Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value database, a table holds items (records). Each item has a partition key, the attribute DynamoDB uses to decide where the item is stored, and optionally a sort key, which orders items that share a partition key. A Query is a read that requires an exact partition key value and may add a condition on the sort key, such as a range or a 'begins with' prefix. DynamoDB jumps straight to that partition and reads only the matching items. A Scan is a read with no key: it walks through every item in the table, in pages of up to 1 MB each.

Why the difference matters: DynamoDB charges and throttles by read capacity, the amount of data actually read, not the amount returned. A filter expression, a condition you attach to remove items from the result, is applied after the read, so it shrinks the response but not the bill.

Worked example: an Orders table has partition key customerId and sort key orderDate, holding one million 1 KB items, about 1 GB. You want customer C42's 20 orders. Step 1, Query with customerId = C42: DynamoDB reads about 20 KB and returns 20 items in one request. Step 2, Scan with a filter customerId = C42: DynamoDB reads all 1 GB, about 1,000 pages of 1 MB, returns 20 items, and your code must loop through every page using the continuation marker DynamoDB returns. That is roughly 50,000 times more data read for the same answer.

The common mistake is believing a filter expression makes a scan cheap. It does not; every item is still read and billed.

In a running system, a scan in a hot code path eats the table's read capacity, so other requests get throttled, latency climbs as the table grows, and a Lambda function doing it may hit its timeout. Scans are fine for small tables, one-off exports, or occasional offline jobs. When a frequent request cannot be answered by a query, the fix is to design a key or a secondary index that matches that access pattern, not to scan.

questions.prompt: A fitness app stores heart-rate readings in a DynamoDB table called Readings. The partition key is deviceId and the sort key is readingTime. The table holds 400,000 items of 2 KB each, about 800 MB. You need device D7's 60 readings from the last hour, about 120 KB of data. Step 1, Query with deviceId = D7 and a sort key condition that readingTime falls within the last hour: DynamoDB goes straight to D7's partition, reads about 120 KB, and returns 60 items in one request. Step 2, Scan with a filter expression deviceId = D7 and readingTime in the last hour: ______. Step 3, compare: the scan reads roughly 6,700 times more data than the query for the same 60 readings. Which statement correctly completes Step 2?
choices: DynamoDB uses the filter to skip straight to D7's items, so it reads about 120 KB and returns 60 items, costing the same as the query.
DynamoDB reads all 800 MB but bills only for the 120 KB it returns, and it sends all 60 items back in a single response.
DynamoDB reads all 800 MB in about 800 pages of 1 MB, bills read capacity for all of it, returns the 60 matching items, and your code must loop through every page using the continuation marker.
DynamoDB refuses the request, because a scan cannot have a filter expression on the partition key.
questions.why: A scan walks every item in 1 MB pages and the filter is applied only after the read, so the full 800 MB is read and billed even though just 60 items come back.

questions.prompt: A library's DynamoDB table Loans has partition key memberId and sort key loanDate. Which request is a Query rather than a Scan?
choices: Read items where loanDate begins with 2024-03, with no memberId given.
Read every item in the table and keep only those where memberId equals M-310.
Read items where memberId equals M-310 and loanDate begins with 2024-03.
Read every item in the table and keep only those where loanDate is in March.
questions.why: A Query requires an exact partition key value (memberId = M-310) and may add a condition on the sort key, such as a 'begins with' prefix; the other options supply no partition key, so they would have to scan.

questions.prompt: A support-desk Lambda function runs on every page load and scans a 5 GB Tickets table with a filter expression status = open. As the table grows, the function starts hitting its timeout and other requests to the table are being throttled. What is the right fix?
choices: Keep the scan but ask for smaller pages so each request reads less in total.
Design a key or secondary index that matches the 'open tickets' access pattern and query it instead of scanning.
Add a second filter expression so fewer items are read from the table.
Raise the Lambda timeout so the scan has time to finish every page.
questions.why: Filters and page size do not reduce the total data a scan reads, and a longer timeout only hides the growing cost; a key or secondary index matching the access pattern lets a query read only the needed items.

questions.prompt: In which situation is using a Scan a reasonable choice?
choices: An API endpoint, called thousands of times per minute, that finds one user's cart in a 20 GB table.
A once-a-month offline job that exports every item from a small 3 MB settings table.
A checkout Lambda function that scans a large Products table with a filter to find one product's price.
A login check that looks up a single account by its partition key value on every sign-in.
questions.why: Scans are fine for small tables, one-off exports, or occasional offline jobs; frequent or hot-path requests against large tables should use a query on a key or index.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you rejected their pull request that uses a DynamoDB Scan with a filter to look up a user's records, including when a scan would actually be acceptable.
lessons.modelAnswer: A Query needs the partition key value, so DynamoDB goes straight to that user's items and reads only those. A Scan reads every item in the table page by page, up to 1 MB per page, and the filter expression only removes items after they have been read. DynamoDB bills and throttles on data read, not data returned, so this scan costs as much as reading the whole table every time it runs. Today the table is small so it looks fine, but cost and latency grow with the table, it will burn read capacity, throttle other requests, and could push our Lambda past its timeout. Since we look users up often, we should query on a key that matches this access pattern, or add an index if the key is wrong. A scan is acceptable for small tables, one-off exports, or occasional background jobs where reading everything is the point.
rubricPoints: A query requires a partition key value and reads only matching items.
A scan reads every item in the table, in pages of up to 1 MB.
Filter expressions are applied after reading, so they do not reduce the read cost.
Scan cost and latency grow with table size and can throttle other requests.
Scans are acceptable for small tables, one-off exports or occasional offline jobs.
The fix for a frequent access pattern is a matching key or index, not a scan.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises DynamoDB reads directly, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario comparing data read by a query versus a filtered scan builds the judgment the exam tests.

lessons.plain: Serializing means turning the data your program holds in memory, such as a customer record, into a flat form of text or bytes that can be saved or sent. Deserializing is the reverse: reading that saved form and rebuilding the original data. Think of packing furniture into a flat box for shipping and then assembling it again on arrival. The box and the instructions must match, or you end up with spare screws or a wobbly table. A database only stores the types it understands, so your code has to pack data carefully on the way in and unpack it correctly on the way out.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your program holds a price of 19.99 as a number in memory. If you saved it as text and later read it back, what could go wrong, and how could both sides agree on what the text means?
lessons.teach:
Serialization is converting an in-memory object, such as a dictionary or class instance, into text or bytes that can be stored or transmitted. Deserialization rebuilds the object from that text or those bytes. A data store such as Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value and document database, accepts only its own set of types, so your objects must be translated when written and translated back when read.

This works because both sides agree on a format. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation, a text format made of keys, values, lists and nested objects) is the usual choice. DynamoDB's low-level API uses a typed form of JSON. Each value is wrapped in an attribute value, a small object whose key names the type: S for string, N for number, BOOL for true or false, L for list, M for map (a nested object) and B for binary. A number travels as a string inside its N tag, so no precision is lost on the way. The AWS SDKs, the code libraries for calling AWS, provide helpers that add and remove these tags for you. Examples are the boto3 resource layer in Python and the document client or marshall and unmarshall functions in JavaScript.

Worked example. Start with an order {"id": "o-17", "total": 19.99, "paid": true}. Step 1: the helper marshals it, meaning it adds the type tags, to {"id": {"S": "o-17"}, "total": {"N": "19.99"}, "paid": {"BOOL": true}}. Step 2: PutItem stores the item. Step 3: GetItem returns the tagged form. Step 4: the helper unmarshals it, meaning it strips the tags. In Python, total comes back as Decimal("19.99"), an exact decimal number type, not a float.

The first common mistake is passing a Python float to boto3. It raises a TypeError, because floats can be imprecise. Convert to Decimal first.

A second mistake is saving a whole object as one JSON string attribute. The write succeeds. Afterwards, though, you cannot filter, update or index individual fields, and every change rewrites the entire blob.

Dates have no native type. Choose one text format, such as ISO 8601 (for example 2024-05-01T09:00:00Z), which sorts correctly as plain text.

In a running system, format mismatches show up as failed writes, rounding errors in money, or readers that crash on items written by older code. Each item must also stay under DynamoDB's 400 KB item size limit.

questions.prompt:
A bike-rental company's Python Lambda saves a rental record {"rentalId": "r-302", "hours": 4.5, "returned": false, "startedAt": "2024-07-12T14:30:00Z"} to DynamoDB. In DynamoDB's low-level API, a type tag names each value's type, for example S for string, N for number and BOOL for true or false. Marshalling means the SDK helper adds these tags.

Step 1: The developer converts hours to Decimal("4.5"), an exact decimal number type, because boto3 rejects a Python float with a TypeError.

Step 2: The helper marshals the record. rentalId becomes {"S": "r-302"}, hours becomes ???, returned becomes {"BOOL": false}, and startedAt becomes {"S": "2024-07-12T14:30:00Z"}.

Step 3: PutItem stores the item.

Step 4: Later, GetItem returns the tagged form. The helper unmarshals it by stripping the tags, and hours comes back as Decimal("4.5").

What does hours become in Step 2?
questions.why: A number is tagged N, and its value travels as a string inside that tag so no precision is lost.

questions.prompt: A weather service's Lambda calls GetItem and receives {"city": {"S": "Oslo"}, "rainMm": {"N": "3.2"}}. The SDK helper then turns this into {"city": "Oslo", "rainMm": Decimal("3.2")}. What is this step, and what does it do?
choices: Unmarshalling, a form of deserialization: it strips the type tags and rebuilds a normal object.
Encryption: it protects the item so that only the Lambda can read it.
Compression: it shrinks the item so it stays under the 400 KB item size limit.
Marshalling, a form of serialization: it adds type tags so DynamoDB will accept the item.
questions.why: Removing the type tags to rebuild the in-memory object is unmarshalling, which is deserialization.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking app stores appointment times in DynamoDB. DynamoDB has no native date type, so the times are stored as text. The team needs the times to sort in time order when compared as plain text. Which text format should they choose?
choices: Tuesday 11 March, 14:00
questions.why: ISO 8601 puts the year first, then the month, day and time, so plain-text order matches time order.

questions.prompt: A fitness app stores each member as a single DynamoDB attribute called profile. Its value is one JSON string holding name, email, plan and city. The writes succeed. What problem will the team run into later?
choices: Every write fails with a TypeError, because DynamoDB rejects JSON strings.
They cannot filter, update or index fields such as city on their own, and every change rewrites the whole string.
DynamoDB automatically splits the string into separate attributes, which doubles the storage cost.
Reads return each field as a Decimal, so the name and email come back as numbers.
questions.why: A JSON blob saved as one attribute hides its fields from DynamoDB, so you cannot filter, update or index them individually, and each change rewrites the entire blob.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what happens to an object between your Lambda code and a DynamoDB table on a write and on a read. Name one tradeoff or limit they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: When we write, our code serializes the object. The SDK helper marshals it into DynamoDB's typed format, so every value gets a tag: S for strings, N for numbers sent as text, BOOL, M for nested maps, L for lists. When we read, the helper unmarshals those tags back into native objects. The format is agreed on both sides, so nothing gets lost in translation. Here are the limits to watch. In Python, numbers come back as Decimal, and boto3 rejects floats, so we convert money to Decimal ourselves. Dates have no native type, so we store them as ISO 8601 strings, which sort correctly. There is also a tradeoff. Dumping the whole object into one JSON string attribute is quick to write, but we lose the ability to filter, update or index single fields, and every change rewrites the whole thing. Each item also has to stay under 400 KB.
rubricPoints: Defines serialization as converting in-memory data into storable text or bytes, and deserialization as the reverse.
Explains that DynamoDB uses typed attribute values such as S, N, BOOL, M and L, and that SDK helpers marshal and unmarshal them.
Notes that numbers travel as strings and come back as Decimal in Python, and that floats are rejected.
Names a tradeoff such as storing a JSON blob versus separate attributes, or the date format choice.
Mentions a limit or a production consequence, such as the 400 KB item limit or readers breaking on mismatched formats.

suggested.rationale: Converting CSV rows into JSON makes the learner serialize real data and handle number types, which is the core skill behind persisting items to a store.

lessons.plain: Data has a life: it is created, used a lot while it is fresh, read less as it ages, and eventually becomes useless or even risky to keep. Managing a data store means planning that whole life up front. You decide when old records get deleted automatically, when rarely read files move to cheaper storage, and how you can recover if something is lost by accident. Think of a kitchen. Today's food stays on the counter, leftovers go in the fridge, bulk goods go to the basement, and expired items go in the bin on a schedule, not when the smell gets bad.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app stores login sessions that are useless after 24 hours, and you never clean them up. What do you think happens to the table and your bill after a year, and what would you want the database to do for you instead?
lessons.teach:
A data lifecycle is the set of rules that decide what happens to data as it ages. On AWS, developers mostly meet three tools for this.

The first is DynamoDB Time to Live (TTL). Amazon DynamoDB is a managed key-value database. TTL lets you name one attribute on each item that holds an expiry time, written as a Unix epoch timestamp in seconds, meaning the number of seconds since 1 January 1970. A background process deletes items whose time has passed, and these deletes cost no write capacity. The delete is not instant. It can lag by hours or even days, so your read code should still ignore items that are past their expiry.

The second is S3 lifecycle rules. Amazon S3 is managed object storage, meaning a store for whole files. A lifecycle rule can transition objects, which means moving them to a cheaper storage class such as Infrequent Access or Glacier, where storage costs less but reading costs more or takes longer. A rule can also expire objects, which means deleting them after a set age.

The third is backups. DynamoDB point-in-time recovery keeps a rolling window of up to 35 days you can restore from. On-demand backups are snapshots you keep until you delete them. S3 versioning keeps older copies of an object when it is overwritten or deleted.

Here is a worked example. A user logs in at epoch 1,700,000,000. The session item is written with expiresAt set to 1,700,086,400, which is that time plus 86,400 seconds, or one day. The next day a read finds the item still present, but the code compares expiresAt to the current time and treats the session as dead. Later, TTL removes the item for free.

A common mistake is to write the expiry in milliseconds or as a date string. TTL quietly skips values in the wrong format, so nothing ever expires. In a running system, the table then grows without limit, storage costs climb, and stale data piles up that you may have been obliged to delete.

questions.prompt:
A concert-ticketing app holds a seat for a buyer for 15 minutes. A DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database) stores each hold, and Time to Live (TTL, the feature that deletes items after an expiry time you store on them) is enabled on an attribute called heldUntil. A hold is created at Unix epoch time 1,720,000,000 (seconds since 1 January 1970).

Step 1: Convert the hold length to seconds: 15 × 60 = 900.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: Write the hold item with that heldUntil value.
Step 4: At checkout, the code compares heldUntil to the current time and rejects the hold if the time has passed, even if the item still exists.

Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: Set heldUntil to 1,720,000,900,000, the time in milliseconds for extra precision
Set heldUntil to 1,720,000,900, the creation time plus 900 seconds
Set heldUntil to 1,720,000,015, the creation time plus 15
Set heldUntil to the readable date string "2024-07-03 09:55"
questions.why: TTL expects an epoch timestamp in seconds, so the expiry is the creation time plus 900 seconds; milliseconds or date strings are silently skipped, and adding 15 would expire the hold after only 15 seconds.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing company stores user uploads in Amazon S3 (managed storage for whole files). Photos are rarely viewed after 90 days, and company policy says they must be deleted after 2 years. Which setup fits this lifecycle best?
choices: An S3 lifecycle rule that transitions objects to a cheaper storage class such as Glacier at 90 days and expires them at 730 days
An S3 lifecycle rule that expires objects at 90 days and transitions them to Glacier at 730 days
Enable DynamoDB TTL on the S3 bucket with an expiry of 730 days
Turn on S3 versioning so older photos move to cheaper storage automatically
questions.why: A lifecycle rule can transition (move to a cheaper class) objects as they age and expire (delete) them later; TTL is a DynamoDB feature and versioning only keeps old copies.

questions.prompt: At a logistics company, a bug wrote bad data into a DynamoDB table 10 days ago. Point-in-time recovery (a rolling window of restorable history) is enabled on the table, but nobody took a manual backup. What is the best way to get the table back to its state before the bug?
choices: Restore using point-in-time recovery to a moment just before the bug, since 10 days is within its window of up to 35 days
Nothing can be done, because point-in-time recovery only covers the last 24 hours
Enable TTL so the bad items are deleted for free
Use S3 versioning to retrieve the older copies of the items
questions.why: Point-in-time recovery lets you restore to any moment in a rolling window of up to 35 days, so a 10-day-old problem is recoverable.

questions.prompt: A fitness app enables DynamoDB TTL on an attribute called deleteAfter. Its code writes values like 1,715,000,000,000 into that attribute. Months later, no items have ever been removed and the table keeps growing. What is the most likely cause?
choices: TTL only deletes items when the table has spare write capacity
The values are in milliseconds instead of seconds, so TTL quietly skips them
TTL needs the value stored as a date string such as "2024-05-06"
TTL deletes can lag by hours or days, so months of waiting is normal
questions.why: TTL requires an epoch timestamp in seconds; a 13-digit millisecond value is the wrong format, so TTL ignores it and nothing ever expires.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make old session records and old log files clean themselves up on AWS, and name one limit or tradeoff of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: For sessions in DynamoDB, I'd turn on Time to Live and give each item an expiry attribute holding a Unix epoch timestamp in seconds, set to the login time plus the session length. DynamoDB deletes expired items in the background without charging write capacity. The limit is that deletion is lazy and can lag by hours or days, so my read code still checks the expiry and treats old items as gone. I also have to write the timestamp in seconds, because milliseconds or a date string are silently ignored. For log files in S3, I'd add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to a cheaper storage class after about 30 days and expires them after a year. The tradeoff is that colder classes cost less to store but more to read, and reads can be slower. Separately, I'd enable point-in-time recovery so I can undo accidental deletes.
rubricPoints: Uses DynamoDB TTL with an epoch-seconds expiry attribute to auto-delete items.
Notes TTL deletion is delayed, so reads must filter out expired items.
Uses S3 lifecycle rules to transition objects to cheaper classes and expire them.
Names the tradeoff that colder storage is cheaper to keep but costlier or slower to read.
Mentions backups or versioning for recovering from accidental loss.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine exercises TTL or storage tiering directly, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about expiry formats, transition timing and recovery is the most useful practice.

lessons.plain: A data cache is a small, very fast storage area that keeps copies of information your application asks for often, so it does not have to fetch it from the slower main database every time. Think of a chef who keeps the most-used spices on the counter instead of walking to the pantry for each dish. The pantry is still the real store, and the counter copy can run out or get old. On AWS, managed caching services hold these copies in memory, close to your code, making repeat reads much faster and taking load off the database.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app shows each vehicle's last known position, and you keep a copy in a fast cache for 30 seconds. A vehicle moves at second 10. What will a user who asks at second 20 probably see, and why?
lessons.teach:
A data cache is a fast, temporary store that holds copies of data your code reads often, so repeat reads skip the slower source of truth, meaning the database that holds the real data. Amazon ElastiCache is a managed in-memory key-value store that runs Redis-compatible engines or Memcached. Amazon DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache that sits in front of DynamoDB and accepts the same API calls. Caching works because memory is far faster than a database query, and most traffic tends to ask for a small set of popular items.

There are two common ways to fill a cache. In lazy loading, also called cache-aside, the code checks the cache first. On a hit (the item is found), it returns the item. On a miss (the item is not found), it reads the database, stores the result in the cache, and then returns it. Only data that is actually requested gets cached, but the first read is slow and the copy can go stale, meaning out of date. In write-through, every database write also updates the cache. This keeps copies current, but it adds cost to every write and can fill the cache with data nobody reads.

A TTL (time to live) is an expiry time placed on each cached item, and it puts an upper limit on how stale that item can get. Eviction is the cache dropping items when its memory is full, usually the least recently used ones first.

Worked example: a Lambda function serves positions using cache-aside with a 30-second TTL. At 0 s, a request for vehicle 42 misses, so the function reads DynamoDB, caches the result, and returns it. At 5 s, the request hits and returns in under a millisecond. At 31 s, the item has expired, so the next request misses and refreshes it.

A common mistake is setting no TTL, or giving every key the same TTL. With no TTL, users see old data indefinitely. With identical TTLs, or after a deploy empties the cache, many keys miss at the same moment and the whole load lands on the database. This is called a cache stampede. Adding random jitter to TTLs and letting one request rebuild each hot key prevents it.

questions.prompt: A bookshop's Lambda function looks up book prices. It uses cache-aside (lazy loading) with a 120-second TTL. Step 1: At 0 s, a request for book 7781 checks the cache and misses. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: At 50 s, another request for book 7781 checks the cache, hits, and returns in under a millisecond. Step 4: At 125 s, the cached copy has expired, so the next request misses and refreshes it. What happens in Step 2?
choices: The function reads the price from the database, stores it in the cache with a 120-second TTL, and returns it.
The function writes the price to both the database and the cache, then returns it.
The function returns a 'not found' result and waits for the next database write to fill the cache.
The function reads the price from the database and returns it, but leaves the cache unchanged.
questions.why: In cache-aside, a miss means reading the source of truth, storing that result in the cache with its TTL, and then returning it, which is why the request at 50 s can hit.

questions.prompt: A team sets a TTL (time to live) of 10 minutes on every item in their ElastiCache cluster. What does that TTL guarantee about each cached item?
choices: A cached copy can be out of date for at most about 10 minutes before it expires and is reloaded.
The cache will evict the item after 10 minutes only if its memory is full.
The database will refuse writes to that item for 10 minutes.
The item will always match the database exactly for its first 10 minutes.
questions.why: A TTL is an expiry time on each item, so it puts an upper limit on how stale that copy can get. It does not keep the copy current during that window.

questions.prompt: A sports app shows live match scores. Scores are written to the database a few times per minute, and fans must never see an old score in the cache. The team accepts some extra cost on each write. Which way of filling the cache fits best?
choices: Cache-aside with a long TTL, so the first read of each score is cached
Write-through, so every score write to the database also updates the cache
Cache-aside with no TTL, so popular scores stay cached forever
Relying on eviction to remove old scores when memory fills up
questions.why: Write-through updates the cache on every database write, which keeps cached copies current at the cost of extra work per write, exactly the trade-off this team accepts.

questions.prompt: A news site caches articles with cache-aside, and every key has the same 300-second TTL. Right after each deploy empties the cache, and then roughly every 5 minutes, the database is flooded with reads and slows down. What is happening, and what is the fix?
choices: A cache stampede. The fix is to raise every key's TTL to the same 3600 seconds.
Stale data. The fix is to remove the TTL so items never expire.
Eviction is removing items too early. The fix is to add more cache memory.
A cache stampede. The fix is to add random jitter to the TTLs and let one request rebuild each hot key.
questions.why: Identical TTLs and an emptied cache make many keys miss at once, which is a stampede. Jitter spreads the expiry times out, and allowing one rebuild per hot key stops duplicate database reads. A longer identical TTL still expires keys together, and having no TTL leaves users seeing old data indefinitely.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how cache-aside caching with a TTL speeds up reads, and name the tradeoff you accept by choosing the TTL length.
lessons.modelAnswer: We put a fast in-memory cache, such as ElastiCache or DAX in front of DynamoDB, between our code and the database. With cache-aside, the code checks the cache first. A hit returns immediately. A miss reads the database, stores a copy, and then returns it, so only data people actually ask for gets cached. Each copy has a TTL, an expiry time, so it eventually gets refreshed. The tradeoff is freshness against load. A long TTL means more hits and less database work, but users can see data that is up to that old. A short TTL keeps data fresher but sends more reads to the database. We also shouldn't let many keys expire together, for example by using identical TTLs or flushing the cache on deploy, because the burst of misses can overwhelm the database. Adding jitter to TTLs and letting a single request rebuild each hot key avoids that stampede.
rubricPoints: A cache holds copies of frequently read data in fast memory, while the database stays the source of truth.
Cache-aside checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and fills the cache.
A TTL limits how stale a cached item can become.
Longer TTLs trade freshness for fewer database reads.
Mass expiry or an emptied cache can cause a stampede of misses that overloads the database.

suggested.rationale: The mission has the learner diagnose a slowdown caused by a cache emptying after a deploy, which exercises cache misses, TTLs and stampede prevention directly.

lessons.plain: Different questions need different storage. A key-value database is brilliant when you already know the exact key, like finding a book by its catalogue number. It is poor at answering "which books mention lighthouses and storms, best matches first?" A specialized data store is one built around a particular kind of question. A search engine such as Amazon OpenSearch Service (a managed search and analytics engine) handles free-text, fuzzy, ranked search. Other specialized stores handle relationships (graph databases) or readings over time (time-series databases). Choosing well means looking at how the data will be asked for, then picking the store designed for that kind of question.
lessons.guessPrompt: An online shop keeps its products in a database where you can only look items up quickly by product ID. Customers now want to type "waterproof hiking boot" and see the best matches first, even if they misspell a word. Do you think the existing database can do this well, and if not, what kind of tool would you add?
lessons.teach:
An access pattern is a description of how your application reads or writes data: which fields it filters on, whether it needs exact matches or ranked results, and how often. A specialized data store is a database designed to make one family of access patterns fast and cheap. Amazon DynamoDB, a managed key-value and document database, is fast when you supply a partition key, but it has no built-in way to search inside text. Amazon OpenSearch Service is a managed search engine. It builds an inverted index, which is a lookup table from each word to the documents containing it, so a text query jumps straight to matching documents and scores them by relevance. It also supports fuzzy matching (tolerating typos), filters and aggregations (counts and groupings). Other examples of matching store to pattern: a graph database such as Amazon Neptune for "friends of friends" relationship queries, and a time-series database such as Amazon Timestream for readings indexed by time.

Worked example. A shop stores products in DynamoDB keyed by productId. A customer searches "waterprof boots". Step one: DynamoDB stays the source of truth, the authoritative copy. Step two: DynamoDB Streams, a change feed of every write, triggers a Lambda function. Step three: the function copies the product's name and description into an OpenSearch index. Step four: the search API queries OpenSearch, which tolerates the typo, ranks waterproof boots first, and returns product IDs. Step five: the app fetches full details from DynamoDB by ID if needed.

A common mistake is forcing search into the key-value store with a scan plus a "contains" filter. A scan reads every item, so cost and latency grow with the table, results are unranked, and typos fail. The opposite mistake is treating the search index as the only copy of data. The tradeoff of the two-store design is that the index is eventually consistent: a newly saved product may take a moment to appear in search results, and you now run and pay for a second system.

questions.prompt: A city council runs a help-desk app. Each support ticket is saved in a DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database) keyed by ticketId. A DynamoDB Streams change feed triggers a Lambda function that copies each ticket's title and description into an Amazon OpenSearch Service index (a managed search engine), so staff can search text like "streetlight brokn". The design is worked through as follows. Step A: DynamoDB is the source of truth, the authoritative copy of every ticket. Step B: searches go to OpenSearch, which tolerates the typo and ranks the best matches first. Step C: a clerk saves a new ticket about a broken streetlight and searches for it two seconds later, but it is not in the results. A minute later it appears. Step D (missing): the explanation for Step C. Which statement correctly completes Step D?
choices: The DynamoDB write failed the first time and was retried automatically, so the ticket did not exist in the table until a minute later.
OpenSearch can only match words already in its index, so new words are added in a scheduled overnight rebuild and the ticket matched by luck.
The search index is eventually consistent: the change has to flow through the stream and the Lambda copy before OpenSearch can return it, so brief lag is expected.
The partition key ticketId was chosen badly, so DynamoDB hid the new item from queries until its partition was rebalanced.
questions.why: In a two-store design the index is updated after the source-of-truth write via the change feed and function, so newly saved items can take a moment to appear in search.

questions.prompt: A developer explains that OpenSearch can answer a text query without reading every document. Which description of an inverted index supports that claim?
choices: A log of every write in time order, so the engine replays recent changes to find the documents a query needs.
A cache of the most recent query results, so repeated searches return instantly without touching any documents.
A copy of the table sorted by partition key, so the engine reads items in key order until it finds a match.
A lookup table from each word to the documents that contain it, so a query jumps straight to the matching documents.
questions.why: An inverted index maps words to the documents containing them, so matching documents are found directly instead of by reading everything.

questions.prompt: A professional networking startup needs to answer queries like "which people have worked with someone who has worked with me?" quickly as its user base grows. Based on matching the store to the access pattern, which choice fits best?
choices: A time-series database such as Amazon Timestream, because each working relationship has a start date.
A key-value store such as DynamoDB with a scan and a contains filter over every user's colleague list.
A graph database such as Amazon Neptune, because the query follows relationships between people in several hops.
A search engine such as Amazon OpenSearch Service, because it ranks people by how relevant their profile text is.
questions.why: Friends-of-friends style queries traverse relationships, which is the access pattern a graph database like Neptune is designed for.

questions.prompt: A recipe website stores 2 million recipes in DynamoDB keyed by recipeId. To add search, a developer runs a scan with a "contains" filter on the recipe description for every search request. Users type queries such as "chiken curry". What should the team expect?
choices: Each search reads every item, so cost and latency grow with the table, results come back unranked, and the misspelled query finds nothing.
Typo-tolerant results, because DynamoDB applies fuzzy matching to filters, though results are not ranked by relevance.
Fast, ranked results, because the contains filter uses the partition key to jump to matching items.
Correct results but only for the first 2 million items, after which DynamoDB automatically moves the data into OpenSearch.
questions.why: A scan reads the whole table, and a contains filter neither ranks results nor tolerates typos, so this is the common mistake of forcing search into a key-value store.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we would add OpenSearch next to DynamoDB for product search instead of doing everything in DynamoDB, and name at least one tradeoff of doing so.
