Common mistake: expecting a public ACM certificate to work on a self-managed web server, or forgetting to distribute the private root to clients. In production, an expired or untrusted certificate breaks every connection at once, which is why automatic renewal matters.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain wants HTTPS for its public ordering site, menu.crumbco.com, which sits behind a load balancer. Here is the plan, traced step by step. Step 1: In AWS Certificate Manager (ACM, the managed certificate service), request a free public certificate for menu.crumbco.com. Step 2: ??? Step 3: ACM issues the certificate, and the team attaches it to the load balancer. Step 4: Browsers trust it because it chains to a public CA they already trust, and ACM renews it automatically before it expires. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Create a root CA in AWS Private CA and add it to every customer's browser trust store.
Prove control of menu.crumbco.com, usually by adding the DNS record that ACM provides.
Import the certificate back into ACM so that ACM will begin renewing it automatically.
Export the certificate's private key from ACM and copy it onto the load balancer.
questions.why: ACM issues a public certificate only for a name you prove you control, and this is usually done by adding a DNS record.

questions.prompt: A startup runs its web server software directly on its own virtual machine, with no load balancer, CloudFront or API Gateway in front of it. The team requested a public ACM certificate for app.tidelog.io and now wants to install it on that server. What is the problem, and what is a workable fix?
choices: Public ACM certificates expire after one day on servers, so the team should switch on renewal in the server settings.
Public ACM certificates are trusted only by machines the team configures, so the team should give its root certificate to every visitor.
The private key of a public ACM certificate cannot be exported, so the team should put an ACM-integrated load balancer in front and attach the certificate there.
There is no problem, because the team can download the certificate and its key from ACM and install both on the server.
questions.why: ACM keeps the private key of a public certificate and will not export it, so the certificate only works on integrated services such as a load balancer.

questions.prompt: A travel agency bought a certificate from an outside certificate authority. It imported the certificate into ACM and attached it to its load balancer. The certificate is valid for 13 months. What must the team do to avoid an outage?
choices: Get a new certificate and re-import it before the current one expires, because ACM does not renew imported certificates.
Nothing, because ACM automatically renews every certificate that it stores.
Convert the certificate into an AWS Private CA certificate so that browsers keep trusting it.
Export the private key from ACM each month so that the load balancer keeps a fresh copy.
questions.why: ACM renews only the certificates it issues itself; an imported certificate stays your responsibility to replace before it expires.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs 40 containers that call each other over mutual TLS (mTLS), where both sides present a certificate. The containers use internal names such as stock.corp. Each container needs its certificate and private key installed inside it. Which approach fits?
choices: Use AWS Private CA to create the company's own CA, issue exportable private certificates, and make every container trust the private root.
Skip certificates and rely on the load balancer's DNS records to prove each container's identity.
Import certificates from a public CA into ACM, and rely on ACM to renew them inside the containers.
Request free public ACM certificates for the stock.corp names and export them with their private keys into the containers.
questions.why: Private CA issues private certificates for internal names, and those certificates can be exported with their keys; they work only on machines configured to trust your private root.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate when you would use a public ACM certificate and when you would use AWS Private CA, and name one limit or tradeoff of each.
lessons.modelAnswer: A certificate proves a service's name and carries its public key, signed by a CA the client trusts. For anything the public internet reaches, like our customer-facing load balancer or CloudFront site, I'd use a public ACM certificate: it's free, browsers already trust it, and ACM renews it automatically. The limit is that we can't export its private key, so it only works on integrated services, not on our own servers, and imported certificates aren't renewed for us. For internal traffic, such as mTLS between microservices, I'd use AWS Private CA to run our own CA and issue certificates for internal names. Those can be exported for instances and containers. The tradeoffs are cost, and that every client must have our private root in its trust store, or connections fail even with a valid certificate.
rubricPoints: Defines a certificate as binding a name to a public key, signed by a trusted CA.
Public ACM certificates suit internet-facing integrated services and renew automatically.
Public ACM certificate private keys cannot be exported, and imported certificates are not auto-renewed.
AWS Private CA issues certificates for internal names, such as service-to-service mTLS.
Clients must trust the private root, and Private CA carries a cost.

suggested.rationale: No mission or engine exercises certificates, so reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which certificate source fits which endpoint adds the most.

lessons.plain: Encryption scrambles data so only someone holding the right key can read it. The question here is who does the scrambling. With server-side encryption, you hand readable data to a storage service, and the service locks it before saving it to disk. With client-side encryption, your own program locks the data before sending it, so the service only ever holds scrambled data. Think of a storage company. Either you hand them your papers and they lock them in their safe, or you lock the papers in your own box before handing it over. Then the company never sees what is inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app saves customers' passport numbers in a database that the cloud provider encrypts on disk. A support engineer has permission to read rows from that table. When they open a row, do you think they see the passport number or scrambled text? Why?
lessons.teach:
Server-side encryption means your app sends plaintext (readable data) to a storage service. The service encrypts it before writing to disk and decrypts it for any caller allowed to read it. Client-side encryption means your app turns the data into ciphertext (scrambled data) before it leaves your code, so the service stores only ciphertext. The real difference is where plaintext exists and who can decrypt it.

Amazon S3, an object store, offers three server-side options. With SSE-S3, S3 manages the keys entirely. With SSE-KMS, the keys live in AWS KMS, a managed key service, and a separate key policy plus an audit log control who may decrypt. With SSE-C, you send your own key with each request, and S3 uses it and then discards it. For client-side encryption, a library such as the AWS Encryption SDK encrypts inside your process, usually by envelope encryption. A fresh data key encrypts the record, and a KMS key encrypts that data key. Field-level encryption protects chosen attributes rather than whole records.

Worked example: an app stores a passport number in DynamoDB, a managed database.

Server-side only: the app sends the number over an encrypted connection, and DynamoDB encrypts it on disk. Anyone with read permission on the table sees it in clear.

Client-side: the app gets a data key from KMS, encrypts the number, and stores the ciphertext plus the encrypted data key. A table reader sees gibberish unless they are also allowed to decrypt with that KMS key.

The tradeoff: server-side encryption is nearly effortless. Client-side encryption keeps plaintext away from the storage service and anyone with only storage access. The cost is more code, no searching or indexing on encrypted fields, and key handling becomes your job.

Common mistake: believing that bucket or table encryption hides data from people who can read it through the API. It protects disks, not authorized reads.

Consequence: lose a client-side or SSE-C key and that data is gone for good, because AWS cannot recover it.

questions.prompt:
A veterinary clinic's app stores lab results as objects in Amazon S3 and uses client-side envelope encryption. Each stored object holds two things: the encrypted lab result and an encrypted data key, which a KMS key protected when the object was written. A vet now opens result #4471, and the app reads it back like this.

Step 1: The app downloads the object from S3. It receives the encrypted lab result and the encrypted data key, and neither is readable yet.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The app uses the now-readable data key to decrypt the lab result inside its own process.
Step 4: The app shows the plaintext result to the vet and discards the readable data key.

What is Step 2?
choices: The app asks S3 to decrypt the object with the bucket's default encryption setting, which returns the readable data key.
The app sends the encrypted data key to KMS, which decrypts it only if the app is allowed to use that KMS key.
The app requests a brand-new data key from KMS and uses that new key to unlock the stored lab result.
The app decrypts the encrypted data key with the lab result, because the two were encrypted together.
questions.why: In envelope encryption a KMS key encrypts the data key, so the app must have KMS decrypt that data key, and this works only if the caller has permission on the KMS key, before the data key can unlock the record.

questions.prompt: A travel agency stores booking spreadsheets in an S3 bucket that uses SSE-S3, where S3 manages the encryption keys entirely. A contractor has an IAM role that allows downloading objects from that bucket and nothing else. What does the contractor get when they download a spreadsheet through the S3 API?
choices: Readable plaintext, because server-side encryption decrypts for any caller allowed to read
An access-denied error, because SSE-S3 requires a separate KMS key policy
Ciphertext plus an encrypted data key that they must send to KMS
Ciphertext, because the bucket is encrypted and the contractor holds no key
questions.why: Server-side encryption protects data on disk, and the service decrypts it for any caller with read permission. SSE-S3 adds no extra key permission check, so the contractor sees plaintext.

questions.prompt: A delivery company keeps orders in a DynamoDB table. Its database administrators can read the whole table, but they must never see customers' phone numbers. The app still needs to look up orders by order ID. Which approach meets both needs?
choices: Turn on SSE-KMS for the table so the phone numbers are encrypted on disk
Use client-side field-level encryption on the phone number only, leaving the order ID readable
Switch the table to SSE-C so the company supplies its own key with each request
Encrypt each whole order record client-side, order ID included, before writing it
questions.why: Field-level client-side encryption keeps phone numbers as ciphertext even for table readers who lack KMS decrypt rights, while the unencrypted order ID can still be searched and indexed.

questions.prompt: A small analytics startup uploads reports to S3 using SSE-C, sending its own key with every request. An engineer accidentally deletes the only copy of that key. What happens to the reports encrypted with it?
choices: AWS Support can restore access, because S3 keeps a backup of every customer-provided key
They are permanently unreadable, because S3 discarded the key after use and AWS cannot recover it
The startup can decrypt them by asking KMS to generate a replacement data key
S3 automatically re-encrypts them with SSE-S3 so the startup can still read them
questions.why: With SSE-C, S3 uses the supplied key and then discards it, so if the customer loses the key, the encrypted data is gone for good.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "Our DynamoDB table is encrypted, so the customer PII is safe." Explain to them the difference between client-side and server-side encryption, who can actually read the data in each case, and one cost of switching to client-side encryption.
lessons.modelAnswer: Table encryption is server-side. DynamoDB encrypts data before it hits disk and decrypts it automatically for anyone allowed to read the table. That protects against someone stealing the storage, not against our own admins, a debugging script, or a leaked read credential. Those all see plaintext. With client-side encryption, our code encrypts the PII fields before writing, often with a data key protected by a KMS key. The table then holds only ciphertext. To read it, you need table access and permission to decrypt with that KMS key, so two separate controls must both allow it. The cost: we can no longer query, filter, or index on those encrypted fields. We also add code and own the key handling. If a key we manage is lost, that data is unrecoverable.
rubricPoints: Server-side encryption means the service encrypts on write and decrypts for any authorized reader.
Client-side encryption means the app encrypts before sending, so the service stores only ciphertext.
Storage-level encryption does not hide data from callers who have read permission.
Client-side encryption with KMS requires both data access and decrypt permission on the key.
Names a tradeoff such as losing query or index on encrypted fields, added complexity, or unrecoverable data if the key is lost.

suggested.rationale: Encrypting a field yourself in an envelope encryption lab, and then seeing what a plain table reader sees, makes the difference in who can decrypt concrete in a way reading alone does not.

lessons.plain: Encrypting data means scrambling it with a secret value called a key, so it is useless to anyone without that key. Decrypting means using the right key to turn it back into readable form. On AWS, a managed key service called AWS Key Management Service (KMS) keeps your most important keys locked inside itself, and your code asks it to use them. Think of a bank vault that holds the master key and never lends it out. You bring small locked boxes to the counter to be opened, and the bank checks your ID every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: A bank holds your master key and will never let it leave the building, and it only opens small envelopes at the counter. You need to protect a 2 GB file. How could you use that master key without ever carrying the whole file to the bank?
lessons.teach:
Encrypting means feeding plaintext (readable data) and a key into an algorithm to produce ciphertext (unreadable output). Decrypting means feeding the ciphertext and the right key back in to recover the plaintext. On AWS, keys are held by AWS Key Management Service (KMS), a managed key store whose master keys never leave it unencrypted. A KMS key is that master key, named by an ID or an alias. Your code never sees its raw bytes. It asks KMS to use the key. Every request is checked against the key policy (the permissions document attached to the key) and against IAM permissions, and every request is logged.

KMS can encrypt data directly, but only small payloads of up to 4 KB, and each call is a network round trip. For real data you use envelope encryption. KMS generates a data key, which is a key your code uses locally, and returns it twice: once in plaintext and once encrypted under your KMS key.

Worked example: encrypting a 2 MB customer file. Step 1: the code calls GenerateDataKey and names the KMS key. Step 2: KMS returns a plaintext data key and an encrypted copy of it. Step 3: the code encrypts the file locally with the plaintext data key, using a standard algorithm such as AES-256. Step 4: the code wipes the plaintext key from memory and stores the ciphertext file next to the encrypted data key. Reading the file later takes two more steps. Step 5: the code sends the encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt. KMS checks that the caller is allowed kms:Decrypt and returns the plaintext data key. Step 6: the code decrypts the file locally and wipes the key again.

This works because only KMS can unwrap the data key. Control over the data therefore equals control over who may call Decrypt on that KMS key, and the large data never travels to KMS.

A common mistake is storing the plaintext data key in a database column, a log or an environment variable, which silently defeats the encryption. Another is sending large payloads to Encrypt, which fails with a size error. In a running system, if a role loses kms:Decrypt or the key is disabled, reads fail with access denied even though the data is intact. If the key is deleted, the data cannot be recovered.

questions.prompt: A logistics company called Harbourline has a nightly job that writes a 300 MB shipment export to storage using envelope encryption. Next to the encrypted export it stores the encrypted copy of the data key. A separate reporting function, running under a role that has been granted kms:Decrypt on the same KMS key (the managed master key held inside AWS Key Management Service), now needs to read the export. Step 1: the reporting function loads the encrypted export and the encrypted data key from storage. Step 2: ??? Step 3: the function decrypts the 300 MB export locally with AES-256 using the plaintext data key. Step 4: it wipes the plaintext data key from memory once the report is built. What is Step 2?
choices: Send the full 300 MB encrypted export to KMS Decrypt so that KMS returns the readable export directly.
Read the plaintext data key from an environment variable that the nightly job set when it first encrypted the export.
Call GenerateDataKey on the same KMS key to get a fresh plaintext data key, then use that fresh key to decrypt the export.
Send the encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt, which checks the role's kms:Decrypt permission and returns the plaintext data key.
questions.why: Only KMS can unwrap the encrypted data key, so the function sends that small encrypted key to Decrypt and gets back the plaintext data key it needs to decrypt the large export locally.

questions.prompt: A fitness app called PulseTrack encrypts each user's workout history with envelope encryption. Each record is encrypted locally with its own data key, and each data key is stored encrypted under one KMS key. An auditor asks what actually decides who can read these records. What is the most accurate answer?
choices: Whoever is allowed to call kms:Decrypt on that KMS key, because only KMS can unwrap the stored data keys.
Whoever knows the KMS key's alias, because the alias is enough to unwrap the data keys locally.
Whoever has the raw bytes of the KMS key, which the app downloads once at startup and caches.
Whoever can read the database table, because the encrypted data keys are stored right next to the records.
questions.why: The stored data keys are useless until KMS unwraps them, so control over the data equals control over who may call Decrypt on the KMS key, as checked by the key policy and IAM permissions.

questions.prompt: At an online bookshop called Pagewise, an invoice service reads envelope-encrypted invoices without trouble. After a permissions cleanup, every read starts failing with an access denied error. Nobody touched the stored invoices or the KMS key itself, and the key is still enabled. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The KMS key was deleted, so the invoices can no longer be recovered by anyone at all.
The service's role lost the kms:Decrypt permission, so KMS will not unwrap the data keys, though the invoices are intact.
The encrypted data keys grew past the 4 KB limit, so KMS rejects them with an access error.
The invoices were corrupted during the cleanup, so KMS refuses to process the damaged ciphertext.
questions.why: When a caller loses kms:Decrypt, KMS denies the request to unwrap the data key, so reads fail with access denied even though the encrypted data is unharmed.

questions.prompt: A developer at a video studio called Reelbox writes code that sends each 20 MB raw video clip straight to the KMS Encrypt operation, naming the studio's KMS key. What will happen, and what is the right approach?
choices: It works, but slowly; the fix is to send the clips in parallel so the network round trips overlap.
It fails with a size error because KMS Encrypt only accepts small payloads of up to 4 KB; use envelope encryption with a data key instead.
It fails with access denied because KMS keys can only encrypt other keys; grant kms:Encrypt to the role to fix it.
It works, but the clips are stored in plaintext; the fix is to store the KMS key's raw bytes alongside each clip.
questions.why: KMS Encrypt handles only payloads of up to 4 KB, so large data must be encrypted locally with a data key from GenerateDataKey, which is envelope encryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how your service should encrypt and later decrypt a large customer record using a KMS key. Say why you would not just call KMS Encrypt on the record, and name one risk or tradeoff of relying on KMS.
lessons.modelAnswer: We use envelope encryption. The service calls GenerateDataKey on our KMS key and gets back a data key in two forms: plaintext and encrypted. We encrypt the record locally with the plaintext data key, throw that key away, and store the ciphertext together with the encrypted data key. To read the record, we send the encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt. KMS checks our IAM and key-policy permissions, hands back the plaintext key, and we decrypt locally. We don't call Encrypt directly on the record because KMS only accepts about 4 KB, and shipping big data over the network on every call is slow. The tradeoff is dependency. Every decrypt needs KMS to be reachable and our role to keep kms:Decrypt. If the key is disabled, reads fail. If the key is deleted, the data is gone for good. We must also never persist the plaintext data key.
rubricPoints: Defines a KMS key as a master key that stays inside the managed service and is used by request.
Describes envelope encryption: GenerateDataKey, encrypt locally, store the encrypted data key with the ciphertext.
Explains decryption as sending the encrypted data key to KMS Decrypt, which is gated by key policy and IAM permissions.
Notes the roughly 4 KB direct-encrypt limit as the reason not to send large data to KMS.
Warns never to store or log the plaintext data key.
Names a dependency risk, such as lost permissions, a disabled key, or a deleted key making data unreadable.

suggested.rationale: The planned envelope encryption lab would have the learner generate, wrap, store and unwrap data keys step by step, which is exactly this objective.

lessons.plain: A key pair is two matching pieces of data: a public key you can hand to anyone, and a private key that only you keep. It works like a padlock and its only key. You give out open padlocks (public keys) freely, and only your key (private key) proves the lock is yours. SSH keys use this to let you log in to a remote server without a password. A certificate is a public key wrapped in an ID card that says who owns it. During development you often make these yourself, cheaply and quickly, while keeping the private half secret.
lessons.guessPrompt: You want to log in to a new cloud server from your laptop using a key pair. Which half of the pair should be copied onto the server, and which half should never leave your laptop?
lessons.teach:
A key pair is a matched public key and private key: data scrambled with one half can only be checked or unscrambled with the other. SSH (Secure Shell) is the protocol used to log in to remote machines. It uses key pairs so that the server stores your public key, and you prove you hold the matching private key without ever sending it.

There are two common ways to get an SSH key for an EC2 virtual server. You can let AWS create an EC2 key pair, and you download the private key file once. AWS does not keep a copy you can fetch later. Or you can generate the pair yourself with a tool like ssh-keygen and import only the public key into AWS. The same idea applies when you register an SSH public key on an IAM user for Git access.

Worked example: you run ssh-keygen on your laptop and get dev_key (private) and dev_key.pub (public). You import dev_key.pub into EC2 and launch an instance with it. At boot, the instance places that public key in its list of authorized keys. When you connect using dev_key, the server sends a challenge, your SSH client signs it with the private key, the server checks the signature against the public key, and you are let in.

A certificate is a public key plus identity details (such as a domain name), signed by a certificate authority (CA), which is an issuer that clients trust. TLS is the encryption protocol that uses certificates to secure connections like HTTPS. For local testing you can make a self-signed certificate (signed by its own key) with a tool like openssl. Clients will not trust it by default and will show warnings. Public certificates from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) are free and renew automatically, but they attach to AWS services such as load balancers, and you cannot export their private keys.

A common mistake is committing a private key to a repository, or disabling certificate checks in code to silence self-signed warnings and then shipping that code. In a running system, the first mistake lets anyone with repo access log in. The second leaves production traffic open to interception.

questions.prompt: Priya joins a small logistics firm, Harbourline, and needs to push code to a Git repository that authenticates people through their IAM user's SSH keys. Step 1: on her workstation she runs ssh-keygen, which produces two files, hl_git (private key) and hl_git.pub (public key). Step 2: ??? Step 3: she points her Git client at hl_git. Step 4: when she pushes, the Git server sends a challenge, her client signs it with hl_git, and the server checks the signature against the key on file for her IAM user and lets her push. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Upload hl_git, the private key, to her IAM user, so the server holds the exact key she will sign with.
Make a self-signed certificate with openssl and attach it to her IAM user in place of either key file.
Upload hl_git.pub, the public key, to her IAM user, and keep hl_git only on her workstation.
Upload both files to her IAM user, so the server can match the pair itself.
questions.why: The server only needs the public key to check signatures, and with SSH you prove you hold the private key without ever sending it, so only hl_git.pub is registered.

questions.prompt: At a weather-data startup, Tomás launches an EC2 virtual server and lets AWS create the key pair. He downloads the private key file, then accidentally deletes it a week later. Based on how AWS-created EC2 key pairs work, what is true?
choices: He can connect without it, because the instance keeps the private key in its authorized keys list.
He cannot download that private key from AWS again, because AWS does not keep a copy he can fetch later.
He can download it again from the EC2 console, because AWS keeps the private key for every key pair it creates.
He can rebuild the private key from the public key that AWS still stores.
questions.why: With an AWS-created EC2 key pair you download the private key file once, and AWS does not keep a copy you can retrieve later.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company is putting a public HTTPS website behind an AWS load balancer. The team wants a certificate that browsers trust, that costs nothing, and that renews without anyone remembering to do it. Which option fits?
choices: A self-signed certificate made with openssl and uploaded to the load balancer
An exported ACM certificate whose private key is copied onto each web server
An SSH key pair from ssh-keygen, with the public key placed on the load balancer
A public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), attached to the load balancer
questions.why: Public ACM certificates are free, renew automatically, and attach to AWS services such as load balancers, whereas a self-signed certificate is not trusted by clients by default, an SSH key pair is not a certificate, and ACM private keys cannot be exported.

questions.prompt: While testing an order service against a local HTTPS endpoint that uses a self-signed certificate, a developer at a furniture retailer gets trust warnings. To make them stop, she turns off certificate checking in the HTTP client code, and that code later ships to production unchanged. What is the main risk in the running system?
choices: Production traffic is open to interception, because the client no longer verifies who it is talking to.
Anyone with access to the repository can now log in to the production servers over SSH.
The ACM certificate on the production load balancer will stop renewing automatically.
The production service will refuse every connection, because certificate checking was turned off.
questions.why: With certificate checks turned off, the client will accept any certificate, so an attacker can sit in the middle of production connections and read or change the traffic.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would set up an SSH key and a TLS certificate for a development environment on AWS, where each private key lives, and what the limits of a self-signed certificate are.
lessons.modelAnswer: For SSH, I generate a key pair myself with ssh-keygen, or let EC2 create one. Either way, the public key goes to AWS and onto the instance, and the private key stays only on my machine. If EC2 creates the key pair, I get exactly one chance to download the private key, and it never goes into Git. When I connect, the server checks a signature made with my private key against the stored public key, so the private key is never sent anywhere. For HTTPS in dev, I can make a self-signed certificate with openssl. It encrypts traffic, but no trusted certificate authority vouches for it, so browsers and clients warn. That makes it fine for local testing and wrong for production. For real endpoints I'd use an ACM certificate on a load balancer, which renews automatically. The tradeoff is that ACM public certificates can't be exported to run on my own server. I also never turn off certificate verification in code just to get past self-signed warnings.
rubricPoints: The public key goes on the server or AWS, and the private key stays only with the user.
An EC2-created private key can be downloaded only once, or you can generate your own pair and import just the public key.
SSH login works by proving possession of the private key, not by sending it.
A self-signed certificate encrypts traffic, but clients don't trust it, so it suits development only.
ACM public certificates are free and auto-renew, but their private keys can't be exported.
Never commit private keys or disable certificate verification in shipped code.

suggested.rationale: This objective is mostly about which tool or service creates each key or certificate and where each half belongs, which is best absorbed by reading and recall rather than through a listed mission or engine.

lessons.plain: Encryption across account boundaries means letting a program in one cloud account use data that was locked with an encryption key owned by a different account. Each account is a separate walled-off space with its own owners and permissions, so by default nobody outside can touch your keys. To share, both sides must agree: the key's owner writes a rule saying 'that other account may use this key,' and the other account separately decides which of its own users or programs actually get that power. Think of a safe-deposit box. The bank has to list you as allowed, and you still have to hand your key to a specific family member before they can open it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Account A encrypts files with its own key and shares them with Account B. Account A adds a rule saying Account B may use the key, but Account B's program still gets 'access denied.' What do you think is still missing?
lessons.teach:
Cross-account encryption is the practice of letting principals (users, roles, or services that can act) in one AWS account encrypt or decrypt with a key held in another account. On AWS the key lives in AWS KMS (Key Management Service), a managed service that stores encryption keys and performs cryptographic operations without ever handing out the raw key.

Two kinds of permission decide who may use a KMS key. A key policy is a permission document attached directly to the key; every key has one, and it is the primary gatekeeper. An IAM policy is a permission document attached to a principal inside an account. Within one account, the key policy can delegate to IAM. Across accounts, both must say yes: the key policy in the owning account must allow the other account (or a specific role in it), and the other account's IAM policy must allow its own principal to call actions such as kms:Decrypt on that key's full identifier, its ARN (Amazon Resource Name, a unique address for a resource). A grant, a narrower delegated permission attached to the key, is an alternative to editing the key policy.

Worked example. Account A stores reports in an S3 bucket encrypted with a customer managed KMS key (a key A created and controls). A Lambda function in Account B, running as role ReportReader, must read them. Step 1: A edits the key policy to allow Account B's ReportReader role to use kms:Decrypt. Step 2: A's bucket policy lets that role call s3:GetObject. Step 3: B attaches an IAM policy to ReportReader allowing kms:Decrypt on A's key ARN and s3:GetObject on the bucket. Step 4: Lambda calls GetObject; S3 asks KMS to decrypt the object's data key; KMS checks both policies, both allow, and the object returns.

Common mistake: encrypting with an AWS managed key (the default key AWS creates per service, such as aws/s3). Its key policy cannot be edited, so it can never be shared across accounts. In a running system this shows up as access-denied errors at read time, even though the S3 permissions look correct, and the fix requires re-encrypting data under a customer managed key.

questions.prompt: A freight company keeps its customer managed KMS key in Account Hub. Messages on an SQS queue (a managed message queue) in Account Hub are encrypted with that key. A container app in Account Depot, running as role ManifestConsumer, must read and decrypt those messages. Step 1: Account Hub edits the key policy to let Depot's ManifestConsumer role use kms:Decrypt. Step 2: Account Hub's queue policy lets ManifestConsumer receive messages. Step 3: ??? Step 4: The app reads a message. KMS checks the permissions on both sides, both allow, and the decrypted message is returned. What is Step 3?
choices: Account Depot attaches an IAM policy to ManifestConsumer allowing kms:Decrypt on the key's full ARN in Account Hub.
Account Hub switches the queue to the AWS managed key for SQS so Depot can use it without policy edits.
Account Hub attaches an IAM policy to its own admin role that allows kms:Decrypt on behalf of Account Depot.
Nothing further is needed, because the key policy in Account Hub already names the ManifestConsumer role.
questions.why: Across accounts, both the key policy in the owning account and an IAM policy in the calling account must allow the action, so Depot must grant its own role kms:Decrypt on the key's ARN.

questions.prompt: Which statement about a KMS key policy is accurate?
choices: It is optional, and keys without one fall back to IAM policies in the account.
It is attached directly to the key, every key has one, and it is the primary gatekeeper for using the key.
It is attached to a user or role and lists which keys that principal may use.
It only matters for keys that are shared with other accounts.
questions.why: A key policy is a permission document on the key itself; every key has one and it is the main control over who may use the key.

questions.prompt: A clinic's Account Records writes patient files to S3 using the default aws/s3 encryption key. A billing service in Account Claims gets access-denied errors when reading them, even though the bucket policy and the service's IAM policy both allow s3:GetObject and kms:Decrypt. What fixes this?
choices: Give the billing role s3:GetObject a second time in the bucket policy.
Add kms:Decrypt for Account Claims to the aws/s3 key policy.
Re-encrypt the files under a customer managed key whose policy allows the Claims role.
Wait for the IAM changes to propagate; the errors will clear on their own.
questions.why: An AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited, so it can never be shared across accounts; the data must be re-encrypted under a customer managed key that can grant access.

questions.prompt: A retailer's Account Ledger owns a customer managed KMS key. A role in Account Storefront has an IAM policy allowing kms:Decrypt on that key's ARN, but the key policy does not mention Storefront at all, and no grant exists. What happens when the role calls Decrypt?
choices: It succeeds, because KMS returns the raw key to any account that requests it.
It is denied, because customer managed keys can never be used across accounts.
It is denied, because the owning account's key policy (or a grant) must also allow it.
It succeeds, because the caller's IAM policy names the key's ARN.
questions.why: Cross-account use needs both sides to say yes: the caller's IAM policy and the key policy (or a grant) in the owning account.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what has to be configured so a service in another AWS account can decrypt data encrypted with your KMS key, and name one limit or tradeoff of this setup.
lessons.modelAnswer: Cross-account decryption needs agreement from both accounts. In our account, the KMS key's key policy has to name the other account or, better, the specific role that needs access, and allow only the actions it needs, like kms:Decrypt. That alone isn't enough: the other account must also attach an IAM policy to its role allowing kms:Decrypt on our key's ARN. If the data is in S3 or another service, that resource's own permissions must allow access too. A grant can stand in for a key policy edit when we want narrow, revocable access. The big limit is that this only works with a customer managed key; AWS managed keys like aws/s3 have fixed policies and can't be shared, so data encrypted under them would need re-encrypting. The tradeoff is that we own and maintain the key policy, and naming a whole account instead of one role widens who can decrypt.
rubricPoints: The key policy in the owning account must allow the other account or a specific principal.
The other account's IAM policy must also allow its principal to use the key's ARN.
Both sides must allow; one side alone still results in access denied.
AWS managed keys cannot be shared cross-account, so a customer managed key is required.
Grant only needed actions to a specific role rather than a whole account, or use a grant for narrow access.
The data's resource permissions, such as a bucket policy, must also allow access.

suggested.rationale: Cross-account encryption is fundamentally a two-sided permission check, and an authorization policy evaluator would let the learner see a decrypt fail until both the key policy and the IAM policy allow it.

lessons.plain: Key rotation means swapping the secret material inside an encryption key for fresh material on a schedule, while everything that points at the key keeps working. Think of a building that changes the lock cylinder every year but keeps the same front door and the same door number. New visitors get new keys, and the building manager keeps the old cylinders in a drawer so old keys still open old safes. Rotation limits how much data any one piece of key material protects. Enabling it turns the schedule on; disabling it turns the schedule off, without destroying anything.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a company swaps the secret inside its encryption key every year, what do you think must happen so that files encrypted three years ago can still be opened?
lessons.teach:
In AWS Key Management Service (KMS, a managed service that stores encryption keys and performs encryption for you), a KMS key is a named key with an ID, an ARN (Amazon Resource Name, its unique address) and a key policy (the rules saying who may use it). Inside it sits key material, the actual secret bits. Automatic key rotation, when you enable it on a customer managed key (a key you created and control), makes KMS generate new key material on a schedule, by default once a year, and you can usually choose a different period or trigger an on-demand rotation. AWS managed keys (keys AWS creates for a service on your behalf) rotate yearly on their own and you cannot change that.

Why it works: the key ID, ARN, alias and policy never change, so no code or permission needs editing. KMS keeps every older version of the material. Each ciphertext (encrypted output) carries a hidden reference to the material that produced it, so KMS picks the right version when decrypting. Nothing has to be re-encrypted.

Worked example: in January you enable rotation on key orders-key. You encrypt invoice A; KMS uses material version 1. A year later rotation adds version 2. You encrypt invoice B with version 2. You then decrypt invoice A; KMS reads its reference, uses version 1, and it works. Next you disable rotation. Versions 1 and 2 both stay; future encryption keeps using version 2 and no version 3 appears.

Limits: automatic rotation applies to symmetric encryption keys made by KMS. Asymmetric keys, HMAC keys and keys with imported material do not get it; for those you rotate manually by creating a new key and moving an alias (a friendly name) to it, while keeping the old key so old data can still be decrypted.

Common mistake: confusing disabling rotation with disabling the key. Disabling the key blocks every encrypt and decrypt call, so a running application immediately starts failing, while disabling rotation only stops future material from being created.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic stores pet medical notes encrypted with a customer managed symmetric KMS key named vet-notes-key. Trace what happens. Step 1: In March 2023 the team turns on automatic rotation, and KMS creates key material version 1. Step 2: The app encrypts note P-17 with version 1. Step 3: In March 2024 the yearly rotation adds version 2. Step 4: The app encrypts note P-42 with version 2. Step 5: In June 2024 the team disables rotation. Step 6: In August 2025 the app asks KMS to decrypt note P-17. What happens in Step 6?
choices: The call fails because disabling rotation deleted version 1, keeping only the newest material.
KMS decrypts it with version 2, because version 2 is the current material when rotation stops.
KMS reads the hidden reference inside P-17's ciphertext, uses version 1, and the decryption succeeds.
The call fails until the team re-encrypts P-17 with version 2, because older notes must be migrated after rotation.
questions.why: KMS keeps every older version of the key material, even after rotation is disabled, and each ciphertext points to the version that made it, so P-17 is decrypted with version 1.

questions.prompt: An engineer at a ticketing company wants to stop new key material from being generated for the customer managed key that the live payments service uses. By mistake, they disable the key itself instead of disabling rotation. What does the running payments service experience?
choices: Encryption keeps working, but decrypting older data fails.
Every encrypt and decrypt call using that key fails immediately, so the service starts erroring.
Only data encrypted after today is affected; existing ciphertext still decrypts.
Nothing changes now; only the next scheduled rotation is skipped.
questions.why: Disabling a key blocks all encrypt and decrypt calls with it, unlike disabling rotation, which only stops future key material from being created.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup created a KMS key using key material it imported from its own hardware. Auditors ask the team to rotate this key. Which approach fits?
choices: Enable automatic rotation on the key and choose a 180-day period.
Create a new key, move the alias to it, and delete the old key right away so nobody can use it.
Disable the key, then re-enable it, which forces KMS to generate fresh key material.
Create a new key, move the alias (the key's friendly name) to it, and keep the old key so older data can still be decrypted.
questions.why: Keys with imported material do not get automatic rotation, so you rotate manually by moving an alias to a new key while keeping the old key for decrypting existing data.

questions.prompt: A bookshop's order service calls KMS using the ARN (unique address) of a customer managed symmetric key. The team enables automatic rotation, and a rotation happens six months later. What must the developers change in their code or permissions?
choices: Update the code to use the new ARN that rotation produces.
Re-encrypt all existing orders so the new material can read them.
Nothing; the key ID, ARN, alias and key policy stay the same after rotation.
Update the key policy so the service may use the new key material.
questions.why: Rotation only adds new key material inside the same KMS key, so the ID, ARN, alias and policy are unchanged and old ciphertext still decrypts without re-encryption.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what turning on automatic rotation for a KMS key actually changes, why old encrypted data still decrypts afterwards, and name one limit or tradeoff they should know about.
lessons.modelAnswer: Turning on rotation tells KMS to generate fresh key material for that customer managed key on a schedule, a year by default. The key's ID, ARN, alias and key policy stay the same, so our code and permissions do not change. KMS keeps all old material, and every ciphertext records which material encrypted it, so decrypting old data just works without re-encrypting anything. New encryptions use the newest material, which limits how much data any single piece of material protects. Disabling rotation only stops new versions; existing ones remain. A limit: automatic rotation only covers symmetric keys whose material KMS generated. Asymmetric, HMAC or imported-material keys need manual rotation: create a new key, point the alias at it, and keep the old key for old data. And never confuse disabling rotation with disabling the key, which breaks every call.
rubricPoints: Rotation replaces the key material while keeping the key ID, ARN, alias and policy unchanged.
Old material is retained, so existing ciphertext decrypts without re-encryption.
Disabling rotation stops new versions but deletes nothing.
Customer managed keys rotation is opt-in, while AWS managed keys rotate yearly automatically.
Asymmetric, HMAC and imported-material keys need manual rotation via a new key and alias change.
Disabling the key itself is different and breaks all encrypt and decrypt calls.

suggested.rationale: An envelope encryption lab lets the learner rotate a key, then watch old and new ciphertexts both decrypt, which makes the idea of retained key material concrete.

lessons.plain: Data classification means sorting the information your application handles by how much harm it would cause if it leaked, so you know how carefully to treat each piece. Personally identifiable information (PII) is anything that can point to a specific person, such as a name, email address or passport number. Protected health information (PHI) is health data, like a diagnosis or prescription, that is tied to an identifiable person. Think of a post room that stamps envelopes ordinary, private or confidential before deciding which ones go in the locked cabinet. The stamp comes first. The protection follows from it.
lessons.guessPrompt: A clinic app stores a patient's email address, their blood test result, and the app's colour theme preference. Which of these would you protect most carefully, and why?
lessons.teach:
Data classification is the practice of labelling each kind of data by sensitivity, then applying protection that matches the label. A typical scheme has levels such as public, internal, confidential and restricted. Personally identifiable information (PII) is data that identifies a person directly, like a full name or national ID number, or indirectly when pieces are combined, like a postcode plus a birth date plus a gender. Protected health information (PHI) is a term from HIPAA, a United States health privacy law. It means health information, such as conditions, treatments or payments for care, that is linked to an identifiable individual. PHI is almost always placed in the highest level.

This works because protection costs effort. Encryption, tight access rules, audit logging and masking all add work. Classifying first lets you spend that effort where a leak would hurt, instead of guessing field by field.

Here is a worked example with one DynamoDB item from a clinic booking app, where DynamoDB is AWS's managed key-value database. Step 1: the field appointmentId is a random value that identifies no one, so it is internal. Step 2: patientName and phone are PII, so they are confidential. Step 3: diagnosisCode sits in the same item as the name, so it is PHI and therefore restricted. Step 4: the item takes the protection of its highest field. That means restricted handling for the whole record: encryption, the fewest readers, and no copies in logs.

On AWS, you can record a classification as a tag on a resource, for example a key-value label such as DataClass=PHI. Amazon Macie is a managed service that scans S3 storage buckets and reports objects that appear to contain PII. If you handle PHI, use only services that AWS lists as HIPAA eligible, under a signed agreement with AWS.

A common mistake is to judge each field on its own. A diagnosis code with no name attached looks harmless, but once it sits beside a name it becomes PHI. In a running system, unclassified PHI ends up in debug logs, test copies and analytics exports, where far too many people can read it.

questions.prompt: A city transit agency gives a research team a CSV file of trips. Each row has rideCount, homePostcode, birthDate and gender. The team classifies the file like this. Step 1: rideCount is just a number of journeys and identifies no one, so it is internal. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: the file takes the protection of its most sensitive columns, so the whole file is handled as confidential. It is encrypted, only a few named researchers can read it, and the bucket is tagged DataClass=Confidential. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: homePostcode, birthDate and gender describe a person's body and home, so they are PHI and the file must be restricted.
homePostcode, birthDate and gender each identify no one on their own, so they are internal like rideCount.
homePostcode is printed on public maps, so these columns are public and need no protection.
homePostcode, birthDate and gender look harmless one at a time, but together they can single out one person, so they are PII and confidential.
questions.why: PII includes data that identifies someone indirectly when pieces are combined. A postcode plus a birth date plus a gender is exactly that kind of combination, so the columns are confidential and not PHI, because no health information is linked.

questions.prompt: An insurance company stores one database record per claim. A record holds the policyholder's full name, the claim number, and a payment made for the policyholder's knee surgery. Under a scheme of public, internal, confidential and restricted, how should this record be classified?
choices: Internal, because claim numbers are random values that identify no one.
Restricted only for the payment field, while the rest of the record stays internal.
Restricted, because a payment for medical care linked to a named person is PHI, and the record takes the level of its most sensitive field.
Confidential, because the name is PII and payment amounts are only financial data.
questions.why: PHI covers payments for care that are linked to an identifiable individual, and PHI is almost always placed in the highest level. A record gets the protection of its highest field.

questions.prompt: A telehealth company copies its production customer table into a test environment that the whole engineering department can read. Each item holds customerName and bloodType. The team labelled bloodType as internal because a blood type alone identifies no one. What is the problem?
choices: The problem is cost, because classified data must always be stored in a separate database.
bloodType sits beside a name, so it is PHI. Misjudging it field by field has put restricted health data where far too many people can read it.
The only issue is customerName, which is PII. bloodType is correctly internal.
There is no problem, because test environments never need the same protection as production.
questions.why: Judging each field on its own is the common mistake. Health data linked to a name becomes PHI, and unclassified PHI tends to leak into test copies with broad access.

questions.prompt: An online retailer suspects that some objects in its S3 storage buckets contain customer PII nobody knew about. It also wants each bucket to carry a visible label of its sensitivity. Which approach fits?
choices: Turn on Amazon Macie, which encrypts every object it finds and so removes the need for labels.
Use Amazon Macie to scan the buckets and report objects that appear to contain PII, then record each bucket's classification as a tag such as DataClass=Confidential.
Add a DataClass tag to each bucket, because tagging a bucket automatically scans and encrypts its contents.
Check the HIPAA eligible services list, which reports which S3 objects contain PII.
questions.why: Macie is a managed service that scans S3 buckets and reports likely PII. A tag is a key-value label that records the classification, and the tag itself does not scan or encrypt anything.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would classify the fields in a new customer table and why it matters, including one limit or tradeoff of classifying data.
lessons.modelAnswer: Classification means labelling each type of data by how harmful a leak would be, then matching the protection to that label. PII is anything that identifies a person, either directly, like a name or ID number, or through combinations such as postcode plus birth date. PHI is health information linked to an identifiable person, and it goes in the top tier. I would walk through the table field by field, remembering that combinations matter. A record takes the level of its most sensitive field, so one diagnosis column makes the whole row restricted. I would tag the table with its classification and keep those fields out of logs and test data. The tradeoff is that higher tiers cost more: encryption, narrower access and auditing slow developers down. If you overclassify, everything becomes painful to use. If you underclassify, PHI quietly ends up in places like debug logs.
rubricPoints: Defines classification as labelling data by sensitivity to decide its protection.
Defines PII, including indirect identification through combined fields.
Defines PHI as health data linked to an identifiable person and places it in the highest tier.
States that a record inherits the level of its most sensitive field.
Names a tradeoff, such as protection cost versus usability, or the risk of under-classifying.

suggested.rationale: Classifying data is mainly a judgement skill, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario where you sort a record's fields into PII, PHI and harmless builds it better than reading or any existing mission.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function, which is a piece of code AWS runs for you on demand, often reads settings from environment variables: named values like DB_PASSWORD that sit next to the code instead of inside it. Some of those values are sensitive. Encrypting them means storing them scrambled, so that only someone holding the right key can read them. Think of a hotel safe in your room. The hotel locks every safe by default, but staff with the master code can still open it. Setting your own code means only you can open it.
lessons.guessPrompt: If AWS already encrypts your function's environment variables automatically, can a colleague who is allowed to view the function's settings in the console still read your database password? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Encrypting environment variables means keeping sensitive values unreadable without a key held in AWS KMS (Key Management Service), a managed service that stores encryption keys and performs encrypt and decrypt operations for you. Lambda does two levels of this.

The first level is automatic encryption at rest, which means the values are scrambled while they are stored. By default Lambda uses an AWS managed key, a KMS key that AWS creates and controls for your account. You can switch to a customer managed key, a KMS key you create and whose key policy (the rules for who may use it) you write. Lambda decrypts the values when the function starts, so your code reads plain text.

The second level is the console's encryption helpers, which encrypt a value with your KMS key before it is saved. The stored value stays ciphertext (scrambled text) even in the console and API. Your code must then call KMS Decrypt itself, and the execution role, the IAM role the function runs as, needs kms:Decrypt permission on that key.

Worked example: you store DB_PASSWORD using a helper and a customer managed key. Step 1: the console sends the password to KMS and saves the ciphertext. Step 2: a teammate opening the function sees only gibberish. Step 3: on a cold start, your code calls KMS Decrypt once, outside the handler function, and keeps the result in memory. Step 4: later invocations reuse it with no KMS call.

Common mistake: assuming default encryption hides the value. With the AWS managed key, anyone allowed to view the function's configuration sees plain text. A customer managed key lets you limit who can read it, because viewers then need kms:Decrypt on that key.

In a running system, decrypting on every invocation adds latency and cost and can hit KMS request limits, causing failures under load. A missing kms:Decrypt permission makes the function fail at startup. For values that must be rotated, a dedicated secrets service is often the better home.

questions.prompt:
A shipping company's Lambda function, a piece of code AWS runs on demand, needs a partner token. Trace the setup and pick the missing step.

Step 1: A developer stores CARRIER_TOKEN with the console's encryption helpers, using a customer managed KMS key named ship-app-key. The stored value is ciphertext.
Step 2: Outside the handler function, the code calls KMS Decrypt on CARRIER_TOKEN.
Step 3: On the first test, the function fails at startup with an access-denied error from KMS.
Step 4: ???
Step 5: After redeploying, one cold start decrypts the token once. The next 3,000 invocations reuse it from memory with no KMS calls.

What is Step 4?
choices: Move the KMS Decrypt call inside the handler so the token is decrypted on every invocation.
Give the function's execution role kms:Decrypt permission on ship-app-key.
Give the developers who view the function kms:Decrypt permission on ship-app-key.
Give the function's execution role kms:Encrypt permission on ship-app-key.
questions.why: The code runs as its execution role, so that role needs kms:Decrypt on the key that encrypted the value, or the function fails at startup.

questions.prompt: A clinic's Lambda function stores PATIENT_API_KEY as an environment variable. The team relies only on Lambda's default encryption at rest with the AWS managed key. A contractor is allowed to view the function's configuration but has no special KMS permissions. What does the contractor see for PATIENT_API_KEY?
choices: Ciphertext only, because all Lambda environment variables are encrypted at rest.
Ciphertext, unless the contractor also has kms:Encrypt permission.
The key in plain text, because the default AWS managed key does not limit who can read the value in the configuration.
Nothing, because environment variables are never shown in the console.
questions.why: With the AWS managed key, anyone allowed to view the function's configuration sees the value in plain text. Limiting readers needs a customer managed key, where viewers must hold kms:Decrypt.

questions.prompt: A ticketing site's Lambda function encrypts an environment variable with the console helpers. Its code calls KMS Decrypt inside the handler function, so it runs on every request. During a sale the function receives about 2,500 requests per second and starts failing. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The AWS managed key expired. Switch to a customer managed key.
The execution role lacks kms:Encrypt. Add that permission.
The environment variable is too large. Split it into two variables.
Decrypting on every invocation hits KMS request limits. Decrypt once outside the handler and keep the result in memory.
questions.why: A Decrypt call on every invocation adds latency and cost and can exceed KMS request limits under load. Decrypting once per cold start and reusing the value avoids this.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's developer stores SUPPLIER_PASSWORD using the console's encryption helpers with a customer managed KMS key. The function code reads the variable directly and uses it as the password without any other step. What happens?
choices: The code receives ciphertext, so the login fails. The code must call KMS Decrypt itself.
The console refuses to save the variable until a secrets service is configured.
It works, but only when the execution role has kms:Encrypt permission.
It works, because Lambda always decrypts environment variables before the code runs.
questions.why: Values encrypted with the helpers stay ciphertext in storage and in the environment, so the code must call KMS Decrypt to get the plain text.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would protect a database password stored in a Lambda environment variable, who can actually read it under each option, and one tradeoff of your choice.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lambda always encrypts environment variables at rest with KMS. By default it uses an AWS managed key, but that only protects storage: anyone who can view the function's configuration sees the password in plain text. If I switch to a customer managed key, I write the key policy, so only people and roles with kms:Decrypt on that key can see the value. For stronger protection I'd use the encryption helper, so the value stays ciphertext even in the console, and the function's execution role calls KMS Decrypt itself. I'd do that decrypt once during a cold start, outside the handler, and cache it, because decrypting every invocation adds latency, costs money and can hit KMS request limits. The tradeoff is more code and permissions to manage. If the password must rotate regularly, a dedicated secrets service is a better fit.
rubricPoints: States that Lambda encrypts environment variables at rest with KMS by default, using an AWS managed key.
Notes that with the default key anyone who can view the function's configuration sees plain text.
Explains that a customer managed key or encryption helper limits reading to principals with kms:Decrypt on that key.
Says the execution role needs kms:Decrypt when the code decrypts values itself.
Recommends decrypting once per cold start and caching, citing latency, cost or KMS request limits.
Names a tradeoff, such as extra code and permissions, or rotation being better served by a secrets service.

suggested.rationale: Encrypting a value with a key, then decrypting it under a role that does or does not hold decrypt permission, makes clear who can read the secret and why.

lessons.plain: A secret is any value that unlocks something, such as a database password or an API key. Secret management means keeping those values in a dedicated, locked store and having the program ask for them when it runs, instead of typing them into the code. Think of a hotel: staff do not write the safe combination on the wall. They ask the front desk, which checks who they are, hands over the code, and writes down who asked. On AWS, the front desk is a service such as Secrets Manager or Parameter Store, and anyone who reads the code never sees the password.
lessons.guessPrompt: A developer pastes a database password directly into a Python file and pushes it to a shared Git repository. Later they delete the line and push again. Is the password safe now? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A secret is any value that grants access, such as a database password, a payment provider's API key, or a signing key. Secret management means storing those values in a dedicated service and having code fetch them at runtime, instead of writing them into source code, config files, or container images.

On AWS there are two main options. AWS Secrets Manager is a managed secret store. It encrypts each secret with a key from AWS KMS (Key Management Service, the managed service that holds encryption keys). It controls who can read the secret through IAM (Identity and Access Management, AWS's permission system). It can also rotate the secret automatically, meaning it replaces the value on a schedule, often by running a small Lambda function. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store is a simpler configuration store. Its SecureString type also encrypts values with KMS and costs less, but it has no built-in rotation.

Why this works: the secret is no longer in the code, so anyone who can read the repository, a build log, or an image still cannot read the password. Reading it requires two permissions: permission to get the secret, and permission to use the KMS key that decrypts it. Every read is recorded in CloudTrail, the AWS audit log.

Worked example: a Lambda function needs a database password. Step 1: store the password in Secrets Manager under the name prod/orders/db. Step 2: give the function's execution role (the IAM role the function runs as) permission to read only that secret and to decrypt with its key. Step 3: in code, fetch the secret once when the function starts and keep it in memory. Step 4: connect to the database. When rotation changes the password, the next fresh fetch picks up the new value without a redeploy.

One common mistake is fetching the secret on every request. This adds latency and cost, and under a traffic surge it can hit API rate limits and make the function fail. Instead, cache the value and refresh it after a time limit or when authentication fails. A second mistake is committing a secret just for testing. Once a secret is in Git history, deleting the line does not remove it, so treat it as leaked and rotate it.

questions.prompt: A small clinic's scheduling app sends text reminders through an SMS provider. While testing, a developer pasted the provider's API key into a test file and pushed it to the team's Git repository. The team fixes it as follows. Step 1: They recognise that removing the line in a new commit does not erase it from Git history, so the key must be treated as leaked. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: They store the new key in a dedicated secret service, such as Secrets Manager or a Parameter Store SecureString, both encrypted with a KMS key. Step 4: They change the app so it fetches the key at runtime and caches it, instead of reading it from a file. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Make the repository private so outsiders can no longer browse the commit that held the key
Rotate the key: generate a replacement with the SMS provider so the leaked value stops working
Move the key out of the test file into a separate config file that is committed alongside the code
Push a new commit that deletes the line containing the key, so the current code no longer shows it
questions.why: A secret that has reached Git history must be assumed exposed, so the only real fix is to replace it so the old value no longer grants access, and then store the new one properly.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup keeps a mapping-service API key that is sensitive but never needs to change on a schedule. They want it encrypted with KMS, readable only by permitted IAM roles, and stored as cheaply as possible. Which option fits best?
choices: A Systems Manager Parameter Store SecureString parameter
An environment variable written into the container image at build time
An AWS Secrets Manager secret with automatic rotation turned on
A plain-text value in a config file kept in the source repository
questions.why: Parameter Store SecureString encrypts with KMS, is controlled by IAM, and costs less than Secrets Manager; its lack of built-in rotation does not matter here.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function at a ticketing company runs under an execution role that is allowed to get the secret named prod/tickets/api. The secret exists and is encrypted with a customer-managed KMS key, yet every attempt to read it is denied. What is the most likely missing piece?
choices: The function must fetch the secret on every request rather than once at startup
The secret must be moved to Parameter Store because Secrets Manager cannot be read from Lambda
The execution role lacks permission to use the KMS key that decrypts the secret
CloudTrail logging must be turned off so the read is not blocked
questions.why: Reading a stored secret requires two permissions, one to get the secret and one to use the KMS key that decrypts it, and only the first has been granted here.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery company's Lambda function fetches its payment API key from Secrets Manager on every single invocation. During a lunchtime surge of about 6,000 requests per minute, invocations start failing with throttling errors from the secret service. What is the best fix?
choices: Switch off automatic rotation so the secret service receives fewer calls
Give the execution role permission to read every secret in the account
Hard-code the key into the function's source so no fetch is needed during surges
Fetch the key once, keep it in memory, and refresh it after a time limit or when authentication fails
questions.why: Caching the value removes a fetch from each request, which avoids rate limits, latency and cost, while refreshing on a timer or on an authentication failure still picks up rotated values.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our service should read its database password from Secrets Manager or Parameter Store instead of keeping it in the code or a config file. Include how the code gets permission to read it, and name one tradeoff or limit of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: If the password sits in code or a config file, anyone with access to the repo, a build log, or the container image can read it. Deleting it later doesn't help, because Git history keeps it, so it has to be rotated. Instead, we store it in Secrets Manager, or as a SecureString in Parameter Store, where it is encrypted with a KMS key. Our function's execution role gets IAM permission to read that one secret and to decrypt with that key, and nothing more. Every read lands in CloudTrail. Secrets Manager can also rotate the password automatically; Parameter Store is cheaper but has no built-in rotation. The tradeoff is that fetching is a network call that adds latency, cost, and a rate limit. So we fetch once at startup, cache the value, and refresh when authentication fails or the cache expires.
rubricPoints: Secrets in code, config files, or images are exposed to anyone who can read them, and Git history keeps them even after they are deleted.
Secrets Manager or Parameter Store SecureString stores the value encrypted with a KMS key.
Access is granted through the app's IAM role, with least-privilege permission to read the secret and use the key.
Secrets Manager offers automatic rotation, while Parameter Store is simpler and cheaper but has no built-in rotation.
Fetching adds latency, cost, and rate limits, so cache the value and refresh it on failure or expiry.
A leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.

suggested.rationale: That mission has the learner wire a deployment to a secret store without exposing the secret, which is exactly this objective in practice.

lessons.plain: Sanitizing sensitive data means removing or hiding private values, such as card numbers, passwords, email addresses or tokens, before they leave the safe place where they are needed, for example before they are written to a log, shown on a screen or put in an error message. Data masking is one way to sanitize: you replace most of a value with filler characters and keep only a harmless piece, like showing a card as ************4242. Think of a bank statement that prints only the last four digits: you can still recognise your card, but anyone reading over your shoulder cannot use it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app logs every incoming checkout request so you can debug failures later, and each request contains the customer's full card number and email address. Who might end up seeing those values, and what would you change before the log line is written?
lessons.teach:
Sanitizing is the practice of stripping or disguising sensitive values before data crosses into a less trusted place: logs, metrics, error messages, analytics exports or a user interface. Sensitive values include secrets (passwords, API keys, bearer tokens) and personally identifiable information, or PII, meaning data that identifies a person, such as a name, email or card number. There are three common techniques. Redaction removes the value entirely and leaves a placeholder like [REDACTED]. Masking keeps a small, harmless part so humans can still recognise it, for example j***@example.com. Tokenization swaps the value for a random stand-in whose mapping to the real value is kept in a separate, protected store.

It works because the safest copy of sensitive data is the one never made. Logs are copied, retained for months and readable by many engineers, so anything written there spreads.

Worked example. A handler receives {email: ana@example.com, card: 4111111111114242, token: abc123}. Step one: a sanitize function walks the fields. Step two: the token is redacted to [REDACTED] because no part of a secret is safe to show. Step three: the card is masked to keep only the last four digits, ************4242. Step four: the email is masked to a***@example.com. Step five: only this sanitized copy is passed to the logger; the original stays in memory for the real payment call.

On AWS, CloudWatch Logs (the managed log service) can apply a data protection policy that detects and masks patterns like emails or card numbers in a log group, and Amazon Macie scans S3 storage buckets to find PII you did not know was there. These are safety nets; masking in your own code comes first.

Common mistake: masking only what the screen displays while logging the raw request, or treating masking as encryption. Masking is one-way and partial; it does not protect the stored original. In a running system, one unsanitized debug line can copy thousands of card numbers into logs that many people and tools can read.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic's booking API writes a debug log line for each request. One request body is {patientName: "Liam Ortiz", phone: "07700 900318", partnerApiKey: "pk_live_7Qx2m9Lw"}. The developer traces the sanitize step like this. Step one: a sanitize function walks each field of a copy of the request. Step two: (missing). Step three: the phone number is masked so that only its last three digits remain, giving ********318. Step four: the name is masked to L*** O***. Step five: only the sanitized copy goes to the logger, and the original object is still used to send the SMS reminder. What should step two do with partnerApiKey?
choices: Leave it unchanged, because a CloudWatch Logs data protection policy will catch it later.
Redact it completely, replacing it with a placeholder such as [REDACTED].
Mask it to pk_l************ so engineers can tell which partner key was used.
Tokenize it, and write the token-to-key mapping into the same log line for convenience.
questions.why: An API key is a secret, and no part of a secret is safe to show, so redaction removes it entirely. Masking would leave part of it visible, and a data protection policy is only a safety net, not a replacement for sanitizing in your own code.

questions.prompt: A bookshop chain exports purchase data to an analytics team. Before the export, each customer's email address is replaced with a random value such as tk_83jd91. A table that links each tk_ value back to the real email is kept in a separate database that only the billing team can read. Which sanitizing technique is this?
choices: Masking
Partial display
Tokenization
Redaction
questions.why: Tokenization swaps the real value for a random stand-in and keeps the link back to the real value in a separate, protected store. That is exactly what the bookshop does with the tk_ values and the restricted lookup table.

questions.prompt: A logistics company suspects that years of old uploads have left files containing customer names and card numbers in its S3 storage buckets. Nobody knows which buckets are affected. Which AWS service is designed to scan those buckets and find PII the team did not know was there?
choices: Amazon Macie
A sanitize function added to the upload Lambda handler
Masking the card numbers on the customer web page
A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy on each log group
questions.why: Amazon Macie scans S3 buckets to discover PII you did not know was stored there. A CloudWatch Logs data protection policy works on log groups, not buckets, and code changes or screen masking do nothing about files that are already stored.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app shows customers their saved card as ************7781 on the checkout page. To investigate a bug, a developer adds a debug line that logs the full incoming request body, and that body includes the complete card number. Which statement best describes this situation?
choices: It is unsafe, because full card numbers are now copied into logs that many people and tools can read.
It is safe, because masking the card on screen also protects every other copy of it.
It is safe, because masking is a form of encryption, so the logged value cannot be read.
It is only a risk if the logs are kept for longer than a year.
questions.why: Masking only changes what the screen displays. It does not protect the raw request, and it is not encryption, so logging the full body copies every card number into widely readable, long-retained logs. The data should be sanitized before it reaches the logger.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what sanitizing and masking sensitive data at the application level means, where in the code it should happen, and one limit or tradeoff of relying on it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Sanitizing means we clean sensitive values out of data before it goes somewhere less trusted, like logs, error messages, metrics or the UI.
