Masking is one technique: we keep a recognisable fragment, such as the last four card digits, and hide the rest. Secrets like tokens or passwords should be fully redacted, because even part of one is risky. The right place is in our own code, just before the data is written or returned, so the raw value never lands in a log that is retained and widely readable. Tools like CloudWatch Logs data protection or Macie are useful backstops, not replacements. The tradeoff is debuggability: heavily masked logs make some problems harder to trace, so we may need correlation IDs instead. Also, masking is not encryption; it does nothing to protect the original value wherever it is stored.
rubricPoints: Defines sanitizing as removing or disguising sensitive values before they reach less trusted places such as logs or error messages.
Distinguishes masking (keep a harmless fragment) from redaction (remove entirely), and redacts secrets fully.
Says sanitizing should happen in application code before data is logged or returned.
Notes that managed tools like CloudWatch Logs data protection or Macie are backstops, not the primary control.
Names a limit: masking is not encryption, or masked logs reduce debuggability.

suggested.rationale: That mission makes the learner fix a deployment while keeping a secret out of output and logs, which directly practises the habit of sanitizing sensitive values.

lessons.plain: A multi-tenant application serves many separate customers, called tenants, from one shared system. A data access pattern for it is the plan for where each tenant's data sits and what stops one tenant from ever seeing another's. Think of an apartment building. Some buildings give every family its own house (separate storage per tenant). Others put everyone in one block, where each flat has its own locked door (shared storage, with every record labelled by tenant). The shared block is cheaper to run, but it is only safe if every door is locked by something stronger than residents promising to stay out.
lessons.guessPrompt: Imagine 500 customer companies all store their orders in one shared table. What would you add to every row, and do you think it is safe to rely only on the application code remembering to filter by customer? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
A multi-tenant data access pattern decides how each tenant's records are stored and how requests are kept inside one tenant's data. A tenant is one customer organisation using your shared application. There are three common shapes. In silo, each tenant gets its own table, database, or even AWS account. It gives the strongest isolation, but it costs the most and is the most work to operate. In pool, all tenants share one table and every item carries a tenant ID. It is the cheapest option, and its safety depends entirely on how strictly that tenant ID is enforced. Bridge mixes the two, for example a shared table for small tenants and dedicated tables for large ones.

In a pooled Amazon DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database), put the tenant ID at the start of the partition key. The partition key is the attribute DynamoDB uses to group and find items, for example pk = TENANT#acme#ORDER#981. Then enforce isolation below your own code. An IAM policy is a JSON document that grants AWS permissions. It can use the condition key dynamodb:LeadingKeys, which allows a request only if the partition key it touches matches a value taken from the caller's identity. That value can come from a session tag, which is a key-value label attached to temporary credentials when a role is assumed, such as tenant=acme.

Here is a worked example. An acme user signs in, and the tenant comes from their verified token. The backend assumes a role and passes the session tag tenant=acme. The policy allows reads only on partition keys starting with TENANT# followed by that tag value. A Query on TENANT#acme#ORDER#981 matches, so it is allowed. Now suppose a bug builds TENANT#globex#ORDER#5. The condition fails and DynamoDB returns AccessDenied, so the faulty code leaks nothing.

The common mistake is relying only on application filtering. One example is scanning the whole table and then filtering by tenant. Another is trusting a tenant ID sent in the request body. One missed filter exposes another customer's data. A Scan, which reads every item in the table, also burns capacity across all tenants.

In a running pooled system, one heavy tenant can also eat the shared throughput and slow everyone else. This is the noisy-neighbor problem, and silo isolation avoids it.

questions.prompt:
A dental-clinic booking app keeps every clinic's appointments in one shared (pooled) DynamoDB table. The partition key looks like TENANT#brightsmile#APPT#3307. Here is how a request is handled.
Step 1: A receptionist from the Brightsmile clinic signs in and receives a verified token that names their clinic.
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The IAM policy on that role uses dynamodb:LeadingKeys to allow reads only on partition keys that begin with TENANT# followed by the caller's tenant tag value.
Step 4: A Query for TENANT#brightsmile#APPT#3307 matches the rule and is allowed. A buggy Query for TENANT#pinecrest#APPT#12 does not match and is denied.
Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: The backend reads the clinic name from a tenantId field in the JSON request body and uses it to choose which items to return.
The backend runs a Scan of the whole table and keeps only the items whose tenant attribute equals brightsmile.
The backend assumes a role and attaches the session tag tenant=brightsmile, taken from the verified token.
The backend creates a separate DynamoDB table named brightsmile and copies that clinic's appointments into it.
questions.why: The LeadingKeys condition in Step 3 needs a tenant value that comes from the caller's identity, and the session tag tenant=brightsmile, set from the verified token when the role is assumed, provides that value.

questions.prompt: A project-tracking SaaS stores its hundreds of small customers in one shared table, where every item carries a tenant ID. Its three largest enterprise customers each get their own dedicated table. Which multi-tenant pattern is this?
choices: Bridge, because it mixes shared and dedicated storage
Leading-key isolation, because each item has a tenant ID
Pool, because most tenants share one table
Silo, because some tenants have their own tables
questions.why: Bridge combines pool and silo, for example a shared table for small tenants and dedicated tables for large ones.

questions.prompt: A fitness-studio platform uses a pooled DynamoDB table. To list one studio's class bookings, its code Scans the entire table and then filters the results by the studioId that the browser sends in the request body. What is the main problem with this design?
choices: Scans can only read items in a single partition, so some bookings will be missed.
The approach is safe, because IAM automatically checks the studioId in the request body.
Isolation depends only on application code and an untrusted ID, so one bug or a forged ID exposes other studios' data, and the Scan uses capacity across all tenants.
DynamoDB rejects Scans on pooled tables unless the table has a sort key.
questions.why: Relying only on application filtering and a client-supplied tenant ID leaves no enforcement below your code, and a Scan reads every item in the table, which burns shared capacity.

questions.prompt: In a pooled table shared by forty logistics companies, one company starts running large hourly reporting jobs. Every other company now sees slow responses. What is this problem called, and which storage shape avoids it?
choices: The noisy-neighbor problem, which a pool shape avoids
A partition-key collision, which a Scan-then-filter design avoids
The noisy-neighbor problem, which silo isolation avoids
A LeadingKeys failure, which session tags avoid
questions.why: When one heavy tenant consumes shared throughput and slows everyone else, that is the noisy-neighbor problem, and giving tenants their own resources (silo) prevents it.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would keep tenants' data apart in a shared DynamoDB table, and name one tradeoff between putting all tenants in one table versus giving each tenant its own.
lessons.modelAnswer: We serve many customers, or tenants, from one system, so every piece of data must belong to exactly one tenant, and nothing should be able to cross that line. In a shared (pool) DynamoDB table, I'd start every partition key with the tenant ID, like TENANT#acme#ORDER#981. I wouldn't trust our code alone to filter. The tenant ID comes from the verified sign-in token, gets passed as a session tag when we assume a role, and an IAM policy with the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition only allows keys starting with that tenant's prefix. Then even a buggy query for another tenant's key gets AccessDenied. The tradeoff is that pooling is cheap and simple to run, but tenants share throughput, so one busy tenant can slow others. Isolation also rests on that policy being right. Separate tables or accounts per tenant (silo) isolate data and load more strongly, but they cost more and multiply operational work.
rubricPoints: Defines a tenant and the goal of keeping each tenant's data separate.
Distinguishes silo (separate storage per tenant) from pool (shared storage labelled by tenant ID).
Puts the tenant ID at the start of the DynamoDB partition key.
Enforces isolation with an IAM condition such as dynamodb:LeadingKeys tied to the caller's identity, not just application filters.
Takes the tenant ID from verified identity, never from client-supplied input.
Names a tradeoff such as cost versus isolation or the noisy-neighbor effect.

suggested.rationale: Evaluating whether requests with different tenant session tags pass a LeadingKeys policy condition makes the learner see enforced isolation succeed and fail directly.

lessons.plain: Your code almost never runs alone. It leans on other people's libraries, on settings such as which database table to use, and on a particular language version. Managing dependencies inside the package means making sure everything the code needs travels with it to the cloud, because the server will not have your laptop's extras. Think of packing for a trip to a remote cabin with no shops. Anything you forgot stays forgotten. Settings that change between places, like an address, go on a note you can swap out instead of being sewn into your clothes.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your Python function imports a popular library that you installed on your laptop months ago. You zip only your one source file and upload it to a cloud function service. What do you think happens the first time the function runs, and why?
lessons.teach:
A dependency is anything your code needs in order to run that you did not write in that file: a third-party library, a language runtime, a setting. In AWS Lambda, the managed service that runs your function on demand, there are three main ways to supply these.

First, bundle libraries into the deployment package, the zip file you upload. Lambda provides the language runtime and a few built-in modules, but your third-party libraries must be inside the zip. Second, keep values that change between environments out of the code and in environment variables. These are named key-value settings attached to the function, such as TABLE_NAME=orders-dev, that your code reads when it runs. Lambda caps their combined size at 4 KB, so larger structured settings can live in a configuration file packaged alongside the code. Third, ship a container image. This is a snapshot built from a recipe file, called a Dockerfile, that includes a base operating system layer, the runtime, the libraries and your code together. Images can be up to 10 GB, while a zip must stay within 250 MB once unzipped.

Worked example. A handler imports requests. Step 1: run pip install -r requirements.txt -t build/ so the library lands in a local folder. Step 2: copy handler.py into build/. Step 3: zip the contents of build/ and deploy. Step 4: the code reads os.environ['TABLE_NAME'], so the same zip works in dev and prod with different variable values.

A common mistake is trusting what is installed on your laptop. If you skip step 1, the function fails on every invocation with a module-not-found error. A related trap is a compiled library built on a Mac, which will not load on Lambda's Linux machines. Build on Linux or inside a container that matches Lambda's environment. Also avoid putting secrets in plain config files. Anyone who can read the package can read the file.

questions.prompt: A wildlife charity is moving a Python image-tagging function to AWS Lambda, the managed service that runs code on demand. Its machine-learning libraries plus code total about 3 GB once unzipped. Step 1: the team measures the unzipped size at roughly 3 GB. Step 2: they compare this to the limits. A zip deployment package must stay within 250 MB unzipped, so a zip will not work. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the code reads os.environ['PHOTO_BUCKET'], an environment variable (a named key-value setting attached to the function), so the same package runs in test and production with different bucket names. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Move the library code into environment variables, so the package itself shrinks below the 250 MB zip limit.
Remove the libraries and rely on the built-in modules that Lambda provides with the runtime.
Build a container image from a Dockerfile that holds the base OS layer, runtime, libraries and code, since images can be up to 10 GB.
Compress the zip at a higher setting, so the uploaded file falls under 250 MB.
questions.why: A container image can hold up to 10 GB, so it fits a 3 GB bundle that a zip cannot.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Lambda function needs about 9 KB of structured feature-flag settings that differ between staging and production. The settings contain no secrets. Based on Lambda's limits, where should these settings go?
choices: In a separate container image used only for settings, because zips cannot hold any files except code.
In a configuration file packaged alongside the code, because environment variables are capped at 4 KB combined.
In environment variables, because they have no practical size limit and suit any amount of settings.
Hard-coded in the handler file, because settings should never be kept outside the code.
questions.why: Environment variables are capped at 4 KB combined, so larger structured settings belong in a configuration file packaged with the code.

questions.prompt: A developer at a logistics firm builds a deployment package on a Mac. It includes a compiled library, meaning a library that contains machine code built for a specific operating system. It runs fine locally but will not load on Lambda. What is the best fix?
choices: Increase the zip size limit in the function's settings to make room for the library.
Rename the library folder to match the handler name, so Lambda can find it.
Add the library's name as an environment variable, so Lambda installs it when the function starts.
Rebuild the package on Linux, or inside a container that matches Lambda's environment.
questions.why: Lambda runs on Linux machines, so a compiled library built on a Mac will not load; it must be built on Linux or in a matching container.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking startup puts its payment provider's API key in plain text in settings.json inside its Lambda deployment package. What is the main risk?
choices: Anyone who can read the deployment package can read the key, because a plain config file offers no protection.
The key will push the environment variables over their 4 KB limit, so the deployment will fail.
Lambda will reject the package, because config files are only allowed inside container images.
The function will fail with a module-not-found error, because JSON files cannot be included in a zip.
questions.why: A plain config file is readable by anyone who can read the package, so secrets should not be stored there.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make sure a Lambda function has the libraries and settings it needs in each environment. Say when you would pick a container image over a zip, and name one limit or tradeoff.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lambda only gives us the language runtime. Any third-party library has to be inside what we deploy. For a zip, I install the requirements into a build folder, ideally on Linux so compiled libraries match, then add our code and zip it. Anything that differs between dev and prod, like the table name or the log level, goes in environment variables. The code reads them at runtime, so one artifact works everywhere. The tradeoff is that environment variables are capped at 4 KB, so bigger structured settings go in a config file in the package. Secrets don't belong in either place in plain text. If our dependencies push past the 250 MB unzipped limit, or we need a custom runtime or system packages, I'd build a container image instead, which can reach 10 GB. The cost is that we have to maintain a Dockerfile and keep the base image patched.
rubricPoints: Third-party libraries must be bundled into the package because Lambda provides only the runtime.
Environment variables hold values that change per environment, so one artifact deploys everywhere.
Compiled dependencies must be built for Lambda's Linux environment.
Container images suit large or unusual dependencies, up to 10 GB versus 250 MB unzipped for a zip.
Names at least one limit or tradeoff, such as the 4 KB environment variable cap, image maintenance, or not storing secrets in plain config.

suggested.rationale: The skill shows up as exam-style scenarios, such as an import error after deploy, a package that is too large, or values that differ per stage, where the learner reasons about whether the fix is bundling, environment variables, or a container image.

lessons.plain: Organizing files for deployment means arranging your project folders so the tools that build and run your code find everything exactly where they expect it. Think of packing a moving box for someone else to unpack in the dark: if the label says the kettle is on top, it had better be on top. Cloud services follow fixed rules. A function's entry file must sit at a specific spot inside its package. Build and deploy instruction files must sit at the top of the project. Shared libraries must live in specific folders. When the layout matches the rules, deployments just work.
lessons.guessPrompt: You zip a folder called my-function that contains app.py, then tell a cloud function service to run app.py. The function fails with an error saying it cannot find app. What do you think went wrong with how the zip was made?
lessons.teach:
A deployment package is the bundle of code and libraries you upload so a service can run it. Its internal layout is a contract: the service looks for files at exact paths, not wherever they happen to be.

On AWS Lambda, a managed service that runs your function on demand, you set a handler string such as app.lambda_handler. It means: open the file app.py and call the function lambda_handler. Lambda searches for that file starting at the root, meaning the top level, of the zip. Libraries your code imports must also be at the root, or in a subfolder the language already searches. Lambda layers, which are shared add-on zips mounted under the /opt directory, use language-specific folders: python/ for Python libraries and nodejs/node_modules/ for Node.js.

In an AWS SAM project (SAM is a framework that describes serverless apps in a template file), template.yaml sits at the project root. Each function's CodeUri property points to that function's own folder, for example src/orders/. Pipeline files have fixed homes too. buildspec.yml, the step list for AWS CodeBuild, a managed build service, is expected at the root of the source by default. appspec.yml, the instructions for AWS CodeDeploy, a managed deployment service, must be at the root of the bundle it receives.

Worked example. Handler is app.lambda_handler. You right-click the my-function folder and zip it. Inside the zip the path is now my-function/app.py. Lambda looks at the root, finds only a folder, cannot load app, and reports an import error. Fix: zip the contents of the folder, so app.py lands at the root, or change the handler to my-function/app.lambda_handler.

The common mistake is exactly that: zipping the parent folder instead of its contents. The upload succeeds, so the deployment looks green, but every invocation fails in production. A clear per-function folder layout with CodeUri pointing at each folder prevents this.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking team writes a shared Node.js library called fare-rules and wants several Lambda functions to reuse it through a Lambda layer (a shared add-on zip that Lambda mounts under the /opt directory). Their packaging steps are: Step 1, create an empty working folder named layer-build. Step 2, inside layer-build, create the folder path that Node.js layers are expected to use: ________. Step 3, copy the fare-rules library into that folder. Step 4, zip the contents of layer-build, not the layer-build folder itself, so the path from Step 2 starts at the root of the zip. Step 5, publish the zip as a layer and attach it to the functions. At runtime the library then sits at /opt/<path from Step 2>/fare-rules, where Node.js can find it. Which folder path belongs in Step 2?
choices: nodejs/node_modules/
lib/fare-rules/
node_modules/ at the root, with no parent folder
python/
questions.why: Lambda layers use language-specific folders, and for Node.js the expected path is nodejs/node_modules/, so the library becomes findable under /opt.

questions.prompt: A payroll company sets a Lambda function's handler string to payslips.generate_pdf. What does Lambda do with this string when the function is invoked?
choices: It opens the file payslips.py at the root of the deployment zip and calls the function generate_pdf inside it.
It searches every folder in the zip for any file containing a function named generate_pdf.
It opens the file generate_pdf.py inside a folder named payslips and runs that whole file.
It opens the file payslips.py under the /opt directory and calls generate_pdf.
questions.why: A handler string names the file first and the function second, and Lambda looks for that file starting at the root of the deployment package.

questions.prompt: A food-delivery startup builds an AWS SAM project (SAM is a framework that describes serverless apps in a template file). The project root holds template.yaml and a src folder containing two folders, src/menus/ and src/riders/, one for each function's code. What should the CodeUri property of the riders function point to?
choices: The template.yaml file itself
The project root, so the function can see both folders
src/riders/, the folder holding only that function's code
src/, the shared parent of both function folders
questions.why: In SAM, each function's CodeUri points to that function's own folder, which keeps a clear per-function layout and keeps the handler file at the root of what gets packaged.

questions.prompt: A logistics firm deploys to servers with AWS CodeDeploy, a managed deployment service. Their bundle has this layout: a scripts folder, an app folder, and a deploy folder that contains appspec.yml. The upload itself succeeds, but the deployment cannot proceed because CodeDeploy does not find its instructions. What is the fix?
choices: Move appspec.yml into the app folder next to the application code
Put appspec.yml inside a Lambda layer so it is mounted under /opt
Rename appspec.yml to buildspec.yml so CodeDeploy recognises it
Move appspec.yml out of the deploy folder to the root of the bundle
questions.why: CodeDeploy expects appspec.yml at the root of the bundle it receives, so placing it in a subfolder means the instructions are not found.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why file layout matters when deploying a function, using the handler setting as your example, and name one tradeoff or limit of a strict per-function folder structure.
lessons.modelAnswer: Deployment tools do not search your bundle; they look at exact paths. For a function, the handler setting such as app.lambda_handler tells the service to load app.py from the root of the zip and call lambda_handler. If you zip the parent folder, the file ends up at my-function/app.py, the upload still succeeds, but every call fails with an import error. The same rule applies elsewhere: the build spec and the deploy spec sit at the root of what each service receives, and layer libraries go in language-specific folders like python/. A per-function folder, with the template pointing each function at its own folder, keeps packages small and makes these paths predictable. The tradeoff is duplication: code shared by several functions must be copied, put in a layer, or packaged deliberately, which adds structure to maintain.
rubricPoints: Services look for files at fixed paths rather than searching the bundle.
The handler names a file and function that must sit at the package root.
Zipping the parent folder instead of its contents breaks invocations even though the upload succeeds.
Build and deploy instruction files belong at the root of the source or bundle.
Names a tradeoff, such as shared code needing a layer or duplication across function folders.

suggested.rationale: This is mostly fixed layout rules best cemented by reasoning through exam-style 'deploy succeeded but the function cannot find its module' scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine exercises package layout directly.

lessons.plain: A code repository is a shared, versioned storage place for your project's files, usually managed with Git, a tool that records every change as a numbered snapshot. Using a repository in deployment means the servers never get code straight from someone's laptop. Instead, an automated release process pulls an exact snapshot from the repository and ships that. Think of a restaurant where cooks may only use recipes from the official binder, never from scribbled notes. Every dish can be traced back to one page, and if a dish goes wrong, you can go back to the previous page.
lessons.guessPrompt: If two developers each deploy to production straight from their own laptops, and a bug appears an hour later, what makes it hard to work out which code is actually running?
lessons.teach:
Using a code repository in deployment means the repository is the single source of truth: the only place a release process takes code from. A repository is versioned storage, usually Git. Each saved change is a commit, a snapshot with a unique ID. A branch is a named line of commits, such as main.

A pipeline is an automated sequence of stages: source, build, test, deploy. AWS CodePipeline is a managed pipeline service. Its first stage is the source action, which watches a repository and branch. The repository can be GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket, linked through AWS CodeConnections, an authorized link between AWS and an outside Git host. It can also be AWS CodeCommit, AWS's managed Git service, which no longer accepts new customers. When the watched branch changes, the source action takes that exact commit. It saves the code as an artifact, a zip file stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, which is managed file storage. Later stages use only that artifact.

This works because every deployment ties back to one commit ID. Builds can be repeated, an approved change was reviewed before merge, and nobody needs production credentials on a laptop.

Here is a worked example. A developer merges a fix into main, creating commit a1b2c3. The source action sees the change on main and zips a1b2c3 into the artifact bucket. AWS CodeBuild, a managed build service, builds and tests from that zip. The deploy stage releases it and records a1b2c3. Later, an error appears. The team sees exactly which commit is live and redeploys the previous commit's artifact.

A common mistake is committing secrets, such as database passwords or access keys, into the repository. Everyone with read access, and every old commit, now holds them. Keep secrets in a secrets store and give the pipeline an IAM role, which is a set of AWS permissions it uses without stored keys. A second mistake is hand-patching a running server. The next pipeline run overwrites the patch, and the live code silently differs from the repository until then.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company runs a pipeline whose deploy stage records the commit ID of each release. On Monday it released commit 4d7e91. On Thursday it released commit c03f5a, and checkout errors began within minutes. Step 1: the on-call engineer reads the deploy stage's record and confirms that c03f5a is the commit currently live. Step 2: the engineer checks the release history and sees that 4d7e91 was the last commit that ran without errors. Step 3: ??? Step 4: the deploy stage now records 4d7e91 as live, and the checkout errors stop. What is Step 3?
choices: Redeploy the artifact already built from commit 4d7e91, the zip file stored in the pipeline's S3 artifact bucket.
Copy the project folder from a developer's laptop, which still holds an older version, onto the production servers.
Sign in to each production server and edit the checkout code by hand until it matches what 4d7e91 contained.
Run the pipeline again on commit c03f5a, because a fresh build of the same commit will remove the errors.
questions.why: Every release ties back to one commit ID, so the team can roll back by redeploying the saved artifact of the last good commit rather than by patching or copying code by hand.

questions.prompt: A shipping company's CodePipeline source action watches the branch named prod in its GitLab repository, which is linked to AWS through AWS CodeConnections. A developer pushes three new commits to a branch named experiment-routing. What does the pipeline do?
choices: Nothing. The source action only reacts to changes on the branch it watches, which is prod.
It refuses the push, because CodeConnections only lets commits be pushed to the watched branch.
It deploys all three commits at once, one after another, as soon as they arrive.
It zips the newest commit on experiment-routing and deploys it, because any change in the repository starts the pipeline.
questions.why: The source action watches one specific repository and branch, so commits on any other branch do not trigger a release.

questions.prompt: A developer at a fitness app company commits a file containing the production database password to the Git repository. An hour later, they make a second commit that deletes the file. Which statement best describes the situation?
choices: The problem is fixed, because the newest commit no longer contains the password.
The password is safe as long as the pipeline uses an IAM role instead of stored keys.
The password is still exposed. The older commit still holds it, and anyone with read access to the repository can retrieve it. It belongs in a secrets store instead.
The problem is fixed, but only if the pipeline has not run since the first commit.
questions.why: Each commit is a saved snapshot, so deleting the file in a later commit leaves the secret in the old commit, where everyone with read access can still reach it.

questions.prompt: At 2 a.m., an engineer at an online grocery company fixes a pricing bug by editing the code directly on the running production server. They never commit the change to the repository. What happens next?
choices: The pipeline detects the edit on the server and automatically commits it back to the repository.
The pipeline stops working until someone deletes the edited file from the server.
The next pipeline run overwrites the hand patch. Until that run, the live code silently differs from what the repository says is deployed.
The fix stays in place permanently, because the pipeline only deploys code to servers that have no running application.
questions.why: The repository is the only source the pipeline releases from, so a change made on a server is lost on the next deploy and leaves the live code out of step with the repository until then.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why your team deploys only from the repository through a pipeline instead of from laptops, and name one limit or tradeoff of doing it this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: We treat the Git repository as the single source of truth. The pipeline's source stage watches a branch, such as main, through a connection to GitHub or CodeCommit. When a commit lands, the source stage takes that exact snapshot and saves it as a zip artifact in S3. Build, test and deploy all use that artifact. Every release therefore maps to one commit ID. We can repeat a build, see exactly what is live, and roll back by redeploying an earlier commit. Changes get reviewed before they merge. Nobody needs production credentials on a laptop, because the pipeline uses an IAM role. One tradeoff is speed: even a one-line hotfix must go through commit, build and test, so an emergency fix takes minutes, not seconds. The repository also becomes sensitive. Anything committed, such as a leaked secret, stays in its history, so secrets belong in a secrets store.
rubricPoints: The repository is the single source of truth that deployments pull from.
A pipeline source stage watches a specific branch and captures an exact commit as an artifact.
Each deployment is traceable to a commit ID, which enables repeatable builds and rollback.
Secrets must not be committed; the pipeline should use a role or connection instead of stored keys.
A real tradeoff is named, such as slower hotfixes or manual changes drifting from the repository.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red CI pipeline makes the learner trace how code moves from the repository through build stages, which grounds the idea of the repository as the pipeline's source.

lessons.plain: Every program needs a certain amount of working memory and processing power to run well. When you deploy code to the cloud, you usually have to say up front how much of each it gets, because the cloud reserves that capacity for you and bills you for it. Think of booking a workspace: too small a desk and you cannot spread out your papers, so the job stalls or fails; too big and you pay for empty space. Applying resource requirements means picking the right size, writing it into your deployment settings, and checking that the choice holds up under real work.
lessons.guessPrompt: A serverless function that resizes photos is slow. On this platform you can only adjust one size setting, memory, and there is no separate processor setting. What do you think happens to the function's speed if you double its memory, and why might that be?
lessons.teach:
Resource requirements are the memory, processor (CPU) capacity, temporary disk and time limit you declare for your code so the platform can reserve them. You write them into deployment configuration, such as an AWS SAM template (an infrastructure-as-code file describing serverless resources), so every environment gets the same size.

For AWS Lambda, a managed service that runs your function on demand, memory is the main setting. You choose it from 128 MB up to 10,240 MB. There is no separate CPU setting: Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory, reaching about one full virtual CPU (vCPU, a share of a physical processor core) near 1,769 MB and up to six vCPUs at the maximum. Two other settings matter too. The timeout caps how long one run may last, up to 15 minutes. Ephemeral storage is scratch disk space under /tmp, from 512 MB up to 10 GB. In SAM these appear as MemorySize, Timeout and EphemeralStorage.

For containers on Amazon ECS (a managed container service), a task definition, which is the recipe for running containers, states CPU in units where 1,024 equals one vCPU, plus memory. On AWS Fargate, the serverless way to run those containers, only certain CPU and memory pairings are allowed.

Worked example: Lambda bills by GB-seconds, meaning memory in gigabytes times run time in seconds. An image-resize function at 512 MB runs 4 seconds: 0.5 × 4 = 2 GB-seconds. Raise it to 1,024 MB; the extra CPU cuts the run to 1.8 seconds: 1 × 1.8 = 1.8 GB-seconds. It is faster and cheaper. The gain stops once the work is no longer CPU-bound, so measure at several sizes.

Common mistake: sizing memory only to what the code holds in RAM, leaving a CPU-heavy function starved of processor time, or hunting for a CPU dial Lambda does not have.

In a running system, too little memory causes out-of-memory crashes and too little CPU causes timeouts. Retries of failed runs then add load and cost.

questions.prompt:
A travel company's Lambda function renders booking PDFs. It is CPU-bound. Lambda bills by GB-seconds (memory in gigabytes times run time in seconds).

Step 1: At 256 MB it runs 10 seconds, so 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 GB-seconds.
Step 2: The team raises memory to 2,048 MB. Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory, so the run drops to 1.2 seconds.
Step 3: [missing] Work out the GB-seconds at the new size.
Step 4: Compare the two results to decide whether the larger size is cheaper per run as well as faster.

Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: 0.25 × 1.2 = 0.3 GB-seconds, because billing keeps using the original memory size
1.2 ÷ 2 = 0.6 GB-seconds, because more memory divides the run time
2,048 × 1.2 = 2,457.6 GB-seconds, so it costs far more than before
2 × 1.2 = 2.4 GB-seconds, slightly less than the 2.5 GB-seconds before
questions.why: 2,048 MB is 2 GB, and 2 GB × 1.2 seconds = 2.4 GB-seconds, which is just under the 2.5 GB-seconds at 256 MB.

questions.prompt: A developer at a logistics firm wants their Lambda function to get more processor (CPU) power for a heavy calculation. What should they change in the function's configuration?
choices: Increase EphemeralStorage, since more /tmp space adds processor capacity
Increase the memory setting, because Lambda allocates CPU in proportion to memory
Set a separate vCPU count property next to MemorySize in the SAM template
Increase the Timeout, which also raises the CPU share
questions.why: Lambda has no separate CPU setting; it gives CPU in proportion to the memory you choose, so raising memory raises CPU.

questions.prompt: A retail team is writing an Amazon ECS task definition (the recipe for running their containers) and wants the task to have two full virtual CPUs. What CPU value should they enter?
questions.why: In an ECS task definition 1,024 CPU units equal one vCPU, so two vCPUs is 2 × 1,024 = 2,048.

questions.prompt: A media startup has a Lambda function that compresses audio files. It is set to 256 MB, and its code only ever holds about 100 MB in RAM. The work is CPU-heavy, and the function keeps hitting its timeout; failed runs are retried, adding load and cost. What is the best fix?
choices: Lower memory to 128 MB, because the code is not using the RAM it already has
Raise the memory setting to get more CPU, then measure run time at several sizes
Add a CPU property to the SAM template to request more processor time
Only raise the timeout to 15 minutes so every run has time to finish
questions.why: The function is starved of CPU, not RAM, and in Lambda more memory brings more CPU; measuring at several sizes finds where the speed gain stops.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would choose the memory setting for a Lambda function that is CPU-heavy, and name one limit or tradeoff they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lambda has no CPU knob. You set memory, from 128 MB to about 10 GB, and CPU scales with it, reaching roughly one vCPU near 1,769 MB. So a CPU-heavy function often needs more memory than its code actually holds. I would test the function at a few memory sizes with a realistic payload and record the duration of each run. Cost is memory times duration in GB-seconds, so a bigger size that finishes much faster can cost the same or less. Then I would put the winning value in the SAM template's MemorySize, along with a sensible Timeout, so every environment matches. The tradeoff is that the benefit flattens. Once the work waits on a network or a database instead of the CPU, more memory just costs more. Also, single-threaded code cannot use the extra vCPUs that come at high memory settings.
rubricPoints: States that Lambda CPU is allocated in proportion to memory, with no separate CPU setting.
Explains billing as memory times duration, so more memory can be faster and not more expensive.
Recommends measuring several sizes with realistic input instead of guessing.
Records the chosen values in deployment configuration such as a SAM template.
Names a limit, such as diminishing returns for I/O-bound or single-threaded code, or timeouts and out-of-memory failures.

suggested.rationale: This skill is mostly about reasoning through sizing scenarios that weigh speed, cost and failure, which exam-style situations practise better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: Environment-specific configuration means keeping the settings that differ between development, testing and production (database names, timeouts, feature switches, log levels) outside your code, so the same built package can run anywhere and simply read the right settings for where it lives. Think of a travel adapter: the appliance stays the same, and only the plug changes per country. AWS AppConfig is a managed configuration service that stores these settings per environment, checks them for mistakes, and rolls changes out gradually, so you can change behaviour without rebuilding or redeploying the application.
lessons.guessPrompt: You build one package for your app and want it to use a small test database in development and the real database in production. Where would you put the database name so you never have to rebuild the package to switch?
lessons.teach:
Environment-specific configuration is any value that changes between environments while the code stays identical. The rule is build once, configure per environment: the deployable artifact (the packaged code) is the same everywhere, and settings are injected or fetched at runtime.

AWS AppConfig is a managed service for this. Its terms: an application is a logical name for your workload; an environment is a deployment target such as dev or prod; a configuration profile points to where the data lives, either AppConfig's own hosted store or another source such as Systems Manager Parameter Store (a key-value settings store) or an S3 bucket; a feature flag is a simple on/off switch, optionally with attributes; a validator checks data before release, using a JSON Schema (a description of the allowed shape) or a Lambda function; a deployment strategy controls how fast a change spreads, with a growth rate and a bake time (a watch period after rollout). If a linked CloudWatch alarm fires during deployment or bake time, AppConfig rolls the configuration back automatically.

Worked example: a checkout Lambda function has a flag newPricing. Step one, you create profile pricing-flags with newPricing on in dev and off in prod. Step two, testers confirm it in dev. Step three, you start a prod deployment with a strategy of 20 percent every two minutes plus ten minutes of bake time. Step four, the function reads configuration through the AppConfig Lambda extension, a local helper that caches values and polls for updates. Step five, the error-rate alarm fires at 40 percent, so AppConfig reverts to the previous version. No code was rebuilt at any point.

A common mistake is storing passwords or API keys as plain AppConfig values. Secrets belong in Secrets Manager, which encrypts and rotates them. Another mistake is calling the configuration API on every request instead of caching; this adds latency and cost and can hit request limits under load. Getting this right means a bad setting is contained and reversed in minutes rather than causing a full redeploy.

questions.prompt: A city library runs a room-booking service as a Lambda function. The same packaged code runs in staging and prod. The value maxBookingDays should be 21 in staging and 7 in prod. The team works through these steps. Step one: in AWS AppConfig they create an application called library-booking with two environments, staging and prod. Step two: they create a hosted configuration profile called booking-limits that holds maxBookingDays. Step three is missing. Step four: an engineer edits the prod value and accidentally types the word "seven" instead of the number 7. That bad version is rejected before any function receives it. Step five: a corrected version is released with a strategy of 25 percent every three minutes plus fifteen minutes of bake time. Which step three explains why the bad version in step four never reached any function?
choices: Link a CloudWatch error-rate alarm to the prod environment so AppConfig rolls back bad versions
Turn on the AppConfig Lambda extension so the function caches values and polls for updates
Attach a validator to booking-limits, using a JSON Schema that requires maxBookingDays to be a whole number
Rebuild and redeploy the Lambda package with maxBookingDays hard-coded to 7 for prod
questions.why: A validator checks configuration data against an allowed shape before release, so a text value where a number is required is rejected before it is deployed, whereas an alarm only reacts once a deployment is already running.

questions.prompt: A team at a shipping company sets an AWS AppConfig deployment strategy with a bake time of 20 minutes. What does that bake time do?
choices: It is the time AppConfig waits before running the validator on the new configuration data
After the change has reached all targets, AppConfig keeps watching for 20 more minutes, and a linked CloudWatch alarm firing in that window triggers an automatic rollback
It sets the growth rate, so the new configuration reaches another share of targets every 20 minutes until all are covered
It is how long the AppConfig Lambda extension caches a value before it checks for a newer version
questions.why: Bake time is a watch period after the rollout finishes, and if a linked alarm fires during it, AppConfig reverts to the previous configuration.

questions.prompt: A weather-alerts startup has a Lambda function that calls a paid third-party SMS service. The function needs the endpoint URL, which differs between dev and prod, and an API key for the service. Following good practice, where should each value live?
choices: The API key in AppConfig as a feature flag attribute, and the endpoint URL in Secrets Manager
Both values hard-coded into separate dev and prod builds of the deployment package
Both values as plain values in an AppConfig hosted configuration profile, one profile per environment
The endpoint URL in AppConfig as environment-specific configuration, and the API key in Secrets Manager, which encrypts and rotates it
questions.why: Non-secret settings that vary by environment suit AppConfig, but secrets such as API keys belong in Secrets Manager rather than stored as plain AppConfig values.

questions.prompt: A ticket-sales site's Lambda function calls the AppConfig configuration API directly on every incoming request to read a discount flag. During a big concert on-sale, traffic jumps from 50 to 5,000 requests per second. What problem is most likely, and what is the fix?
choices: Responses get slower, costs rise, and calls may hit request limits, so the function should read through the AppConfig Lambda extension, which caches values locally and polls for updates
The validator runs on every call and rejects the flag under load, so the team should remove the JSON Schema
Each call forces AppConfig to rebuild the deployment package, so the team should switch the profile to an S3 bucket source
The flag will be rolled back automatically because AppConfig treats the extra calls as a failed deployment, so the deployment strategy needs a longer bake time
questions.why: Calling the configuration API on every request adds latency and cost and can exceed request limits under load, and caching through the Lambda extension avoids this.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why we should use one build artifact with AppConfig for per-environment settings instead of separate builds per environment, and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: We build the code once and keep everything that differs between dev, test and prod in configuration, so what we tested is exactly what reaches production. AppConfig holds that configuration per environment under an application and a configuration profile. It validates changes with a JSON Schema or a Lambda validator, then rolls them out using a deployment strategy with a growth rate and bake time. If a CloudWatch alarm fires, it reverts automatically. That lets us flip a feature flag or change a timeout without a redeploy. The tradeoffs: the app now depends on fetching configuration, so we need caching, such as the Lambda extension, and sensible defaults. AppConfig is also not a secrets vault, so credentials stay in Secrets Manager. Finally, configuration changes can break production just like code, which is why validators and gradual rollout matter.
rubricPoints: Same artifact everywhere, with only configuration varying per environment.
Names AppConfig pieces: application, environment, configuration profile, feature flags.
Mentions validation before release, using a JSON Schema or a Lambda validator.
Describes gradual rollout with bake time and automatic rollback on an alarm.
Names a limit, such as needing caching, or that secrets belong in Secrets Manager.

suggested.rationale: No current mission exercises AppConfig, and the exam tests it through scenarios about where settings live, how they are validated and how a bad change is rolled back, so reasoning through situations teaches it best.

lessons.plain: Testing deployed code means checking that your application actually works after it lands in the cloud, not just on your laptop. Code that passes every test locally can still fail once deployed, because the cloud copy runs with different permissions, settings, network paths and real neighbouring services. It is like test-driving a car after it leaves the factory floor: the parts were checked individually, but you only learn whether the assembled car starts on a real road by turning the key there. On AWS you send a real request to the deployed function or API, then read its logs and traces to confirm what happened.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function works perfectly when you run it on your laptop, but it fails within seconds of being deployed to AWS. Before reading anything, list two things that could be different between your laptop and the cloud copy.
lessons.teach:
Testing deployed code is sending real input to the copy of your application that is running in AWS and checking both the response and the evidence it leaves behind. It works because a deployed resource has things your laptop lacks. One is its execution role: the set of permissions AWS grants the running code, written as an IAM policy. The others are its configured environment variables, its network placement, and the live services it calls. A quick post-deployment check that the basics work is called a smoke test.

The main tools are these. The Lambda console Test tab and the command-line call aws lambda invoke run a deployed Lambda function (AWS's managed run-your-code-on-demand service) with a JSON event you supply. The command sam remote invoke does the same through AWS SAM, a tool for defining serverless apps. API Gateway, a managed front door for HTTP APIs, has a console test feature that calls the backend behind one method. CloudWatch Logs stores what the code printed. AWS X-Ray records a trace, a timeline of each downstream call with its duration and errors. A pipeline can also run smoke tests automatically in a build step after deploying.

Worked example. You deploy an orders function and run aws lambda invoke with a sample order. Step one: the response shows a function error. Step two: you open CloudWatch Logs and find an AccessDenied error on a DynamoDB write. Step three: the X-Ray trace shows the DynamoDB call failing quickly. Step four: you add the missing write permission to the execution role, redeploy, and invoke again, and it succeeds.

A common mistake is trusting sam local invoke alone. It runs with your own credentials, which are often broad, so a missing role permission stays hidden until production. A similar trap is that the API Gateway console test skips authorization and the public stage URL. Passing that test does not prove callers can reach the API. Skipping deployed tests means users find these failures first.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental company deploys a returns function to AWS Lambda. The function saves a receipt file to an S3 bucket (S3 is AWS's managed file storage). An engineer tests the deployed copy. Step 1: she runs sam remote invoke with a sample event for a return of 4 bikes, and the response shows a function error. Step 2: ______. Step 3: the X-Ray trace shows the S3 upload call failing after about 12 milliseconds. Step 4: she adds the missing S3 write permission to the function's execution role, redeploys, and invokes again, and this time it succeeds. Which action best fills Step 2?
choices: Run the API Gateway console test against the returns method to confirm the backend responds
Add S3 write permission to her own IAM user so the deployed function can reuse her access
Open CloudWatch Logs for the function and find an AccessDenied error on the S3 write
Run sam local invoke with the same event to see whether the error also happens on her laptop
questions.why: CloudWatch Logs holds what the deployed code printed, so it reveals the AccessDenied error that explains the failure and points to the missing execution-role permission fixed in Step 4.

questions.prompt: A team at a pet-supplies retailer finishes deploying a new version of its inventory service. Right away, a pipeline build step sends a few simple requests to the deployed service and checks that the basic responses are correct. What is this quick post-deployment check called?
choices: An execution role check
A smoke test
A trace, a timeline of each downstream call
A local invocation
questions.why: A smoke test is a quick check, run after deployment, that the basics of the running application work; a pipeline can run one automatically in a build step.

questions.prompt: A travel agency builds an HTTP API with API Gateway that calls a booking function. The API Gateway console test for the POST /bookings method returns a successful response. Yet partner companies calling the public stage URL get rejected. Which explanation fits best?
choices: The console test skips authorization and the public stage URL, so passing it does not prove callers can reach the API
The console test runs the code on the engineer's laptop with broad local credentials
The booking function's execution role must be missing a permission for its database
CloudWatch Logs only records requests that come from the console test feature
questions.why: The API Gateway console test calls the backend directly without going through authorization or the public stage URL, so a pass there does not show that real callers can get in.

questions.prompt: A developer at a fitness app tests a new function only with sam local invoke on her laptop, and every run succeeds. After deployment, the function fails with AccessDenied when it writes to its table. What is the most likely reason the local test did not catch this?
choices: sam local invoke ran with her own, often broad, credentials, hiding a permission missing from the function's execution role
X-Ray must be turned on during local runs before permission errors can appear
Deployed functions ignore their execution role and use the caller's permissions instead
sam local invoke cannot read JSON test events, so it never really ran the write
questions.why: sam local invoke uses your own credentials rather than the deployed execution role, so a missing role permission stays hidden until the code runs in AWS.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why a function that passes local tests still needs to be tested after it is deployed, which AWS tools you would use, and one limit of one of those tools.
lessons.modelAnswer: Local tests prove the logic, but the deployed copy runs differently. It runs under its own execution role, with the environment variables configured in AWS, inside its network setup, and against real services. So after deploying I'd run a smoke test against the real thing. I'd use aws lambda invoke or sam remote invoke with a sample JSON event, or a request to the API, and check the response. If it fails, CloudWatch Logs shows what the code printed and the error, and an X-Ray trace shows which downstream call failed or was slow. A pipeline can run these checks automatically after each deploy. One limit is that sam local invoke uses my own credentials, so it can hide a missing role permission. Another is that the API Gateway console test skips authorization and the public stage URL, so passing it doesn't prove real callers can get in.
rubricPoints: The deployed copy differs from local in its role permissions, configuration, network and live dependencies.
Tests should invoke the real deployed function or API, for example with aws lambda invoke or sam remote invoke.
CloudWatch Logs and X-Ray traces are used to diagnose what happened inside the deployed code.
Smoke tests can run automatically in the pipeline after deployment.
Names a limit, such as local runs using your own credentials or the API Gateway console test bypassing authorization.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing the right post-deployment check and reading logs and traces for a given failure, which is best practised by reasoning through exam-style scenarios.

lessons.plain: An integration test checks that several pieces of your application work correctly together, such as your function, its database, and the outside services it calls. Some of those outside services are slow, cost money, or are run by someone else, so you replace them during testing with a mock: a stand-in that pretends to be the real service and gives answers you choose. Think of a flight simulator. A pilot practises real procedures with real controls, but the weather and engine failures are staged so every situation can be rehearsed safely and repeatedly.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function charges a card through a third-party payment service. If your automated tests called the real payment service every time they ran, what problems might you run into?
lessons.teach:
An integration test runs several real parts of your code together and checks the combined result. A unit test, by contrast, checks one small function on its own. An external dependency is anything your code relies on but does not own: a third-party HTTP API, a managed database, a queue. A mock is a fake version of a dependency that returns scripted responses and records how it was called. A stub is a simpler fake that only returns canned data. You make mocking easy through dependency injection: your code receives its clients as inputs instead of creating them internally, so a test can pass in a fake.

Mocking works because your code only sees the interface, meaning the requests it sends and the responses it gets back. If the fake honours that interface, your code cannot tell the difference. You can then rehearse cases that are hard to trigger for real, such as timeouts or error codes, quickly and for free.

Worked example: a Lambda function (AWS's run-on-demand compute service) receives an order, calls a payment API, then writes the order to a DynamoDB table (AWS's managed key-value database). Step 1: the test builds a mock payment client scripted to return a 402 "card declined" response. Step 2: it injects that mock into the handler. Step 3: it invokes the handler with a sample order. Step 4: it asserts the handler returned a clear failure, and that no order row was written. Step 5: a second test scripts a timeout and checks that the handler retries once and then fails cleanly. The database can be a local emulator or a dedicated test table, so the database interaction stays real.

Common mistake: mocking everything, including your own modules. The test then only proves the mocks agree with each other. A related trap is contract drift, where the real API changes its response format but your mock does not. In a running system the result is a green pipeline and a broken production release. Keep a small number of tests that hit real test endpoints so you can catch that drift.

questions.prompt: A ski resort's function getSlopeReport calls a third-party weather API and then saves a summary row into a reports table. The function receives its weather client as an input parameter, which is called dependency injection: the code is handed its clients instead of creating them itself. A developer wants to prove that when the weather API answers 503 "service unavailable", the function returns the message "report unavailable" and saves nothing. The reports table is a dedicated test table, so that part stays real. Step 1: build a mock weather client, a fake that returns scripted responses and records how it was called, and script it to return a 503. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: call getSlopeReport for resort "peak-7". Step 4: assert that the result is "report unavailable", that the test table has zero new rows, and that the mock recorded exactly one call. What is Step 2?
choices: Call the real weather API once first, to confirm it is online before the test runs.
Replace getSlopeReport itself with a mock that always returns "report unavailable".
Pass the mock weather client into getSlopeReport in place of the real client.
Swap the test reports table for a mock as well, so that no real storage is touched.
questions.why: The scripted 503 only reaches the code under test if the mock is injected where the real weather client would normally go.

questions.prompt: A test needs a fake currency-rates service. In one version, the fake simply returns a fixed rate of 1.08 every time. In another version, the fake returns scripted answers and also records how many times it was called and with what arguments, so the test can check those calls. Which description is correct?
choices: The first is a stub and the second is a mock.
Both are stubs, because both return canned data.
Both are integration tests, because both replace a real service.
The first is a mock and the second is a stub.
questions.why: A stub only returns canned data, while a mock also records how it was called so the test can check those calls.

questions.prompt: A function sendInvoice creates its own SMS client inside its body, which means it builds the client itself each time it runs. Because of this, tests always send real text messages. Which change most directly lets a test use a fake SMS client instead?
choices: Wrap sendInvoice in a try/catch block so that failed messages are ignored.
Write more unit tests for the other functions that call sendInvoice.
Change sendInvoice so it receives the SMS client as an input, and let the test pass in a fake.
Run the test suite only at night, when sending real messages costs less.
questions.why: Dependency injection means handing the code its clients as inputs, so a test can supply a fake client in place of the real one.

questions.prompt: A team's tests mock a shipping partner's API, so they never call the real thing. The partner renames a response field from "eta" to "estimatedArrival", but nobody updates the mock. What is the likely outcome, and what guards against it?
choices: Nothing breaks, because mocked code cannot tell the difference from the real API.
The tests fail straight away, so it is enough to watch the pipeline.
The pipeline stays green but the production release breaks; keep a few tests that call real test endpoints.
The tests fail only in production; the fix is to mock the team's own modules as well.
questions.why: This is contract drift: the real API changed its response format but the mock did not. Tests pass against the outdated mock, and only tests against real endpoints can reveal the change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why our integration tests mock the payment API but not our own code, and name one risk that mocking introduces.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our integration tests run the handler, its logic, and the database together, because the goal is to prove that those parts cooperate. The payment API is an external dependency: it costs money, it is slow, and we cannot make it fail on demand. So we inject a mock that returns scripted answers such as success, declined, or timeout. That lets us test every branch quickly and repeatably. We do not mock our own modules, because then the test would only be checking fakes against fakes. The risk is contract drift. If the provider changes its response shape and our mock still returns the old shape, our tests stay green while production breaks. To limit that, we keep the mocks close to real recorded responses and run a few tests against the provider's real test endpoint.
rubricPoints: Defines an integration test as checking several real components working together.
Explains a mock as a scripted stand-in for an external dependency.
Gives reasons to mock: cost, speed, reliability, and the ability to simulate failures.
Mentions injecting dependencies so a test can swap in the fake.
Warns against over-mocking, which leaves the test proving nothing.
Names contract drift and a mitigation such as some tests against real test endpoints.

suggested.rationale: Fixing a flaky test properly makes the learner confront unreliable external calls in tests and replace them with controlled fakes, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Before you let real users hit a new version of your web API, you try it at a separate test address first. Amazon API Gateway, a managed front door that receives web requests and passes them to your code, lets one API have several named copies called stages, such as dev, test and prod. Each stage has its own web address. Testing against a development endpoint means calling the dev address on purpose, checking what comes back, and only then promoting the change. It is like a restaurant tasting a new dish in the back kitchen before putting it on the menu.
lessons.guessPrompt: You changed your API and saved it, but when you call the dev stage's web address you still get the old response. What do you think is missing between saving the change and the dev address showing it?
lessons.teach:
An endpoint is a web address a client calls. In Amazon API Gateway, a stage is a named, live version of your API, such as dev or prod, with its own invoke URL, the address clients call. For a REST API the URL looks like https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/dev/orders, where abc123 is the API's id, us-east-1 is the AWS region, dev is the stage name and /orders is the resource, meaning the path.

Why this works: editing an API only changes its draft configuration. A deployment is a frozen snapshot of that draft, and you attach each deployment to a stage. So dev can run today's snapshot while prod keeps last week's, letting you test without touching real users. Each stage also has its own settings, such as logging and throttling (a cap on request rate).

Worked example. You add a status field to the /orders response. First, save the change; dev does not see it yet. Second, deploy the API to the dev stage. Third, call the dev invoke URL with a test tool or curl and confirm a 200 status code and the new field. Fourth, read the dev stage's logs if anything looks wrong. Fifth, only then deploy the same snapshot to prod.

The console's built-in test button is useful for a quick check of one method, but it calls the method directly rather than through a deployed stage, so it does not prove the stage URL, stage settings or the full client path work. Always finish with a real call to the stage URL.

A common mistake is forgetting to redeploy, so you test the old snapshot and wrongly decide your fix failed or succeeded. Another is pointing tests at the prod URL by accident, which sends test data to real users and real databases in a running system. Some newer HTTP APIs offer a default stage that redeploys automatically, which removes the first mistake but means every saved change goes live on that stage at once.

questions.prompt: A developer at a bike-rental company fixes a bug in the /bikes resource of a REST API in Amazon API Gateway. The stage called qa should now return a field named batteryLevel. Here is how the work went. Step 1: She edits the /bikes method and saves the change. Step 2: She calls https://k4m2p9.execute-api.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/qa/bikes with curl. She gets a 200 status code, but batteryLevel is missing. Step 3: ??? Step 4: She calls the same qa URL again. batteryLevel now appears, and she confirms it in the qa stage's logs. What is the missing Step 3?
choices: Deploy the API to the qa stage, so qa gets a new frozen snapshot that includes the saved edit.
Run the console's built-in test button on the /bikes method, because a pass there shows the qa stage is serving the fix.
Conclude the fix is wrong and rewrite it, because a saved edit is live on every stage at once.
Deploy the API to the prod stage, because a change only reaches the other stages once prod has it.
questions.why: Saving only changes the draft, so the qa stage keeps serving its old snapshot until you deploy a new snapshot to it.

questions.prompt: A team's REST API in Amazon API Gateway is called at https://q7w8e9.execute-api.ap-southeast-2.amazonaws.com/staging/invoices/42. Which part of this address is the stage name?
choices: staging
invoices/42
q7w8e9
ap-southeast-2
questions.why: In a REST API invoke URL, the stage name is the first path segment after the host, so here it is staging. q7w8e9 is the API id, ap-southeast-2 is the region and /invoices/42 is the resource path.

questions.prompt: At a ticketing startup, the console's built-in test button returns a correct 200 response for the /seats method. However, a load-test tool calling the beta stage's invoke URL gets many requests rejected for exceeding the request rate. What best explains the difference?
choices: Throttling is set once for the whole API, so the load-test tool must be calling the wrong region.
The beta stage has no snapshot attached, so it rejects every request until the test button has been run.
The test button always uses the prod stage, and prod has a higher throttling cap than the beta stage does.
The test button calls the method directly rather than through the deployed stage, so it never applied the beta stage's own throttling settings.
questions.why: The test button bypasses the stage, so it does not prove that stage settings such as throttling, a cap on request rate, behave as expected. Only a real call to the stage URL shows that.

questions.prompt: A developer at a weather-data firm uses a newer HTTP API with a default stage that redeploys automatically. She saves a half-finished change to the /forecast route, intending to test it later. What is the main risk?
choices: The change is ignored until she deploys it manually, so the testers keep seeing old data.
The console's test button stops working until she creates a separate dev stage.
The default stage freezes its snapshot, so she can never update /forecast again.
Every saved change goes live on that stage at once, so clients calling it get the half-finished /forecast right away.
questions.why: An auto-deploying default stage means you never forget to redeploy. The trade-off is that each save is published immediately to anyone calling that stage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would test an API change against a development stage in API Gateway before it reaches production, and name one limit or risk of the approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: API Gateway lets one API have several stages, like dev and prod, and each stage has its own invoke URL. Editing the API only changes a draft, so after saving I deploy it to the dev stage, which freezes a snapshot there while prod keeps its old snapshot. Then I call the dev URL, the region-and-stage address ending in /dev/ plus the path, check the status code and response body, and read the dev stage logs if something is off. When it passes, I deploy the same snapshot to prod. The console test button is fine for a quick look, but it skips the deployed stage, so it does not prove the real URL works. The main risks are forgetting to redeploy, so I test stale code, and accidentally aiming tests at the prod URL. Also, dev only proves things as far as its settings and backends match prod's.
rubricPoints: A stage is a named live version of the API with its own invoke URL.
Changes must be deployed to a stage before that stage's URL reflects them.
Testing means calling the dev stage URL and checking status, body and logs before promoting to prod.
The console test button skips the deployed stage, so it is not a full substitute.
Names a risk such as stale tests from not redeploying or accidentally hitting the prod URL.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine exercises API Gateway stages directly, so reasoning through exam-style situations like a stale dev URL or a test hitting prod builds the needed judgment best.

lessons.plain: Once an application is described in a template (a text file listing every piece of cloud infrastructure it needs), you can deploy that same file many times. Each deployment creates or updates a stack, a named group of resources that AWS manages together. Updating a stack means changing an existing environment in place rather than building from scratch. Pointing the same template at a different stack name, such as a staging stack, gives you a separate copy of the environment. It works like a building blueprint: one plan can produce a test house and a real house, and later revisions to the plan can be applied to either house.
lessons.guessPrompt: If you deploy the same template twice under two different stack names, such as my-app-staging and my-app-prod, do you get one environment or two? What do you think happens if both try to create a database table with the exact same fixed name?
lessons.teach:
A stack update applies a changed template, or changed inputs to that template, to a stack that already exists. AWS CloudFormation is the managed infrastructure-as-code service that does the work. AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) is a shorthand template format for serverless apps that CloudFormation expands into full resources. The stack name is the key fact. A new name creates a new environment. A name that already exists updates that environment.

This works because CloudFormation compares the desired state in the template with the current state of the stack. It then changes only what differs. Before anything changes, it can build a change set, which is a preview listing each resource as Add, Modify or Remove. Some property changes force Replacement, meaning the old resource is deleted and a new one is created. Parameters are named inputs, such as Stage, that let one template behave differently in each environment. SAM can store per-environment settings, including stack name, Region and parameter overrides, in a samconfig.toml file. Each environment gets its own section.

Worked example: you run sam deploy with --config-env staging. First, SAM packages the code and uploads it to an S3 bucket. Second, it reads the staging section, which sets the stack name my-app-staging and the parameter Stage=staging. Third, CloudFormation finds that this stack already exists, so it builds a change set: modify the Lambda function code and add one alarm. Fourth, you confirm and the update runs. If any step fails, CloudFormation rolls back to the last working state and the stack ends in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.

A common mistake is hard-coding physical names, such as a table named Orders, instead of building them from the Stage parameter. A staging deploy then collides with production's resource and fails. Renaming such a resource later forces replacement, and replacing a database table can delete its data. Always read the change set for Replacement entries before you approve an update to a running environment.

questions.prompt: A dental clinic runs its booking app from a SAM template. A developer makes three edits: raise a Lambda function's memory from 256 MB to 512 MB, add a new reminder queue, and rename the hard-coded patients table from Patients to clinic-patients. Step 1: she runs sam deploy with --config-env uat, whose section sets the stack name booking-uat. Step 2: CloudFormation finds that booking-uat already exists, so it compares the template with the current stack. Step 3: it builds a change set: Modify the function, Add the queue, and Replacement for the patients table. Step 4: ??? Which choice correctly completes Step 4?
choices: Approve it. If anything goes wrong, rollback restores the table's data.
Do not approve it yet. Replacement deletes the table and creates a new one, which can lose data, so revise the change first.
Delete the booking-uat stack and deploy again under a new stack name to avoid the change set.
Approve it. Modify and Add are safe, so one table entry can be ignored.
questions.why: A Replacement entry means the old table is deleted and a new one is created, which can destroy its data, so you must catch it in the change set before approving the update.

questions.prompt: A team's production stack for a payments service is named payments-prod. A developer changes the template and deploys it with the stack name payments-prod-v2, expecting to update production. What actually happens?
choices: CloudFormation updates payments-prod, because it matches stacks by template content.
CloudFormation refuses to deploy because the two names are too similar.
CloudFormation creates a new, separate environment, and payments-prod is left unchanged.
CloudFormation updates payments-prod and renames that stack to payments-prod-v2.
questions.why: The stack name decides the outcome: a name that does not exist yet creates a new environment, while only an existing name updates that environment.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's SAM template defines a queue with the fixed physical name ShipmentQueue. Production already runs from this template. When the team deploys the same template as a new test stack in the same account and Region, the deploy fails. What is the best fix?
choices: Deploy the test stack in the production stack's name so the two share one queue.
Remove the queue from the template and create it by hand for each environment.
Read the change set more carefully, because Replacement entries cause the failure.
Build the queue's name from a Stage parameter so each environment gets its own name.
questions.why: A hard-coded physical name makes the test deploy collide with production's resource, and building the name from the Stage parameter gives each environment a unique name.

questions.prompt: A travel site updates its existing stack, flights-staging. Partway through, creating a new alarm fails. Assuming CloudFormation handles the failure normally, what is the result?
choices: CloudFormation rolls back to the last working state, and the stack ends in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.
The stack stays half-updated until the developer manually reverses each change.
