CloudFormation deletes the flights-staging stack, so it must be created again from scratch.
The stack ends in UPDATE_COMPLETE, keeping the changes that worked before the failure.
questions.why: When any step of an update fails, CloudFormation returns the stack to its last working state and the stack ends in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how one SAM template can be used to update a staging environment without touching production, and name one risk or tradeoff of updating a stack in place.
lessons.modelAnswer: We keep one SAM template and deploy it under a different stack name for each environment, such as my-app-staging and my-app-prod. The stack name decides which environment we touch. If the stack already exists, CloudFormation compares our template with what is deployed and changes only the differences. A Stage parameter, set per environment in samconfig.toml, lets resource names and settings differ between environments so they never collide. Before we approve, we look at the change set, which shows every resource that will be added, modified or removed. The risk is replacement. Some edits, such as renaming a table, make CloudFormation delete the old resource and create a new one, which can lose data in a running environment. If the update fails partway, CloudFormation rolls back automatically. That keeps the environment safe, but the rollback takes time and does not undo any data that was already lost.
rubricPoints: The stack name identifies the environment: a new name creates one, an existing name updates it.
CloudFormation compares desired and current state and changes only the differences.
Parameters or per-environment config let one template serve several environments without name collisions.
Change sets preview the changes before they are applied.
Some changes force replacement, which can destroy data.
A failed update rolls back to the last working state.

suggested.rationale: The skill is mostly about predicting what a given deploy command and template change will do to a specific stack, which exam-style scenarios practise better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: An event-driven application is one where pieces of code run because something happened, like a file being uploaded or a message landing in a queue, rather than because someone called them directly and waited. Testing one is like testing a relay race: checking that each runner can run is not enough. You also check that the baton is handed over, that a dropped baton is noticed, and that nobody runs the same leg twice. Testing event-driven code means checking the code, the trigger that delivers the event, and what happens when delivery is late, repeated, or fails.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function runs whenever a file lands in a storage bucket and writes a record to a database. Your test uploads a file and immediately checks the database. Sometimes it passes and sometimes it fails, with no code changes. Why might that be?
lessons.teach:
Testing an event-driven application means proving three things: the handler (the function that receives an event) does the right work, the wiring (the trigger, filter rules and permissions that deliver events) actually connects source to handler, and the failure behaviour is safe. An event is a JSON document describing something that happened. Delivery is usually asynchronous, meaning the sender does not wait for the result, and at-least-once, meaning the same event can arrive more than once.

This works best in layers. Unit tests call the handler directly with a saved sample event, which is fast and needs no cloud. Tools such as AWS SAM can run a Lambda function locally against such an event. Integration tests then cause a real event in a test environment and look for the side effect. Event-routing rules, such as an Amazon EventBridge pattern (a filter deciding which events reach which target), should be tested with a matching and a non-matching event.

Worked example: an upload to an S3 bucket (object storage) triggers a Lambda function that writes a row to a DynamoDB table (a key-value database). Step 1: the unit test passes a sample upload event to the handler and checks it builds the right row. Step 2: the integration test uploads a test file with a unique name. Step 3: it polls the table every second for up to 30 seconds until the row appears, failing only on timeout. Step 4: it sends the same event twice and checks there is still one row. Step 5: it sends a malformed event and checks it ends up in the dead-letter queue (a holding queue for events that failed every retry).

A common mistake is checking for the result immediately, or after a fixed sleep. Asynchronous delivery has variable delay, so tests become flaky. Another is testing only the handler: a missing permission or wrong filter means production never invokes it, and events silently pile up or vanish.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain publishes an "OrderPlaced" event to Amazon EventBridge (an event bus with routing rules) whenever a customer pays. A rule whose pattern matches source "bakery.orders" sends the event to a Lambda function that saves a PDF receipt into an S3 bucket (object storage) named after the order ID. The team's test plan is: (1) a unit test calls the handler directly with a saved sample OrderPlaced event and checks the receipt content it builds; (2) a routing test sends one event with source "bakery.orders" and one with source "bakery.inventory" and confirms only the first reaches the function; (3) an integration test publishes a real OrderPlaced event in the test account with a unique order ID such as test-7f3a; (4) ??? ; (5) the test publishes the same event a second time and confirms there is still exactly one receipt for test-7f3a. Which step (4) best completes the plan?
choices: Check the bucket for the test-7f3a receipt every 2 seconds for up to 20 seconds, failing only if it never appears
Skip checking the bucket and instead assert that the handler returned a success value in step (1)
Immediately after publishing, list the bucket once and fail the test if the receipt is not there yet
Sleep for exactly 10 seconds, then check the bucket once and fail if the receipt is missing
questions.why: Delivery is asynchronous with a variable delay, so repeatedly polling until a timeout avoids the flaky failures caused by checking immediately or after a single fixed sleep.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Lambda function receives "SeatReserved" events from a queue. Delivery is described as at-least-once. Which test does that property make necessary?
choices: Send one event and confirm the function replies to the sender before it continues
Send the same SeatReserved event twice and confirm the seat is reserved only once
Send no events and confirm the function never runs on its own
Send events in strict order and confirm none ever arrives out of sequence
questions.why: At-least-once means the same event can arrive more than once, so the test must prove that a duplicate does not produce a duplicate effect.

questions.prompt: A logistics startup has thorough unit tests: each one calls its Lambda handler directly with a saved "ParcelScanned" sample event, and all of them pass. After release, the function is never invoked in production and scan events seem to disappear. What gap in testing most likely let this through?
choices: The unit tests used JSON sample events instead of real parcel scanners
The handler should have been tested with more sample events to cover more fields
The unit tests ran too fast to notice the handler's real processing delay
No test checked the wiring, such as the trigger, filter rule and permissions, with a real event
questions.why: Unit tests prove only the handler's logic; a wrong filter or missing permission means events never reach it, which only an integration test causing a real event would reveal.

questions.prompt: A media company adds an EventBridge rule whose pattern should send only events with "videoType": "premium" to a transcoding function. What is the most complete way to test this rule?
choices: Call the transcoding handler directly with a premium sample event
Send a malformed event and confirm it lands in the dead-letter queue
Send one premium event and one with a different videoType, and confirm only the premium one reaches the function
Send one premium event and confirm the function receives it
questions.why: A routing rule must be shown both to let matching events through and to keep non-matching events out, which needs one of each.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would test a function triggered by queue messages, and name one limit or tradeoff of your approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: I would test in layers. First, unit tests call the handler directly with saved sample messages, including a valid one, a malformed one, and the same one twice, so I know the logic is right and duplicates are harmless. Second, an integration test in a test environment puts a real message on the queue with a unique ID and polls for the expected side effect with a timeout, because delivery is asynchronous and I cannot assume it is instant. That proves the trigger, permissions and filters work. Third, I check failure paths: a bad message should be retried and then land in the dead-letter queue instead of blocking others. The tradeoff is that integration tests are slower, cost a little, and need a real environment, while local tests are fast but cannot prove the wiring, so I keep many unit tests and a few integration tests.
rubricPoints: Separates testing the handler logic from testing the wiring that delivers events.
Uses sample JSON events to test the handler directly.
Waits for asynchronous results by polling with a timeout rather than checking immediately or sleeping a fixed time.
Tests duplicate delivery and confirms the handler is safe to run twice.
Tests the failure path, such as retries ending in a dead-letter queue.
Names a tradeoff, such as integration tests being slower and needing a real environment.

suggested.rationale: Writing an event handler that must survive duplicate delivery makes the learner exercise the core event-driven test case of sending the same event twice and checking the outcome.

lessons.plain: A test event is a sample message you hand to your code to pretend something happened, such as a web request arriving or a file being uploaded. On AWS, a Lambda function (a small piece of code that runs only when triggered) always receives its input as JSON, a text format of named fields. Each trigger wraps its data in its own fixed shape. Writing a realistic test event is like a fire drill: the alarm is fake, but if the drill matches the real thing, you find the problems before an actual fire. A test event that does not match the real shape only rehearses the wrong emergency.
lessons.guessPrompt: When a web request reaches your function through an API, the request body arrives inside a JSON event. Do you think the body arrives as a ready-made object with named fields, or as one long piece of text your code must unpack first? Why might it be designed that way?
lessons.teach:
A test event is a JSON payload (a block of structured text) that you feed to a function to imitate a real trigger. Lambda, the AWS service that runs functions on demand, passes every invocation one event object. The shape of that object depends on the trigger. A direct invoke receives whatever JSON you send. Amazon API Gateway, a managed front door for HTTP APIs, uses a proxy integration (a mode that forwards the whole request untouched) and wraps the request in fields such as httpMethod, path, headers, queryStringParameters and body. Queues, storage buckets and streams each use their own wrapper as well, usually a Records list.

There are three common ways to create these payloads. In the Lambda console you can save named test events. Private ones are visible only to you, while shareable ones are visible to others who have access to the function. The AWS SAM CLI (the command-line tool for the Serverless Application Model, a shorthand for describing serverless apps as templates) can print a correctly shaped sample with sam local generate-event, for example for apigateway aws-proxy. You save that sample to a file, edit it, and run it with sam local invoke -e event.json against the function named in your template. You can also keep event files in your repository so teammates and pipelines reuse them.

Here is a worked example. Generate an API Gateway proxy event, then set body to the string "{\"orderId\":\"42\"}" and httpMethod to POST. Invoke the function locally. The handler reads event body, which is text, parses it into an object, takes orderId 42, and returns statusCode 200 with a body string.

A common mistake is testing with the bare payload {"orderId":"42"}, or with body written as a nested object instead of a string. The tests pass, but behind the real API the handler cannot find orderId or fails to parse it. Callers then get 500 errors or 502 malformed-response errors in production. A test event earns its value only when it matches the exact shape the real trigger sends.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental startup has a Lambda function behind API Gateway with proxy integration. The handler reads the request body, parses it, and uses bikeId to reserve a bike. A developer builds a local test with the SAM CLI. Step 1: run sam local generate-event apigateway aws-proxy and save the output as reserve.json. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: run sam local invoke -e reserve.json against the function named in the template. Step 4: the handler parses the body text into an object, finds bikeId 7, and returns statusCode 200 with a body string. Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: In reserve.json, add a header named bikeId with value 7 and leave body empty
Replace the whole contents of reserve.json with {"bikeId":"7"} so the handler receives only the data it needs
In reserve.json, set body to the nested object {"bikeId":"7"} without quotes and set httpMethod to POST
In reserve.json, set body to the string "{\"bikeId\":\"7\"}" and set httpMethod to POST
questions.why: A proxy event delivers the request body as text inside the body field, so the test must put the JSON in body as a string, keeping the wrapper the handler will get from the real API.

questions.prompt: A developer at a museum ticketing company saves a named test event for a Lambda function in the Lambda console. Two teammates who also have access to that function need to run the same event. What kind of saved test event should the developer create?
choices: A shareable test event, which others with access to the function can see
A shareable test event, which only works when invoked through API Gateway
A private test event, then copy its name into the function's description
A private test event, which every teammate on the account can see by default
questions.why: Private test events are visible only to their creator, while shareable ones are visible to others who have access to the function.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team has a Lambda function triggered by messages arriving on a queue. A developer wants a test event that matches what the function will really receive. Which shape should the test event follow?
choices: An API Gateway shape with httpMethod, path, headers and a body field
An empty JSON object, since the queue adds the message at run time
The queue's own wrapper, typically a Records list holding the messages
Just the message content itself, such as {"palletId":"88"}, with no wrapper
questions.why: Each trigger has its own wrapper, and queues, storage buckets and streams usually deliver a Records list, so the test must imitate that shape.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking team tests its Lambda function by invoking it directly with {"slotId":"15"}, and every test passes. After the function goes live behind API Gateway with proxy integration, callers get 500 errors because the handler cannot find slotId. What is the most likely cause?
choices: API Gateway removes the request body before it reaches the function, so slotId is lost
The real event wraps the request in fields like body and headers, so slotId is not at the top level
The function needs more memory, because API Gateway requests are larger than direct invokes
Direct invokes and API Gateway use the same event shape, so the template must be wrong
questions.why: Proxy integration wraps the request, putting the payload as text in the body field, so a test using the bare payload passes locally but does not match what the real trigger sends.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why you generate test events with the SAM CLI or save them in the console, rather than typing a quick JSON object by hand. Name one limit of what a passing local test event proves.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each trigger hands a Lambda function a JSON event in its own fixed shape. An API Gateway proxy event, for example, nests the request inside fields like headers, queryStringParameters and body, and the body is a string we have to parse ourselves. A JSON object typed by hand usually skips that wrapper, so the handler looks correct in testing and then breaks behind the real API. sam local generate-event gives us a correctly shaped template that we edit and run with sam local invoke -e. We can also save shareable events in the console or keep event files in the repo so everyone runs the same cases. There is a limit, though. A passing test event only proves the code handles that one payload. It says nothing about permissions, timeouts, or how the real deployed trigger and its settings behave, so we still need tests against the deployed environment.
rubricPoints: A test event is a JSON payload that imitates what a real trigger sends to a function.
Each trigger, such as API Gateway proxy or a queue, wraps data in its own shape, and the API Gateway body is a string.
The SAM CLI generates sample events, and sam local invoke -e runs a function locally with one of them.
The console can save private or shareable test events, and event files can be kept in the repository.
Using the wrong shape gives tests that pass while production fails with errors.
A passing local event does not prove permissions, configuration or real integration behavior.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is picking and reasoning about the right event shape for a given trigger, so working through exam-style scenarios about payload mismatches adds the most.

lessons.plain: An API is the front door other programs use to talk to your application. Deploying it to different environments means publishing the same door design in separate places, usually development, testing and production, so you can try changes safely before real customers see them. Think of a theatre: rehearsals happen on the practice stage, and only once the show works is it put on the main stage. In Amazon API Gateway, a managed service that hosts APIs, editing your API design changes nothing live until you take a snapshot and attach it to a named environment.
lessons.guessPrompt: You add a new path to your API in the editor and save it, but you have not published anything yet. Do you think callers using the production web address can already reach the new path? Why or why not?
lessons.teach:
Deploying an API to an environment means taking a frozen copy of your API's definition and making it reachable at an address that belongs to one environment. In Amazon API Gateway, three terms matter. A resource is a path such as /orders, and a method is an action on it, such as GET or POST. A deployment is a snapshot of all resources and methods at one moment. A stage is a named environment, such as dev, test or prod, that points at exactly one deployment and has its own invoke URL, the web address callers use.

This works because editing the API only changes a working draft. Nothing callers see changes until you create a deployment and attach it to a stage. Each stage can point at a different snapshot, so dev can run new code while prod keeps running the old, proven version.

Worked example. Your API has GET /orders, deployed as snapshot D1, and both dev and prod point to D1. Step 1: you add POST /orders in the draft. Neither stage changes yet. Step 2: you deploy to the dev stage, which creates snapshot D2, and dev now points to D2 while prod still points to D1. Step 3: testers call the dev invoke URL and confirm POST works. Step 4: you point prod at D2. Now both stages serve the new method. If prod misbehaves, you point prod back to D1, a quick rollback because the old snapshot still exists.

A common mistake is editing the API, testing against prod's address, and wondering why nothing changed: the edit was never deployed. The opposite mistake is deploying every edit straight to prod. In a running system that publishes untested changes to every customer at once, and a broken method can cause errors for all live traffic. Promoting one known snapshot from dev to test to prod keeps environments separate and makes each release traceable.

questions.prompt: A bike-rental company's API has one method, GET /bikes. Two stages exist, beta and live, and both point to deployment R3. The team wants to add a new method, GET /bikes/{id}/availability, without affecting live customers. Step 1: a developer adds the new method in the working draft, and neither stage changes yet. Step 2: [missing]. Step 3: QA engineers call the beta invoke URL and confirm the new method works, while live callers still see only GET /bikes. Step 4: the team points the live stage at the same snapshot QA tested. Which choice correctly fills in Step 2?
choices: Do nothing extra, because the beta stage automatically picks up draft edits since it is the non-production environment
Deploy to the beta stage, which creates snapshot R4; beta now points to R4 while live still points to R3
Create a new stage named R4 and attach the working draft to it directly
Deploy to the live stage first so the new snapshot exists, then copy it to beta for QA
questions.why: Draft edits only reach callers after a deployment creates a new snapshot and a stage is pointed at it, so deploying to beta gives QA the new method while live stays on R3.

questions.prompt: In Amazon API Gateway, which statement correctly describes a stage?
choices: It is the working draft of the API, which updates as soon as you edit a method
It is a named environment with its own invoke URL that points at exactly one deployment
It is a snapshot of all resources and methods taken at one moment in time
It is a single path, such as /invoices, together with the actions allowed on it
questions.why: A stage is a named environment such as dev or prod that has its own invoke URL and points at one deployment, which is the snapshot.

questions.prompt: A weather-data team changes the response of GET /forecasts in their API's working draft. They then call the prod stage's invoke URL and still get the old response. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The edit was never deployed, so prod still points at an older snapshot
Edits only appear after every stage is deleted and recreated
API Gateway caches edits for 24 hours before they reach any stage
The prod stage needs its invoke URL changed before it can show edits
questions.why: Editing only changes the draft; callers see nothing new until a deployment is created and attached to the stage they call.

questions.prompt: A payments team moved its prod stage from deployment W5 to deployment W6. Within minutes, the new method in W6 starts returning errors to live customers. W5 still exists. What is the quickest way to roll back?
choices: Delete the prod stage so traffic falls back to the dev stage automatically
Create a brand-new deployment from the current draft and attach it to dev
Edit the draft to remove the new method and wait for prod to update itself
Point the prod stage back at deployment W5
questions.why: Because the old snapshot W5 still exists, pointing prod back at it restores the proven version immediately without any new deployment.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how one API can serve different versions in dev and prod at the same time, and name one limit or risk of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Edits to the API's paths and methods only change a draft. To publish, you create a deployment, which is a frozen snapshot of the whole API, and attach it to a stage. A stage is a named environment like dev or prod with its own invoke URL, and each stage points at one snapshot. So dev can point at the newest snapshot while prod still points at last week's one. We test on dev's URL, then point prod at the same snapshot we tested. If prod breaks, we point it back to the previous snapshot. The risk is that nothing goes live until you deploy, so people forget and test stale behaviour, or they skip dev and deploy edits straight to prod, which exposes every customer to untested changes. Also, stages only separate the API layer; the backends they call must be kept separate too.
rubricPoints: Edits change only a draft until a deployment is created.
A deployment is a frozen snapshot of the API definition.
A stage is a named environment with its own URL pointing at one deployment.
Different stages can point at different snapshots, enabling safe promotion from dev to prod.
Rollback means pointing a stage back at an earlier snapshot.
Names a risk such as forgetting to redeploy or deploying untested changes straight to prod.

suggested.rationale: The skill is reasoning about which stage serves which snapshot after a sequence of edits and deployments, which an exam-style scenario exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: When several people test an application while developers keep changing it, testers need something that holds still. An approved-version environment is a named place that always runs one specific, frozen copy of your code until someone deliberately moves it forward. Think of a library shelf labelled 'Book club pick': the label stays the same, but the librarian decides which exact edition sits under it. Testers always go to the label. AWS offers several such labels: Lambda aliases, container image tags, AWS Amplify branches, and AWS Copilot environments. Each lets you say 'test against this exact build' without chasing changing code.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team keeps editing a serverless function several times a day, and a tester needs to run a two-hour integration test suite against it. What could go wrong if the tester simply calls 'whatever the newest code is', and what would you give the tester instead?
lessons.teach:
An approved-version environment is a stable name that points at one frozen, known build of your code, so integration tests (tests that check your code working together with real services) run against exactly what you intend to ship.

AWS Lambda, the managed run-your-function service, gives you versions and aliases. A version is a numbered, unchangeable snapshot of the code and settings. The special name $LATEST is the editable draft and changes whenever you upload. An alias is a named pointer, such as 'test' or 'prod', that refers to one version and can be moved later. Callers use the alias, so they never need to know version numbers.

Container image tags are labels on a packaged container image stored in a registry such as Amazon ECR. A tag like 'latest' can be reassigned to a different image, while a tag based on the commit ID, or the image digest (a fingerprint of the exact contents), identifies one build for good. ECR can also be set to refuse re-tagging.

AWS Amplify, a hosting service for web front ends, can connect each Git branch to its own deployed copy with its own web address, so a 'staging' branch becomes a staging site.

AWS Copilot, a command-line tool for container apps, lets you create named environments such as 'test' and 'prod', each with separate infrastructure, and deploy a chosen service build into each one.

Worked example: a function has versions 1 to 3, and the 'test' alias points to 3. A developer finishes changes and publishes version 4. Testers still hit 'test', so they still see 3. After a review, you move 'test' to 4 and tests run on it. When they pass, you move 'prod' to 4. No caller changed its configuration.

Common mistake: testing $LATEST or the 'latest' image tag. The code can change mid-test, so what passed is not what ships, and a production failure cannot be reproduced because nobody knows which build was actually tested.

questions.prompt:
A logistics company, Harbourline, runs its tracking service as a container. Its pipeline must give integration testers one frozen build. The steps are below, with Step 3 missing.

Step 1: Build the container image from Git commit 7f3e91c.
Step 2: Push the image to Amazon ECR, a registry that stores container images. Give it two tags, 'latest' and '7f3e91c'. ECR is set to refuse re-tagging.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The integration tests pass. The same image, tagged '7f3e91c', is deployed to production.

Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Deploy the image tagged '7f3e91c' to the test environment and run the integration tests against it
Deploy the image tagged '7f3e91c' straight to production and run the integration tests there
Rebuild the image from commit 7f3e91c in the test account so testers get their own fresh copy
Deploy the image tagged 'latest' to the test environment, because it was pushed with the newest build
questions.why: The commit-based tag identifies exactly one build and cannot be moved, so the image that was tested is guaranteed to be the image that ships.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment-reminder Lambda function has published versions 7, 8 and 9. Its 'staging' alias points to version 8. A developer then uploads new code but does not publish a new version. Which code runs when a caller invokes the 'staging' alias?
choices: The newly uploaded code, because uploads update every alias
Version 9, because an alias always follows the highest published version
Version 8, because the upload only changed $LATEST and the alias still points to version 8
Nothing runs, because the upload invalidated the alias until it is reset
questions.why: An alias points to one fixed version until someone moves it. The upload changes only the editable $LATEST draft.

questions.prompt: A small retail team runs its order service as a container app. They want separate 'test' and 'prod' setups, each with its own infrastructure. They also want to deploy a chosen build of the service into each one from the command line. Which option fits best?
choices: Connect a Git branch to AWS Amplify so the branch becomes the test setup
Point a Lambda alias named 'test' at the container image
Create named AWS Copilot environments, 'test' and 'prod', and deploy the chosen build into each
Push the image with the 'latest' tag and let both setups pull it
questions.why: AWS Copilot is a command-line tool for container apps. It creates named environments with separate infrastructure and deploys a chosen service build into each one.

questions.prompt: A fintech start-up ran its integration tests against the image tagged 'latest'. The tests passed and the image was released. A day later production fails, and the team cannot reproduce the failure in test. What is the most likely underlying cause?
choices: The registry deletes untagged images after release, so production lost its code
Image digests change every time an image is pulled, so test and production always differ
The 'latest' tag can be reassigned to a different image, so nobody knows which build was actually tested
Integration tests cannot detect problems in container images, only in Lambda functions
questions.why: The 'latest' tag can be moved to a different image. The build that passed testing may not be the one that shipped, and that makes the failure impossible to trace.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why integration tests should target a Lambda alias or a fixed image tag instead of $LATEST or 'latest', and name one limit or tradeoff of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: An integration test is only useful if what it tested is what we ship. $LATEST and the 'latest' image tag are moving targets: someone can upload new code halfway through a test run, and afterwards we cannot say which build passed. So we publish a Lambda version, which is a frozen snapshot, and point a 'test' alias at it, or we tag the container image with the commit ID or use its digest. Testers always call the alias or tag, and promoting is just moving the 'prod' alias to the same version that passed. Amplify branches and Copilot environments give the same idea for web front ends and container services. The tradeoff is extra bookkeeping: versions pile up and need cleaning, someone must deliberately move pointers, and a mutable tag still gives no protection unless tag immutability is turned on or digests are used.
rubricPoints: Defines an approved-version environment as a stable name pointing at one frozen build.
Explains that a Lambda version is immutable while $LATEST is editable, and an alias is a movable pointer to a version.
Notes that 'latest' image tags can move, while commit-based tags or digests identify one exact build.
Connects Amplify branches and Copilot environments to the same idea of separate named deployed copies.
Explains promotion as moving a pointer to the build that passed tests, with no caller changes.
Names a tradeoff such as version clutter, manual pointer management, or mutable tags undermining guarantees.

suggested.rationale: Moving named pointers such as aliases and tags between frozen builds and watching which build each environment serves is best learned by doing it in a deployment simulator.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing the cloud resources your application needs, such as functions, tables and queues, in a text file instead of clicking them together by hand. A service then reads that file and builds exactly what it describes, every time. Think of it like a recipe card rather than cooking from memory. Anyone can follow the same card and get the same dish, and when you change the recipe you can see what changed. On AWS, CloudFormation is the service that reads these files. AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) is a shorthand layered on top that makes serverless pieces quicker to write.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your template says a function is called OrderHandler. A teammate renames it to OrdersHandler in the template and redeploys. Do you think the cloud service will treat this as a rename of the same function, or as deleting one function and creating a new one? Why?
lessons.teach:
Infrastructure as code (IaC) is the practice of declaring infrastructure in a versioned text file. AWS CloudFormation is AWS's IaC engine. You give it a template, a YAML or JSON file listing resources (each cloud thing to create), parameters (inputs that change per deployment, like a stage name) and outputs (values to report afterwards, like an API URL). CloudFormation turns the template into a stack, which is the live group of resources it manages together. You can create, update or delete a stack as one unit.

This works because CloudFormation compares the template you submit with what the stack currently holds. It then works out the creates, updates and deletes needed, and does them in dependency order. If any step fails, it rolls the stack back to the last working state. A change set is a preview of those planned actions that you can review before running them.

AWS SAM is an extension of CloudFormation. A SAM template carries a Transform line that tells CloudFormation to expand short serverless resource types into full ones. For example, one AWS::Serverless::Function with an API event becomes a function, an execution role, an API and a permission. The SAM command-line tool runs sam build to package code and sam deploy to upload it and create or update the stack.

Worked example: you add a table resource and set the function's environment variable to reference it. You run sam deploy, and a change set lists one Add (the table) and one Modify (the function). You approve it. CloudFormation creates the table first because the function refers to it, then updates the function.

Common mistake: renaming a resource's logical ID, which is the name the template uses for it. CloudFormation sees that as removing one resource and adding another. For a database table, that can delete the old table and its data. Changing resources by hand in the console is also risky, because it causes drift, where reality no longer matches the template and later deployments behave unexpectedly.

questions.prompt: A cinema chain called ReelTime keeps its booking service in a SAM template. Here is a deployment, traced step by step. Step 1: a developer runs sam build, which packages the function code. Step 2: the developer runs sam deploy, which uploads the code and produces a change set (a preview of planned actions) listing two Adds (a message queue and a notification topic) and one Modify (the booking function). Step 3: the developer reviews the change set and approves it. Step 4: CloudFormation creates the queue successfully, but creating the topic fails because one of its settings is invalid. Step 5: ______. Which choice correctly completes step 5?
choices: CloudFormation rolls the stack back to its last working state, so the new queue is removed and the function is unchanged
CloudFormation deletes the whole stack, including the resources that existed before this deployment
CloudFormation keeps the new queue, stops there, and leaves the stack partly updated until someone fixes it
CloudFormation skips the failed topic and carries on updating the booking function as planned
questions.why: When any step of a stack update fails, CloudFormation rolls the whole stack back to its last working state instead of leaving it half-changed or deleting it.

questions.prompt: A developer opens a template and sees a Transform line near the top along with a resource of type AWS::Serverless::Function. What does that Transform line do?
choices: It tells CloudFormation to expand short SAM resource types into full CloudFormation resources
It locks the stack so that nobody can change its resources by hand in the console
It converts the YAML template into JSON so that CloudFormation is able to read it
It packages the function code and uploads it, just as the sam build command does
questions.why: SAM is an extension of CloudFormation, and the Transform line tells CloudFormation to expand short serverless types into full resources, such as a function, a role, an API and a permission.

questions.prompt: A florist's ordering app has a database table with the logical ID (the name the template uses for a resource) OrdersTable, and the table holds 40,000 orders. A developer renames the logical ID to CustomerOrdersTable for clarity, changes nothing else, and deploys. What is the most likely result?
choices: CloudFormation sees a simple rename and updates the table's label in place, keeping all the data
CloudFormation refuses to deploy because logical IDs can never be changed once a stack exists
CloudFormation creates a second table and keeps both, copying the 40,000 orders into the new one
CloudFormation treats it as removing one table and adding another, so the old table and its data can be deleted
questions.why: Changing a logical ID looks to CloudFormation like a delete plus an add, so the old table and its data can be lost.

questions.prompt: At a parcel-tracking company, an engineer uses the console to raise a function's memory from 512 MB to 1,024 MB, but never changes the template that manages the function. What is this situation called, and why is it risky?
choices: A rollback: CloudFormation will undo the change immediately and restore the memory to 512 MB
A transform: SAM will expand the console change into extra resources at the next deployment
A change set: the console change is held as a preview until someone approves it in CloudFormation
Drift: the real resource no longer matches the template, so later deployments can behave unexpectedly
questions.why: Changing resources by hand causes drift, where reality no longer matches the template, and this makes later deployments behave unexpectedly.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how SAM and CloudFormation relate and what happens when you deploy a template change. Include one limit or risk they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: CloudFormation is the engine. You hand it a template listing resources, parameters and outputs, and it builds them as a stack it manages as a unit. SAM is a shorthand on top of it. A Transform line expands compact serverless types, like a function with an API event, into the full set of underlying resources. When we deploy a change, CloudFormation diffs the new template against the current stack. It plans adds, modifies and deletes, which we can preview as a change set, and applies them in dependency order. If something fails, it rolls back to the last good state. The risk to watch is that the logical ID is how CloudFormation recognises a resource. If you rename it, the old resource is deleted and a new one is created, which for a table can mean losing data. Hand edits in the console cause drift, so every change should go through the template.
rubricPoints: Defines a template and a stack, and says CloudFormation builds the stack from the template.
Explains that SAM is a CloudFormation extension whose transform expands shorthand serverless resources.
Describes deployment as a diff of template against stack, with a change-set preview and dependency ordering.
Mentions automatic rollback on failure.
Names a risk such as logical ID renames causing replacement or manual changes causing drift.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine has the learner write templates, so the most value comes from reasoning through exam-style scenarios about what a template change will do to a stack.

lessons.plain: Most teams keep at least three copies of an application: development for trying things, test for checking them, and production for real users. Some services let you keep all three inside one resource instead of building three separate ones. In Amazon API Gateway, a managed service that puts a web address in front of your backend code, these copies are called stages. Think of a theatre with one script but three rooms: a rehearsal room, a dress-rehearsal room and the main stage. The script is shared, but each room runs whichever saved draft you last handed it, and has its own lighting and seating rules.
lessons.guessPrompt: You edit a route in your API, save it, then call the production web address. Do you think production users see your edit straight away? Why might a service deliberately make you wait?
lessons.teach:
Managing environments inside a single service means one resource definition holds several named environments, and each can run a different version with its own settings. In API Gateway, three terms matter. The API definition is your working draft of routes and backend connections. A deployment is a frozen, unchangeable snapshot of that draft taken at one moment. A stage is a named, live environment, such as dev, test or prod, that points to exactly one deployment and gets its own URL that includes the stage name.

This works because editing the draft never changes what callers see. A stage only changes when you deploy a snapshot to it. Each stage also has its own settings: request throttling limits, logging level, response caching, and stage variables, which are name-value pairs a stage can pass to your backend.

Worked example. You add a new route, /orders, to the draft. Step 1: you deploy to dev, which creates snapshot A. The dev URL now serves /orders, and the prod URL does not. Step 2: testers check dev and find no problems. Step 3: you point the test stage at snapshot A, the same frozen snapshot, without making a new one. Step 4: after tests pass, you point prod at snapshot A. Each stage now runs exactly the code that passed through the earlier stages. To roll back, you point prod at the previous snapshot.

A common mistake is editing the draft and expecting the change to go live. Nothing changes until you deploy. A related mistake is taking a new snapshot for prod after more edits have been made. Prod then runs something nobody tested.

In a running system, stages share one API, one account and its limits, and the same people with edit access. A careless deployment or a shared throttling limit can affect prod. For this reason, many teams also use separate accounts for stricter isolation.

questions.prompt: A city library runs a book-search API in API Gateway with two stages, staging and live. The live stage currently points to deployment L4. A developer adds a new route, /holds, to the API definition. Step 1: she deploys to staging, which creates a new deployment, L5. The staging URL now serves /holds, and the live URL does not. Step 2: librarians test /holds on staging and approve it. Step 3: while waiting for approval, a teammate edited the API definition to rename an unrelated route, and nobody has tested that edit. Step 4: ??? Step 5: a week later, a fault appears in /holds, so the team points live back at L4 to roll back. Which action belongs in Step 4 so that live runs exactly what the librarians approved?
choices: Give library users the staging URL, because staging already serves /holds and has been tested.
Deploy the current API definition to the live stage, which creates a new deployment L6 that holds the approved /holds route.
Save the API definition again, because saved edits go to every stage automatically and live will pick up /holds.
Point the live stage at deployment L5, the same frozen snapshot that staging used, without creating a new deployment.
questions.why: L5 is the frozen snapshot the librarians tested, so pointing live at it releases exactly the approved version, while a new deployment would also pick up the teammate's untested rename.

questions.prompt: In API Gateway, which term names the frozen, unchangeable snapshot of the API definition taken at one moment?
choices: A deployment
The API definition
A stage variable
A stage
questions.why: A deployment is the unchangeable snapshot, while a stage is a named live environment that points to one deployment, and the API definition is the editable working draft.

questions.prompt: At a ticketing company, a developer changes the backend connection for the /seats route in the API definition and saves it. He then calls the prod stage URL and still gets the old behaviour. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The prod URL must be rebuilt by hand after any edit to the API definition.
Stage variables override every change made to the API definition.
Editing the API definition does not change any stage, and nothing goes live until a deployment is made and a stage points to it.
The prod stage caches every response forever, so changes never show up.
questions.why: A stage only changes when it is pointed at a deployment, so a saved edit to the draft has no effect on what prod callers see.

questions.prompt: A fitness-app team keeps dev, test and prod as three stages of one API Gateway API in a single account. During a heavy load test against the test stage, prod users start getting throttled requests. Which explanation and fix best match how stages work?
choices: The test stage was accidentally pointed at the prod deployment, so the team should create a new snapshot for prod.
Each stage has its own account by default, so this can only be a bug in the backend code.
Stages share one API and one account with its limits, so test traffic can affect prod; many teams use separate accounts for stricter isolation.
Load tests always delete the prod stage's settings, so the team should redeploy the API definition to prod.
questions.why: Stages in one API share the same account and its limits, so a careless or heavy use of one stage can reach prod, which is why separate accounts are used for stronger isolation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how one API can serve dev, test and prod at the same time, how a change moves from dev to prod, and one limit of keeping all environments inside a single API.
lessons.modelAnswer: In API Gateway we edit one API definition, which is just a draft. When we deploy, it takes a frozen snapshot called a deployment. Each stage, like dev, test or prod, is a live environment with its own URL. It points at one snapshot and has its own throttling, logging, caching and stage variables. Editing the draft changes nothing live. To promote a change, we deploy to dev, test it there, then point test and later prod at that same snapshot, so prod runs exactly what was tested. Rolling back means pointing prod at the previous snapshot. The tradeoff is weak isolation. All stages share one API, one account, the same account limits and the same people with edit access, so one mistake can reach prod. That is why stricter teams also separate environments into different accounts.
rubricPoints: A stage is a named live environment with its own URL and settings.
A deployment is an immutable snapshot; editing the draft changes nothing until you deploy.
Promotion means pointing later stages at the same tested snapshot.
Rollback means pointing a stage back at an earlier snapshot.
Names a limit: stages share the API, account, quotas and permissions, so isolation is weaker than separate accounts.

suggested.rationale: The skill shows up as exam-style scenarios, such as why a change is not live or which snapshot prod is running, and reasoning through those cases builds it best since no current mission covers API stages.

lessons.plain: An application rarely lives in one place. It is usually a function, a database table, a message queue, an API, permissions and stored secrets all working together. An environment is one complete, separate copy of that whole set, such as development for experimenting, test for checking, and production for real customers. Managing environments across services means each copy is complete and walled off, so the development function only ever talks to the development table and queue. Think of three identical kitchens in one restaurant chain. Each must have its own fridge, oven and staff, because a trainee cook should never be pulling ingredients from the flagship kitchen's fridge.
lessons.guessPrompt: You copy your production setup to make a test copy, but the test function still has the production table's name written directly into its code. What do you think happens when you run tests?
lessons.teach:
An application environment is a full, isolated set of every resource an app needs, across all the services it uses. That can include an AWS Lambda function (code that runs on demand), an Amazon DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database), an Amazon SQS queue (a managed message queue), an API, IAM roles (permission identities) and secrets. Managing environments broadly means keeping each set complete, consistent and separated, instead of only splitting things inside one service.

The usual technique is one infrastructure-as-code template (a text file that describes resources) with an environment parameter, an input value such as dev or prod. You deploy that template once per environment as a separate stack, which is a named group of resources created and deleted together. Every resource name and reference is built from the parameter, so each stack wires only to its own pieces. It works because the template is identical everywhere, and only the parameter changes. That keeps environments alike, and it keeps them from overlapping.

Worked example. You deploy the template with Env=dev, creating stack orders-dev. Step one: it creates table orders-dev and queue orders-dev-queue. Step two: it creates the function and sets its configuration value TABLE_NAME to the table's actual name from this same stack. Step three: you deploy again with Env=prod, creating stack orders-prod with orders-prod and its own function. Neither function can see the other's table name, and the IAM role in each stack grants access only to that stack's resources.

For stronger isolation, many teams put each environment in a separate AWS account, so a mistake in dev cannot touch prod at all. Tagging every resource with its environment also helps with cost reports and cleanup.

A common mistake is hard-coding a name like orders-table. The second deployment may then fail on a name clash. Worse, development code may silently read and write production data. In a running system that means test records appearing in customer orders, or a dev cleanup script deleting live data.

questions.prompt:
A dental clinic builds an appointment-reminder app with one infrastructure-as-code template (a text file that describes resources) that takes an environment parameter called Env. The team deploys it with Env=staging, creating a stack (a named group of resources created and deleted together) called reminders-staging.
Step one: the stack creates a DynamoDB table named reminders-staging-patients and an SQS queue (a managed message queue) named reminders-staging-sms.
Step two: ???
Step three: the team deploys the same template again with Env=live. This creates stack reminders-live with its own table, queue and function, and each stack's IAM role grants access only to that stack's resources.
Which step two keeps the staging environment complete and separate from live?
choices: It creates the function and sets its QUEUE_NAME configuration value to the fixed name reminders-sms so both stacks share one queue.
It creates the function and sets its QUEUE_NAME configuration value to the queue's actual name from this same reminders-staging stack.
It creates the function and points its QUEUE_NAME configuration value at reminders-live-sms so staging tests use the real queue.
It copies the template into a new file for staging and edits the function's queue name by hand before deploying it.
questions.why: Building the reference from the same stack, which follows from the Env parameter, wires the staging function only to the staging queue while the template stays identical for every environment.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing startup says it has separate test and production environments. Which description best matches what an application environment means when environments are managed broadly across AWS services?
choices: A single shared DynamoDB table where test rows and production rows are marked with a different attribute value
A naming convention applied only to the API, so callers know whether they are calling test or production
Two versions of the Lambda function code inside one service, while the database, queue and secrets are shared by both versions
A full, isolated set of every resource the app needs (functions, tables, queues, API, IAM roles and secrets), kept complete and separate from other sets
questions.why: An environment is a complete, isolated set of resources across all the services an app uses, not a split inside one service.

questions.prompt: A library's book-loan app has a template that hard-codes its DynamoDB table name as loans, instead of building the name from an environment parameter. The team has already deployed the production stack and now deploys the same template again for development. Which outcome is a realistic risk?
choices: Hard-coded names only affect cost reports, so the two environments still behave independently
The deployment may fail on a name clash, or dev code may read and write the live loans table, mixing test data into real loans
The development stack automatically gets a renamed table, loans-2, so nothing is shared
The development stack is merged into the production stack and both are deleted together
questions.why: A fixed name gives no separation, so the second deployment can clash with the first or wire development code to production data.

questions.prompt: A payments team already deploys one template per environment with an Env parameter. After a developer's experiment nearly altered live resources, they want a mistake in development to be unable to touch production at all. What does the teaching suggest for this stronger isolation?
choices: Put each environment in a separate AWS account
Tag every resource with its environment name
Deploy both environments as a single shared stack
Give the dev and prod stacks the same IAM role
questions.why: Separate AWS accounts give stronger isolation, so a mistake in dev cannot reach prod, while tags help mainly with cost reports and cleanup rather than isolation.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would run dev, test and production versions of an app that uses a function, a table and a queue, and name one tradeoff in how strongly you separate them.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each environment is a complete copy of everything the app uses, so the function, the table, the queue, the permissions and the secrets all get duplicated. I'd write one template with an environment parameter and deploy it as a separate stack for dev, test and prod. Names are built from that parameter, and the function gets its table and queue names from its own stack rather than from hard-coded strings. Its role only grants access to that stack's resources. That keeps environments identical in shape but unable to touch each other. I'd tag everything with the environment too. The tradeoff is the strength of separation. Separate accounts per environment give the strongest walls, so a dev mistake can't reach prod, but they add setup, access management and cost overhead. One shared account is simpler but has a bigger blast radius if a permission or a name is wrong.
rubricPoints: An environment is a full set of resources across all services, not just one service.
Use one template with an environment parameter, deployed as a separate stack per environment.
Resource names and references come from the parameter or the stack, never hard-coded.
Permissions are scoped so each environment can only reach its own resources.
Names a tradeoff, such as separate accounts versus one shared account.
Names the risk of cross-wiring, such as dev code touching production data.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine builds multi-service environments, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario about cross-wired or hard-coded resources teaches this best.

lessons.plain: Amazon Q Developer is an AI coding assistant from AWS that works inside your code editor and can suggest code, explain it, and draft automated tests for it. An automated test is a small piece of code that runs your real code with chosen inputs and checks that the output is what you expected. You point the assistant at a function, and it writes a first draft of those checks. Think of it as a keen intern who drafts a checklist quickly. It saves you time, but you still have to read it, because it can miss things or get them wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: If an AI assistant writes tests by reading a function you already wrote, and that function has a bug in it, what might the generated tests end up checking for?
lessons.teach:
Amazon Q Developer is a generative AI assistant. That means it produces new text or code from a request. It runs as a plugin in common code editors. One of its jobs is drafting unit tests. A unit test checks one small piece of code, such as a single function, on its own. In the editor you select a function or file and ask the assistant to write tests for it. Usually you type a test command or a plain request in its chat panel. It reads the code and infers what the code seems meant to do. It then proposes test cases: a normal input, boundary values, empty or invalid input, and the errors the code should raise. Where the code calls something outside itself, such as a database or another service, it can add mocks. A mock is a stand-in object that returns canned answers, so the test runs fast and offline. The suggestion uses your project's test framework, such as pytest for Python or Jest for JavaScript. You choose whether to accept it.

Worked example: a function apply_discount(price, percent) should reject percentages above 100. First you select it and ask for tests. Second, the assistant proposes four cases: 10 percent off 200 gives 180, 0 percent gives the full price, 100 percent gives 0, and 150 percent raises an error. Third, you run them. The 150 percent test fails, because the function silently returns a negative price. Fourth, you fix the function instead of the test. Now all four pass.

The common mistake is accepting generated tests without reading them. The assistant infers intent from the code, so it can assert the buggy behavior as correct. It might, for example, expect a negative price. It also cannot know business rules that the code never states.

In a running system, the consequence is a pipeline that shows green while the bug ships to production. Generated tests speed up coverage, but a human must still review what each test checks and confirm that it matches the requirements.

questions.prompt:
A city library's billing code has a function late_fee(days_overdue). The written library policy says the fee is 0.25 dollars per day, capped at 5.00 dollars, but the code never applies the cap. A developer selects the function in the editor and asks Amazon Q Developer, a generative AI assistant that runs as an editor plugin, to draft unit tests (tests that each check one small piece of code on its own).

Step 1: The assistant proposes four cases: 4 days gives 1.00, 0 days gives 0.00, a negative number of days raises an error, and 40 days gives 10.00.
Step 2: The developer runs the tests, and all four pass.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: The developer corrects the function so it caps the fee, and all four tests pass against the corrected code.

Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: Ask the assistant to regenerate the tests several times until one version picks up the 5.00 dollar cap from the code on its own.
Delete the 40-day test, because a value that large is an unusual outlier and should not count toward the test suite.
Read each assertion against the written policy, spot that the 40-day test expects 10.00 instead of the capped 5.00, and change it to expect 5.00.
Accept all four tests as written, because every test passing shows the function already matches the library's billing policy.
questions.why: The assistant inferred intent from code that has no cap, so it asserted the buggy 10.00 as correct, and only a human comparing each test to the stated policy can catch and correct that expectation.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking service has a function reserve_seat(event_id) that calls an external payment provider over the network. When Amazon Q Developer drafts unit tests for it, it adds a mock for the payment provider. What is the main purpose of that mock?
choices: It converts the tests into the project's test framework, such as Jest or pytest, so they can be run in the editor.
It records every real payment request made during the test, so the team can audit charges sent to the provider afterward.
It acts as a stand-in that returns canned answers, so the test runs fast and offline without contacting the real payment provider.
It checks the business rules for seat pricing that the code never states, so the test can confirm the real pricing policy.
questions.why: A mock is a stand-in object with canned responses, which keeps a unit test isolated, quick, and independent of outside services.

questions.prompt: A warehouse team used Amazon Q Developer to generate tests for a stock-count function and accepted them without reading them. The CI/CD pipeline (the automated build, test, and release process) showed every test green, yet a bug that let stock counts go below zero reached production. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The assistant inferred intent from the buggy code and asserted the negative count as correct, so the tests passed while confirming the bug.
The pipeline skipped the generated tests, because tests produced by a generative AI assistant cannot run in an automated pipeline.
Mocks always hide bugs, so any test that uses a mock will pass no matter what the code does.
The project used the wrong test framework, so the tests appeared to pass even though they never actually executed.
questions.why: Because the assistant infers what code seems meant to do, it can encode buggy behavior as expected, and unreviewed tests then turn green while the bug ships.

questions.prompt: An insurance company's function quote_premium(age) contains no mention of a company rule that applicants under 18 must be refused. A developer asks Amazon Q Developer to write unit tests for the function. What should the developer expect about that under-18 rule?
choices: The assistant will add an under-18 test automatically, because it always checks boundary values that match company policy.
The assistant will refuse to generate any tests until the developer adds the under-18 rule as a comment in the code.
The assistant will create a mock of the company's policy database so the under-18 rule is tested against the real requirements.
The assistant cannot know a rule the code never states, so the developer must review the tests and add a check for it.
questions.why: The assistant only infers intent from the code it reads, so business rules missing from the code must be added and confirmed by a human reviewer.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use Amazon Q Developer to add unit tests to an existing function, and name one limit you must guard against before merging those tests.
lessons.modelAnswer: Amazon Q Developer is an AI assistant inside the editor. I select the function and ask it to write unit tests. It reads the code and drafts cases in our test framework: a normal input, edge values, invalid input and expected errors. Where the function calls a database or another service, it adds mocks so the test runs without the real dependency. That gets us a lot of coverage quickly. The limit is that it guesses intent from the code itself. If the code has a bug, the generated test may assert the bug as correct. It also does not know business rules that aren't written down. So I read every assertion, run the tests, and check them against the requirements. If a test fails, I decide whether the code or the test is wrong. Otherwise CI goes green while broken behavior ships.
rubricPoints: Amazon Q Developer is an AI assistant in the editor that drafts unit tests from selected code.
Generated tests cover normal, edge, and error cases in the project's test framework.
It can add mocks for external dependencies so tests run in isolation.
Tests are inferred from existing code, so they may encode bugs or miss unstated business rules.
A human must review, run, and compare tests to requirements before merging.

suggested.rationale: The skill tested is judging whether AI-generated tests check the right behavior, which is best practiced by reasoning through a scenario with a buggy function and its drafted tests.

lessons.plain: A Lambda function is code that AWS runs for you on demand, without you managing a server. Before AWS can run it, you have to hand over your code and everything it needs, such as the libraries it imports. That bundle is the deployment package. Lambda accepts two main kinds. One is a .zip archive, a compressed folder of files. The other is a container image, a sealed snapshot of a small operating system plus your code. Think of a .zip as packing a carry-on bag: it is quick and light, but there is a size limit. A container image is more like shipping a crate: it is bigger and you control everything inside.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your Python function needs a data-science library that is about 400 MB once unpacked. Do you think a small compressed .zip upload or a larger self-contained image is the better way to hand it to Lambda, and why?
lessons.teach:
A deployment package is the bundle of code and dependencies that Lambda runs. You choose its package type when you create the function, and you cannot switch an existing function to the other type later. To change type, you create a new function.

The first option is a .zip archive. This is a compressed file that holds your handler, which is the function Lambda calls, along with any libraries it needs. You can upload a .zip directly when it is up to about 50 MB compressed. For a larger file, you upload it to Amazon S3, AWS's object storage service, and point Lambda at it. Either way, the unpacked total must stay within 250 MB. That total also counts layers. A layer is a separate .zip of shared libraries that you attach to a function, and you can attach up to five. Layers let several functions reuse the same dependencies without each one bundling its own copy.

The second option is a container image. This is a packaged file system with a runtime, your code, and your libraries, stored in Amazon ECR, AWS's managed container registry. An image can be up to 10 GB. It must include the Lambda runtime interface, which is the small piece that receives events from Lambda. The easiest way to get that is to start from an AWS-provided base image. Container images cannot use layers. You put everything inside the image instead.

Here is a worked example. A team's function imports a library that unpacks to 400 MB. First, they try a .zip and find that 400 MB is more than the 250 MB unpacked limit, so the .zip is out. Second, they build a container image from an AWS Python base image and copy in the code and libraries. Third, they push the image to ECR. Finally, they create the function with the image package type and give it the image's address.

A common mistake is building dependencies on a laptop and zipping them as they are. Some libraries contain compiled native code. Code compiled on macOS or Windows, or for the wrong processor architecture (x86_64 or arm64), will not run on Lambda's Linux environment. In a running system, every invocation then fails with an import error. You avoid this by building on a matching Linux environment or inside a container.

questions.prompt: A logistics company runs three Lambda functions that all use the same 150 MB (unpacked) reporting library. Each function's own code compresses to 8 MB and unpacks to 20 MB. Step 1: Because 8 MB is under about 50 MB compressed, they upload each function's .zip directly instead of going through Amazon S3. Step 2: They put the shared reporting library into one layer, a separate .zip of shared libraries, and attach it to all three functions so no function bundles its own copy. Step 3: ______. Step 4: Satisfied with the check, they deploy all three functions as .zip archives. Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: They count only each function's own code, 20 MB, against the 250 MB limit, because attached layers are not part of the unpacked total.
They switch every function to a container image in Amazon ECR, because any function that uses a layer must be packaged as an image.
They add each function's unpacked code to the unpacked layer, 20 MB + 150 MB = 170 MB, and confirm it stays within the 250 MB unpacked limit.
They skip any size check, because the 8 MB compressed file already passed the 50 MB direct-upload limit and that is the only limit.
questions.why: The 250 MB unpacked limit covers the function's code plus all attached layers, so the check is 20 + 150 = 170 MB, which fits.

questions.prompt: A research group is writing a Lambda function that loads a 3 GB machine-learning model plus about 200 MB of Python libraries. Which deployment package type fits this function?
choices: A .zip archive uploaded directly, because the code itself is small and the model does not count.
A .zip archive uploaded through Amazon S3, because S3 removes the 250 MB unpacked limit.
A container image stored in Amazon ECR, because an image can be up to 10 GB.
A .zip archive with the model split across five layers, because layers add capacity beyond 250 MB.
questions.why: About 3.2 GB is far beyond the 250 MB unpacked limit for .zip (which includes layers and applies even when uploading via S3), but within the 10 GB limit for container images.

questions.prompt: A developer on a Windows laptop installs a Python library that contains compiled native code, zips it with the handler, and deploys it as a .zip Lambda function. Every invocation fails with an import error. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: The library must be moved into a layer, because Lambda cannot import native code from the main .zip.
The handler name is wrong; renaming the function Lambda calls would make the library import correctly.
The .zip was over 50 MB compressed; uploading it through Amazon S3 instead would fix the import error.
The native code was built for Windows, not Lambda's Linux; rebuilding on matching Linux or in a container fixes it.
questions.why: Compiled native code built on Windows (or for the wrong architecture) will not run in Lambda's Linux environment, so it must be built on a matching Linux environment or inside a container.

questions.prompt: A team has a production Lambda function deployed as a .zip archive. Their dependencies have grown, and they now want this workload to run from a container image. What must they do?
choices: Edit the existing function's settings and change its package type from .zip to image.
Attach the container image to the existing function as a layer so it can load the new code.
Upload the container image to Amazon S3 and point the existing .zip function at that S3 object.
Create a new function with the image package type and point it at the image in Amazon ECR.
questions.why: Package type is fixed when a function is created and cannot be switched later, and container images cannot use layers, so a new image-type function is required.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would decide between a .zip package, a .zip with layers, and a container image for a new Lambda function. Name at least one limit or tradeoff of each option.
lessons.modelAnswer: For a small function with few libraries, I'd use a plain .zip. It's simple and quick to deploy. We can upload it directly if it's under about 50 MB compressed, or go through S3 if it's bigger, but it has to stay within 250 MB once unpacked. If several functions share the same libraries, I'd move those libraries into a layer. Every function then reuses one copy, but layers still count toward the 250 MB, and a function can attach at most five. If the dependencies are huge or we need full control of the environment, I'd use a container image stored in ECR. It can be up to 10 GB, but we have to maintain the image, include the Lambda runtime interface, and give up layers. Whatever we choose, we pick it at creation, because we can't switch package type later. We also have to build native dependencies for Lambda's Linux and the right processor architecture.
rubricPoints: Names the two package types: .zip archive and container image.
States the .zip limits: about 50 MB for direct upload, S3 for larger files, and 250 MB unpacked including layers.
Explains that layers share dependencies across functions, with a maximum of five per function.
States that container images can be up to 10 GB, are stored in ECR, need the runtime interface, and cannot use layers.
Mentions that the package type is fixed at creation, or that native dependencies must match Lambda's Linux environment and processor architecture.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine packages Lambda code, so reasoning through exam-style size and dependency scenarios is the most useful way to practise choosing between .zip, layers, and container images.

lessons.plain: When you build a web API, the outside world needs an address to call it and a way to tell the test version from the live one. Amazon API Gateway is a managed front door that receives web requests and passes them to your code. A stage is a named, published copy of the API, such as dev or prod, and each stage gets its own web address. A custom domain lets customers use a friendly name like api.example.com instead of a long generated one. Think of a shop with a back room for trying things out and a showroom for customers, both behind a sign you chose yourself.
lessons.guessPrompt: You edit an API in API Gateway, adding a new path. Your teammate calls the production web address straight away and gets a 'not found' error. What step do you think was skipped between editing the API and the change reaching the live address?
lessons.teach:
Amazon API Gateway (a managed front door for HTTP APIs) separates editing an API from publishing it. A deployment is a frozen snapshot of the API's routes and settings at one moment. A stage is a named pointer to one deployment, for example dev, test or prod. Each stage has its own invoke URL, the generated address clients call, shaped like https://abc123.execute-api.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/prod. Each stage also has its own settings, such as request throttling (limits on requests per second), logging and caching. This works because stages are independent, so dev can move forward while prod stays on a snapshot you trust.

A custom domain name is your own hostname, such as api.example.com, attached to API Gateway. It needs three things. The first is a TLS certificate (the file that proves you own the name and enables HTTPS), usually from AWS Certificate Manager. The second is an API mapping, also called a base path mapping, which links a path on the domain to a specific API and stage. The third is a DNS record (the internet's name-to-address lookup), for example in Route 53, pointing your name at the target address API Gateway gives you. An edge-optimized endpoint routes through a global content network and needs its certificate in us-east-1. A regional endpoint needs the certificate in the same region as the API.

Worked example: you add a /orders route, then create a deployment and attach it to the dev stage. You test against dev's invoke URL and it works, so you point the prod stage at that same deployment. Your mapping sends api.example.com/ to prod, so customers now see /orders. Later you map api.example.com/v2 to a second API's prod stage, and old clients on /v1 keep working.

A common mistake is editing routes and forgetting to deploy them to a stage, so the live address keeps serving the old snapshot. Another is giving clients the raw invoke URL. If the stage or API is later rebuilt, that address changes and every client breaks. A custom domain hides the change, because you only update the mapping.

questions.prompt:
A bike-rental company, CycleHub, runs a regional API Gateway API in the eu-west-2 (London) region. The team wants customers to call rentals.cyclehub.io instead of the generated invoke URL. Here is their plan, with one step missing.

Step 1: ______
Step 2: Create an API mapping that links rentals.cyclehub.io/ to the API's live stage.
Step 3: Add a DNS record in Route 53 that points rentals.cyclehub.io at the target address API Gateway provides for the custom domain.

What belongs in Step 1?
choices: Request a TLS certificate for rentals.cyclehub.io in AWS Certificate Manager in eu-west-2, the same region as the API
Request a TLS certificate for rentals.cyclehub.io in AWS Certificate Manager in us-east-1, because certificates for custom domains always live there
Create a new deployment and point the live stage's invoke URL at rentals.cyclehub.io
Skip the certificate, because a regional endpoint serves HTTPS on custom domains without one
