questions.why: A regional endpoint needs its TLS certificate in the same region as the API, so the certificate must be in eu-west-2; us-east-1 is only required for edge-optimized endpoints.

questions.prompt: A payroll team uses Amazon API Gateway with three stages named alpha, beta and live. In this setup, what is a stage?
choices: A named pointer to one deployment, with its own invoke URL and its own settings such as throttling and logging
A DNS record that points a hostname at the API's target address
A frozen snapshot of the API's routes and settings taken at one moment
Your own hostname, such as pay.example.com, attached to the API
questions.why: A stage is a named pointer to a single deployment, and each stage has its own invoke URL and settings; the frozen snapshot itself is the deployment.

questions.prompt: A developer at a ticketing startup adds a new /refunds route to their API in the API Gateway console and saves it. Customers calling the live stage's address still get a 'not found' response for /refunds. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The TLS certificate was created in the wrong region, so new routes are blocked
The live stage's request throttling limit is set too low to allow new routes
The DNS record in Route 53 must be recreated every time a route is added
The change was never deployed, so the live stage still points to an older deployment snapshot without /refunds
questions.why: Editing routes does not publish them; until a new deployment is created and attached to the live stage, that stage keeps serving the old snapshot.

questions.prompt: A weather-data company has its forecasts API served through the custom domain forecasts.example.net, mapped to the API's prod stage. They have to rebuild the API, and the new API gets a different generated invoke URL. What do they change so existing clients keep working without any changes on the client side?
choices: Email every client the new raw invoke URL and ask them to update their code
Rename the new API's stage to match the old invoke URL
Request a new TLS certificate for forecasts.example.net
Update the API mapping so forecasts.example.net points to the new API's prod stage
questions.why: Because clients call the custom domain rather than the raw invoke URL, only the API mapping needs to change to send that domain to the rebuilt API's stage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how API Gateway stages and a custom domain work together to keep dev and prod separate behind one friendly hostname, and name one limit or tradeoff you must watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: In API Gateway, editing an API doesn't change what clients get. You create a deployment, which is a snapshot, and attach it to a stage like dev or prod. Each stage has its own generated invoke URL and its own throttling, logging and caching settings, so we can test in dev while prod stays on a known-good snapshot. To give customers a stable name, we create a custom domain such as api.example.com. It needs a certificate from Certificate Manager, an API mapping that sends a path to one API and stage, and a DNS record pointing at the API Gateway target. Clients never see the raw URL, so we can repoint the mapping without breaking them. Tradeoffs: changes are invisible until you deploy them to a stage, and certificate region matters. Edge-optimized endpoints need the certificate in us-east-1, while regional endpoints need it in the API's own region.
rubricPoints: A deployment is a snapshot and a stage is a named pointer to one deployment with its own URL.
Each stage has independent settings such as throttling, logging and caching.
Edits are not live until they are deployed to a stage.
A custom domain needs a certificate, an API (base path) mapping to an API and stage, and a DNS record.
Certificate region depends on the endpoint type: us-east-1 for edge-optimized, the API's own region for regional.
Custom domains shield clients from changes to the generated invoke URL.

suggested.rationale: No mission or planned engine models API Gateway stages or domain mappings, so reasoning through exam-style situations like 'my change isn't live' or 'the certificate won't attach' builds the judgment best.

lessons.plain: Infrastructure as code means describing your cloud setup (functions, tables, queues, permissions) in a text file called a template, and letting a service build it for you. Updating an existing template means editing that file and asking the service to change the live setup to match, instead of clicking around by hand. Think of a renovation plan for a house that already has people in it: some changes are a new coat of paint, some mean closing a room for a day, and some mean knocking a wall down and rebuilding. Before you start, you want to know which kind each change is.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a running database table built from a template, and you change only the table's name in the template, then apply the update. What do you think happens to the data already in the table?
lessons.teach:
In AWS CloudFormation, a template is a JSON or YAML file listing resources, and a stack is the live set of resources built from it. AWS SAM (Serverless Application Model) is a shorter template style for serverless apps that turns into CloudFormation underneath. To update, you edit the template and submit it against the same stack; CloudFormation compares old and new and changes only what differs.

Each property you change has an update behavior. No interruption: the resource is changed in place while it keeps working, such as a Lambda function's memory setting. Some interruption: the resource is changed in place but briefly unavailable. Replacement: the old resource cannot be changed that way, so CloudFormation creates a new one, switches references to it, then deletes the old one.

To see this before it happens, create a change set: a preview listing every resource that will be added, modified or removed, and whether it needs replacement. Nothing changes until you execute it.

Worked example. A template defines a DynamoDB table (a managed key-value database) with TableName orders. You change it to orders-v2. Step one, create a change set. Step two, it shows the table as Modify with Replacement True. Step three, if executed, a new empty orders-v2 table is built, the function now points to it, and orders is deleted along with its data. A safer path is to set DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain on the table, which tell CloudFormation to keep the old resource instead of deleting it, or to avoid changing that property at all.

A common mistake is renaming a resource's logical ID, the name the template uses for it internally. CloudFormation treats that as deleting one resource and creating another. Another is editing resources by hand in the console, which causes drift: the live setup no longer matches the template, and the next update may fail or undo the manual fix.

If an update fails partway, CloudFormation by default rolls the stack back to its last working state, so the system returns to how it was rather than staying half-changed.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup keeps its uploads in an Amazon S3 bucket (managed object storage) defined in a CloudFormation template with the bucket name photo-uploads-2023. A developer changes the name to photo-uploads-main and works through the update like this. Step 1: create a change set against the existing stack instead of updating directly. Step 2: the change set lists the bucket as Modify with Replacement True. Step 3: ______. Step 4: before executing, the developer sets DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain on the bucket, or drops the rename. Which statement correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Read it as a warning: executing would build a new empty bucket, point references to it, then delete the old bucket and its photos.
Read it as a block: CloudFormation refuses to execute any change set that contains a replacement.
Read it as an in-place change: the bucket keeps running under the new name, so the stored photos carry over.
Read it as already applied: creating the change set has renamed the bucket, so the only option left is a rollback.
questions.why: Replacement True means CloudFormation will create a new resource, switch references to it and delete the old one along with its contents, and nothing happens until the change set is executed.

questions.prompt: An operations engineer at a logistics firm raises a Lambda function's timeout directly in the AWS console to fix an urgent problem. The CloudFormation template that built the function still shows the old timeout. What is this mismatch called, and what risk does it create?
choices: Drift. The live setup no longer matches the template, so the next stack update may fail or undo the manual fix.
Rollback. CloudFormation automatically restores the template's timeout within a few minutes.
A change set. The console edit is saved as a preview and waits for someone to execute it.
Replacement. The console builds a new function and deletes the old one on the next update.
questions.why: Manual console edits cause drift, where the live resources differ from the template, and a later update may fail or overwrite the hand-made fix.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's template defines a message queue with the logical ID TicketQueue. To match a naming guide, a developer renames only the logical ID to TicketsQueue and changes nothing else. What will CloudFormation do on the next update?
choices: Skip the queue entirely, because none of its properties changed.
Mark the stack as drifted and wait for someone to fix it in the console.
Update the existing queue with no interruption, because a logical ID is only a label inside the template.
Treat it as removing one resource and adding another: create a queue for TicketsQueue and delete the one under TicketQueue.
questions.why: CloudFormation identifies resources by logical ID, so a new logical ID looks like deleting one resource and creating a different one.

questions.prompt: A clinic's booking app is deployed from one CloudFormation stack. An update changes four resources. The first three change successfully, but the fourth fails. Assuming default settings, what state is the stack left in?
choices: Half-changed: the first three updates stay in place and only the fourth is left as it was.
Deleted: CloudFormation removes the whole stack so it can be recreated from the new template.
Paused: CloudFormation holds the first three changes as a change set until someone executes or discards it.
Back to its last working state: CloudFormation rolls back all four changes, so the app runs as it did before the update.
questions.why: By default a failed update rolls the stack back to its last working state rather than leaving it partly updated.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would safely change a property on a resource in an existing CloudFormation or SAM stack, and name one limit or risk of relying on the automatic update.
lessons.modelAnswer: I edit the template in the repository instead of changing anything in the console, so the template stays the single source of truth and I avoid drift. Then I create a change set against the existing stack, which previews every add, modify and remove without touching anything. I look closely at the Replacement column, because some properties, like a DynamoDB table name, cannot be changed in place; CloudFormation builds a new resource and deletes the old one, which for a table means losing the data. For stateful resources I set DeletionPolicy and UpdateReplacePolicy to Retain. I also never rename logical IDs casually, since that looks like delete plus create. The limit: automatic rollback only restores what CloudFormation manages. It cannot bring back data from a replaced resource that was already deleted, so the preview step matters more than the rollback.
rubricPoints: Changes are made by editing the template and updating the same stack, not by hand in the console.
A change set previews the update before anything is changed.
Properties have update behaviors, and replacement creates a new resource and deletes the old one.
Replacing a stateful resource such as a table can lose data unless a Retain policy or a different approach is used.
Renaming a logical ID or manual edits causing drift are recognised risks.
Failed updates roll back by default, but rollback does not recover deleted data.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine updates templates, and the core skill is reasoning through exam-style scenarios about which edits cause replacement, drift or data loss.

lessons.plain: A deployment strategy is the plan for swapping old code for new code while real users keep using the system. Think of replacing the tyres on a delivery fleet. You could change a few trucks at a time (rolling). You could prepare a whole second fleet and switch drivers over in one go (blue/green). Or you could give the new tyres to one truck, watch it for a day, then do the rest (canary). Each plan trades cost, speed and safety differently. The aim is that a bad release hurts as few people as possible and can be undone quickly.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have a new version of an app and you are nervous it might have a bug. Would you rather send it to every user at once, or to a small slice of users first? What would you watch before sending it to everyone else?
lessons.teach:
A deployment strategy is the rule for how traffic moves from the old version of your code to the new one. Three names matter.

Rolling replaces servers in batches. A batch is a slice of the fleet, say 25%. Each batch is taken out of service, updated, health-checked and returned before the next one starts. It is cheap because no extra servers are needed. But capacity drops during the update, and old and new versions serve users at the same time. Elastic Beanstalk, a managed app-hosting service, offers "rolling with additional batch". It launches extra instances first, so capacity never dips.

Blue/green builds a complete second environment, called green, that runs the new version beside the live one, called blue. You test green, then switch all traffic at once by swapping a DNS name or a load balancer target. Rolling back is just switching back, which is fast. The cost is paying for two environments for a while.

Canary sends a small share of traffic, the canary, to the new version, watches it, then sends the rest. Linear is a variant that shifts equal steps on a timer.

All three limit the blast radius, meaning how many users see a bad release, and all three keep a known-good version within reach.

Worked example: a Lambda function (a managed service that runs your code when an event arrives) has version 7 behind an alias named live. An alias is a named pointer to a version. You publish version 8, and AWS CodeDeploy, a managed deployment service, applies the configuration Canary10Percent5Minutes.

Step 1: the alias sends 10% of invocations to version 8 and 90% to version 7.

Step 2: for five minutes, CodeDeploy watches a CloudWatch alarm on the error rate.

Step 3: if the alarm stays quiet, the alias shifts 100% to version 8. If it fires, the alias points fully back to version 7 automatically, and only about a tenth of requests ever hit the bug.

A common mistake is setting up canary or linear shifting without any alarm or health check. The tool then has nothing to judge, so it promotes a broken version on schedule. All you have gained is a delay before every user meets the bug.

questions.prompt:
A ticketing company runs a Lambda function (code that runs when an event arrives) for seat reservations. Its alias named prod (a named pointer to a version) points at version 3. The team publishes version 4 and uses AWS CodeDeploy with a linear configuration that shifts 20% more traffic every 2 minutes, while watching a CloudWatch alarm on the error rate.

Step 1: the alias sends 20% of invocations to version 4 and 80% to version 3.
Step 2: the alarm stays quiet for 2 minutes, so the alias moves to 40% on version 4 and 60% on version 3.
Step 3: one minute later the alarm fires. What happens next?
choices: The shift carries on as scheduled, moving to 60% on version 4 after the next 2-minute step
The alias steps back to 20% on version 4, undoing only the most recent shift
The alias points fully back to version 3 automatically, so only part of the traffic ever hit the bug
The alias holds at 40% on version 4 and waits for an engineer to choose the next step
questions.why: When the watched alarm fires during a canary or linear shift, CodeDeploy returns the alias fully to the known-good version, which limits the blast radius to the share already shifted.

questions.prompt: A payments team must release a new version of its web service. They want to test the new version fully before any user sees it, and if something goes wrong after release they need to undo it almost instantly. They accept paying for extra servers for a short time. Which strategy fits best?
choices: Rolling with additional batch: launch extra instances, then update in batches
Blue/green: build a full second environment, test it, then switch all traffic at once
Rolling: update the existing servers in batches of 25%
Canary: send 5% of traffic to the new version, then the rest
questions.why: Blue/green lets you test a complete separate environment before switching, and rollback is just switching traffic back, at the cost of running two environments for a while.

questions.prompt: A small online shop runs on 8 servers managed by Elastic Beanstalk (a managed app-hosting service). It cannot afford to lose any serving capacity during an update, but it also does not want to pay for a whole second environment. Which option matches these needs?
choices: Canary with no alarm, because it delays the release
Blue/green, because it keeps two complete environments
Plain rolling, because it needs no extra servers at all
Rolling with additional batch, because it launches extra instances before updating
questions.why: Rolling with additional batch adds extra instances first so capacity never dips, without building a full second environment like blue/green.

questions.prompt: A developer configures a canary deployment that sends 15% of traffic to a new version for 10 minutes and then shifts the rest, but sets up no alarm or health check. The new version has a bug that fails every request. What is the most likely result?
choices: After 10 minutes the broken version is promoted on schedule, and every user meets the bug
Only the 15% canary share ever sees the bug, because canary always limits the blast radius
The deployment stays at 15% forever because nothing confirms the new version is healthy
The deployment detects the failures and rolls back to the old version after 10 minutes
questions.why: Without an alarm or health check the tool has nothing to judge, so it promotes the broken version on schedule and the canary only adds a delay.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between rolling, blue/green and canary deployments. For each one, name the main tradeoff, and say which you would pick for a risky change to a Lambda function and why.
lessons.modelAnswer: All three are ways to move traffic from the old version to the new one without a big-bang outage. Rolling updates the existing servers in batches. It is cheap, but capacity dips and two versions run side by side unless you add an extra batch. Blue/green stands up a full copy running the new version and flips all traffic at once. Rollback is an instant flip back, but you pay for double infrastructure during the switch, and everyone moves together. Canary sends a small slice, like 10%, to the new version, watches metrics, then promotes or reverts. For a risky Lambda change I would use a canary: an alias shifting traffic through CodeDeploy, tied to an error-rate alarm. A bug then reaches only a fraction of requests, and rollback is automatic. The catch is that canary only helps if alarms exist. Without them, it promotes the bad version on a timer anyway.
rubricPoints: Rolling updates batches of existing capacity, so it is cheap but mixes versions and can reduce capacity.
Blue/green runs a full parallel environment and switches all traffic at once, giving fast rollback at extra cost.
Canary sends a small share of traffic first and promotes only if health looks good.
The strategies limit blast radius and keep a known-good version available for rollback.
For Lambda, an alias shifts traffic between versions under CodeDeploy, driven by alarms.
Shifting traffic without alarms or health checks gives no real protection.

suggested.rationale: Choosing a strategy, shifting traffic and watching an alarm trigger a rollback is best learned by doing it in a planned deployment-strategies simulator.

lessons.plain: Committing code means saving a set of changes into a shared code repository, a central store that keeps every version of a project. In a modern team, that save is also a trigger. The moment a change lands on a watched branch, an automated pipeline wakes up. It builds the code, runs the tests, and if everything passes, deploys it. Think of a factory conveyor belt with a sensor at the start. Drop a part on the belt and machines downstream assemble it, inspect it, and box it. Nobody presses a button. The commit is the part, and the pipeline is the belt.
lessons.guessPrompt: If a pipeline runs its tests automatically after every commit, what do you think should happen to the deploy step when one test fails, and why?
lessons.teach:
A repository is a versioned store of code, such as a Git repository on GitHub or AWS CodeCommit. A commit is one recorded set of changes, and a branch is a named line of commits, for example main. A pipeline is an ordered series of stages that runs automatically. On AWS, AWS CodePipeline is the managed orchestrator that strings stages together. AWS CodeBuild is a managed build service that runs commands in a temporary container. It reads them from a file called buildspec.yml at the root of the repository. AWS CodeDeploy is a managed service that pushes a built release onto servers, containers, or Lambda functions.

This works because the pipeline's source stage watches one specific branch. When a change event fires, it pulls that exact commit and passes it along as an artifact, meaning a packaged bundle of files. The change event can be a webhook from GitHub or an Amazon EventBridge event from CodeCommit. Each later stage only starts if the stage before it succeeded. A failing command returns a non-zero exit code, and CodeBuild treats that as failure. When CodeBuild fails, the pipeline stops.

Worked example. A developer pushes a fix to main. First, the source stage detects the push and captures commit a1b2c3. Second, the build stage starts CodeBuild, which reads buildspec.yml, installs dependencies, and compiles the code. Third, the test commands in the same buildspec run the unit tests, and one fails with exit code 1. Fourth, CodeBuild marks the build failed and the pipeline halts. Fifth, the deploy stage never runs, and production keeps the last good version. The developer pushes a corrected commit, and the whole chain runs again from the top.

A common mistake is pointing the source stage at the wrong branch, such as main when the team merges to master. Another is writing test commands that swallow errors so they always exit 0. In a running system, the first means commits silently never deploy. The second means broken code sails through to production because the safety gate never closes.

questions.prompt: A small logistics company keeps its parcel-tracking API in a GitHub repository. Its CodePipeline source stage watches a branch named release, and the deploy stage uses CodeDeploy to update a set of Lambda functions. A developer merges commit 7d4e19 into release. Step 1: GitHub sends a webhook, and the source stage pulls commit 7d4e19 and passes it on as an artifact. Step 2: The build stage starts CodeBuild, which reads buildspec.yml, installs dependencies, compiles the code, and runs 42 unit tests. Every command exits with code 0. Step 3: ??? Step 4: CodeDeploy pushes the new release onto the Lambda functions. What belongs in Step 3?
choices: The pipeline waits for the developer to push a second commit before it moves on, because one commit is never enough to deploy.
CodeBuild marks the build as succeeded, so the pipeline allows the next stage, deploy, to start.
The deploy stage had already started in parallel with the build, because stages run at the same time regardless of results.
CodeBuild copies the compiled files directly onto the Lambda functions, and CodeDeploy only confirms the copy afterwards.
questions.why: Each later stage starts only when the stage before it succeeded, and CodeBuild treats a run where every command exits 0 as a success, which releases the deploy stage.

questions.prompt: A veterinary clinic's development team merges all of its finished work into a branch called trunk. Their CodePipeline source stage was set up to watch a branch called main, which nobody uses any more. For two weeks, developers merge fixes into trunk. What happens in the running system?
choices: The pipeline detects the trunk merges anyway, because the source stage watches every branch in the repository.
The build stage fails with a non-zero exit code on every merge, which stops the pipeline and alerts the team.
None of the fixes reach production, and nothing fails loudly, because the source stage never sees a change on the branch it watches.
CodeDeploy rolls production back to the last commit that was on main.
questions.why: The source stage only reacts to changes on the one branch it watches, so commits on a different branch silently never trigger a build or deploy.

questions.prompt: At an online bookshop, a developer edits the test step in buildspec.yml so that the test command always reports success, even when tests fail. The goal is to stop the pipeline from being blocked. A later commit contains a bug that makes 3 of 60 tests fail. What is the most likely result?
choices: The source stage refuses to pull the commit because it contains failing tests.
CodeBuild notices the failed tests in the output and marks the build failed anyway.
The test command exits with code 0, CodeBuild marks the build succeeded, and the buggy code is deployed to production.
The deploy stage runs but CodeDeploy automatically skips any release with failing tests.
questions.why: CodeBuild judges success only by exit codes, so a test command that always exits 0 never closes the safety gate and broken code reaches production.

questions.prompt: A fitness-app team is setting up an automated release process on AWS. Which pairing correctly describes what each managed service does?
choices: CodePipeline strings the stages together in order; CodeBuild runs the build and test commands from buildspec.yml in a temporary container; CodeDeploy pushes the built release onto servers, containers, or Lambda functions.
CodePipeline stores commits; CodeBuild sends the webhook when a developer pushes; CodeDeploy runs the unit tests before release.
CodePipeline pushes releases onto servers; CodeBuild watches the branch for new commits; CodeDeploy compiles and tests the code.
CodePipeline runs the commands in buildspec.yml; CodeBuild stores the versioned code and its branches; CodeDeploy decides which stage runs next.
questions.why: CodePipeline is the orchestrator of stages, CodeBuild is the managed build service that reads buildspec.yml, and CodeDeploy delivers the built release to its targets.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a single git push ends up running a build, tests, and a deployment on AWS, and name one way this automation can fail to protect production.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our pipeline's source stage watches the main branch of our repository. When I push a commit there, a webhook or EventBridge event tells CodePipeline, which grabs that exact commit as an artifact. The build stage hands it to CodeBuild. CodeBuild spins up a temporary container and runs the steps in buildspec.yml: install dependencies, compile, then run the tests. Every command's exit code matters. If anything returns non-zero, the build fails and the pipeline stops, so the CodeDeploy stage never touches production. If everything passes, CodeDeploy rolls out the new version. The limit is that the gate is only as good as what we feed it. If the pipeline watches the wrong branch, our commits never deploy. If a test script hides failures and always exits zero, or our tests are thin, broken code goes straight to production with a green checkmark.
rubricPoints: The pipeline's source stage watches a specific branch and is triggered by a commit event.
CodeBuild runs build and test commands defined in buildspec.yml.
A non-zero exit code fails the stage and stops later stages, including deploy.
CodeDeploy (or a deploy stage) only runs after build and tests succeed.
Names a limit, such as a wrong watched branch, swallowed test errors, or weak tests letting bad code through.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red CI pipeline makes the learner trace how a commit flows through build and test stages and why a failed step blocks the rest.

lessons.plain: An orchestrated deployment workflow is an automated assembly line for releasing software. Instead of a person copying files to each server by hand, a pipeline runs a fixed sequence of steps: fetch the code, build it, put it in a practice environment, check it, and only then put it in the real one that customers use. Think of a car factory where each car moves station to station and stops if an inspection fails. On AWS, the service that runs this line is AWS CodePipeline, a managed release-pipeline service. The point is that every release follows the same path, in the same order, every time.
lessons.guessPrompt: If your team tests a release in a practice environment and it passes, should the pipeline rebuild the code again before sending it to production, or reuse exactly what was tested? Why?
lessons.teach:
An orchestrated workflow is a pipeline: a defined, automated sequence that moves one release through several environments. An environment is a separate copy of your application, such as dev (for developers), test or staging (a near-copy of production for checks), and prod (what customers use). In AWS CodePipeline, a managed pipeline service, the pipeline is split into stages, which are ordered groups of work. Each stage holds actions, the individual steps. Common action types are source (fetch code from a repository), build (compile and package, often with AWS CodeBuild, a managed build service), test, deploy (for example with AWS CodeDeploy or CloudFormation), and manual approval, a pause where a person must click approve before the pipeline continues. Actions pass artifacts to each other. An artifact is a file bundle, such as a zipped package, stored in an S3 bucket between stages.

Why it works: the order is enforced by the tool, a failed action stops the release before it reaches the next environment, and every run is recorded, so you can see who approved what and when.

Worked example. A developer commits change number 42. The source stage fetches it and saves it as an artifact. The build stage packages it into app-42.zip. The deploy-dev stage installs app-42.zip in dev. A test action runs integration checks against dev; if any fail, the pipeline stops and prod is untouched. Here they pass. A manual approval action waits until a release manager approves. The deploy-prod stage then installs the same app-42.zip in prod.

Common mistake: rebuilding the code separately for each environment. A second build can pull a newer dependency or a different commit, so production receives bits that were never tested. Build once, then promote that single artifact, changing only environment settings. In a running system, skipping this rule means a release that passed every check can still break customers, and nobody can say exactly what differs.

questions.prompt: A city library team runs a pipeline for its book-reservation app. Change number 317 is committed. The source stage fetches it and stores it as an artifact (a file bundle kept in an S3 bucket between stages). The build stage packages it into reserve-317.zip. The deploy-staging stage installs reserve-317.zip in staging, a near-copy of production. A test action runs checks against staging, and they all pass. A manual approval action pauses until the head librarian clicks approve. Missing step: what should the deploy-prod stage do next?
choices: Run a fresh build from the newest commit on the main branch, so production gets the latest code, then install it in prod
Skip installing anything and point customers at the staging environment, since it already passed its checks
Install the same reserve-317.zip in prod, changing only the production environment settings
Rebuild change 317 from source a second time, so the prod package is made specifically for production
questions.why: Build once and promote that single tested artifact, so production receives exactly the bits that passed the staging checks, with only environment settings changed.

questions.prompt: In AWS CodePipeline, a managed pipeline service, how do stages and actions relate to each other?
choices: A stage is an ordered group of work, and each stage holds actions, which are the individual steps such as build, deploy or manual approval
A stage is the zipped file bundle passed along the pipeline, and an action is the S3 bucket that stores it
Stages and actions are two names for the same thing, an environment such as dev or prod
An action is an ordered group of stages, and each stage is one copy of the application
questions.why: The pipeline is split into ordered stages, and each stage contains the individual steps called actions.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking company's pipeline builds trips-58.zip, deploys it to a test environment, and then runs an integration test action. Two of the tests fail. Assuming the pipeline is set up as an orchestrated workflow, what happens to production?
choices: Production receives trips-58.zip anyway, because the deploy-prod stage runs on a fixed schedule
The pipeline rebuilds the code and tries production with a new package instead
Nothing changes in production, because a failed action stops the release before it reaches the next environment
Production receives trips-58.zip after a manual approval action automatically approves it
questions.why: The tool enforces the order, so a failed test action halts the pipeline and later environments such as prod stay untouched.

questions.prompt: A payments startup's pipeline builds its app once for staging, where all checks pass, and then runs a separate build for production. A day later, the production release breaks customer checkouts even though staging looked fine. What is the most likely reason this setup allowed the problem?
choices: Building twice always corrupts the S3 bucket that stores artifacts
The manual approval action was placed before the test action, which reverses the order of the stages
The second build may have pulled a newer dependency or a different commit, so production got code that was never tested
Production cannot run a package that was built by AWS CodeBuild, a managed build service
questions.why: Rebuilding per environment means prod can receive different bits than the ones tested, so a release that passed every check can still break and nobody can say exactly what differs.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how a deployment pipeline moves one release from dev to production, and name one tradeoff of adding a manual approval step.
lessons.modelAnswer: A pipeline is an automated, ordered workflow. In CodePipeline it is made of stages, and each stage has actions like source, build, test, deploy and manual approval. A commit starts it: the source action grabs the code, the build action packages it once into an artifact stored in S3, and that same artifact is deployed to dev, tested, and then promoted to staging and prod. Only the environment configuration changes between environments, never the package, so prod gets exactly what was tested. If a test fails, the pipeline stops and later environments stay safe. A manual approval step adds a human check before prod, which catches things automated tests miss and gives an audit trail. The tradeoff is speed: releases wait on a person, which slows delivery and can become a bottleneck if approvers are unavailable.
rubricPoints: Defines a pipeline as ordered stages containing actions such as source, build, test, deploy and approval.
Explains that artifacts are passed between stages and stored between them.
States that one build artifact is promoted through environments rather than rebuilt for each.
Notes that a failed action stops the release before later environments.
Names a real tradeoff of manual approval, such as slower releases versus an added human check.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red CI pipeline makes the learner work directly with ordered stages, artifacts and failing steps, which is the core of an orchestrated deployment workflow.

lessons.plain: Rolling back means putting the last version of your application that worked back in front of users after a new release turns out to be broken. It is like the undo button in a document editor. Undo only works because the editor kept the earlier copy. A good release process does the same thing. It keeps the old version ready and makes the switch through the same route used to release the new one. That way, going back is fast and dull, not a panic rebuild at 2 a.m. Rollback is about getting users back to safety first. You find and fix the bug afterwards.
lessons.guessPrompt: You release version 8 of a function to 10% of users while 90% stay on version 7, and the error rate jumps. What is the quickest safe move, and why is it quicker than fixing the bug?
lessons.teach:
A rollback returns live traffic to the last known-good version using the deployment strategy that is already in place. That strategy is your chosen way of moving traffic from old to new. In blue/green, two full environments exist side by side. In canary, a small slice of traffic tries the new version first. In rolling, servers are replaced in batches. Rollback works because each strategy keeps the old version as an immutable artifact, meaning a saved build that is never changed. Going back is then a traffic switch, not a rebuild.

On AWS this ties together a few pieces. A Lambda version is a frozen, numbered copy of a function. A Lambda alias is a named pointer, such as live, that can send weighted traffic to one or two versions. AWS CodeDeploy is a managed release service that shifts the alias weights step by step. Amazon CloudWatch alarms watch metrics such as the error count and change state when a threshold is crossed. If an attached alarm fires during the deployment, CodeDeploy stops and reverses the shift on its own. AWS CloudFormation, the infrastructure-as-code service, does something similar for a whole stack. If a stack update fails, it returns the resources to their previous state.

Here is a worked example. The alias live points 100% to version 7. You deploy version 8 with a canary of 10% for five minutes, and an error alarm is attached. At minute three, errors cross the threshold and the alarm goes into ALARM. CodeDeploy marks the deployment failed and sets live back to 100% on version 7. Users see good responses again within moments. You then fix forward in a new version 9.

A common mistake is deploying without attaching alarms. The canary then promotes itself to 100% even while it is failing. Another mistake is deleting old versions or overwriting image tags, which leaves nothing to roll back to. Rollback also does not undo data or schema changes the bad release already wrote, so database changes must stay compatible with the previous code.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-booking company runs its checkout code as a Lambda function. The alias prod points 100% to version 21. The team deploys version 22 through CodeDeploy using a canary of 20% for ten minutes, with a CloudWatch alarm on the function's error count attached to the deployment.

Step 1: CodeDeploy moves the prod alias to 80% on version 21 and 20% on version 22.
Step 2: At minute six, the error count crosses the threshold and the alarm changes to the ALARM state.
Step 3: ???
Step 4: Customers get working checkouts again within moments, and the team starts work on a fixed version 23.

Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: CodeDeploy rebuilds version 21 from the source code and publishes it as a new version before switching prod to it
CloudFormation deletes version 22 and restores any database rows that version 22 wrote during the canary
CodeDeploy keeps the 20% split until the ten minutes end, then sends prod 100% to version 22 as planned
CodeDeploy marks the deployment failed and sets the prod alias back to 100% on version 21
questions.why: An alarm attached to the deployment makes CodeDeploy stop and reverse the shift, so the alias goes back to the saved, unchanged version 21 with a traffic switch rather than a rebuild.

questions.prompt: A payroll team uses a blue/green strategy: two complete environments run side by side, and the old one is kept as a saved build that is never changed. After a bad release, they move traffic back in under a minute. Why can the rollback be that fast?
choices: The pipeline recompiles the old code very quickly because it was cached on the build server
Blue/green deployments never let errors reach users, so nothing really needs to change
CloudWatch alarms automatically repair the faulty code in the new environment
Going back is only a traffic switch to the immutable old version, not a rebuild
questions.why: Each strategy keeps the previous version as an immutable artifact, so rollback simply points traffic back at it instead of building anything.

questions.prompt: A sports-news startup deploys version 4 of a Lambda function through CodeDeploy with a 15% canary for eight minutes. No CloudWatch alarms are attached to the deployment. Version 4 returns errors on most requests during the canary. What is the most likely outcome?
choices: CloudFormation detects the failed requests and rolls the whole stack back
The canary finishes its window and promotes version 4 to 100% of traffic while it is still failing
The canary pauses indefinitely at 15% until an engineer approves or rejects it
CodeDeploy notices the errors on its own and returns the alias to the previous version
questions.why: Without an attached alarm, nothing tells CodeDeploy the release is bad, so the canary promotes itself to full traffic even though it is failing.

questions.prompt: A clinic-scheduling app releases version 30, which renames a database column that version 29 reads. Users report errors, and CodeDeploy rolls the alias back to version 29 because an alarm fired. Errors continue after the rollback. What best explains this?
choices: Rollback switches code but does not undo the schema change, and version 29 is not compatible with the renamed column
The rollback failed because Lambda versions are numbered copies that can be edited after release
Version 29 had been deleted, so the alias could not point to it
CodeDeploy only rolls back blue/green deployments, not deployments that use aliases
questions.why: A rollback does not reverse data or schema changes the bad release already made, which is why database changes must stay compatible with the previous code.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how our canary deployment rolls back a bad Lambda release, and name one thing rollback cannot fix for us.
lessons.modelAnswer: Our function's live alias points to a numbered, frozen version. When we release, CodeDeploy sends a small slice of traffic, say 10%, to the new version while CloudWatch alarms watch errors. If an alarm fires before the canary finishes, CodeDeploy marks the deployment failed and moves the alias back to 100% on the old version. Rollback is just a pointer change, so it takes seconds, not a rebuild. That only works if we keep old versions around and actually attach the alarms. Without alarms, the bad version gets promoted anyway. The limit is that rollback restores code, not data. If the bad release wrote broken records or changed a table shape, the old code may still fail. So database changes need to be backward compatible, and data cleanup is a separate job. After rolling back, we fix forward with a new version.
rubricPoints: Rollback returns traffic to the last known-good version through the existing strategy.
It is fast because the old version is kept as an unchanged artifact, so it is a traffic switch, not a rebuild.
Automatic rollback depends on alarms attached to the deployment, such as CloudWatch alarms with CodeDeploy.
Deleting old versions or overwriting artifacts removes the ability to roll back.
Rollback does not undo data or schema changes, so those must stay compatible.
After rolling back, the team fixes forward with a new release.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner roll back a bad release quickly and then fix forward, which is exactly the skill in this objective.

lessons.plain: A branch is a separate line of work in a code repository (the shared, version-tracked store of your code), like a parallel draft of a document that can later be merged back. A label, usually called a tag, is a permanent name pinned to one exact snapshot of the code, such as "v1.4.0". Think of a book: branches are drafts still being edited, while a tag is the printed edition with a fixed number. Teams use branches to keep unfinished work apart from what is shipped, and tags to know exactly which code is running and to get back to it.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your team shipped version 1.4.0 last week and has merged lots of new, unfinished work since. A customer reports a serious bug in 1.4.0. How would you fix just that bug and ship it without also shipping the unfinished work?
lessons.teach:
A commit is one saved snapshot of the code with a unique ID. A branch is a named pointer to the latest commit in one line of work; it moves forward every time someone commits to it. A tag is a named pointer to one specific commit that is meant never to move. Branches answer "where is work happening?"; tags answer "what exactly did we release?"

A common layout: the main branch holds integrated, releasable code; short-lived feature branches hold one change each and merge into main after review; a release branch (for example release/1.4) is cut when a version is prepared, so it can be stabilised and patched while main keeps moving. Tags follow semantic versioning, a numbering scheme MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: bump MAJOR for breaking changes, MINOR for new compatible features, PATCH for compatible bug fixes.

Worked example. Step 1: main reaches a good state; you create branch release/1.4 and tag its commit v1.4.0, and the pipeline builds and deploys that tag. Step 2: main gains new, unfinished features. Step 3: a bug appears in production. You commit the fix on release/1.4, not on main. Step 4: you tag that commit v1.4.1 and deploy it; the unfinished work is untouched. Step 5: you merge or copy the fix into main so it is not lost in 1.5.

The same idea appears in AWS: a published Lambda version is an immutable numbered snapshot, much like a tag, while an alias is a movable named label pointing at a version; container images also carry tags, but a tag like "latest" can be moved, while an image digest (a content hash) cannot.

Common mistake: deploying a moving reference such as a branch name or "latest", or deleting and re-creating a tag on a different commit. Consequence: two deployments of "the same version" can contain different code, you cannot reproduce a bug, and rollback to a known-good release becomes guesswork. Treat release tags as permanent and deploy from them.

questions.prompt: A warehouse-software company runs a container service that tells pickers which shelf to visit. Its pipeline uses a container image, a packaged copy of the app that a server can run. Step 1: the pipeline builds an image from the Git tag v5.0.2 and pushes it to the image registry, the storage service for images, under the image tag "latest". Step 2: the registry reports the image's digest, a content hash such as sha256:ab12..., which can never point at different content. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: Three weeks later a new build pushes different code under "latest". The production service crashes and restarts, and it still runs exactly the v5.0.2 code. Which action belongs in Step 3?
choices: The production deployment configuration names the image by "latest" so it always picks up the newest build.
The production deployment configuration names the image by the Git branch main, since main holds releasable code.
The team deletes the Git tag v5.0.2 and re-creates it on the newest commit so the tag stays current.
The production deployment configuration names the image by its digest, sha256:ab12..., rather than by "latest".
questions.why: Only an immutable reference such as a digest guarantees that a restart pulls the same code; "latest", a branch name, and a re-created tag can all move to different code.

questions.prompt: A shared date-formatting library is at version 2.3.4 under semantic versioning, a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH numbering scheme. The team adds a new optional setting. Code that already uses the library keeps working unchanged. What should the next release tag be?
questions.why: A new feature that stays compatible bumps MINOR and resets PATCH to zero, so 2.3.4 becomes 2.4.0.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company invokes its Lambda function through an alias named "live". An alias is a movable named label that points at a published version, and a published version is an immutable numbered snapshot of the code. "live" pointed at version 7 until a deployment moved it to version 8, which is now failing. What is the cleanest rollback?
choices: Point the "live" alias back at version 7, the known-good snapshot.
Edit the code inside version 7 so it matches version 8 minus the bug.
Rename version 8 to version 7 so callers see the old number.
Delete the "live" alias so callers fall back to whatever code was uploaded most recently.
questions.why: Versions are immutable snapshots and the alias is the movable label, so moving the alias back to version 7 restores the known-good code exactly.

questions.prompt: A clinic-booking team deploys to its staging environment from the branch name main on Monday. On Tuesday it deploys to production, also from main. A bug that staging never showed now appears in production, and nobody can reproduce it in staging. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Production requires a MAJOR version bump before every deployment.
main is a moving pointer, so new commits landed between Monday and Tuesday and the two deployments contain different code.
Staging and production must always be built from separate feature branches.
Branches cannot be deployed to more than one environment.
questions.why: A branch moves forward with every commit, so deploying it by name on two different days can ship different code; deploying a fixed release tag avoids this.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a branch and a tag for release management, how you would ship a hotfix to an older release, and one limit or tradeoff of keeping long-lived release branches.
lessons.modelAnswer: A branch is a moving pointer for ongoing work: each commit advances it. A tag is a fixed pointer to one commit, used to name a release like v1.4.1 under semantic versioning, where the patch number signals a compatible bug fix. We deploy from tags, not branches, so we always know exactly which code is in production and can redeploy or roll back to it. For a hotfix to 1.4 while main has moved on, I commit the fix on the release/1.4 branch, tag it v1.4.1, deploy that tag, then bring the fix into main so the next release keeps it. The tradeoff is that every long-lived release branch must be maintained: fixes need copying across branches, they can drift apart, and merges get harder, so we keep few of them and retire old ones. Never move or reuse a tag, or releases stop being reproducible.
rubricPoints: A branch is a movable pointer for a line of work; a tag is a fixed pointer to one commit.
Release versions are named with tags, often using MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH semantic versioning.
A hotfix is made on the release branch, tagged as a new patch version, deployed, then merged back to main.
Deploying from immutable tags makes releases reproducible and rollback reliable.
Moving tags or deploying a moving name like latest or a branch breaks reproducibility.
Long-lived release branches cost effort to keep in sync and can drift.

suggested.rationale: Rolling back to a known-good release and then fixing forward makes the learner rely on exactly the fixed, named release points that tags and release branches provide.

lessons.plain: A dynamic deployment is one where the same deployed code decides at runtime which backend, database or setting to use, based on configuration attached to the environment rather than baked into the code. In Amazon API Gateway, a managed service that puts a web address in front of your functions, each stage (such as dev or prod) can carry its own small set of named values called stage variables. Think of a hotel key card: the same card design opens different rooms depending on what is written on it. One API definition reaches different function versions depending on which stage's values are read.
lessons.guessPrompt: You have one API with a dev stage and a prod stage, and one Lambda function with a dev version and a prod version. Without copying the API, how could each stage send requests to its matching function version?
lessons.teach:
Stage variables are name-value pairs stored on an API Gateway stage. A stage is a named, deployed snapshot of an API with its own URL, such as /dev or /prod. In the integration, the setting that says which backend handles a request, you can write a placeholder like ${stageVariables.alias} instead of a fixed value. API Gateway fills it in from the calling stage on every request, so one API definition behaves differently per stage without being redeployed.

This pairs naturally with Lambda aliases. Lambda is AWS's run-your-function-on-demand service. An alias is a named pointer, such as dev or live, to a specific published version of a function. The function's address with the alias appended is called a qualified ARN, meaning the Amazon Resource Name plus a version or alias name.

Worked example. The integration target is set to the orders function's ARN followed by :${stageVariables.alias}. The dev stage has alias=dev; the prod stage has alias=live. A request to /dev/orders arrives, API Gateway reads alias=dev, and it invokes orders:dev. A request to /prod/orders resolves to orders:live. To promote new code, you point the live alias at the newer version or change the prod stage's variable, with no change to the API. Stage variables are also passed to the function inside the request event, so code can read, for example, a table name per stage.

Common mistake: forgetting permissions. Lambda must explicitly allow API Gateway to invoke each qualified ARN through a resource-based policy, which is the function's own list of who may call it. Granting it for one alias does not cover the others. In a running system the newly wired stage returns HTTP 500 errors while the other stage keeps working, which looks confusingly like a code bug.

Stage variables are plain text visible in configuration, so they must never hold passwords or keys; use a secrets service for those.

questions.prompt: A bakery chain's API Gateway API has two stages, /test and /main. The integration target is set to the pricing function's ARN followed by :${stageVariables.env}. The test stage has the stage variable env=candidate. The main stage has env=stable. The candidate and stable aliases each point to a different published version of the pricing function. Step 1: A request to /test/prices arrives at API Gateway. Step 2: (missing). Step 3: The version of the pricing function that the candidate alias points to runs and returns its response. Which choice is the missing Step 2?
choices: API Gateway reads env=stable, because every stage of an API shares the values of the most recently deployed stage
The pricing function receives the request first, reads env from the event, and then forwards the request to its candidate alias
API Gateway reads env=candidate from the test stage, fills in the placeholder, and invokes pricing:candidate
API Gateway invokes the unqualified pricing function, because placeholders are filled in only when the API is first deployed
questions.why: API Gateway fills in the placeholder on every request from the stage that was called, so a call to /test resolves env to candidate and invokes the qualified ARN pricing:candidate.

questions.prompt: A developer at a travel startup writes ${stageVariables.target} inside an API Gateway integration setting. What does API Gateway do with this placeholder?
choices: It replaces the placeholder once at build time and stores the result permanently in the API definition
On each request, it replaces the placeholder with the value of the target variable stored on the stage that was called
It sends the placeholder text unchanged to the backend, which must work out what it means
It looks the value up in a secrets service, because stage variables are meant to hold sensitive data
questions.why: Stage variables are name-value pairs stored on a stage, and API Gateway fills in the placeholder from the calling stage on every request, so one API definition behaves differently per stage.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's API has a working /prod stage whose integration invokes invoices:live. The team adds a new /qa stage with the stage variable alias=qa, so it invokes invoices:qa. The qa alias exists and its code passes unit tests. Calls to /qa now return HTTP 500 errors, while /prod keeps working. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The /prod stage is holding a lock on the function, so it blocks all other callers
The function's resource-based policy allows API Gateway to invoke invoices:live but not invoices:qa
Stage variables only work on the first stage of an API, so /qa cannot use them
The function code has a bug that only shows up when the code runs on Lambda
questions.why: Each qualified ARN needs its own permission in the function's resource-based policy, and a missing grant for the new alias causes 500 errors on that stage only, which can look like a code bug.

questions.prompt: A fitness app team uses stage variables so that its dev and prod stages each pass a different table name to the Lambda function. The team now also needs to give the function a different third-party payment API key per stage. What should the team do?
choices: Keep each key in a secrets service, and use a stage variable to hold only a non-secret value, such as which secret to look up
Put the key in the alias name, so that the qualified ARN carries the secret to the function
Store the key in a stage variable, but only on the prod stage, where fewer people can see it
Store each key directly in a stage variable, because stage variables are encrypted and hidden from configuration views
questions.why: Stage variables are plain text that anyone can see in the configuration, so passwords and keys belong in a secrets service, never in a stage variable on any stage.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how API Gateway stage variables let one API send dev and prod traffic to different Lambda aliases, and name one limit or risk of this approach.
lessons.modelAnswer: Each API Gateway stage, like dev or prod, can hold stage variables, which are simple name-value pairs. Instead of hard-coding the Lambda target, we put a placeholder such as ${stageVariables.alias} on the end of the function ARN. When a request hits /dev, API Gateway substitutes dev and calls the dev alias; /prod substitutes live and calls the live alias, which points at a specific published version. So one API definition serves every environment, and we promote code by moving the alias or changing the variable rather than rebuilding the API. The function also receives the stage variables in its event, so it can pick per-stage settings like a table name. Limits: the function's resource-based policy must allow API Gateway to invoke every alias separately, or that stage returns 500 errors. And the values are plain text, so secrets must never go in them.
rubricPoints: Stage variables are name-value pairs attached to a specific API Gateway stage.
The integration uses a placeholder resolved per request, so one API definition serves several environments.
A Lambda alias is a named pointer to a published version, and the stage variable selects which alias is invoked.
Each qualified alias ARN needs its own permission for API Gateway to invoke it, otherwise the stage returns errors.
Stage variables are plain text and must not hold secrets.

suggested.rationale: No current mission or planned engine wires stage variables to aliases, so reasoning through an exam-style scenario where one stage returns 500 errors builds the right mental model fastest.

lessons.plain: Debugging is the work of finding exactly which part of your code is wrong and why, before you change anything. A defect (often called a bug) is a mistake in code that makes it behave differently from what was intended. Debugging is like a mechanic tracing a strange noise. They don't replace parts at random. They reproduce the noise, narrow down where it comes from, confirm the cause, and only then repair it. In cloud applications you rarely watch the code run. Your evidence is the error messages and records the running service leaves behind.
lessons.guessPrompt: A function crashes with an error that names a file and a line number. Should you start reading the code at the top of the file, or at the line the error points to? Why?
lessons.teach:
Debugging means locating the exact cause of a defect, which is code that does something other than intended, and proving it is the cause before you fix it. The reliable loop has four steps: reproduce, read the evidence, form one hypothesis, and confirm it.

The key evidence is the stack trace. This is the list of function calls that were active when an error was raised, and it ends with the error type, its message, and the file and line. In AWS Lambda, which is a managed service that runs your function in response to events, this trace lands in the function's log stream in CloudWatch Logs, AWS's managed log store. The input that caused the failure is called the event.

Worked example: an order API returns errors for some users. Step 1: open the log and find the trace. It ends with "TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'id') at handler.js:12". Step 2: read line 12, which is customer = event.body.customer.id. The message says customer is undefined, so the event had no customer field. Step 3: hypothesis: guest checkouts send no customer object. Step 4: save that failing event as a test event and run it locally, for example with the SAM CLI's local invoke, which runs a Lambda function on your machine. It fails the same way, so the hypothesis is confirmed. The fix handles a missing customer explicitly, and you add a unit test using that event so the defect cannot quietly return.

This works because each step shrinks the search space. You move from the whole system to one line, and then to one input.

A common mistake is fixing the symptom by wrapping the code in a try/catch that logs nothing and returns success. The function then reports success to Lambda. For asynchronous invocations, Lambda will not retry the event or send it to a failure destination, so bad events are lost silently. The real defect stays hidden until it causes damage somewhere harder to trace. Either let real errors fail loudly, or catch them, log them with context, and re-raise.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing startup runs a Lambda function that makes thumbnails whenever a picture is uploaded. About 1 in 50 uploads produce no thumbnail. Step 1: in the function's log stream in CloudWatch Logs, the stack trace ends with "KeyError: 'width' at thumbs.py:27". Step 2: line 27 is size = event['metadata']['width'], so the incoming event had no width field in its metadata. Step 3: hypothesis: pictures uploaded from the older mobile app do not include a width value. Step 4: ??? Step 5: the fix computes the width from the image itself when the field is missing, and a unit test is added that uses that event. Which action belongs in Step 4?
choices: Wrap line 27 in a try/except that returns success, so the missing thumbnails stop showing up as errors
Save one failing upload's event as a test event and run it locally, such as with SAM CLI local invoke, to see it fail the same way
Raise the function's memory and timeout settings, because occasional failures usually mean the function is short on resources
Deploy the fix to production right away, because the trace already names the exact line that failed
questions.why: Replaying the real failing event locally and getting the same failure is what proves the hypothesis before any fix is made.

questions.prompt: A billing team's Lambda function fails, and the last line of the stack trace reads "ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'N/A' at invoice.py:41". Based on what a stack trace contains, what is the most useful next step?
choices: Restart the function, since a value error usually means the runtime is in a bad state
Search the whole codebase for every int() call, since any of them could be the cause
Open invoice.py at line 41 and see which input field is being turned into a number
Add a try/except around the entire handler so the function reports success
questions.why: A stack trace ends with the error type, its message, and the file and line, so it narrows the search straight to line 41 and the value 'N/A' being converted there.

questions.prompt: A logistics company's Lambda function is invoked asynchronously for each shipment event. A developer wraps the handler in a try/catch that logs nothing and returns success. Later, a malformed shipment event arrives and the code inside throws an error. What happens to that event?
choices: It is lost silently, because Lambda sees success and neither retries it nor sends it to a failure destination
Lambda retries it automatically until the code succeeds or the retry limit is reached
Lambda sends it to the configured failure destination so it can be inspected later
The error is still written to CloudWatch Logs with a full stack trace for later review
questions.why: Because the function reports success, Lambda has no reason to retry or route the event to a failure destination, and nothing was logged, so the bad event disappears without a trace.

questions.prompt: A ticketing app's developer has traced a crash to events that contain an empty seat list, confirmed it by replaying one such event locally, and written a fix. What should they add so this exact defect cannot quietly come back in a later release?
choices: A unit test that runs the code with that saved empty-seat event
A note in the code comment describing the empty-seat problem
A larger memory setting so the function has more room to run
A try/catch around the seat logic that returns success on error
questions.why: A unit test built from the real failing event will fail if a later change brings the defect back, so the problem is caught before release instead of going unnoticed.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would track down the defect behind a Lambda function that fails for some requests. Name one limit of debugging from logs alone, or one tradeoff in how you handle the error once you find it.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I reproduce it. I find a failing request in CloudWatch Logs and read the stack trace from the bottom. The error type, message, file and line tell me where it broke. Then I look at that line and the event that triggered it. I form one hypothesis, such as "this field is missing for guest users". I prove it by replaying that saved event locally or as a test event and seeing the same failure. Only then do I fix it, and I add a test built from that event. One limit is that logs only show what the code chose to record. If the input wasn't logged, I may not be able to reproduce the failure. The tradeoff when handling the error is that catching it keeps the function from crashing, but swallowing it hides failures and stops retries. So I log it with context and re-raise it unless the case is truly expected.
rubricPoints: Reproduces the failure with the real failing input before changing code.
Reads the stack trace for error type, message, file and line.
Forms and confirms one hypothesis instead of changing code at random.
Adds a test from the failing event so the defect stays fixed.
Warns that swallowing exceptions hides defects and prevents retries.
Names a limit, such as logs lacking the input needed to reproduce.

suggested.rationale: The mission makes the learner reproduce a failure, read the error output, and fix the root cause instead of masking the symptom, which is the core debugging loop.

lessons.plain: When an app misbehaves, you have three kinds of evidence. Metrics are numbers over time, like a car dashboard showing speed and engine temperature: they tell you something is wrong and when. Logs are written notes from the code, like a driver's diary: they say what happened and why. Traces follow one single request from start to finish across every service it touches, like a parcel tracking history showing where it waited. Each alone gives a partial picture. Used together, the dashboard tells you when to look, the tracking history tells you where, and the notes explain the cause.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your web app's average response time looks normal, but some customers say it is very slow. Which do you think would best show you where those slow requests are spending their time: a graph of average response time, a list of all log lines, or a record that follows one slow request through each service it calls?
lessons.teach:
Interpreting metrics, logs, and traces together means asking each signal the question it answers best, then joining them on time and request ID. A metric is a number measured over time, such as error count or p99 latency (the time that 99 of every 100 requests finish within). Metrics are cheap to keep and show that something changed, and when. A log is a timestamped record written by code that shows what happened inside one component and why. A trace follows one request across services. Each step in it is a segment (also called a span) with its own duration. On AWS, CloudWatch is the managed monitoring service that stores metrics and logs. X-Ray is the managed tracing service, and its service map draws how services connect and where time goes. If your code writes the trace ID (the unique identifier for one request's trace) into each log line, you can jump from a trace to its logs.

Why it works: metrics narrow the time window and the affected service. Traces narrow it to the slow or failing step. Logs explain the cause at that step.

Worked example: an order API's p99 latency jumps from 300 ms to 4 s at 10:05. The average barely moves and the error rate stays flat. Step 1, metrics: the problem started at 10:05 and hits a minority of requests. Step 2, traces: you open slow traces from 10:05 to 10:15. The Lambda function, a serverless function service, spends 3.6 s calling DynamoDB, a managed NoSQL database. Every other step looks normal. Step 3, logs: you filter the function's logs by those trace IDs. They show repeated throttling errors, where the database refused requests because the table had hit its throughput limit, and the client kept retrying. Step 4, back to metrics: the table's throttled-request count rose at 10:05, which confirms the cause. Fixing the table's capacity should bring p99 back toward 300 ms and throttles toward zero.

Common mistake: trusting the average, or relying on a single signal. Averages hide slow outliers, and logs searched with no time window are a haystack. In a running system, that means longer outages and fixes aimed at the wrong part, such as giving the function more memory when the database is the real bottleneck.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking API's p99 latency (the time that 99 of every 100 requests finish within) jumps from 250 ms to 5 s at 09:40. The average latency barely changes, and the error rate stays flat. Step 1, metrics: the problem began at 09:40 and affects a minority of requests. Step 2, traces: you open slow X-Ray traces from 09:40 to 09:50. The Lambda function spends 4.5 s in one segment, a call to an outside pricing service, and every other segment looks normal. Step 3: ??? Step 4, metrics: the pricing call's timeout count rose at 09:40, which confirms the cause. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: Raise the Lambda function's memory, because the slow segment runs inside that function.
Search every log the function wrote over the past week for the word "error" to find whatever went wrong.
Check the average latency again to confirm that most requests are slow.
Filter the function's logs in CloudWatch by the trace IDs of those slow traces, to read why the pricing call took so long, such as repeated timeouts and retries.
questions.why: Once metrics have narrowed the time window and traces have narrowed the problem to one step, filtering the logs by those trace IDs explains the cause at that step.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming team reports that its search endpoint has a p99 latency of 2 s. What does this number tell you?
choices: Only 1 in every 100 search requests has failed.
The fastest search request took 2 s to finish.
The average search request takes 2 s to finish.
99 of every 100 search requests finish within 2 s, and the slowest 1 in 100 take longer.
questions.why: p99 latency is the time within which 99 of every 100 requests finish, so it shows how slow the outliers are, which an average can hide.

questions.prompt: At 16:30, a CloudWatch metric shows the error count for a library's book-loan API climbing sharply. The API passes each request through three services. You now know when the problem started. Which signal should you use next to find which step of the failing requests is breaking?
choices: The average latency metric, because it shows whether most requests are affected.
Logs from all three services with no time filter, because logs explain why things happened.
Traces, because they follow one request across services and show each segment, so the failing step stands out.
More metrics from the same API, because metrics are cheap to keep.
questions.why: Metrics narrow the time window, traces narrow the problem to the slow or failing step, and logs then explain the cause at that step.

questions.prompt: A fitness app's workout-save Lambda function became slow. Without looking at traces, the team doubled the function's memory, but latency did not improve. A trace later shows that 90% of each slow request is spent waiting on a DynamoDB table that was throttling, meaning it refused requests because it had hit its throughput limit. What went wrong?
choices: Throttling only shows up in logs, so traces could never have revealed this problem.
Relying on a single signal led them to fix the wrong part. The database was the bottleneck, so they needed to address the table's capacity.
The team should have trusted the average latency, which would have pointed to the function.
Doubling the memory was too small a change, and quadrupling it would have fixed the problem.
questions.why: Skipping traces sent the fix to the function, but the trace shows the time is spent in the throttled table, so the table's capacity is what needs to change.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use metrics, logs, and traces together to find why some requests are slow. Name one limit or tradeoff of relying on any single one of these signals.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start with metrics, because they are cheap and show when things changed and which service is affected. I look at a percentile like p99, not the average, because averages hide the slow minority. With that time window, I open traces for slow requests. A trace follows one request through every service, so its segments show which step is eating the time, for example a database call. Then I read the logs for that step, filtered by the trace IDs, to see why: an error, a retry, or a throttle. Finally I go back to metrics to confirm the cause lines up in time, and to pick the number my fix should move. The tradeoff is that each signal alone misleads. Metrics say something is wrong but not why. Logs have detail but are hard to search without a window. Traces are often sampled, so they may miss rare requests.
rubricPoints: Metrics show that something changed and when, and percentiles reveal tail latency that averages hide.
Traces follow one request across services and show which step is slow or failing.
Logs explain the cause at that step, and are easier to use when they carry the trace ID.
The signals are joined on time window and request or trace ID.
The cause is confirmed back in metrics, and the fix names the number it should move.
Relying on one signal alone gives an incomplete or misleading picture.

suggested.rationale: Diagnosing a slow API after a deploy makes the learner move from a latency metric to the slow component to the log evidence, which is exactly the skill of reading signals together.

lessons.plain: Querying logs means asking a precise question of your stored log lines and getting back only the ones that answer it. An application can write millions of lines a day, far too many to read. A query works like a search plus a calculator: keep only the errors from the payment service in the last hour, then count them by type. On AWS the store is called CloudWatch Logs, and its query tool is CloudWatch Logs Insights. It is like asking a librarian for every page that mentions one word, published in one week, sorted by date, instead of reading the whole library.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your service logged 2 million lines today, and users say checkout broke around 14:00. Before reading anything, what two or three things would you narrow down first to shrink those lines to the few that matter?
lessons.teach:
Querying logs means filtering and summarizing stored log records so only the relevant ones come back. In CloudWatch Logs, a log event is one timestamped record. A log stream is the sequence of events from one source, such as one Lambda execution environment. A log group collects the streams for one application, for example /aws/lambda/checkout. CloudWatch Logs Insights is the query tool. You choose log groups and a time range, then write commands joined by the pipe symbol |, each passing its output to the next.

The core commands are these. fields picks which fields to show. filter keeps events matching a condition. stats aggregates, for example count() by a field. sort orders the rows. limit caps how many come back. parse pulls fields out of plain text. Built-in fields start with @, such as @timestamp, @message and @logStream. JSON logs are split into named fields automatically. Lambda's end-of-invocation report line supplies @duration.
