This works because filtering first shrinks the data, and aggregation turns thousands of lines into a few numbers.

Worked example: checkout errors began near 14:00. Select the checkout log group and the range 13:30 to 15:00. Run: filter level = "ERROR" | stats count() by errorCode | sort count() desc. The filter keeps only error events. The stats step groups them by errorCode and counts each group. The sort puts the largest group first. The result is 412 TimeoutError and 3 ValidationError. Next, run: filter errorCode = "TimeoutError" | fields @timestamp, requestId, @message | sort @timestamp asc | limit 20. This shows the earliest timeouts and gives you a requestId to follow.

A common mistake is choosing the wrong log group or time range, getting zero rows, and concluding nothing went wrong. Another is text-searching @message when the logs are JSON, where a field condition is more exact. Insights bills by data scanned, so wide ranges across many groups run slower and cost more. To watch for a pattern continuously, use a metric filter, which turns matching lines into a metric, instead of rerunning queries.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company notices that its Lambda function seat-reserve felt slow between 09:00 and 09:45. An engineer opens CloudWatch Logs Insights, selects the log group /aws/lambda/seat-reserve, and sets the range 08:45 to 10:00. She wants the 5 slowest invocations, using the @duration field that Lambda's end-of-invocation report line supplies. Her query is: fields @timestamp, @logStream, @duration | [missing step] | limit 5. Step 1 shows the time, the source stream and the duration of each event. Step 3 keeps only 5 rows. Which command belongs in the missing step?
choices: stats count() by @duration
filter @duration = "slow"
sort @duration asc
sort @duration desc
questions.why: Sorting by @duration in descending order puts the longest invocations first, so the limit 5 that follows keeps exactly the 5 slowest.

questions.prompt: A data team's Lambda function report-builder logs to the log group /aws/lambda/report-builder. During a busy hour, the function runs in three separate execution environments, and each one writes its own run of timestamped records. In CloudWatch Logs terms, what is each environment's sequence of records called?
choices: A log group
A log event
A metric filter
A log stream
questions.why: A log stream is the sequence of events from one source, such as one Lambda execution environment, and the log group collects all of those streams for the application.

questions.prompt: Customers of a grocery delivery app report failed orders between 18:10 and 18:30. An engineer runs filter level = "ERROR" | stats count() by errorCode in Logs Insights. He selected the log group /aws/lambda/inventory-sync and the range 17:00 to 17:30, and the query returns zero rows. What is the most sensible conclusion?
choices: The filter is wrong and should be a text search of @message
The log group and time range must be checked before concluding anything
The stats command removed the rows, so drop it and rerun
No errors happened, so the outage reports are false
questions.why: His range ends before the failures began, and he may have chosen the wrong log group, so zero rows says nothing about whether errors occurred.

questions.prompt: A payments startup wants to be told whenever log lines containing PaymentDeclined appear in its /aws/lambda/charge-card log group, around the clock. A developer suggests rerunning a Logs Insights query every few minutes. What is the better approach based on how CloudWatch Logs works?
choices: Create a metric filter that turns matching lines into a metric
Run one Insights query across every log group for the past month
Add a limit command so the repeated query scans less data
Search @message for the text instead of using a field condition
questions.why: A metric filter continuously turns matching log lines into a metric. Rerunning Insights queries rescans data each time, and Insights bills by the data it scans.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use CloudWatch Logs Insights to find why a Lambda function started failing, and name one limit or tradeoff of querying logs this way.
lessons.modelAnswer: I'd start by picking the right log group, the function's /aws/lambda/name group, and a tight time range around when failures began. Then I'd chain commands with pipes. I'd filter to error-level events and use stats count() by errorCode, sorted descending, so thousands of lines collapse into a short list showing which error dominates. Then I'd filter to that one error and show @timestamp, requestId and @message, sorted oldest first with a limit. That shows when it started and gives me a request to follow. Filtering early keeps each step small. The tradeoff is that Insights charges by data scanned, so a wide time range across many log groups is slower and costs more. It is also an on-demand tool. For continuous alerting on a pattern, I'd use a metric filter instead. And if the time range or group is wrong, zero results don't prove nothing happened.
rubricPoints: Defines log event, log stream and log group and chooses the right group and time range first.
Describes chaining commands with pipes, such as filter, stats, sort, fields and limit.
Uses aggregation like count by error type to find the dominant failure before reading lines.
Drills from the summary to individual events, for example by requestId or earliest timestamp.
Names a limit, such as cost per data scanned, slowness on wide ranges, or misleading empty results.
Notes that a metric filter, not repeated queries, suits ongoing alerting.

suggested.rationale: The log detective mission makes the learner narrow a large log down to the lines explaining an API failure, which is the same filter-then-summarize skill Logs Insights queries use.

lessons.plain: A custom metric is a number your own code reports, such as orders placed or payment time, instead of one the platform measures for you, like CPU use. Amazon CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service, can graph and alarm on these numbers. The embedded metric format lets your code write one structured log line that carries the number along with a short label explaining it. CloudWatch reads that label and turns the log line into a metric for you. Think of a shop receipt with a tear-off coupon: one piece of paper, but the counter clerk files the coupon separately.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your function already writes a log line for every order. If you wanted a graph of orders per minute, would you rather make a separate network call to the monitoring service on every order, or somehow mark up the log line you already write? Why?
lessons.teach:
A metric is a named series of numbers over time. In CloudWatch each metric lives in a namespace, which is a folder name for your app such as FleetApp. It is identified by its name plus its dimensions. A dimension is a name-value pair that splits the series, such as Service=checkout. A custom metric is any metric your code publishes. You can publish one in two ways.

The first way is the PutMetricData API call, a direct request to CloudWatch. It is immediate, but it adds a network call inside your request path, and those calls can be throttled or fail.

The second way is the embedded metric format (EMF). EMF is a JSON log line with a reserved _aws block. That block lists a Timestamp and a CloudWatchMetrics array giving the Namespace, the Dimensions to use, and each metric's Name and Unit. The actual values sit as ordinary top-level fields. CloudWatch Logs spots the _aws block and extracts metrics in the background. Your code only writes to standard output, which is cheap and never blocks on a remote call.

Worked example. A Lambda function finishes a checkout and prints: {"_aws":{"Timestamp":1700000000000,"CloudWatchMetrics":[{"Namespace":"FleetApp","Dimensions":[["Service"]],"Metrics":[{"Name":"CheckoutLatency","Unit":"Milliseconds"}]}]},"Service":"checkout","CheckoutLatency":182,"orderId":"A17"}. Step 1: the line lands in the function's log group. Step 2: CloudWatch sees _aws and reads Namespace FleetApp. Step 3: it looks up the dimension Service and finds checkout. Step 4: it reads CheckoutLatency=182 in milliseconds and records a data point. The orderId field is not declared as a dimension. It stays searchable in the log but does not create a metric.

Common mistake: declaring a high-cardinality field, one with many distinct values such as orderId or userId, as a dimension. Every unique combination of dimension values becomes a separate custom metric, and each one is billed. Costs balloon, and the metrics become useless for graphing. A second mistake is writing malformed JSON, or naming a value field that is missing from the line. In both cases no metric appears and nothing reports an error, so dashboards and alarms silently go flat.

questions.prompt: A photo-sharing company, PixelPort, has a Lambda function that resizes uploaded images. After each resize it prints this line to standard output: {"_aws":{"Timestamp":1712345678000,"CloudWatchMetrics":[{"Namespace":"PixelPort","Dimensions":[["Format"]],"Metrics":[{"Name":"ResizeDuration","Unit":"Milliseconds"}]}]},"Format":"png","ResizeDuration":94,"imageId":"img-5521"}. Here is how CloudWatch turns it into a metric. Step 1: the line lands in the function's log group. Step 2: CloudWatch Logs notices the _aws block and reads the namespace PixelPort. Step 3: ??? Step 4: it reads ResizeDuration=94, in milliseconds, and records one data point. The imageId field stays searchable in the log but produces no metric. Which choice correctly fills in Step 3?
choices: It looks up the declared dimension Format and finds the value png in the top-level fields of the line
It creates one dimension for Format and another for imageId, because every top-level field in the line becomes a dimension
It makes a PutMetricData call on the function's behalf, and the call waits for CloudWatch to confirm before the function returns
It reads the value png from inside the _aws block, where EMF stores dimension values next to the metric names
questions.why: The _aws block only declares which field names are dimensions, so CloudWatch reads the value of Format (png) from the ordinary top-level fields, and the undeclared imageId does not become a dimension.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company publishes an EMF metric called SeatLookupTime. A developer adds sessionId, which is unique for every visitor, to the Dimensions list so they can "see each session." The site gets about 200,000 visitors a day. What is the most likely result?
choices: CloudWatch combines all the sessionId values into one metric, so cost and graphs stay the same as before
The function slows down because each new sessionId adds a network call to CloudWatch inside the request
CloudWatch rejects the log line because a dimension may hold only a few allowed values, and it returns an error to the function
Each distinct sessionId value creates its own billed custom metric, so costs climb sharply and the graphs become too fragmented to be useful
questions.why: Every unique combination of dimension values is a separate custom metric that is billed on its own, so a high-cardinality field like sessionId multiplies cost and makes the graphs useless.

questions.prompt: A logistics team's function prints an EMF line that declares a metric named QueueDepth in the _aws block. Because of a typo, the value is written as the top-level field "QueueDept":37. The function runs normally. What will the team observe?
choices: CloudWatch logs an error explaining that QueueDepth is missing, so the team can fix the typo quickly
CloudWatch matches the closest field name and records 37 under QueueDepth
No QueueDepth data point appears and nothing reports an error, so the dashboard and any alarm on it silently go flat
CloudWatch records QueueDepth as 0 for each invocation, so the alarm sees a steady value of zero
questions.why: When a declared metric's value field is missing from the line, no metric is extracted and no error is raised, so the series simply stops receiving data.

questions.prompt: A payments API handles thousands of requests per second. The team wants a custom metric for each request's fraud-check time, but they do not want to add any remote call to the request path that could be throttled or fail. Which approach fits best, and why?
choices: Create a new namespace for every request, because separate namespaces stop calls from being throttled
Call PutMetricData once per request, because a direct call to CloudWatch is immediate and therefore adds no delay
Write an embedded metric format (EMF) line to standard output, because CloudWatch Logs extracts the metric in the background and the code never waits on a remote call
Put the fraud-check time only in a plain log message without an _aws block, because CloudWatch turns any number in a log into a metric
questions.why: EMF only writes to standard output, which is cheap and never blocks, while PutMetricData adds a network call that can be throttled or fail, and a log line without the _aws block produces no metric.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how the embedded metric format turns a log line into a CloudWatch metric, why you might pick it over calling PutMetricData directly, and one limit or tradeoff to watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: With the embedded metric format, our code prints a JSON log line that includes a reserved _aws block. That block names the namespace, which dimensions to use, and each metric's name and unit. The actual numbers are normal fields in the same JSON. CloudWatch Logs sees the block and extracts the metrics asynchronously, so our code only writes to stdout. It never waits on a network call to the monitoring service, which PutMetricData would require on every request. We also keep the full log line for later searching, so one write gives us both a metric and context. The tradeoff is dimensions. Every unique dimension combination is its own billed metric, so putting something like userId in a dimension explodes cost. Keep IDs as plain fields instead. Also, a malformed line fails silently, so verify the metric appears after deploying.
rubricPoints: A custom metric is a number the application itself reports, organized by namespace, name and dimensions.
EMF is a structured JSON log line with an _aws metadata block that CloudWatch Logs converts into metrics.
EMF avoids a synchronous PutMetricData network call in the request path and keeps the log context too.
High-cardinality dimensions create many billed metrics, so IDs should stay as plain fields.
Malformed EMF lines produce no metric without raising an error, so emission must be verified.

suggested.rationale: The skill is choosing between EMF and PutMetricData and picking sensible dimensions, which is best practiced by reasoning through exam-style scenarios, and no current mission or planned engine has the learner emit metrics.

lessons.plain: Reviewing application health means looking at a few well-chosen pictures of your system so you can tell, at a glance, whether it is working and, if not, roughly where it hurts. A dashboard is one screen of charts showing numbers such as errors, speed, and load side by side. An insights feature is a ready-made tool that collects extra detail for a certain kind of workload and points out unusual patterns. Think of a car dashboard: the speedometer and warning lights tell you something is off; the mechanic's diagnostic scanner, like an insights tool, tells you which part to inspect first.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app's error-count chart jumped at 09:00, and someone deployed at 08:58. Which other two charts would you want on the same screen to decide whether the deploy caused it?
lessons.teach:
A dashboard, in Amazon CloudWatch (AWS's monitoring service), is a saved page of widgets. Each widget is a chart or number built from metrics, which are numeric values recorded over time such as request count, error count, or duration. Dashboards are useful because placing related metrics on one shared time axis lets your eye spot cause and effect: a spike in one line that lines up with a change in another.

Insights features add depth without custom work. CloudWatch Lambda Insights collects per-function memory, CPU, and cold-start detail for serverless functions (AWS Lambda). Container Insights does the same for containers and clusters. Contributor Insights ranks the top contributors to a pattern in logs, for example which customer ID or IP address causes the most errors. Application Insights watches a whole application's resources and groups related problems. The X-Ray service map draws each service as a node, with its error rate and latency, so you can see which call is slow. Application Signals adds service-level health and objectives, meaning targets such as 99.9% of requests under 500 ms.

Worked example. The order API feels slow. Step 1: open the dashboard and see p99 duration (the time within which 99% of requests finish) rise from 300 ms to 2 s at 09:00, while invocation count is flat, so load did not change. Step 2: errors rose slightly too. Step 3: Lambda Insights shows memory used at 98% of the configured limit after the 08:58 deploy. Step 4: the conclusion is that the new code needs more memory, and you expect p99 to return near 300 ms once memory is raised.

A common mistake is building dashboards from averages only. An average can stay calm while the slowest 1% of users wait seconds, so plot percentiles alongside averages. Another mistake is treating a dashboard as an alert: nobody stares at it at 3 a.m., so a problem can run for hours. Dashboards are for review and diagnosis; alarms are what wake someone up.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking company runs its checkout on AWS Lambda functions and sells through many partner websites, each identified by a partner API key that is written into every log line. At 11:00 the team investigates. Step 1: the CloudWatch dashboard shows checkout errors rising from about 5 per minute to 400 per minute at 11:00, while the invocation count line stays flat, so traffic did not change. Step 2: duration percentiles are unchanged, so the functions are not slow, just failing. Step 3: [missing]. Step 4: that result shows that 92% of the error lines carry partner key P-17, so the conclusion is that one partner's integration broke, and the team expects errors to fall back near 5 per minute once P-17's requests are fixed. Which action fills Step 3?
choices: Use Contributor Insights on the checkout logs to rank which partner API key produces the most error lines
Open the X-Ray service map to see which downstream service node has the highest latency
Change the error widget to plot the average error rate instead of the total error count
Open Lambda Insights to compare each checkout function's memory use against its configured limit
questions.why: Step 4 depends on a ranking of which key causes the most errors, and Contributor Insights is the feature that ranks the top contributors to a pattern in logs.

questions.prompt: A payments team's dashboard shows only average response time for its API, and it has stayed steady near 120 ms all week. Meanwhile support receives complaints that some payments take 4 to 5 seconds. What is the most likely explanation, and what should the team change on the dashboard?
choices: The average hides a slow tail of requests; add percentile widgets such as p99 alongside the average
The complaints must come from users' own networks, because a steady average proves every request is fast
The dashboard refreshes too slowly; shorten the refresh period so the average catches the slow requests
Averages only work for error counts; replace the latency widget with an invocation count widget
questions.why: An average can stay calm while the slowest 1% of requests take seconds, so percentiles like p99 must be plotted to reveal that tail.

questions.prompt: A small online bookshop built a detailed CloudWatch dashboard for its order service and told staff to check it for problems. One night the order service failed at 01:30 and nobody noticed until the morning shift opened the dashboard at 07:00. What is the right fix?
choices: Switch every widget from averages to percentiles so overnight failures show up more clearly
Create alarms on the key metrics so someone is notified when a threshold is crossed
Add more widgets to the dashboard so a failure is more obvious when someone looks
Ask staff to keep the dashboard open on a screen overnight instead of only in the morning
questions.why: Dashboards are for review and diagnosis while someone is looking, whereas alarms are what notify a person when a problem happens at any hour.

questions.prompt: A travel site's search request calls three services in turn: a flight-pricing service, a hotel-availability service, and a currency-conversion service. Overall search latency has doubled, and the team wants to see quickly which of the three calls is the slow one, with each service's latency and error rate shown side by side. Which feature fits best?
choices: Contributor Insights, because it ranks which customer IDs appear most often in the search logs
Container Insights, because it collects cluster-level CPU and memory for the containers running search
A dashboard showing only the average total search latency, because one line is simplest to read
The X-Ray service map, because it draws each service as a node with its own latency and error rate
questions.why: The X-Ray service map shows each service as a node with its error rate and latency, so the slow call among several services stands out.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate the difference between a CloudWatch dashboard and an insights feature such as Lambda Insights or Contributor Insights, and name one limit of relying on dashboards to know your app is healthy.
lessons.modelAnswer: A dashboard is a page of charts we design ourselves from metrics, like invocations, errors, and p99 duration, all on the same time axis so we can see whether a spike lines up with a deploy or a traffic jump. An insights feature is prebuilt for a workload type: Lambda Insights adds memory, CPU, and cold-start detail per function, Contributor Insights ranks who or what generates the most errors, and the X-Ray service map shows which downstream call is slow. Dashboards tell us something is wrong; insights help narrow where. The limit is that dashboards only help when someone looks, so they do not replace alarms. They also mislead if built only from averages, which hide the slow tail of users, so I always include percentiles and pair related metrics like load against latency.
rubricPoints: Defines a dashboard as a saved set of metric charts on a shared time axis.
Explains that insights features collect extra workload-specific detail or rank contributors without custom setup.
Names at least one concrete insights tool and what it reveals.
States that dashboards show something is wrong while insights help locate where.
Names a limit such as needing someone to look or averages hiding the slow tail.

suggested.rationale: Choosing which chart or insights tool answers a given symptom is a scenario-reasoning skill best practiced through exam-style situations rather than a single hands-on task.

lessons.plain: When you ship new code and the deployment fails, the deployment service writes down what it tried and where it stopped. Troubleshooting from those service output logs means reading that record to find the first real error, not the noise that follows it. Think of a line of dominoes. When it collapses you can see dozens of fallen pieces, but only one tipped first, and that is the one worth investigating. Deployment tools behave the same way: one step fails, then many others are cancelled or rolled back. Your job is to find that first domino, read its message, and fix the cause.
lessons.guessPrompt: A deployment fails, and the event list shows twelve red error lines. Eleven of them say something like 'cancelled' or 'rollback'. Which line would you read first to find the cause, and why?
lessons.teach:
Service output logs are the records a deployment service keeps about its own work: which steps ran, in what order, and what each one returned. On AWS the main sources are these. CloudFormation, the infrastructure-as-code service that builds resources from a template, keeps stack events, which are timestamped status changes for each resource. CodeBuild, the managed build service, streams build logs to CloudWatch Logs, the central log store. CodeDeploy, which copies code onto servers or Lambda functions, reports each lifecycle event. A lifecycle event is a fixed stage such as BeforeInstall, AfterInstall, ApplicationStart or ValidateService, where your own hook scripts run. CodeDeploy also leaves detailed agent and script logs on the server itself.

This works because deployments run in order. One step fails, and the service then stops or undoes the steps around it. So most of the errors you see are consequences of the failure. Only the earliest one is the cause.

Here is a worked example. A CloudFormation stack update fails. First, sort the stack events by time, oldest first. Second, skip the rollback entries and the messages that say 'Resource creation cancelled'. Third, find the first CREATE_FAILED or UPDATE_FAILED event. In this case it says the role is not authorized to perform a certain action on a queue. Fourth, read the resource name and the reason together: the deployment role is missing a permission. Fifth, add that permission to the role's policy and deploy again.

A CodeDeploy failure follows the same pattern. If the deployment stops at ValidateService, the console names the failing script. The script's own output, such as a health check that returned 'connection refused', is in the agent logs on the instance.

The most common mistake is reading the newest error, which is usually a rollback message, and chasing a problem that does not exist. On a running system this wastes time while the failed or rolled-back release stays stuck. Repeated blind retries can also leave a stack in a failed state that blocks every later deploy until someone fixes it.

questions.prompt: A city library's team creates a new CloudFormation stack called catalog-api, and creation fails. Its stack events, sorted oldest first, are: 10:02:11 CatalogTable CREATE_COMPLETE. 10:02:40 SearchFunction CREATE_FAILED, reason 'The runtime python2.7 is no longer supported for creating functions'. 10:02:41 ImagesBucket CREATE_FAILED, reason 'Resource creation cancelled'. 10:03:05 CatalogTable DELETE_COMPLETE. 10:03:20 catalog-api ROLLBACK_COMPLETE. Step 1: the events are already in time order, oldest first. Step 2: set aside the 'Resource creation cancelled' entry and the rollback entries (DELETE_COMPLETE, ROLLBACK_COMPLETE), because they are consequences of a failure, not causes. Step 3: ??? Step 4: change the function's runtime in the template to a supported version and create the stack again. Which choice correctly completes Step 3?
choices: The cause is ImagesBucket, because it is the second CREATE_FAILED event and the one closest to the rollback.
The cause is CatalogTable, because it was deleted at 10:03:05, which means the table definition must be invalid.
The cause is the stack itself, because ROLLBACK_COMPLETE is the newest event and shows the rollback did not work.
The cause is SearchFunction: it is the earliest CREATE_FAILED event, and its resource name plus reason show the function uses an unsupported runtime.
questions.why: Once consequences are set aside, the earliest CREATE_FAILED event, SearchFunction with an unsupported runtime, is the actual cause, and Step 4 fixes exactly that.

questions.prompt: In CodeDeploy, the service that copies code onto servers or Lambda functions, what is a lifecycle event?
choices: A build log line that CodeBuild streams to CloudWatch Logs whenever a command finishes.
An alarm that fires automatically when a deployed application's error rate rises.
A timestamped status change that CloudFormation records for each resource in a stack.
A fixed stage of a deployment, such as BeforeInstall or ValidateService, where your own hook scripts run.
questions.why: A lifecycle event is one of CodeDeploy's fixed deployment stages, and it is where your hook scripts run; the other choices describe stack events, build logs, or alarms.

questions.prompt: A freight company deploys an update to its EC2 servers with CodeDeploy. The deployment stops at the AfterInstall lifecycle event, and the console names the failing hook script as set_permissions.sh. The console does not show what the script printed. Where should the engineer look next to see the script's own output?
choices: The CodeDeploy agent and script logs on the server where the script ran.
The CloudFormation stack events for the stack that created the servers.
The newest rollback message in the CodeDeploy console, since it summarizes all script output.
Nowhere; the engineer should rerun the deployment until the script succeeds.
questions.why: CodeDeploy leaves detailed agent and script logs on the server itself, and those hold the failing script's actual output.

questions.prompt: A payments team's CloudFormation update fails. An engineer reads only the newest event, a rollback message, and retries the deployment four times without changing anything. What is the most likely result for the running system?
choices: The fourth retry succeeds, because rollback messages mean the problem was temporary.
Time is wasted on a problem that does not exist, the release stays stuck, and the stack can end up in a failed state that blocks later deploys until someone fixes it.
Nothing changes in the stack, because failed updates are never recorded in stack events.
The retries are harmless, because CloudFormation always fixes a missing permission on its own after a few attempts.
questions.why: The newest error is usually a consequence of the real failure, so blind retries leave the actual cause unfixed and can leave the stack in a failed state that blocks later deploys.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would find the cause of a failed deployment from the service's own logs. Name one limit of those logs and what you would check next when they are not enough.
lessons.modelAnswer: Start where the deployment service records its own steps. For a CloudFormation stack, that is the stack events. For a build, it is the CodeBuild log in CloudWatch Logs. For CodeDeploy, it is the lifecycle events plus the agent logs on the instance. Sort the entries by time and find the earliest failure. Ignore the rollback and 'cancelled' entries, because those are the service cleaning up after the first error. Then read the resource name and the reason together, for example a missing permission on a role or a hook script that failed at ValidateService, and fix that one thing before you redeploy. The limit is that service logs show where the deployment stopped and a short reason, but often not why your code misbehaved. A health check that 'failed' tells you nothing about the crash inside the app. When that happens, move to the application's own logs on the host or in the log store.
rubricPoints: Names the right log source for the deployment service in use.
Sorts the entries by time and looks for the earliest failure.
Treats rollback and cancelled messages as consequences, not causes.
Reads the failing resource or lifecycle step together with its reason.
Notes that service logs may not show the application's internal error, so you check the app or host logs next.

suggested.rationale: Repairing a red pipeline makes the learner read deployment and build output to find the first real failure, which is exactly this skill.

lessons.plain: A service integration issue is a failure that happens where one piece of a system hands work to another, rather than inside either piece. Your code may be correct, and the other service may be healthy, yet the handoff still breaks. Common causes are a missing permission, a message in the wrong shape, a timeout that is too short, or a network path that does not exist. Think of a relay race: both runners are fast, but the baton gets dropped at the exchange. Debugging integrations means watching that exchange zone, the boundary between the two services, closely.
lessons.guessPrompt: A web API returns an error to users, but the backend function's own logs say it finished successfully every time. Where would you look next, and why?
lessons.teach:
Debugging a service integration means finding which handoff between two services failed and why. Examples on AWS are an API front door (API Gateway) calling a function (Lambda), a managed queue (SQS) feeding a function, or a function writing to a managed database (DynamoDB). Most integration failures fall into four groups. Permissions: the caller lacks the right. That can be the function's execution role, which is the identity the function uses when it calls other services, or a resource-based policy, which is a rule on the target service listing who may invoke it. Contract: the data is in the wrong shape, for example a missing field the receiver requires. Limits: a timeout or a throttle, meaning the service refused a request because a rate limit was exceeded. Network: the function runs inside a private virtual network (VPC) that has no route to the target service.

This works because each boundary leaves its own evidence, such as HTTP status codes, service logs and traces. A 403 or AccessDenied points to permissions. A 429 or a throttling error points to limits. A 502 often means a contract problem. A 504 or a timeout means the caller waited too long.

Worked example. Users get a 502 from the API. First, the function logs show success, so the code ran. Second, the API's execution logs show the error "malformed Lambda proxy response". Third, you compare the function's return value with the format the API expects, which is a status code, headers and a string body. You find the function returned a raw object. Fourth, you wrap the result in that format, and the 502s stop.

A common mistake is reading only one side's logs, or fixing the wrong side. One example is adding a permission to the function's execution role when the missing rule was the target's resource-based policy. In a running system, an unfixed integration fault can fail silently. Queued messages retry until they move to a dead-letter queue, which is a holding queue for messages that kept failing, and real work is lost from view.

questions.prompt:
A bakery chain runs its order pipeline on AWS. A managed queue (SQS) holds new orders and feeds a function (Lambda), and the function writes each order to a managed database table (DynamoDB). On Monday morning, staff notice that the dead-letter queue, a holding queue for messages that kept failing, now holds 340 orders. Nothing has reached the table since 07:15.

Step 1: The growing dead-letter queue shows that the queue-to-function-to-table path is failing and that the messages are being retried until they give up.
Step 2: [missing]
Step 3: The error is AccessDenied. That points to the permissions group, not to contract, limits or network.
Step 4: Because the function is the caller, you add table write permission to its execution role, the identity the function uses when it calls other services. New orders start reaching the table, and the dead-letter queue stops growing.

Which action belongs in Step 2?
choices: Raise the function's timeout, because messages that end up in a dead-letter queue usually mean the function ran out of time.
Delete the 340 messages from the dead-letter queue so the retries stop clogging the pipeline.
Add a resource-based policy to the queue that allows the table to read the orders from it.
Read the function's logs to find the exact error it reported when it tried to write to the table.
questions.why: Each boundary leaves its own evidence, so reading the function's logs is what reveals the AccessDenied error that Step 3 then interprets.

questions.prompt: A ticketing startup puts an API front door (API Gateway) in front of a function (Lambda). Every request fails. The function's logs show no invocations at all. The API's logs say the API is not allowed to invoke the function. A developer suggests adding an invoke permission to the function's execution role. What should actually be fixed?
choices: The function's response format, because a malformed response blocks the invocation.
The API's rate limit, because the API is being throttled before it can reach the function.
The function's execution role, because it controls every permission involving the function.
The resource-based policy on the function, which is the rule on the target listing who may invoke it.
questions.why: The API is the caller and the function is the target. The missing rule belongs in the target's resource-based policy, and changing the execution role would be fixing the wrong side.

questions.prompt: A fitness app's function sends workout records to another AWS service. During an evening peak of about 1,200 requests per second, many calls come back with HTTP status 429. Which group of integration failure does this point to first?
choices: Network: the function's private virtual network has no route to the service.
Limits: the service is throttling, meaning it is refusing requests because a rate limit was exceeded.
Contract: the records are missing a field the receiver requires.
Permissions: the function's execution role is missing a right.
questions.why: A 429 or a throttling error is the evidence left by a rate limit, which places the fault in the limits group.

questions.prompt: A library system's function wrote to a DynamoDB table without problems for months. This week the team moved the function into a private virtual network (VPC) and changed nothing else: the code, the data and the execution role are all the same. Now every write fails because the function can never reach the table. The logs show no AccessDenied errors and no throttling errors. What is the most likely cause?
choices: The VPC has no route to the database service, which is a network fault.
The records now arrive in a different shape, which is a contract fault.
The execution role lost its write permission during the move, which is a permissions fault.
The table started rejecting requests over its rate limit, which is a limits fault.
questions.why: The only thing that changed was the move into the VPC, and there is no AccessDenied or throttling evidence. That fits a network fault: the private network has no route to the target service.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would track down a failure between two AWS services, and name one limit of relying on logs alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: I start by finding which hop failed, not which service is broken, because both sides can be healthy while the handoff fails. I read the error at the boundary and sort it into a group. A 403 or AccessDenied means permissions, so I check both the caller's execution role and the target's resource-based policy. A 429 or throttling error means a limit. A 502 usually means a contract mismatch, such as a response in the wrong format. A timeout or 504 means a time limit was hit, or a network path is missing, for example a function in a VPC with no route to the service. I check logs on both sides of the hop and compare what was sent with what was expected. The limit is that logs alone show each service separately. Without a trace that follows the request across hops, I can miss where the time went or which call failed first.
rubricPoints: Identifies the specific handoff between services rather than assuming one service is broken.
Classifies the failure as permissions, contract, limits or network.
Uses error codes such as 403, 429, 502 or 504 as clues to the category.
Checks evidence on both sides of the boundary, including the execution role and the resource-based policy.
Names a limitation, such as logs lacking cross-service context or failures retrying silently to a dead-letter queue.

suggested.rationale: This mission has the learner diagnose a broken queue-to-function handoff from its evidence, which is exactly the boundary-focused debugging this objective teaches.

lessons.plain: Logging, monitoring and observability are three related but different jobs. Logging means writing down what happened, one event at a time. Monitoring means watching a few chosen numbers and raising an alarm when one crosses a line you set in advance. Observability is how well you can work out what is going on inside a system just from what it gives off. That includes problems nobody predicted. Think of a car. The trip log is logging. The warning light on the dashboard is monitoring. A mechanic's ability to diagnose a strange new noise from the car's outputs is observability.
lessons.guessPrompt: An alarm tells you your web API got slow five minutes ago. Is that alarm enough on its own to tell you why it got slow? If not, what else would you want to look at?
lessons.teach:
Logging is recording individual events as they happen: a request arrived, a payment failed, an error with its message. A log entry is one record of one moment. On AWS, Amazon CloudWatch Logs is the managed service that collects and stores these records.

Monitoring is collecting metrics and checking them against rules you decided on ahead of time. A metric is a number measured over time, such as error count per minute or request latency. An alarm is a rule like "tell me if latency stays above 2 seconds for 3 minutes." CloudWatch metrics and CloudWatch alarms do this job. Monitoring answers known questions: is the thing I expected to break breaking?

Observability is a property of the system, not a tool. It describes how well you can answer new questions about the system's internal state from its outputs. Those outputs are usually logs, metrics and traces. A trace follows one request across every service it touches and records how long each step took. AWS X-Ray is a tracing service. Observability is what lets you explain failures you never wrote an alarm for.

Worked example. First, an alarm on checkout latency fires. That is monitoring, and it tells you something is wrong. Second, you open the logs and see slow requests but no errors. That is logging, and it tells you what happened to individual requests. Third, you open a trace of one slow request. It shows 1.8 of its 2 seconds spent waiting on a database call. Because the system emits traces, you could answer a question you had not planned for. That is observability.

A common mistake is to treat "we have dashboards and lots of logs" as observability. Huge unstructured logs and a wall of graphs can still leave you unable to say why something failed. The consequence in a running system is that alarms fire, people know something is wrong, and the outage drags on while they guess. Each of the three plays a different part, and you usually need all three working together.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking app starts failing. Step 1: a CloudWatch alarm with the rule "tell me if the booking error rate stays above 5% for 2 minutes" fires. This is monitoring; it tells the team something is wrong. Step 2 is missing: it is the step that tells the team what happened to individual failed bookings. Step 3: the team opens an X-Ray trace of one failed booking and sees that 2.7 of its 3 seconds were spent waiting on a call to an outside payment provider. Because the app emits traces, they answered a question no alarm was written for. This is observability. Which choice correctly completes Step 2?
choices: They read the CloudWatch Logs entries for the failed bookings and see that each one records a "payment request timed out" error with its message. This is logging.
They build a dashboard that graphs bookings per minute next to error count. This is observability, because it shows many numbers at once.
They create a second alarm on payment-provider latency with a 1-second limit. This is logging, because it records each slow call.
They follow one booking across every service it touched and see how long each step took. This is monitoring, because it checks a known rule.
questions.why: Reading the recorded entries for individual requests, each one a record of one moment with its error message, is logging, and it shows what happened to each failed booking.

questions.prompt: A teammate says, "We bought a tool, so now we have observability." Based on how observability is defined, what is wrong with this statement?
choices: Observability is a property of the system: how well you can answer new questions about its internal state from its outputs. It is not a tool you install.
Observability only describes log storage, so the tool must be CloudWatch Logs specifically.
Observability only means having alarms on every metric, so a tool alone is not enough until every alarm is written.
Nothing is wrong. Observability is the name for a tracing tool such as X-Ray, so buying one gives you observability.
questions.why: The text defines observability as a property of the system, meaning its ability to explain unplanned questions from logs, metrics and traces, not as a product.

questions.prompt: An order-processing service puts jobs on a managed queue. The team sets up a rule: "Notify the on-call engineer if the number of waiting messages stays above 500 for 5 minutes." Which of the three practices is this, and why?
choices: Logging, because it records each message that arrives on the queue as an individual event.
Tracing, because it follows one message across every service it touches.
Monitoring, because it checks a metric measured over time against a rule decided ahead of time.
Observability, because it lets the team explain failures they never planned for.
questions.why: A metric (waiting messages over time) checked against a predefined threshold is an alarm, which is monitoring and answers a known question.

questions.prompt: A video-streaming company has 40 dashboard graphs and stores millions of unstructured log lines a day. During an outage, alarms fire and everyone knows playback is broken, but after two hours nobody can say why. What does this situation show?
choices: The team has too much observability. Removing some dashboards would make the cause obvious.
Logging is not useful during outages. Only alarms matter once something breaks.
Lots of dashboards and logs is not the same as observability. Without outputs that can answer new questions, such as traces, the team guesses and the outage drags on.
Monitoring has failed, because the alarms should have stated the cause of the outage.
questions.why: The text warns that a wall of graphs and huge unstructured logs can still leave you unable to explain a failure, so alarms fire while the outage drags on.

lessons.explainPrompt: A teammate says, "We already have CloudWatch alarms, so we're observable." Explain in your own words how logging, monitoring and observability differ. Name one limit of relying on monitoring alone.
lessons.modelAnswer: Those are three different things. Logging is writing down individual events, like this request failed with this error. Monitoring is watching chosen metrics, such as error rate or latency, and alarming when they cross thresholds we set in advance. Observability is how well we can figure out what is happening inside the system from its outputs, including problems nobody predicted. It usually comes from good logs, metrics and traces used together. A trace shows one request's path through every service and where the time went. The limit of monitoring alone is that it only answers questions we thought of beforehand. An alarm tells us latency is high, but not that a downstream database call is the cause. Without useful logs and traces we would know something is broken and still be guessing why. The tradeoff is that richer telemetry costs storage and effort to add.
rubricPoints: Logging records individual events as discrete entries.
Monitoring watches predefined metrics and alarms on thresholds set in advance.
Observability is a property of the system: the ability to answer new, unplanned questions from its outputs.
Traces follow a single request across services and show where time is spent.
Monitoring alone tells you that something is wrong but not why.
Having many logs or dashboards does not by itself make a system observable.

suggested.rationale: The core skill here is telling apart three concepts that are often confused, so explaining the difference back with an example is the most direct way to learn it.

lessons.plain: A logging strategy is a deliberate plan for what your application writes down about itself while it runs, so that later someone can reconstruct what happened and why. Think of a ship's logbook: the captain does not record every wave, but does record course changes, weather, position and anything unusual, each with a time. A good application log works the same way. It records the important events, the key values at those moments, and enough identifying detail to follow one request from start to finish, without drowning the useful lines in noise or leaking private data.
lessons.guessPrompt: A payment function sometimes fails, and the only log line it writes is "Error processing payment". What extra pieces of information would you want on that line to figure out which payment failed and why?
lessons.teach:
An effective logging strategy decides four things: which events to record, what state to attach to each event, how important each line is, and where the lines go and for how long.

Events are meaningful moments: a request arrives, a call to another service starts and finishes, a decision branch is taken, an error is caught. State is the data that explains the moment: the order ID, the input size, the retry count, how long a call took. A correlation ID (also called a request ID) is a unique value attached to every line produced by one request, so you can filter the log to that single journey. Log levels label importance: DEBUG for fine detail, INFO for normal milestones, WARN for something odd but recovered, ERROR for a failure. A configurable level lets you keep production quiet and turn on detail when investigating.

In AWS Lambda, anything the function prints goes to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, a managed log store, into a log group (a container for one function's logs) with a retention period you set.

Worked example: an order handler receives order 812. It logs INFO "order received" with requestId abc and orderId 812. It calls the inventory service and logs INFO "inventory checked" with durationMs 340 and inStock false. It then logs WARN "order rejected, out of stock". When a customer complains, you search requestId abc and see three lines that tell the whole story, including the cause and the timing.

A common mistake is logging the wrong amount: either a bare "error occurred" with no state, or everything at DEBUG in production. The first makes failures impossible to diagnose; the second inflates storage cost and buries the important line. Another mistake is logging secrets, passwords or full card numbers, which turns your logs into a security leak. In a running system, a good strategy means a failure is diagnosed in minutes from the logs alone, instead of needing to reproduce it.

questions.prompt: A print shop runs a Lambda function that resizes uploaded photos. One upload produces these log lines. Step 1: INFO "upload received" with correlationId q7 and fileSizeKb 5200. Step 2: INFO "resize finished" with correlationId q7 and durationMs 1800. Step 3: the function tries to save the resized photo to storage, retries 3 times, and every attempt fails, so the photo is never saved. Step 4 is missing: which line should the function log at this point?
choices: ERROR "error occurred" with no extra fields, so the log line stays short and storage stays cheap
DEBUG "save failed" with correlationId q7 and the full photo contents attached for later review
ERROR "save failed" with correlationId q7, retryCount 3 and the storage error message
WARN "save slow" with correlationId q7 and retryCount 3, because the function did try again before giving up
questions.why: The save failed and was not recovered, so it is an ERROR, and it carries the correlation ID plus explaining state (retry count, error message) so the failure can be diagnosed from the log alone.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking service handles hundreds of requests at once, and their log lines are interleaved in the same log. What is a correlation ID (also called a request ID) for in this situation?
choices: It is the name of the log group that stores one function's logs for a set retention period
It is a number that ranks how important each log line is, so ERROR lines appear above INFO lines
It is a unique value attached to every line from one request, so you can filter the log down to that single request's journey
It is a counter of how many times a request was retried, used to decide when to stop retrying
questions.why: A correlation ID is a unique value shared by every line produced by one request, which lets you isolate that request among many interleaved ones.

questions.prompt: A weather-alert app's Lambda function logs everything at DEBUG in production. Its CloudWatch Logs bill has grown sharply, and on-call engineers say the important lines are hard to find. Which change best fits an effective logging strategy?
choices: Keep DEBUG on but shorten every line to a bare message such as "error occurred"
Make the log level configurable, run production at INFO, and switch on DEBUG only while investigating
Remove all logging from production and rely on reproducing problems in a test environment
Change every DEBUG line to ERROR so the important information is always labeled as urgent
questions.why: A configurable level keeps production quiet and cheap while still allowing fine detail to be turned on when a problem needs investigating.

questions.prompt: A gym-membership signup function logs the full request it receives, including the member's password and full card number, to help debug signup failures. What is the main problem with this?
choices: Nothing, as long as the log group has a short retention period
It only matters if the lines are logged at ERROR rather than INFO
It breaks the correlation ID, so the lines can no longer be filtered by request
It turns the logs into a security leak, because secrets are now readable by anyone with log access
questions.why: Writing secrets such as passwords or full card numbers into logs exposes them to anyone who can read the logs, which is a security leak regardless of level or retention.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what makes a logging strategy effective for a Lambda-based service, and name one tradeoff you have to manage when deciding how much to log.
lessons.modelAnswer: A good logging strategy means we log the meaningful events in a request, like when it arrives, when we call another service, which decision we took and any errors, and we attach the state that explains each one, such as the order ID, retry count and how long a call took. Every line carries a correlation ID so we can pull up one request's whole story in CloudWatch Logs. We use levels: INFO for milestones, WARN and ERROR for problems, and DEBUG only when we turn it on to investigate. We never log secrets or full personal data. The tradeoff is detail versus cost and noise: logging everything makes storage expensive and hides the important line, while logging too little leaves us unable to explain a failure. We also set a retention period so we do not keep logs forever.
rubricPoints: Log meaningful events, not everything.
Attach state such as IDs, durations and decision values to each event.
Use a correlation or request ID to follow one request across lines.
Use log levels and keep production at a sensible level.
Never log secrets or sensitive personal data.
Names the tradeoff between detail and cost or noise, or sets retention.

suggested.rationale: Choosing what to log and why is a judgement call best learned by explaining the plan and its tradeoffs back in your own words.

lessons.plain: Structured logging means writing each log entry as a set of named fields, usually in JSON, instead of a free-form sentence. Rather than 'User 42 bought 3 items', the program records something like event equals order_placed, user equals 42, items equals 3. Think of the difference between a diary and a spreadsheet. A diary is pleasant to read, but finding every entry where someone spent over fifty dollars means rereading the whole thing. A spreadsheet has columns, so you can sort and filter in seconds. Structured logs give your application's history those columns, so people and tools can search it reliably when something goes wrong.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your app writes the log line 'Payment failed for user 42 after 3 retries'. A teammate asks you to count every failed payment that needed more than 2 retries last week. What makes that hard with this kind of line, and how could the line be written differently to make it easy?
lessons.teach:
Structured logging is the practice of emitting each log event as machine-readable key-value pairs, most often one JSON object per line. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a plain-text format of named fields such as "userId": "42". Each key is a field name, and each value is the data for that field.

It works because a log service can index fields directly. In AWS, a Lambda function's output goes to CloudWatch Logs, the managed log store. Its query tool, CloudWatch Logs Insights, automatically discovers fields in JSON lines, so you can filter on a field instead of guessing at text patterns.

Useful fields usually include a timestamp, a level (the severity: DEBUG, INFO, WARN or ERROR), an event name, the user or entity involved, and a correlation ID. A correlation ID is a request ID copied into every log line produced while handling one request, so all its lines can be pulled together.

Worked example. A checkout function records a user action. The unstructured version is: 'User 42 bought 3 items for $59.97'. The structured version is: {"level":"INFO","event":"order_placed","userId":"42","itemCount":3,"totalCents":5997,"requestId":"abc-123"}. Now trace a question: which large orders failed later? Step 1: filter event = order_placed and totalCents > 5000. Step 2: take the requestId values from those results. Step 3: search for those requestIds with level = ERROR. With free text, step 1 alone would need a fragile pattern that breaks when someone rewords the sentence.

A common mistake is to switch to JSON but still pack the facts into one message string, or to use different names for the same thing, such as userId in one place and user_id in another. Both defeat filtering. Another mistake is logging secrets, tokens or full card numbers. Once written, they are readable by everyone who has log access.

In a running system, consistent structured logs turn an hour of scrolling during an incident into one query. They also cost money, because every extra field adds stored and ingested bytes.

questions.prompt: A concert-ticket company is converting this unstructured line from its refund function: 'Refund of 12.50 euros issued to customer 908 for show 77'. Every other function in the company already logs the customer as customerId. Step 1: choose the level and event name, giving "level":"INFO" and "event":"refund_issued". Step 2: (missing) record the customer and the amount as fields. Step 3: add "requestId":"rf-5521", copied from the incoming request so every line for this refund shares it. Step 4: an analyst can now run one query for event = refund_issued and amountCents > 1000. Which fields complete Step 2?
choices: "customer_id":"908","amount":"12.50 euros"
"customerId":"908","amountCents":1250,"cardNumber":"4111111111111111"
"message":"Refund of 12.50 euros to customer 908 for show 77"
"customerId":"908","amountCents":1250,"showId":"77"
questions.why: Separate fields that reuse the company's existing name customerId and store the amount as the number amountCents let the Step 4 query filter directly, without hiding facts in a message, renaming a field, or exposing a card number.

questions.prompt: A video-processing service passes each uploaded file through three Lambda functions in turn. One upload fails, and an engineer wants every log line from all three functions about that single upload in one query. What makes this possible?
choices: Each function copies the same job or request ID into every log line it writes, and the engineer filters on that ID
Each function writes one long message string that describes the whole upload in a single sentence
Each function uses its own field name for the upload ID so its lines are easy to tell apart
Each function logs at level DEBUG so that more lines are kept in CloudWatch Logs
questions.why: A correlation ID is one request ID copied into every line produced while handling that request, so filtering on it pulls all of that request's lines together.

questions.prompt: A fitness app logs JSON lines from two Lambda functions. The bookings function writes "memberId":"5" and the payments function writes "member_id":"5". In CloudWatch Logs Insights, a filter on memberId = "5" returns only booking events. What is the cause?
choices: The value "5" must be a number, not text, for any filter to work
The two functions use different field names for the same fact, so the filter on one name misses lines that use the other
The payments function should have used free text instead of JSON
Logs Insights can only discover fields in the first function's output
questions.why: Filtering works by field name, so using memberId in one place and member_id in another splits the same fact across two fields and defeats the query.

questions.prompt: A payroll service adds each user's full session token as a field in every structured log line, which makes it easier to trace sessions. What is the main risk to the running system?
choices: Logs Insights will stop discovering the other fields in those lines
Anyone who has access to the logs can read the tokens, because once written to the logs they are exposed to that whole audience
The lines become unstructured, because tokens cannot be stored in JSON
The correlation ID will be overwritten by the token value
questions.why: Secrets and tokens written to logs become readable by everyone with log access, so they should never be logged.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate, in your own words, why you want the team's Lambda functions to switch from sentence-style logs to structured logs. Include which fields you would require, and name at least one cost or risk of doing it.
lessons.modelAnswer: Right now our logs are sentences, so finding anything means writing text patterns that break whenever someone rewords a message. If every function writes one JSON object per line, CloudWatch Logs Insights picks up the fields automatically and we can filter directly, for example event = payment_failed and retries > 2. I'd require a timestamp, a level, an event name, the user or entity ID, and the request ID as a correlation ID, so we can pull every line from a single request. We also need to agree on the field names, because userId in one function and user_id in another breaks our queries. There are tradeoffs. Extra fields make logs bigger, which raises ingestion and storage cost, so we should keep DEBUG detail off in production. Structured logs also make it easy to dump whole objects, which risks leaking secrets or personal data, so we need a rule about what never gets logged.
rubricPoints: Defines structured logging as emitting key-value fields, typically JSON, instead of free text.
Explains that named fields let log tools filter and aggregate without fragile text matching.
Names core fields, including level, event name, entity or user ID, and a correlation or request ID.
Stresses using the same field names consistently across services.
Names a cost or risk, such as higher log volume and cost, or leaking secrets and personal data.

suggested.rationale: The core skill is justifying which fields to log and why, and the tradeoffs of doing so, which is best built by explaining a logging design back rather than through any current mission.

lessons.plain: A custom metric is a number your own program reports to a monitoring service, such as 'orders placed' or 'checkout took 340 milliseconds', so you can graph it and set alarms on it. The cloud provider already measures generic things like CPU use or request counts, but it cannot know what matters to your business. Think of a car dashboard: the factory gives you speed and fuel, and a custom metric is like fitting your own gauge for something only you care about. On AWS the monitoring service is Amazon CloudWatch, and your code sends it these numbers while it runs.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your checkout function already shows how many times it ran. Your manager wants a graph of how many payments failed because the card was declined. Where would that number have to come from, and why can't the platform measure it for you?
lessons.teach:
Emitting a custom metric means your application code sends a named, timestamped number to a metrics store. In Amazon CloudWatch, AWS's monitoring service, the direct way is the PutMetricData API call, made through an SDK (a library that wraps AWS calls). Each data point has a namespace (a folder that groups your metrics, like Shop/Checkout), a metric name (CardDeclined), a value (1), a unit (Count, Milliseconds, and so on), an optional timestamp, and optional dimensions. A dimension is a name-value label, like PaymentProvider=Stripe, that lets you split one metric into separate series.

This works because CloudWatch stores every unique combination of namespace, name and dimensions as its own metric, then aggregates points into statistics (sum, average, maximum, percentiles) over a period. Alarms and dashboards read those statistics.

Worked example: a payment is declined. Step 1, the code builds a data point: namespace Shop/Checkout, name CardDeclined, value 1, unit Count, dimension PaymentProvider=Stripe. Step 2, rather than sending immediately, it adds the point to an in-memory batch, because one PutMetricData call can carry many points. Step 3, at the end of the request (or every few seconds) it sends the batch. Step 4, CloudWatch sums the points per minute, so a graph shows declines per minute per provider, and an alarm can fire if the sum passes 20.

A common mistake is using a high-cardinality value, one with many possible values like a user ID or order ID, as a dimension. Every distinct value creates a new metric, each billed separately, and you can no longer see a useful total. Put identifiers in logs instead.

Another consequence in a running system: PutMetricData is a network call that adds latency and can be throttled if called once per request at high traffic. Batching, or writing metrics into logs in a structured format that CloudWatch extracts later, keeps metrics from slowing the very code they measure.

questions.prompt: A video platform, StreamCo, wants to track how long each video takes to transcode (convert to another format). Its code runs as follows. Step 1: when a transcode finishes, the code builds a data point with namespace Media/Transcode, metric name TranscodeDuration, value 4200, unit Milliseconds, and dimension Codec=H264. Step 2: ??? Step 3: every 10 seconds, the code sends all collected points in a single PutMetricData call. Step 4: CloudWatch computes the per-minute average and maximum for each codec, and an alarm fires if the maximum goes above 9000 milliseconds. What belongs in Step 2?
choices: Call PutMetricData right away for this single point so it reaches CloudWatch as soon as possible
Change the unit to Count so CloudWatch can add the durations together
Add the point to an in-memory batch instead of sending it immediately
Add VideoId as a second dimension so each video gets its own graph
questions.why: Step 3 sends many collected points in one call every 10 seconds, so Step 2 must hold each point in an in-memory batch until then, which avoids one network call per transcode.

questions.prompt: A ride-sharing app emits a custom metric named TripCancelled in the namespace Rides/Bookings, with the dimension City set to values such as Lisbon, Porto and Faro. What does adding this dimension do in CloudWatch?
choices: It decides which statistic, such as sum or average, CloudWatch calculates for the metric
Each City value becomes its own metric series, so cancellations can be graphed separately per city
It renames the metric, so the app ends up with three metrics named Lisbon, Porto and Faro
It sets the unit of measurement CloudWatch applies when it aggregates the cancellations
questions.why: A dimension is a name-value label, and CloudWatch stores each unique combination of namespace, name and dimensions as a separate metric, so each city gets its own series.

questions.prompt: A banking app emits a LoginFailed metric. A developer adds the dimension CustomerId, and the app has about 50,000 customers. A week later the team cannot see the overall failed-login rate, and the monitoring bill has jumped. What is the best fix?
choices: Add a second dimension, Region, so the customer series roll up by region
Send every point immediately rather than in batches so the series merge
Change the unit from Count to Milliseconds so the points are grouped together
Remove CustomerId as a dimension and record customer IDs in logs instead
questions.why: CustomerId is high-cardinality: each distinct value creates a separate billed metric and hides the total, so identifiers belong in logs, not in dimensions.

questions.prompt: An online ticketing API handles about 3,000 requests per second. Each request calls PutMetricData once to record its own response time. After this change, the API's response times rise, and some metric calls fail because they are throttled (rejected for being too frequent). What change addresses both problems?
choices: Batch points in memory and send them together, or write them to structured logs that CloudWatch extracts
Move the metric to a new namespace so it gets its own call limit
Switch the metric's statistic from average to maximum so fewer calls are needed
Add a RequestId dimension so every call is stored as a separate metric
questions.why: PutMetricData is a network call, so calling it once per request adds latency and invites throttling, while batching or log-based extraction cuts the number of calls.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would make the checkout code report 'card declined' as a custom metric, what each part of the data point is for, and one tradeoff or limit you would watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: The platform only knows generic numbers like invocations and errors; it can't tell a card decline from a crash, so our code has to report it. When a decline happens we create a data point: a namespace like Shop/Checkout to group our metrics, the metric name CardDeclined, value 1, unit Count, and maybe a dimension such as PaymentProvider so we can split the graph by provider. CloudWatch treats each unique name-plus-dimensions combination as its own metric and aggregates the points, so we get declines per minute and can alarm on it. Two things to watch: don't use user or order IDs as dimensions, because every unique value becomes a separately billed metric and the totals become useless. And don't call PutMetricData synchronously on every request; batch points, or log them in a structured format, so the metric call doesn't add latency or get throttled.
rubricPoints: A custom metric is a business or app-specific number the platform cannot measure on its own, so code must send it.
Names the parts: namespace, metric name, value, unit, and dimensions.
Explains that each unique combination of name and dimensions is a separate metric that CloudWatch aggregates into statistics.
Warns against high-cardinality dimensions like user IDs because of cost and lost usefulness.
Notes the call costs latency and can be throttled, so batching or log-based emission is preferred at scale.

suggested.rationale: The skill is mostly judgment, choosing what to emit, which dimensions to use, and how to send without hurting latency, which an exam-style scenario exercises better than any current mission.

lessons.plain: An annotation is a small searchable label you attach to a trace, the record of one request's journey through your services. Think of a trace as a parcel's delivery history. Annotations are the stickers on the box, such as "priority: express" or "customer: 4471". Staff can later ask "show me every express parcel that was late." On AWS, the tracing service X-Ray records these journeys. Annotations let you find the few traces that matter among thousands, such as all slow requests from premium customers, without reading every one by hand.
lessons.guessPrompt: Your checkout service records thousands of traces per hour, and only premium customers are complaining about slowness. What would you want stamped on each trace so you could pull up just the premium customers' requests?
lessons.teach:
An annotation is a key-value pair you add to a trace from your code. AWS X-Ray, a managed distributed-tracing service, indexes annotations so you can search and group traces by them. The value must be a string, a number, or a boolean. A trace is made of segments. A segment is the record of the work one service did for a request. A subsegment is a smaller timed piece inside a segment, such as one database call. Annotations are attached to segments or subsegments, and X-Ray accepts up to 50 annotations per trace.

Annotations work because the service builds an index on them. You search that index with a filter expression, a short query typed in the console or sent through the API. Metadata is the other way to attach data. Metadata can hold any type, including whole objects, but it is not indexed. You can read metadata on a trace you have already opened, but you cannot search for traces by it.

Worked example, step by step. First, your Lambda function, a piece of code AWS runs for you on demand, opens a subsegment called "charge-card". Second, the code adds the annotation customer_tier = "premium" and the annotation order_total = 120. Third, it adds the full order object as metadata, for reading later. Fourth, after some slow requests, you run the filter expression annotation.customer_tier = "premium" AND responsetime > 2. X-Ray returns only the slow premium traces. Fifth, you open one of them and read the order metadata to see what was in the order.

A common mistake is putting a value you will later need to search by into metadata. It is stored, but no filter can find it. A second mistake specific to Lambda is trying to annotate the function's top-level segment. Lambda creates that segment itself, and your code cannot change it. Add annotations to a subsegment you create.

In a running system, good annotations shrink an investigation from scrolling through thousands of traces to one precise query. Avoid putting secrets or personal data in annotations, because annotation values are visible to anyone who can view traces.

questions.prompt:
A delivery company runs a Lambda function (code AWS runs for you on demand) that plans van routes by calling an outside mapping service. The team wants to use AWS X-Ray, a managed distributed-tracing service, to find slow calls for vans in the northern region. Here is the plan, with one step missing.

Step 1: The code opens a subsegment (a smaller timed piece of work inside a segment) named "call-map-api".
Step 2: ???
Step 3: The code attaches the full mapping-service response object as metadata, to read later.
Step 4: After complaints, the team runs the filter expression annotation.region = "north" AND responsetime > 3, and X-Ray returns only the slow northern traces.
Step 5: They open one returned trace and read the response metadata.

Which action belongs in Step 2 so that Step 4 works?
choices: Add region = "north" as an annotation on the "call-map-api" subsegment
Add an annotation named region whose value is the full route object for the van
Add region = "north" as an annotation on the function's top-level Lambda segment
Attach region = "north" as metadata on the "call-map-api" subsegment
questions.why: The filter searches the annotation index, so region must be an annotation with a string value on a subsegment the code created, since Lambda's top-level segment cannot be changed and metadata is not indexed.

questions.prompt: A ticket-booking service uses X-Ray. An annotation is a key-value pair added to a trace from code, and X-Ray indexes it so traces can be searched. Which of these values could be stored as an annotation value?
choices: A list of every seat in the booking
The full HTTP request object
The boolean value false
A map of header names to header values
questions.why: Annotation values must be a string, a number, or a boolean; lists, maps, and whole objects belong in metadata instead.

questions.prompt: A support-desk app records each request's ticket_id as metadata on an X-Ray subsegment. Weeks later an engineer tries to find all traces for ticket_id 88412 with a filter expression (a short search query run in the console or through the API), and nothing comes back, even though the value is visible when a trace is opened. What is the cause and fix?
choices: Filter expressions only work on numbers; store ticket_id as a string
The trace is over the 50-annotation limit; delete other annotations
Metadata is not indexed; record ticket_id as an annotation instead
Metadata only lasts until the trace is opened; re-send the data
questions.why: Metadata is stored and readable on an opened trace but is not indexed, so only an annotation can be searched with a filter expression.

questions.prompt: A clinic's appointment app uses X-Ray. A developer wants to add each patient's email address as an annotation so traces for one patient can be found quickly. What is the main problem with this plan?
choices: Annotations can only be searched by the account that wrote them, so others cannot use them
Adding the annotation would replace the trace's response time, breaking latency filters
Annotation values are visible to anyone who can view traces, so personal data should not go in them
Email addresses are strings, and strings are not allowed as annotation values
questions.why: Anyone with access to view traces can see annotation values, so secrets and personal data such as patient emails should be kept out of them.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate what an X-Ray annotation is, how it differs from metadata, and when you would choose each. Include at least one limit or catch they should watch for.
lessons.modelAnswer: An annotation is a key-value pair we attach to a segment or subsegment of a trace, for example customer_tier = premium. X-Ray indexes annotations, so we can search with a filter expression like annotation.customer_tier = "premium" and pull out only the traces we care about. The catch is that values must be strings, numbers, or booleans, and a trace can carry at most 50 annotations. Metadata holds any type, even full objects, but it isn't indexed. It's useful for reading details once you've opened a trace, but you can't search for traces by it. So put anything you'll filter or group by in annotations, and put rich context in metadata.
