questions.why: Code outside the handler runs once during the cold start, and warm invocations reuse the environment and call only the handler.

questions.prompt: A bookstore stores orders in a DynamoDB table whose partition key is the customer ID. To show one customer's order history, the app reads every item in the table and then keeps only that customer's orders. Read capacity usage is very high. Which change most directly cuts the capacity used per request?
choices: Move the full-table read outside the Lambda handler
Replace the full-table Scan with a Query on the customer ID partition key
Increase the Lambda function's memory so the full read finishes faster
Run the same full-table read twice and cache the second result
questions.why: A Scan consumes read capacity for every item in the table, while a Query reads only the items matching the partition key, so it uses far less capacity for the same answer.

questions.prompt: A ticketing company's Lambda function saves the current user's booking ID in a variable declared outside the handler, to speed things up. Soon, some customers see another customer's booking on their screen. What is the most likely cause?
choices: Lambda gives CPU in proportion to memory, so the function needs more memory to keep users separate
The variable outside the handler survives into later warm requests, so one user's data leaks into another's response
The database connection outside the handler is mixing up rows between tables
Each request gets a new execution environment, so the variable is always empty
questions.why: State outside the handler persists across warm invocations in the reused environment, so per-request data like a booking ID must stay inside the handler; only clients and connections should be reused.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate why moving setup code outside a Lambda handler reduces cost and load, and name one risk or limit of this technique.
lessons.modelAnswer: Lambda bills for configured memory multiplied by run time, so anything that makes each call shorter saves money. Code outside the handler runs only when a new execution environment starts, a cold start. Warm calls reuse that environment, so a database client or SDK client created there is built once and shared by many requests. If setup took 120 ms of a 150 ms call, moving it out cuts warm duration to about 30 ms, which is roughly 80 percent less billed time. The database also benefits, because it holds a few reused connections instead of opening a new one per request. The limits: cold starts still pay the setup cost, so the saving depends on how often environments are reused. Never put request-specific data in those shared variables, because it carries over into the next request and can leak one user's data to another.
rubricPoints: Lambda cost is memory multiplied by duration, and CPU scales with memory.
Code outside the handler runs once per execution environment and is reused on warm invocations.
Reusing clients and connections shortens each call and reduces load on downstream systems such as databases.
Cold starts still pay the setup cost, so the saving depends on how often environments are reused.
Per-request state must not live in shared variables because it leaks between requests.
Reading less data, for example Query instead of Scan, also cuts capacity used.

suggested.rationale: Modeling GB-seconds and capacity before and after an optimization lets the learner name the number a change should move, which is the core of this objective.

lessons.plain: Finding a performance bottleneck means locating the one slow step that holds up everything else. Think of a supermarket checkout. If the card reader takes two minutes per customer, a faster cashier or more bagging space will not shorten the queue. Application logs are the time-stamped lines a program and its platform write as they run. Each line is like a receipt that shows when something happened and how long it took. When you read those receipts side by side, you can see which step eats most of the time. That step is the one worth fixing first.
lessons.guessPrompt: A request takes 3 seconds in total. Your logs show three steps: checking the user's login took 40 ms, reading from the database took 2,700 ms, and formatting the reply took 30 ms. If you could make one step twice as fast, which would you choose, and roughly how fast would the request become?
lessons.teach:
A performance bottleneck is the slowest step in a request, and it limits how fast the whole request can finish. Speeding up any other step barely helps. Application logs are the time-stamped lines your code and the platform write while running. To find a bottleneck, you compare how long each step took and look for the one that dominates.

AWS Lambda is a managed service that runs your function on demand. At the end of every invocation it writes a REPORT line to CloudWatch Logs, the managed log store. That line includes several fields:

Duration is how long your handler ran. Billed Duration is the time you pay for. Memory Size is the memory you configured. Max Memory Used is the peak memory actually used. Init Duration appears only on a cold start, which is when a fresh execution environment has to be created. It is the time spent loading your code and running setup before the first request.

This works because total time is roughly the sum of its steps. If your code logs the elapsed milliseconds around each external call, the biggest number points straight at the cause.

Here is a worked example. Users report slow order lookups.

Step 1: The REPORT lines show Duration of about 2,900 ms and Max Memory Used of 120 MB out of 512 MB. Most lines have no Init Duration. So the problem is neither memory pressure nor cold starts.

Step 2: Your own timing lines show auth at 40 ms, the DynamoDB call at 2,700 ms and formatting at 30 ms.

Step 3: The database step owns about 93% of the time.

Step 4: Looking at that call reveals a Scan, which reads the whole table, where a Query on the key was needed. After the fix, you expect Duration to fall toward a few hundred milliseconds.

A common mistake is judging by averages. An average of 300 ms can hide that one request in twenty takes 4 seconds. Check percentiles instead: p99 is the time that 99% of requests finish within. Another mistake is raising memory when Max Memory Used is far below the limit. That only helps if a step is CPU-bound, because Lambda gives more CPU along with more memory.

In a running system, an unfixed bottleneck pushes requests toward the function timeout. That causes errors and retries, raises billed time, and keeps more copies running at once, which can lead to throttling.

questions.prompt:
A ticket-booking team's Lambda function feels slow at checkout. Here is the investigation, with one step missing.

Step 1: The REPORT lines show Duration of about 1,600 ms and Max Memory Used of 90 MB out of 256 MB. Almost no lines include Init Duration. So memory pressure and cold starts are ruled out.

Step 2: The function's own timing lines show input validation at 20 ms, a call to an outside payment service at 1,450 ms and a DynamoDB write at 60 ms.

Step 3: [missing]

Step 4: The team examines the payment call and finds it opens a brand-new connection on every request. They fix that and expect Duration to drop well below 1,600 ms.

Which choice correctly fills Step 3?
choices: Compare the step times: the payment call takes about 90% of the total, so it is the bottleneck to investigate.
Treat cold starts as the cause, since any request over one second must include environment setup time.
Start with input validation, because it runs first and every later step waits for it to finish.
Raise the memory to 1,024 MB, because a Duration of 1,600 ms means the function needs more resources.
questions.why: A bottleneck is the step that dominates total time, and 1,450 ms out of roughly 1,600 ms makes the payment call the step that limits the whole request.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function's REPORT line in CloudWatch Logs reads: Duration 210 ms, Billed Duration 211 ms, Memory Size 512 MB, Max Memory Used 140 MB, Init Duration 850 ms. What does the Init Duration field tell you about this invocation?
choices: It was a cold start. A fresh execution environment was created, and 850 ms went to loading code and running setup before the request.
The function used memory for 850 ms before it reached its peak of 140 MB.
The handler code itself ran for 850 ms, which is longer than the 210 ms the function was billed for.
It shows the time this request spent waiting in a queue because the function was being throttled.
questions.why: Init Duration only appears on a cold start, and it measures the setup time spent before the first request in a new environment.

questions.prompt: A weather-alerts API runs on Lambda. Its dashboard shows an average response time of 250 ms, which looks healthy. Users still complain that alerts sometimes take several seconds. What should the developer check next?
choices: Max Memory Used, because complaints about slow responses always come from running out of memory.
Nothing. An average of 250 ms shows that the function is fast for nearly all users.
Percentiles such as p99, because an average can hide a small share of requests that take seconds.
Billed Duration, because it is always a better speed measure than Duration.
questions.why: Averages can mask rare slow requests, while p99 shows the time that 99% of requests finish within, so it exposes the slow tail.

questions.prompt: A report-export Lambda function has Duration near 3,000 ms and Max Memory Used of 200 MB out of 2,048 MB. Its timing logs show 2,800 ms spent waiting for a reply from a remote HTTP service. A teammate proposes raising memory to 4,096 MB. What is the best response?
choices: Agree, because extra memory removes cold starts, and cold starts explain the 3,000 ms.
Disagree, because Lambda never gives a function more CPU when its memory is raised.
Agree, because more memory always shortens Duration no matter which step is slow.
Disagree. Memory is far below the limit, and the slow step is waiting on a network reply rather than using the CPU, so more memory will barely help.
questions.why: Adding memory only helps a CPU-bound step, because Lambda adds CPU along with memory, and here memory is unused while the bottleneck is time spent waiting on a remote call.

lessons.explainPrompt: Explain to a teammate how you would use application logs to find why a Lambda-backed API got slow. Name one limit of relying on logs alone or on average timings.
lessons.modelAnswer: First I'd read the Lambda REPORT lines in CloudWatch Logs. Duration tells me how long the handler ran. Max Memory Used compared with Memory Size tells me whether memory is tight. Init Duration tells me whether cold starts are adding setup time. If those rule out memory and cold starts, I look at our own timing log lines around each step, such as auth, the database call and any outside HTTP call. Total time is roughly the sum of the steps, so the step with the biggest share is the bottleneck. That's the only one worth optimizing first, and I'd predict the new Duration after fixing it. One limit is that averages hide slow outliers, so I check p99 rather than the mean. Another is that logs only show steps we chose to time. If a call has no timing line around it, the logs can't reveal it.
rubricPoints: Defines a bottleneck as the single step that dominates total request time.
Uses the REPORT line fields (Duration, Max Memory Used versus Memory Size, Init Duration) to rule causes in or out.
Compares per-step timing log lines to find the step with the largest share.
Names a limit, such as averages hiding outliers (use percentiles like p99) or untimed steps being invisible.
States the expected improvement in a number after fixing the bottleneck.

suggested.rationale: The learner investigates a real slowdown after a deploy and has to find which step dominates response time from the evidence, which is exactly the skill this objective teaches.

scenarios.title: Brightkettle Coffee: Fixing a Flaky Order Pipeline
scenarios.scenario:
Brightkettle Coffee is a fictional chain that takes mobile coffee orders. Each order is placed as a message in an Amazon SQS queue. SQS is a managed message queue, a service that holds messages until a worker takes them. An AWS Lambda function reads the messages. Lambda is a service that runs your code only when an event arrives. For each order, the function calls an outside payment company's web API and then saves the order to an Amazon DynamoDB table. DynamoDB is a managed key-value database.

You have just joined the team. You find four problems.

The function's timeout is 3 seconds. The timeout is the longest a single run may last before Lambda stops it. Its memory is 128 MB. With that little memory, a run often takes 6 to 9 seconds, mostly in code that checks and formats the order. The queue's visibility timeout is 5 seconds. The visibility timeout is how long SQS hides a message after a worker picks it up. If the worker does not delete the message within that time, other workers can see it again. Customers report two problems: some orders are charged twice, and others never finish.

The table's partition key is storeRegion, which has only three values: north, central and south. A partition key is the attribute DynamoDB uses to decide where each item is stored. DynamoDB splits data into storage pieces called partitions. During the morning rush, writes are throttled. Throttled means DynamoDB rejects requests because too many hit the same place at once.

The My Orders screen in the app scans the whole table and keeps only rows where customerId matches. A scan reads every item in the table. The screen is slow and expensive. Right after checkout, the app also needs to show the order the customer just placed, and it must be accurate.

One malformed order message has been failing over and over for two days. Each time, it costs a run and a call to the payment company. When the payment company has a brief outage, the function also fails at once instead of trying again.

Your tasks:
1. Explain why the timeout and visibility timeout settings cause both double charges and unfinished orders. Recommend new values for memory, function timeout and visibility timeout, and give a reason for each.
2. Explain why storeRegion causes throttling. Propose a better partition key and say why it works.
3. Redesign how the My Orders screen and the just-placed-order screen read data. Say which consistency model each read should use.
4. Describe how to stop the malformed message from retrying forever, and how the code should handle brief payment-company outages.
modelAnswer:
A run needs 6 to 9 seconds, but the function timeout is 3 seconds. Lambda therefore kills most runs before they finish. If the kill happens after the payment call but before the DynamoDB save, the order is charged but never recorded, so it looks unfinished.

The visibility timeout is 5 seconds, which is also shorter than the real work time. A message can reappear in the queue while a run is still working on it, or after a run is killed. Another run then picks it up and charges the customer again.

The fixes are as follows. First, raise memory, for example to 512 MB or 1024 MB. Lambda gives a function more CPU as you give it more memory, so the CPU-heavy checking and formatting finishes faster. Test a few sizes and keep the one with good speed for the cost. Second, set the function timeout comfortably above the slowest real run, for example 30 seconds. That leaves room for a slow payment call without letting a stuck run hang forever. Third, set the queue's visibility timeout well above the function timeout. A common guideline is at least six times the function timeout, so about 180 seconds here. That way a message stays hidden for the whole run, including retries.

A strong answer also makes the work idempotent, meaning safe to repeat. For example, send the order ID to the payment API as a duplicate-protection key, and save to DynamoDB with a conditional write that only succeeds if the order ID is not already there. A repeat delivery then does no harm.

DynamoDB places items on partitions according to the partition key value. storeRegion has only three values, which is low cardinality, meaning few distinct values. Every write therefore lands on one of at most three keys. During the rush, the busiest region's key becomes a hot partition, one partition taking far more traffic than it can handle, and DynamoDB throttles it. The table's total capacity doesn't help because the load is not spread out.

The better key is a high-cardinality one, meaning one with many distinct values, such as orderId, a unique ID for each order. Writes then spread across many partitions, so no single one is overloaded. Region can still be kept as an ordinary attribute, or reached through an index if a by-region view is needed.

The common mistake is picking the key that matches how people group data, such as region or date, instead of one that spreads traffic evenly.

My Orders screen: stop scanning. A scan reads and charges for every item in the table and only then filters, so it gets slower and costlier as the table grows. Instead, add a global secondary index (GSI). A GSI is an extra copy of the data, kept up to date by DynamoDB, that is organised by a different key. Give it customerId as the partition key and order time as the sort key. A sort key orders the items that share a partition key. The screen then uses a Query, which reads only the items with one partition key value, in time order. That is fast and cheap. Reads from a GSI are eventually consistent: a brand-new write may take a moment to appear. That is acceptable for an order history list.

Just-placed-order screen: read the base table directly by orderId with a strongly consistent read. A strongly consistent read always returns the latest saved version. This ensures the customer sees the order they just placed. It costs more read capacity than an eventually consistent read, and it is not available on a GSI, which is why this read goes to the base table rather than the index.

Malformed message: give the source queue a dead-letter queue (DLQ). A DLQ is a separate queue where messages go after failing too many times. You set this with a redrive policy on the source queue, using a maximum receive count of, for example, 3 to 5. After that many failed attempts, SQS moves the message to the DLQ. That stops the wasted runs and payment calls, and keeps the bad message so someone can inspect and fix it.

For a queue that triggers Lambda this way, failure handling belongs on the queue's DLQ. Lambda destinations are for asynchronous invocations, so they are not the tool here.

It also helps to report partial batch failures. With this, only the bad message in a batch is retried, not the good ones alongside it.

Payment outages: wrap the payment call in retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter. Exponential backoff means waiting longer after each failed try, for example 0.2, 0.4 and then 0.8 seconds. Jitter adds a small random amount to each wait so many workers don't retry at the same moment. Retry only errors that may pass, such as timeouts or 5xx server errors. Don't retry a declined card or a 4xx error, because trying again won't change the result. Cap the number of tries so the run stays inside its timeout.

For longer outages, add a circuit breaker. A circuit breaker notices repeated failures and stops calling the outside service for a short cool-down period. During that time it fails fast and lets the message return to the queue for later. This protects both the function and the payment company from a flood of doomed calls.

scenarios.title: Cleaning Up the Rental API at Larkspur Bikes
scenarios.scenario:
Larkspur Bikes is a small fictional company that rents electric bikes through a mobile app. You have just joined as a junior developer, and your first task is a security review of the backend before it launches.

The backend is one AWS Lambda function called rental-api. Lambda is a service that runs your code when a request arrives, without you managing any servers. Each Lambda function has an execution role. That is an IAM role the function uses for its permissions. IAM (Identity and Access Management) is the AWS service that decides who may do what. A role is an identity with permissions but no permanent password, and code can borrow it to get short-lived credentials.

Customers sign in through Amazon Cognito, a managed sign-in service. After sign-in, Cognito gives the app a JSON Web Token (JWT). A JWT is a signed piece of text that says who the user is. The app sends it on every request in the Authorization header as a bearer token. A bearer token works for whoever holds it, like cash.

Rental data lives in an Amazon DynamoDB table, a managed key-value database. Payment history lives in a separate PostgreSQL database.

While reading the code, you find four problems.

First, the PostgreSQL password is typed directly into the source file, which is stored in the company Git repository. The same password is also copied into a plain-text Lambda environment variable. An environment variable is a setting passed to the code at start-up.

Second, the code reaches an Amazon S3 bucket (managed file storage) using an access key ID and secret access key. These belong to an IAM user named dev-maria and are pasted into a config file. An IAM user is a long-lived identity for one person.

Third, for debugging, the function writes the whole Authorization header, including the JWT, to Amazon CloudWatch Logs, the service that stores application logs. It then reads the user ID from the token without checking the token's signature or expiry time.

Fourth, each DynamoDB customer item holds full name, email address, home address, and driving licence number. These are personally identifiable information (PII), meaning data that can identify a specific person. The function logs the full customer item on every request. The table uses DynamoDB's default encryption.

Answer the following:
1. Where should the PostgreSQL password live instead, which AWS service should hold it, and who should be able to decrypt it? Include what to do about the copy already in Git.
2. How should the function reach S3 instead of using dev-maria's access keys, and what should happen to those keys?
3. How should the function handle the Cognito JWT correctly, both when checking it and when logging?
4. How should the customer PII be protected in the logs and in the table, so that Larkspur controls who can decrypt it?
modelAnswer:
Remove the password from the source code and from the plain-text environment variable. Store it in AWS Secrets Manager, a managed service that stores secrets encrypted and hands them to authorized callers at run time. Secrets Manager encrypts the secret with a key in AWS KMS (Key Management Service), the AWS service that creates and guards encryption keys. For Larkspur's own control, that should be a customer managed key.

Only the rental-api execution role, plus any admins who truly need it, should be able to read and decrypt the secret. The role needs permission to get the secret value for that one secret, and permission to use that KMS key for decryption, granted in the role policy and the key policy.

At start-up the code fetches the secret through the AWS SDK and caches it in memory for reuse. Because the old password sits in Git history, treat it as exposed. Change (rotate) the database password now and turn on Secrets Manager's automatic rotation. Simply deleting the line from the file is not enough, because anyone with repository access can still see it in history.

Delete the access keys from the config file and give the needed S3 permissions to the Lambda execution role. Grant only the specific actions needed on the specific bucket, which is the idea of least privilege.

The AWS SDK inside Lambda automatically picks up the role's temporary credentials. These are short-lived keys that AWS creates and replaces for you, so no secret has to be stored in code.

dev-maria's keys were exposed in a file, so deactivate and then delete them. Check whether they were used by anyone unexpected. Long-lived keys belonging to a person should never run production code, because they do not expire, are hard to rotate, and tie the application to one employee's identity.

A bearer token grants access to whoever holds it, so it must never be written to logs. Anyone who can read CloudWatch Logs could copy it and act as that customer until it expires. Stop logging the Authorization header. If needed, log only the user ID after the token has been checked.

Before trusting anything inside the token, the function must validate it. Check that the signature matches Cognito's public signing keys, that the issuer is Larkspur's Cognito user pool, that the audience or client ID is Larkspur's app, and that the token has not expired. A simpler option is to put Amazon API Gateway, a managed front door for APIs, in front of the function with a Cognito authorizer, which rejects bad tokens before the code runs.

After validation, use the token's user ID (the sub claim) to decide authorization. For example, a user may only read their own rentals. All traffic should use HTTPS, so the token is encrypted in transit.

First, classify the fields. Name, email, home address, and especially driving licence number are PII and need extra care.

In logs, stop writing the full customer item. Log only an ID, or mask sensitive fields, for example showing only the last four characters of the licence number. This is application-level data masking. It matters because logs are often readable by more people than the database.

In the table, DynamoDB always encrypts data at rest (while stored). The default uses a key owned by AWS, which Larkspur cannot control or audit. Switch the table to a customer managed KMS key. The key policy then decides who can decrypt, for example only the rental-api role and a small admin group, and Larkspur can turn on automatic key rotation and audit use of the key.

For the most sensitive field, the licence number, Larkspur can add client-side encryption. The code encrypts the value with a KMS key before saving it, so even someone who can read the table sees only scrambled data. Data in transit is protected by using HTTPS between the function and AWS services.

scenarios.title: Releasing a Change Safely at Pinecrest Pantry
scenarios.scenario:
Pinecrest Pantry is a small, fictional grocery-delivery company. Its order API has two parts. The first is an AWS Lambda function called orders-handler. Lambda is a managed service that runs your code when an event arrives, so you never manage a server. The second is an Amazon API Gateway REST API. API Gateway is a managed front door: it receives HTTP requests from the mobile app and passes them to back-end code.

The team describes both parts in an AWS SAM template. SAM (Serverless Application Model) is a shorthand form of AWS CloudFormation. CloudFormation is the service that reads a template file and creates or updates the cloud resources it describes. Writing resources in a file like this is called infrastructure as code. Each push to the main branch of the Git repository (the shared, version-tracked store of the team's code) starts a pipeline that builds and deploys the template.

The API has two stages, dev and prod. A stage is a named, separately deployed copy of the API, with its own URL. orders-handler has a published version, which is a frozen, unchangeable snapshot of the code and settings. It also has two aliases, dev and live. An alias is a named pointer to a version that you can move later.

Today a developer, Ravi, has written a new discount calculation. Last month a bad release broke checkout for every customer at once. Your lead, Amara, wants this release to reach only a small share of real users first, and to undo itself automatically if errors rise. You are the developer on this task.

1. Explain how to make the dev stage call the dev alias and the prod stage call the live alias, while both stages share a single API integration. Name one extra setting that is easy to forget.
2. Ravi wants to start by sending 10 percent of production traffic to the new code for 5 minutes, then everyone. Name this strategy, say what you would add to the SAM function resource to get it, and trace what happens to traffic step by step.
3. Halfway through the 5 minutes the error rate jumps. Explain how the release rolls back without a human, and what you must have set up in advance for that to happen.
4. Before any of this, Ravi wants to test the function on his laptop with a fake API Gateway request. Describe the test event he needs and one common mistake that makes it fail.
subParts: Route stages to aliases with stage variables
Configure and trace a canary release
Build a local API Gateway test event
modelAnswer:
Use a stage variable. A stage variable is a key-value setting that belongs to one API Gateway stage, a bit like an environment variable for that stage. On the dev stage, set lambdaAlias=dev. On the prod stage, set lambdaAlias=live. In the single integration, write the Lambda function's ARN with a placeholder for the alias, ending in orders-handler:${stageVariables.lambdaAlias}. An ARN (Amazon Resource Name) is the unique ID string for an AWS resource.

At request time, API Gateway replaces the placeholder with that stage's value. Trace it: a request to the prod URL fills in live, so API Gateway calls orders-handler:live, which points to whatever version live currently names.

The easy-to-forget setting is invoke permission. Each alias needs a resource-based policy (a permission attached to the function itself) that allows API Gateway to call that exact alias. Without it, requests to that stage fail with a permission error even though the ARN is correct. A second common slip is forgetting to redeploy the stage after changing its settings.

This is a canary deployment. A canary deployment sends a small share of real traffic to the new version first, then shifts the rest only if all looks healthy. It is a gradual form of blue/green, where the old (blue) and new (green) versions run side by side.

In the SAM function resource, add AutoPublishAlias: live. This tells SAM to publish a new version on every deploy and point the live alias at it. Then add a DeploymentPreference with Type: Canary10Percent5Minutes. SAM hands the traffic shifting to AWS CodeDeploy, a managed service that moves traffic between versions.

Trace it:
The pipeline deploys the template, and SAM publishes the new version, say version 8, while version 7 is serving.
CodeDeploy sets weights on the live alias: 90 percent of calls go to version 7 and 10 percent to version 8.
This split holds for 5 minutes.
If nothing goes wrong, the alias moves to 100 percent version 8, and version 7 stays available for a later rollback.

For contrast, the Linear options shift traffic in equal steps over time, and AllAtOnce shifts everything immediately.

Automatic rollback depends on Amazon CloudWatch alarms. CloudWatch is the AWS monitoring service, and an alarm watches a metric and changes state when it crosses a threshold you set. You must list one or more alarms under Alarms in the DeploymentPreference ahead of time, for example an alarm on the Errors metric of the new version or alias.

Trace it: during the 5-minute window, errors on version 8 cross the threshold and the alarm enters the ALARM state. CodeDeploy sees this, stops the deployment, and moves the live alias back to 100 percent version 7. Only the roughly 10 percent of users who hit version 8 saw errors, not everyone.

The common mistake is shipping a canary with no alarms attached. Traffic still shifts in steps, but nothing tells CodeDeploy to stop, so the bad version reaches 100 percent anyway. Optionally, PreTraffic and PostTraffic hooks can run check functions before and after the shift.

If a problem is found after the deployment finishes, you roll back by pointing the alias at the earlier version or by redeploying the previous commit through the pipeline.

He needs a JSON payload, a text file of keys and values, that copies the shape API Gateway sends to Lambda in proxy integration. Proxy integration means API Gateway passes the whole request through to the function. The file can be generated with sam local generate-event apigateway aws-proxy and then edited.

Key fields are:
httpMethod, such as POST
path, such as /orders
headers
queryStringParameters
pathParameters
body
requestContext, which includes the stage name

He saves the file as event.json and runs sam local invoke with the -e event.json option. This runs the function locally in a container with that event as input.

The common mistake is writing body as a nested JSON object. In a real request, body arrives as a string, for example "{\"items\":[\"milk\"]}". The code must parse that string first. A test that passes an object can pass on the laptop and then fail in production, or the reverse.

scenarios.title: Throttled checkout at Tidewell Grocers
scenarios.scenario:
You have just joined Tidewell Grocers, a fictional online grocery shop, as a junior developer. Customers report that checkout is slow and sometimes fails with an error at dinner time. Your team lead asks you to investigate and propose fixes.

How the system works: a checkout request arrives at Amazon API Gateway, a managed front door that receives web requests and passes them on. It hands each request to a function called place-order running on AWS Lambda, a service that runs your code on demand without you managing servers. Each running copy of a function lives in an execution environment, a small isolated container that Lambda can reuse for later requests. place-order calls an internal inventory service over HTTP to get the current price list, saves the order in Amazon DynamoDB (a managed key-value database), and then publishes an order event to Amazon SNS. SNS (Simple Notification Service) is a managed publish-and-subscribe service: a publisher sends a message to a topic, and every subscriber of that topic gets a copy. One subscriber is a Lambda function called delay-notifier, which emails customers only when an order's status is DELAYED.

What you found in Amazon CloudWatch, the AWS service that collects metrics (numbers measured over time) and logs (text records written by your code):

At the 6 pm peak, place-order receives about 200 requests per second. Its average Duration metric (how long each invocation runs) is 0.8 seconds. Its ConcurrentExecutions metric (how many copies run at the same moment) flattens at exactly 100, and its Throttles metric (requests Lambda refused because no copy was allowed to start) jumps into the thousands. The function has reserved concurrency set to 100. Reserved concurrency is a setting that caps how many copies of one function may run at once.

You also opened AWS X-Ray, a tracing service. A trace is the recorded path of one request through every component, and each timed piece of work inside it is called a segment or subsegment. A typical trace shows: 650 ms in the HTTP call to the inventory service, 40 ms writing to DynamoDB, 20 ms publishing to SNS, and the rest in your own code. The inventory team tells you the price list is the same for every caller and only changes every 5 minutes.

The current logs are free-text lines such as "order done ok", so you cannot count anything from them.

Finally, delay-notifier is invoked for every order event, but about 80% of invocations simply check the status, see it is not DELAYED, and exit. SNS can attach message attributes, which are small labelled values such as status=DELAYED sent alongside the message body.

Your tasks:
1. Using the metrics and the trace together, explain why requests are being throttled and identify the bottleneck. Show the concurrency calculation.
2. Propose one application-level change to place-order that removes the bottleneck, and state the numbers you expect it to move (duration, concurrency needed, throttles).
3. Describe how you would emit a custom metric called CacheHit from place-order using the CloudWatch embedded metric format, and how structured logging would help you query the logs afterwards.
4. Propose a change that stops delay-notifier from being invoked for orders it ignores, and state the expected effect.
subParts: Custom metric with EMF and structured logs
modelAnswer: Concurrency is the number of copies of a function running at the same instant. A good estimate is requests per second multiplied by average duration in seconds. Here that is 200 x 0.8 = 160 copies needed at peak. Reserved concurrency caps place-order at 100, so the ConcurrentExecutions metric flattens at 100. About 60 copies' worth of demand has no slot, and Lambda rejects those requests, which shows up as the Throttles spike and as customer errors. The metrics show what is happening: the function hits its ceiling. The trace shows why each request takes so long: 650 ms of the roughly 800 ms is spent waiting on the HTTP call to the inventory service. The bottleneck is that slow, repeated downstream call, not DynamoDB (40 ms) or SNS (20 ms). A common mistake is to fix this only by raising reserved concurrency. That treats the symptom and keeps every request slow. It also multiplies the load placed on the inventory service.

Add an application-level cache for the price list. Store the list in a variable declared outside the handler function. That variable lives in the execution environment, so later requests that land on the same reused environment can read it instead of calling the inventory service. Give it a TTL (time to live, how long a cached value is trusted) of 5 minutes or less, because the list only changes every 5 minutes. When the TTL expires, fetch the list again. Expected effect: on a cache hit, roughly 650 ms is removed, so average duration drops from about 0.8 s to about 0.15 to 0.2 s. Occasional refreshes add a little. Concurrency needed becomes about 200 x 0.2 = 40, well under the cap of 100, so Throttles should fall to zero at the current peak. Calls to the inventory service drop from about 200 per second to a handful per environment every 5 minutes. A shorter duration also lowers Lambda cost, because you pay for run time. The mistake to avoid is caching longer than the data stays valid, which would charge customers stale prices.

The embedded metric format (EMF) lets code turn a log line into a metric. The function writes one JSON log line that contains the normal fields plus a special metadata block named _aws. That block lists the metric namespace (a folder name for metrics, for example TidewellCheckout), the metric names (CacheHit), and any dimensions (labels such as FunctionName). Example line: {"_aws": {"Timestamp": 1700000000000, "CloudWatchMetrics": [{"Namespace": "TidewellCheckout", "Dimensions": [["FunctionName"]], "Metrics": [{"Name": "CacheHit", "Unit": "Count"}]}]}, "FunctionName": "place-order", "CacheHit": 1, "orderId": "o-123"}. Write CacheHit as 1 on a hit and 0 on a miss. CloudWatch reads the line and creates the metric automatically, with no separate API call slowing the request. The average of CacheHit is then your hit rate. Structured logging means every log line is JSON with consistent named fields, such as orderId, status, cacheHit and durationMs, instead of free text like "order done ok". CloudWatch Logs Insights, the query tool for logs, can then filter and count by field. For example: filter cacheHit = 0 | stats count() by bin(5m), or stats avg(durationMs) by cacheHit. This connects slow requests to cache misses.

Add an SNS subscription filter policy to the delay-notifier subscription. A filter policy is a rule stored on the subscription that tells SNS which messages to deliver, based on message attributes. place-order must publish each event with a message attribute status set to the order status. The filter policy then requires status to equal DELAYED, for example {"status": ["DELAYED"]}. SNS drops non-matching messages for that subscriber before they are delivered, so the function never runs for them. Expected effect: delay-notifier invocations fall by about 80%, with a matching cut in its cost and concurrency use. Other subscribers on the topic still receive every message. The common mistake is setting the policy without adding the status attribute when publishing. If the attribute is missing, no message matches, and delayed customers silently get no email.
